en: In the *Preface to the Collection on the Six Realms*, it is said that as secular ways decline day by day, those who establish the teachings must labor increasingly more.

When Shun charged Yu, he said, "The human heart is perilous," and Mencius stated, "That which distinguishes humans from beasts is but slight. Thus, the sages and worthies have passed down this warning to one another.

The language used should be concise yet comprehensive when addressing those of common station, whereas it should be detailed and accessible when speaking with the vulgar; such is the nature of circumstances.
The Buddha’s teaching on the six realms of existence aims to exhaust the transformations of the single mind and to reach the ultimate cause of the hidden and the manifest;
it may be called a cry of bitter lamentation. Yet later generations still regard it with indifference. As for Master Zaiqiu of our own region—
I have therefore compiled accounts of recent events from both ancient and modern times that are well known to every household, composing this work titled *The Collection of the Six Realms*.

This was done because it is unavoidable when preaching the Dharma for those who have not yet attained awakening. I maintain that there are two primary reasons why people remain deluded and fail to awaken:
the first is the thought, "How could I, a human being, sink so low as to become a creature of another realm? and the second is the attachment to the pleasures of human life.

I fear that we are heedless of our future lives. Yet, within the span of a single day, and even in the briefest moment of a single thought, one cannot know how many times one has been a celestial being, a human, or an animal or hungry ghost. Truly, it would be as if a mirror from the state of Qin were suspended before us.

May their livers and gallbladders be laid bare, and their intentions fully exposed; may the various transformations of the six realms appear in chaotic interplay, all manifesting simultaneously within their very hearts. Only then might they be struck with fear and know how to turn back.

Although you, O Venerable Master, have read extensively across all books and authored dozens of works, even as you approach seventy years of age, you have compiled this collection; yet its purport seems increasingly superficial. Its...
My sorrow grows ever deeper. May readers not merely regard this as empty and exaggerated talk, thereby forgetting that it is a reflection from the very core of one’s being.
Written with reverence by Luo Fu’s Chen Gongyin for the preface to the *Six Realms Collection*.
The Venerable Master originally came by the power of his original vows. Entering the Way at a precocious age, his eloquence overflowed and his mastery of scriptural texts was all-encompassing.

In his youth, he sang the "Xinfeng" melody with a tune that would remain sublime for a thousand ages; in his middle years, he concealed his brilliance at Shaoshi Mountain, where he exhaustively investigated the Three Chariots.

Yet, he had no desire to emerge from seclusion to benefit others. Alas, how could the dragons and devas allow it? They refused to let him remain in the abbot’s quarters of Dinghu, and thus compelled his fame—
The price is difficult to repay; ultimately, he did not delight in dwelling there for long. He soon retired to the depths of the Elephant Forest, thinking to himself:

"At the assembly on Vulture Peak, there was no more than one person who could laugh upon the plucking of the flower. Yet, in this age of the Final Dharma, how many fingers can be counted among those who find the kōan through a blow?
Moreover, while the great smelting furnaces for refining ordinary beings are already flourishing everywhere and the fires are glowing red, here in my own place—"

Had he instead hindered his progress and remained in seclusion, aging together with the mists and clouds, how would that compare to preaching the Dharma for a single period to deliver sentient beings of limited capacity?
Which is more beneficial: writing many essential treatises to profit those of future generations, or the former?

Thus, from Shaoshi in the beginning to Xianglin at the end, throughout these fifty-odd years, he produced works exceeding hundreds of millions of words. How fortunate I, Long, am to have received them!

The benefit is indeed great. My only regret is that my faculties are dull and I have little capacity for grasping the profound mysteries. Nevertheless, I most cherish the "Six Realms in One Collection" (*Liùdào yījí*), which painfully awakens the ignorant masses.
For a shadow must follow a form, and a valley must respond to an echo; one cannot plant melon seeds and expect beans, for the production of fruit is invariably determined by its cause.
This is the necessary course of principle and circumstance. Yet, worldly people remain complacent and fail to perceive this, whereas you, O Master, do not abandon them.
How compassionate! How tragic! The multitudes are deluded within the six realms, their cycle of rebirth showing no end. Suddenly, [the Master] picks it up and displays it;

it is as luminous as the sun and moon being raised on high, illuminating every hidden corner so that all people may deeply realize that retribution is unfailing and cause and effect are without deviation.
May they all be able to turn the light back upon themselves and each prepare for their own future. This merit is—
Below the Bodhisattva, how could the dragons dare not receive this with sincere devotion? I merely offer these words after a second prostration, to serve as a preface.
Dated the twenty-first year of the Kangxi era, the Renxu year, by the disciple Li Longbiao of Dongguan, who bows his head in reverence.

Preface to the *Lixiang Liudao Ji* (A Collection on the Six Realms of Existence):
Now, the stations of the three realms are established and the six paths of existence are distinguished; all arise from the sudden stirring of the initial single thought of consciousness.

Deluded conceptualization forms the cause of outflows (*āsrava*), and thus there is the cyclical rotation through the three periods of time and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

When manifesting in substance, form is divided into coarse and subtle; when experiencing retribution, suffering and pleasure follow divergent paths. Within the three realms and six destinies, nothing is exempt from arising and ceasing.
The human realm and the heavens are truly the root of suffering. Therefore, the wise awaken to this truth, wondrously attuning themselves to non-arising.

They transcend the three realms of existence in an instant, tread the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and exhaust the source of birth and death. Abiding in the land of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), they are utterly liberated from saṃsāra.
I bid a long farewell to the realms of suffering; this is the reason for composing this collection.

I hope that all wise ones will realize the impermanence of the three realms, recognize the non-eternal nature of the six destinies, set their aspirations upon the Supreme Vehicle, and seek transcendence from the world, thereby remaining far removed from the scorching of the kalpa-fire.
One avoids sinking into the depths of ruin and reaches the fruits received in this present life, while still repaying the causes of the past.

From fruit one again creates cause; as cause shifts, the fruit ripens. Thus one revolves through the six realms and traverses the three worlds—namely, the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Below, reaching the adamantine base; above, extending to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations; in between, the six destinies dwell intermingled. One.
All sentient beings who have not yet abandoned craving and desire are called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

From the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (*brahmakāyika*) up to the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*akaniṣṭha*), these eighteen heavens, although free from the defilement of desire, still possess material form. Their primary retribution—the physical bodies—resemble the color of white silver;

their secondary retribution—the palaces and mansions—is the color of pure gold. Because the radiance of their bodies illuminates one another, it is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). From the [Heaven of] Infinite Space...
From the heavens up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, these realms are as vast as the azure void and as empty as space.
Because they lack the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), yet consist of the other four aggregates, they are called the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

These three realms are also termed the "Three Existences" (*tri-bhava*), because their causes belong to the outflows (*āsrava*) and their fruits are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), characterized by birth and death. As for the "Six Paths," they are also called the "Six Destinies" (*ṣad-gati*).
"Gati" (destiny) means "to arrive. This refers to the paths by which the causes of one's performed wholesome or unwholesome karma can transport one to their respective destinations;

therefore, they are called "gatis. Furthermore, "gati" carries the meaning of "tending toward. That is to say, the karma one has created tends toward the realms of humans, devas, asuras, pretas, animals, and hells.
Since these realms and destinies are formed through the consciousness-mind, they constitute the sentient and insentient worlds.
In this world, if one reaches the source of the mind, both the subjective emotions and the objective vessel perish. If one awakens to the fundamental permanence, birth and death are thereby severed.

Birth and death and true permanence are originally not two paths; they depend solely upon a single thought-moment of the person. When not a single thought arises, the three realms and the six destinies vanish.

There is no place for them to set foot. (The "sentient world" refers to all sentient beings; they are all provisionally formed through the combination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and arise together as a multitude, each distinct and different from one another; therefore, it is called the "sentient world. The "receptacle world" refers to all insentient worlds;
they are all provisionally formed by mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth, each distinct and different from one another; therefore, it is called the "receptacle world.")
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoliang Forest on the day of the *prātimokṣa* ceremony in the Jiwu year of the Kangxi era.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoliang Forest in Nanhai, Guangzhou, while residing at Zaiqi. *The Collection of the Six Realms*, Volume One.
The term for the Way of Heaven in Sanskrit is *deva*, which here means "heaven. A heaven (*deva*) is so called because it is naturally pure, luminous, and immaculate;

among all realms of existence (*gati*), it is the most excellent, the most blissful, the most virtuous, the most wondrous, the most honorable, and the highest. Thus, it is named "heaven. If it were not the most excellent—

As for the cause: how could one be born in the most excellent and pure realm? The most excellent cause is what is called the ten wholesome paths of action—the three of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind.
By means of these three types of karma, one prevents transgressions and faults, accords with principle and meaning, and opposes the path of unwholesomeness.
Because these ten wholesome actions transport one out of the five destinies, this dharma of the ten wholesome precepts is called the "Vehicle of the Gods" (*devayāna*). All...
Although the devas are numerous, they do not transcend the three realms: namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These three realms are divided into twenty-eight abodes in total. Within the desire realm there are six.

First, ascending forty-two thousand *yojanas* from below is the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). It resides halfway up Mount Sumeru and is the foremost of the upward ascents. Below...
The first heaven of the [four] realms: in the east is the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra (King Who Holds the Nation), who dwells on the eastern flank of Mount Sumeru, made of white silver;

his city is named Uttarakuru (Supreme Virtue). He governs the gandharvas (translated as "Fragrance-Body," the celestial musicians) and the piśācas (translated as "Eaters of Vital Essence" ghosts), protecting the inhabitants of the eastern continent.
In the south is the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka (King of Increase), who dwells on the southern flank of Mount Sumeru, made of blue lapis lazuli; his city is named...
Sudṛśa (Good Vision) presides over the kumbhāṇḍas (translated as "oppressing-demon" spirits) and the preta (translated as "hungry ghosts"), protecting the people of the southern continent.
In the west is the Heavenly King Viśvadeva (Broad-Eyed), who dwells on the western golden terrace of Mount Sumeru;

his city is named Cakravāḍa, and he presides over the nāgas and the pūtana (translated as "stench-hungry ghosts"), protecting the people of the western continent. In the north is the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa (Many-Hearing). He dwells...
To the north of Mount Sumeru, on a terrace of crystal, there are three cities: the first is named Bhīṣma, the second Devasaṃmata, and the third Saṃjñeya.
They lead the yakṣas and rākṣasas to protect the inhabitants of the northern continent. The Four Kings together have thirty-two generals, each of whom has ninety-one sons;
they possess great majesty and power and all protect the ten directions. [In the human realm,] fifty...
One year [of humans] constitutes one day and night for these gods of the Four Great Kings. Their lifespan is five hundred years (calculated as nine million human years).
Ascending forty-two thousand *yojanas* from this realm of the Four Great Kings is the abode of the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa (Trāyastriṃśa means "Thirty-three").
It dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. The summit of the mountain is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, and its center is level.
The area habitable by them is forty thousand *yojanas* in extent. On each of its four sides there are eight heavens, and within the Great City of Sudarśana at the center is a golden wall;
this is the dwelling place of Śakra, the Lord of Devas. Together, these constitute the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*).

One hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and night for this heaven. Their lifespan is one thousand years (calculated in human years, this is thirty-six million years). [Their decline is marked] by the closing of the red lotus and the blue lotus.
The blue lotuses close and the red lotuses open as night; the red lotuses close and the blue lotuses open as day.

From this Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, ascending one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas, there is a place like a cloud, composed of the seven treasures, resembling the great earth, measuring eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
This is the third dwelling place, that of the Yāma Heaven (Yāma means "time" or "division"). Two hundred years in the human realm constitute one day and night for this heaven. Its lifespan is...
Two thousand years [of celestial time] (calculated by human years, this equals fourteen million four hundred thousand years).
From here, ascending thirty-two hundred thousand *yojanas* to the Yāma Heaven, there is a ground like clouds, sixteen hundred thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth;

this is the dwelling place of the fourth heaven, Tuṣita (Tuṣita means "Contentment" in this language). Four hundred years of the human realm constitute one day and night for this heaven, and their lifespan is four thousand years (calculated by human...).
Every other year. (Fifty-seven million six hundred thousand years. From here, one ascends six hundred and forty thousand *yojanas* to the Tuṣita Heaven.

There is a ground like clouds, thirty-two thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth; this is the dwelling place of the fifth heaven, the Nirmāṇarati-devas (who delight in self-created emanations of the five sensory objects).
Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night for this heaven, and their lifespan is eight thousand such years. (Calculated in human years, this is twenty million.)
After thirty million four hundred thousand years, one ascends twelve billion eight hundred thousand *yojanas* from this realm of the Nirmāṇarati devas.
There is a ground like clouds, sixty-four hundred thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth; this is the dwelling place of the sixth [heaven], the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas.
(He manifests palaces, gardens, groves, and all manner of objects of enjoyment, within which he exercises sovereign mastery. This is the highest heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

One thousand six hundred human years constitutes one day and night for this heaven, and its lifespan is sixteen thousand years. (Calculated by human years, this is nine hundred twenty-one million six hundred thousand years.
Ascending from here by double that distance, at twenty-five billion six hundred million *yojanas*, there is a ground like clouds, extending...
It is twelve billion and eighty thousand *yojanas* in extent. This is the dwelling place of the various devas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

There are eighteen heavens in total, collectively designated as the Four Dhyānas. Because they are free from agitation and movement, they are also called the Brahma-worlds (*brahmaloka*), signifying their freedom from the defilement of desire.
Their lifespans are measured in *kalpas*. Their bodies are the color of white silver; they lack male or female characteristics, and their physical forms are of a single type. First...

The three heavens of the dhyāna realm: (1) Brahmakāyika Heaven; lifespan is half a kalpa; these are the subjects. (2) Brahmapurohita Heaven; lifespan is one kalpa; these are the ministers. (3) Mahābrahmā Heaven; lifespan is one and a half kalpas; this is the sovereign.
From here on, they ascend by doubling each time, which can be understood by analogy. The three heavens of the second dhyāna: (1) Parīttābha Heaven; lifespan is two kalpas. (2) Apramāṇābha Heaven;

lifespan is four kalpas. (3) Ābhāsvara Heaven; lifespan is eight kalpas. The three heavens of the third dhyāna: (1) Parīttaśubha Heaven; lifespan is sixteen kalpas. (2) Apramāṇaśubha Heaven; lifespan is thirty-two kalpas. (3) Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; lifespan is sixty-four kalpas. The nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna.

1. Anabhraka Heaven: lifespan is one hundred and twenty-five kalpas. 2. Puṇyaprasava Heaven: lifespan is two hundred and fifty kalpas. 3. Bṛhatphala Heaven: lifespan is five hundred kalpas. 4. Asaṃjñisattva Heaven: lifespan is the same as above. 5. Avṛha Heaven: lifespan is one thousand kalpas. 6. Atapa Heaven: lifespan is two thousand kalpas. 7. Sudarśana Heaven:

lifespan is four thousand kalpas. 8. Sudṛśa Heaven: lifespan is eight thousand kalpas. 9. Akaniṣṭha Heaven: lifespan is sixteen thousand kalpas. This is the zenith of the Rūpadhātu. The final five heavens are called the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) Heavens.

This is the dwelling place of those noble ones who have attained the three fruits. Ascending from here by a further multiple, there is the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which consists of four heavens and is also called the Four Heavens of Emptiness (*catvāry ārūpyāṇi*).

These realms are like the azure void; their nature is like empty space. Because they possess only the four aggregates (*skandha*)—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—and lack the aggregate of form, it is called the Formless Realm.
1. The Heaven of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*; lifespan: twenty thousand great kalpas). 2. The Heaven of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*; lifespan: forty...).

3. The Heaven of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) has a lifespan of sixty thousand great kalpas. 4. The Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) has a lifespan of eighty thousand great kalpas.
However, although the lifespans of the various devas within these three realms are fixed, there are nonetheless those who die prematurely.
Only in the Tuṣita Heaven and the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) are the lifespans entirely fixed, such that premature death is not mentioned. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:

"If one observes the precept against killing, one will be reborn in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings. If one observes the precepts against both killing and stealing, one will be reborn in the [Heaven of] the Thirty[-Three]."
Three days. If one observes the precepts against killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, one will be reborn in the Yāma Heaven.
If one observes the precepts against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech, one will be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

By practicing the Buddha’s precepts while also cultivating the seven wholesome karmas of body and speech, one will be reborn in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states: "If..."

Sentient beings who fully cultivate the ten superior wholesome actions obtain the retribution of the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Those who cultivate the ten wholesome actions associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and conjoined with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) obtain the retribution of the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Those who cultivate the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) obtain the retribution of the heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "When the various gods of the six heavens of the desire realm are first born, they are respectively like humans of five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten years of age."

Thus, their physical forms quickly attain full completion. A male is born upon the right knee of the heavenly father; a female is born upon the left knee of the heavenly mother. All are born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
Alternatively, some are suddenly born by transformation from a flower in the hand of the heavenly mother. As the *Āgama* Sūtra says:
Not long after the children arrived, they became aware of hunger and thirst. Spontaneously, precious vessels appeared, filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors.
For those with great merit, the rice was naturally white; for those of middling merit, it was yellow; and for those of lesser merit, it was red.

If they were thirsty, they drank from the precious vessels the nectar-like juice (*amṛta*), which dissolved gradually upon entering the stomach like butter cast into a fire, leaving no trace or shadow behind, nor did it produce any excrement or urine.
...benefit. Death is like the extinguishing of a lamp’s flame; there are no remains, because they are born by transformation (*upapāduka*).

As for the celestial hosts of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), at the moment of their initial birth, their bodies are fully formed and complete, and they are endowed with exquisite garments. All these celestial hosts speak the noble language (*āryabhāṣā*) without having to study it;
they naturally understand the classical tongue. The *Lokotpatti-sūtra* states: "The various heavens of the Desire Realm all consume morsel food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). The [heavens] of the Form Realm..."
The gods of the various realms from the First Dhyāna up to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven take joy as their food. The gods of the Formless Realm take mental activity as their food.
Some say that the gods of both the Form and Formless Realms take the delight of dhyāna and the joy of the Dharma as their food.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Even if one attains the body of a Caturmahārājika deity, or up to that of a Paranirmitavaśavartin deity, or even the body of a Brahmā or a Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana deity, at the end of life one will still fall back into the three evil realms.

When the celestial retribution is exhausted and the five signs of decay appear, the body undergoes great suffering; this is no different from the suffering of the hells. The *Tattvasiddhi Śāstra* asks: "Regarding birth in the heavens..."

One abandons evil and accumulates goodness. Why, then, does one enter the three miserable realms as soon as the retribution is exhausted? The answer is: since beginningless time, the ordinary person’s evil karma has been inexhaustible.
Even for a single day of greed and anger, they still undergo a thousand forms; how much more so when evil is already abundant, yet one merely suppresses it temporarily before being reborn.
Once the blessings of retribution are exhausted and past karma ripens, one falls back into the three miserable realms. What causes such delusion?

It is because those with conscious minds who have realized the source can shatter the twenty-five states of existence within the triple world. Thus it is said: "If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of land upon the great earth. A sutra states:
"When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the worlds of the ten directions are all brought to extinction. It is like...
If one has not yet been able to reach the fundamental source, one should single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and make a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land.

There, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, one awakens to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), thereby suddenly transcending the three realms and severing the cycle of saṃsāra. (Regarding "Brahma-world": *brahma* means "pure.")
The *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* says: Formerly, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived that his five celestial virtues had departed from him and knew that his life was at its end.
He was destined to be reborn in the human world, taking the form of a donkey in the household of a potter. Knowing that his merit was exhausted, he was filled with great sorrow and anxiety.

He thought to himself, "Within the three realms, there is only the Buddha who can rescue beings from their suffering and distress. Thereupon, he hurried to the place where the Buddha was and prostrated himself.
He first prostrated himself, lying flat on the ground with a sincere heart, and three times took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Holy Sangha.
Before he had even risen, his life suddenly departed, and he was reborn as a son within the womb of a mother donkey at a potter’s workshop.

At that time, the donkey broke free and ran among the unbaked clay vessels, smashing the pottery; its owner struck it, and the fetus was immediately injured. The spirit then returned to its former body.

In the midst [of his life], through the five virtues, he returned to receive blessings and was again made a Heavenly Lord. When the Buddha arose from his meditative concentration, he praised him, saying: "Excellent, O Heavenly Lord!
That you were able, at the moment of your passing, to take refuge in the Triple Gem—your karmic retribution is now exhausted, and you shall no longer undergo further toil and suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse: "All that is conditioned is impermanent; it is the law of arising and decaying. Whatever is born must inevitably die; Nirvana is peace."
"Joy! It is like a potter who shapes clay to make vessels; all must eventually break. The life of man is likewise.

Upon hearing this verse, Śakra understood the essential nature of impermanence, grasped the transformations of sin and merit, and comprehended the root of rise and fall. He took joy in the practice of noble tranquility and received it with devotion, attaining the stage of Srotāpanna.

(The five virtues departed from his body, and the five signs of decay immediately appeared: first, his garments became soiled; second, the flowers upon his head withered; third, [his body emitted a foul odor]; fourth, sweat broke out on his armpits; fifth, his seat grew uncomfortable.)

1. Sweat flows from the armpits; 2. The body smells foul and filthy; 3. One finds no pleasure in one’s own seat. The opposites of these constitute the five virtues. Generally, when it is said "as stated in the Sūtras" or "as stated in the Vinaya," this refers to what was personally taught by Śākyamuni Tathāgata. When it is said "as discussed in the commentaries," this refers to the words of Bodhisattvas and Arhats who annotated the Sūtras and Vinaya.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga of India was a native of the kingdom of Gandhāra. During the millennium following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he was born with keen faculties and clear insight;

having awakened to the Way by catching its fragrance, he left the household life to engage in study. His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, likewise left the household life to receive his teachings.

Extensively learned and possessing a powerful memory, he was a master of scholarship who investigated the subtle workings of the mind. Among the disciples of Asanga was Śīlabuddhi, whose secret practices were unfathomable and whose eminent talent was renowned.
Two or three such worthy sages would often say to one another: "In all our cultivation of the path, we aspire to behold Maitreya.
Should any of us first relinquish this life and succeed in fulfilling our long-cherished wish, we shall inform one another so that we may know where each has gone. Subsequently, Śīlabuddhi...

The elder first relinquished his life, yet for three years there was no sign of rebirth. Vasubandhu Bodhisattva subsequently also relinquished his life; six months passed, yet still there was no sign of rebirth.
At that time, the non-Buddhists all mocked them, saying that Vasubandhu and Siṃhabuddhi had transmigrated into evil realms and thus lacked spiritual efficacy.
Later, during the first watch of the night, Asaṅga Bodhisattva [appeared] at the gate.
As he was instructing people in the methods of meditative concentration, the lamp light suddenly dimmed, and a great radiance appeared in the sky.
A celestial being descended through the void and entered the courtyard, where he paid respectful homage to Asaṅga. Asaṅga asked: "Why have you come so late? What is your name now?"
He replied, "From here, I shall relinquish my life-span and go to Tuṣita Heaven, where I will be born within the inner assembly of Maitreya from within a lotus flower.
As soon as the lotus flower opens, Maitreya will praise me, saying: 'Welcome, Viśālamati! Welcome, Viśālamati!
After I have completed one circuit of circumambulation, I shall immediately return to report this news. The Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked, "Where is Siṃhabuddhi now? He replied, "I am returning..."
While circumambulating, he saw Siṃhabuddhi among the assembly outside, so deeply attached to celestial pleasures that he had no leisure to look back;
how could he have come to report this? The Bodhisattva Asaṅga said, "That matter is finished. What were the marks and signs of Maitreya like? What Dharma did he proclaim?
He replied, "The marks and signs of Maitreya cannot be fully described in words. The sublime Dharma he proclaimed was in meaning no different from this. However, the Bodhisattva..."
Their wondrous voices were clear, resonant, harmonious, and elegant; those who heard them forgot their fatigue, and those who received them never grew weary. (As recorded in the *Xiyu ji*.

Tuṣita—formerly called Doushuai—is the realm of Maitreya [the former name being Chizhi]. Among the three piṭakas of the Buddha’s sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras, there are many accounts of people within the six realms of existence or those who have come from among them. Here, only one or two are recorded to illustrate the rest.
Even regarding those commonly seen and heard in this land, it is impossible to record them all; thus, only the essentials are recorded, as shown below.)
Sun Zhiluo (courtesy name Fahui) of the Jin dynasty was a native of Banya County in Qiguó. His father, Zu, was a Grand Master of the Palace Secretariat (Taizhong Dàfū) under the Jin.
Zhiluo had served the Dharma since childhood; at the age of eighteen, he fell ill and passed away in the eighth month of the first year of the Xiankang era. Afterward, his father moved...
Residing in Wuchang, on the eighth day of the fourth month in the third year, the śramaṇa Yufa was walking through the streets carrying a sacred image.
As he passed by their house, the husband, wife, and all their children came out to observe; they saw Zhì also among the crowd, attending the procession behind the image.
He saw his parents bowing and kneeling to offer greetings; they returned home together. Szu was already ill, and Zhì said, "There is no calamity or malevolent spirit afflicting him;
it is simply because he failed to take proper care of himself. He shall recover in the fifth month. Having finished speaking, he took his leave.

On the fifteenth day of the seventh month of that year, he returned again to offer greetings, appearing exactly as when he was alive. He then spoke of how his maternal grandfather had become the Lord of Mount Tai.
Jian Zhi said, "You should not have come; how did you manage to reach this place? Zhi replied, "My paternal uncle brought me here, intending for me to take his place in punishment.

When the authorities questioned him, they intended to flog and penalize him, but I rescued and explained the matter on his behalf, and he was acquitted. Zhi’s elder brother was named Rong, with the courtesy name Siyuan.
At that time, he was by his side. Zhì said to him, "Although you have left your former body, you remain in a state of ease and joy. Simply continue your studies and do nothing else.
I hope my elder brother will no longer worry; merely apply yourself with diligence and exertion, binding your mindfulness to cultivate goodness, and merit will naturally follow you."
"I completed my studies two years ago and was destined to be born into a royal family. My peers numbered five hundred;
they are currently in the Hall of Blessings, and having completed their studies, they shall all ascend to be born in the sixth heaven.

I originally should have ascended there as well, but because I was bound by the karmic conditions of seeking to save my ancestors, I alone was born into a royal family. On the seventh day of the seventh month in the fifth year, [I shall return]."
Upon returning, he said that there would be an invasion of Zoucheng; the instances of such difficult predictions were numerous, and all came true exactly as he had spoken.

His family members kept this secret, so it was not widely circulated. He further said: "My ancestors have committed many transgressions and been subject to punishment; it is fitting that I should perform meritorious deeds on their behalf.

Now that I have received this body among humans, there is no need for me to strive further; I shall simply save my ancestors. I pray that my father and elder brothers will diligently cultivate merit and perform acts of virtue."

When making offerings to the Sangha, one must ensure that the food is fresh and pure during mealtime. Those who act in every way according to the Dharma receive the highest merit; those who follow it partially receive intermediate merit.
If one cannot act as instructed, the preparations are merely a waste of resources. One should ensure equality and maintain a mind free of "self" and "other"; only then will the merit be great.

At the time of the funeral feast, there was a maidservant who had not yet returned from her youth when she suddenly fell ill and was on the verge of death, with pain throughout her entire body. The youth said: "This..."
The maidservant wished to run away. I previously gave her a whip, so she could no longer leave. The maidservant said, "Previously, it was indeed my intention to run away;
I had made an appointment with someone, and as the day drew near, I simply stayed behind," and so on (Taì Tóngtài).
Dong Qingjian’s father, whose courtesy name was Xianming, served as Commandant of the Yueqi Cavalry at the beginning of the Jianyuan era.

When Qingjian’s mother, Lady Song, was pregnant with him, she dreamed that someone said to her, "You shall certainly give birth to a son; there shall be a green mark upon his body, so you may name him Qingjian.
Upon his birth, it was just as had been said, and he was named accordingly. He possessed dignified deportment, spoke with a pleasant smile, and was by nature broad-minded and harmonious.

His family members never once beheld a look of anger on his face; all who saw him marveled at this. When he reached the age of fourteen, the provincial government appointed him as Assistant Administrator (*zhǔbó*).
At the beginning of the Jiànyuán era, when the Crown Prince was stationed in Fàn and Hàn, he served as Assistant Director of the Water Bureau (*shuǐcáo cānjūn*).

On the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the second year, he fell ill and declared that he would certainly not recover. On the eighteenth day, as he drew near death, he sat up and spoke to his mother.

He said, "My sins are exhausted and my merit has arrived; the bonds of karmic conditions are forever severed. I pray that you, Mother, will cut yourself free from this attachment and need not harbor anxious thoughts.

Because of these seven cries, he wept loudly until his voice failed and he passed away. On the eleventh day of the intercalary month, Xianming dreamed of Jian, who said, "I wish for my father to come out to the Eastern Hall for a moment.
Xianming then bathed himself in fragrant water, observed the precepts, and went out to the Eastern Hall. This continued until the night of the fourteenth.
While he was asleep, he heard the voice of Jian calling him. Startled, he rose and saw Jian before the altar, appearing exactly as he had when alive. His father asked, "Where have you been?
Jian replied, "Since my death, I have resided within the Palace for Refining the Spirit. When one hundred days are complete, I shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
However, I could not bear to see my parents and brothers weeping and grieving, so I stayed for twenty-one days."
I have paid homage to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and requested the Four Heavenly Kings; therefore, I am able to return for a brief time.

I pray that from this day forward, my parents will no longer weep or perform sacrifices. My mother has already made a vow to seek a vision of Jian; she shall not long remain, for her life will soon come to an end.
They were then born together in the same place. His father’s lifespan was seventy-three years;

after his death, he was to undergo the retribution of suffering for three years, but by diligently practicing the Way, he could attain liberation. A questioner asked, "You have come from the middle of the night;
how is it that you possess such radiance? Jian replied, "I have now descended here together with the Bodhisattvas and the various devas; this is simply the light of their bodies. Furthermore—
The questioner asked, "In the heavens, whom do you recognize? Jian replied, "I see King [Liu] and his retinue. [I am] Zhang Yong of Wuxing; my maternal grandfather was from Xihe.
I am not born solely into this one family; from forty-seven years ago until now, [I have been here]."
He had undergone seven deaths and seven births. Having already attained the fruits of the four stages of the path, he had previously made seven vows, vowing to be born among humans;

therefore, he had traversed through birth and death until now, when they were forever ended, and he was able to leave behind the seven sufferings. At the time of his death, Jian saw the seven places of birth and death.
As for why he wept so bitterly, it was because he was parting from the seven families. Someone asked, "In whose families were you born? Jian replied, "I was born into the Jiang family."
The county official Yang Bu; Zhang Yong of Guangzhou; Wang Xuan of the Chiqu Army; Song Mo; Xiao Huiming; the Gishi (Attendant) Liang Jifu;
and the present-life Dong Yueqi—among these, only those born here have lived for seventeen years, while those from other places have lived for no more than three or five years.
From this time forward, pestilence will be frequent year after year; you should diligently cultivate merit and perform good deeds for the sake of those living in the present world.
Once dead, most fall into the three miserable realms; those reborn in heaven are few. By exerting diligent effort, one may attain liberation.

Even if you vow to be reborn in heaven so that we might see one another again, our paths of practice differ, and there will be no time for us to meet. He asked again: "Does your mother grieve and long for you?"
He was on the verge of death. "Can you allow him to see you? Jian replied, "There is no need for him to see me; it would only increase his torment. Simply speak according to what was said before.
Once the devas had departed, he could not remain much longer. With a look of sorrowful anguish, he suddenly vanished.

After he had departed, a fragrant scent still lingered to the left and right of the bamboo grove, and his family members likewise smelled this lingering fragrance. (Sengjian was one who had attained the first fruit, *srotāpanna*.

Having exhausted his outflows (*āsrava*) through seven deaths and seven births, he realized the fourth fruit, that of an *arhat*, and thus transcended the three realms. Hence it is said: "From now on, I have forever finished; I have attained liberation from all suffering. However, the places where Jian was born were all auspicious gates.)

In Liyang, there was a man named Zhang Ying who had previously served a local folk deity and engaged in the ritual drumming and dancing of licentious sacrifices. In the eighth year of the Xianhe era, he moved his residence to Wuhu.
His wife fell ill, and Ying offered prayers with such exhaustive devotion that his wealth and property were nearly exhausted. His wife, however, was a disciple of the Legalist school.

He said, "Now my illness grows daily more severe; seeking spirits is of no benefit. I beg you to perform Buddhist rites on my behalf. [The master] granted his request. He went to the monastery and saw Zhu Tankai.
Tankai said, "The Buddha is like medicine for curing illness. If one sees the medicine but does not take it, though one has seen it, there is no benefit.
You should grant permission to serve the Buddha. Tankai made an appointment with him, saying, "Tomorrow I shall go to the vegetarian feast; you should return. That night, he dreamed of a...
A person over ten feet tall came from the south and entered the gate, saying, "Your home is in such a state of disorder;

it is so utterly impure. Seeing Tanka following behind him, he said, "He has only just begun to resolve his mind; you should not yet reproach him. Once Tanying had awakened from his sleep, he immediately lit lamps and prepared a high seat as well as a seat for Hārītī.
The next morning, Tanka went there, and Tanying recounted his dream in detail. He subsequently received the five precepts and renounced [the world].
He removed the spirit’s image and made extensive offerings of merit. His wife’s illness was immediately cured. In the second year of the Xiankang era, Sengying went to Magou to purchase salt;
on his return, he moored at Wuhu Port for the night. There he dreamed of three men who used iron hooks to hook him.

Sengying said, "I am a disciple of the Buddha. They pulled him relentlessly and would not let him go. He said, "You have been running away from me for a long time. Terrified, Sengying said, "Release me! I shall..."
"I give you one *sheng* of wine. He then released him. [The monk] said to Ying: "I only fear that others will take you back again.

Upon waking from his sleep, Ying suffered from abdominal pain and diarrhea; when he reached home, he was extremely distressed. Ying had already been seriously ill for some time, so he sent someone to call for Kai. It happened that Kai was not at home.
Ying soon lost consciousness, but after a day he revived and recounted how several men had used iron hooks to hook him.
As he was about to go north, he descended a slope. At the foot of the slope, he saw cauldrons of boiling water, swords, and instruments of cruel torment.
Instantly, he realized this was hell. He wished to call out his teacher’s name, but he forgot the character "Tang" (曇) in the name Tangkai (曇鎧);

he could only cry out, "Preceptor, save me! At times, he also called upon the Buddha. After a short while, a man came from the west, over ten feet tall, holding a golden pestle and intending to strike him.
The man who had been seized said, "I am a disciple of the Buddha; why have you brought me here? At this, the seizer was terrified and dispersed.
The tall man led him away, saying to him, "Your life is at its end and you will not live much longer. You may return home for a short while to recite three gāthās and take the name of your preceptor.
In three days, your life shall pass away, and you will immediately be reborn in heaven. When Ying regained consciousness, he immediately returned [to his home].
He was struck with a sudden sense of foreboding. Thereafter, for three days, he observed the fast and recited hymns (*bhāṣya*). He sent someone to record the name of Tan-kai.
When midday had come and the meal was finished, he prostrated before the Buddha, recited hymns, and took his leave of all his family members.

Having washed himself and put on his robes, he fell asleep and passed away immediately. (Note: *Bhāṣya* means praise; it refers to extolling the Three Jewels. Reciting scriptures is also called *bhāṣya*. A *gāthā* is a verse found within Buddhist sutras. The pronunciation of *chù* is like that of *chū*; it signifies sorrow, anxiety, and trepidation.)
Shi Shiguang of Xiangyang died at Wuchang in the eighth year of the Xianhe era.

Seven days later, he invited the śramaṇa Zhi Fashan to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Small Version). While Fashan was weary and dozing, he heard what sounded like a human voice from atop the spirit altar.
Shi’s household had a maidservant named Zhang Xin, who saw Shiguang upon the altar wearing a ceremonial cap (*xià*) and dressed exactly as he had been when alive.

Ping said to Xin, "I was originally destined to fall among the dragons. But because Master Zhi recited the sutras for me, Tanhu and Tanjian have welcomed me up to the seventh Brahma Heaven, a place of great joy. Hu and Jian were both śrāmaṇeras of that mountain.
He had already passed away. Later, when Zhi Fashan went to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for him, [Sheng] again appeared in his seat.
When Sheng was alive, he had offered two banners in the temple; he then called out to Zhang Xin, saying, "Hold these banners and escort me.
Xin replied, "Yes," and immediately died. Taking Xin and holding the banners, they flew together toward the northwest and ascended upon a green mountain.
It was the color of lapis lazuli. Upon reaching the mountain peak, he gazed toward the Gate of Heaven (Devadāruvana).
Shiguang then personally took up the banner and sent a messenger back, giving him a piece of blue incense the size of a *bādara* fruit and instructing him: "Offer this to Master Zhishi.

Before the messenger had even returned, Shiguang was seen from afar entering the Gate of Heaven directly. The messenger retraced his path and returned; in an instant, [Zhishi] revived, yet he no longer saw [Shiguang].
The incense in her hand was still there, and the banner remained in the temple as before.
When Shiguang and Xin were leaving their home, their six-year-old son saw them and pointed, saying to his grandmother, "Father is flying up to heaven; did you see him, Grandmother?
Later, Shiguang returned to her home accompanied by more than ten heavenly beings; they hovered about before departing. Every time she came, she would invariably see the hairpin.
[His] *qia* [cap] was removed, and his hair-knot was necessarily exposed. Xìn asked him about this, and Guāng replied, "In heaven there are crowns; one does not wear this here.
Thereafter, he wore a heavenly crown and, together with the various heavenly beings, played the lute and sang as they went directly to his mother’s hall.
Xìn asked, "Why do you come so often? Guāng said, "I come wishing to make you and your kind understand the nature of sin and merit, while also providing entertainment for my mother."
The sound of the lute was pure and exquisite, unlike any worldly noise. All the family members, both young and old, heard it;

yet though they heard the sound, it was as if there were a wall or screen between them, and they could not perceive its source. Only Xinxin heard it with distinct clarity. After a short while, he departed.
Xìn saw a light enter a black gate; after a short while, he emerged and said to Xìn, "My uncle was here.

He was constantly subjected to flogging and beatings, and the agony was unbearable. I have returned from visiting him. Because my uncle committed the sin of killing during his lifetime, he is now receiving this retribution."
"You may inform your maternal aunt to invite a monk to recite the scriptures; you shall then be somewhat spared from this.
Your uncle was formerly a General of the Light Chariot (the seventh Brahmā Heaven, which is the first dhyāna heaven located above the six heavens of the desire realm)."
In Jiangling of the Song dynasty, there was the monk Huang Qian. When he was twenty years old, he frequently stayed at the home of Yang Daochan to the west of the Jiangling market.

He practiced the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the walking meditation) with diligent austerity for over a year. Consequently, he experienced many spiritual transformations; on some days, he would [suddenly] arrive...

At more than ten locations where vegetarian feasts were held, although the practitioners performed rites and recited scriptures throughout the day and night, Huan Xian was seen present in every household.
The assembly gradually came to regard him with reverence and wonder, considering him one who had attained the Way.

On a certain day in the second year of the Xiaojian era, he announced his own time of death, saying to Daochan: "Tonight, I shall pass away at your home. When the appointed day arrived, Daochan prepared [the offerings].
For eight days they lit lamps throughout the night. During the first and middle watches, they moved among the assembly to lead them in walking meditation;
he remained still and did not differ from the others. After the fourth watch, he claimed to be exhausted and lay down; his complexion gradually changed, and after a short while, he passed away.
The entire district established a three-week *zhāi* (fasting/retreat) ceremony for him, and a stupa was erected, which still exists today. Long after his death, he appeared at Duobao Temple and said:
The practitioner Tánxún said, "On the twenty-third day of the second month next year, I shall go together with the various devas to welcome [the Buddha].
Having spoken these words, he departed. Tánxún immediately established a ninety-day vegetarian feast at the Chan hall in Chángshā and practiced the offering of his body in almsgiving.
When that day arrived, he was so severely exhausted that he knew his end was near; he then extensively invited both monastics and laypeople and grandly prepared a Dharma assembly.
During the third watch of the night, he called out and asked the assembly of monks whether they had heard or seen anything. The monks themselves were unaware of any anomaly.
Hui-xun said, "There is the sound of music being performed in the air, and the fragrant smoke is most extraordinary. The karmic connection of Huang Qianzhi has now arrived.

Only then did the monks return to the hall to take their seats, by which time Hui-xun had already finished [his meal]. (The above five accounts are from the *Mingxiang ji* [Records of Miraculous Signs], a work in ten fascicles compiled by Wang Yan during the Qi dynasty.)

Jiuquan Commandery: Generally, not long after a Governor arrives in the commandery, he dies. Later, Chen Pei of Bohai was appointed to this commandery. Pei was filled with anxiety and found no joy; he went to a diviner to have his fortune told. The diviner said: "Distant from the feudal lords, release the elder’s robe. He who can explain this shall have no sorrow.

Pei still did not understand these words, so the diviner reported [the meaning]: [The interpretation is as follows: "Distant from the feudal lords" refers to the character for "Jiu" (酒), which contains the radical for "water" (氵) and the phonetic "zhou" (酉). To "release the elder’s robe" means to remove the "robe" (衣) from the "elder" (伯). When these two characters are combined, they form "Qiu" (裘). If one understands this, there will be no sorrow. Pei remained unable to comprehend this explanation. The diviner then continued: [The full explanation is: "Distant from the feudal lords" means to remove the "radical for water" (氵) from the character for "Jiu" (酒). "Release the elder’s robe" means to remove the "robe" (衣) from the character for "bo" (伯).

When these two characters are joined, they form "Qiu" (裘). If one can interpret this, there will be no further grief. Pei still could not grasp the meaning of these words. The diviner then informed him: [The final resolution is: "Distant from the feudal lords" means to remove the "radical for water" (氵) from "Jiu" (酒). "Release the elder’s robe" means to remove the "robe" (衣) from "Bo" (伯). When these two characters are combined, they form "Qiu" (裘). If one can understand this, there will be no more sorrow. Pei still could not understand this speech. The diviner then reported [the solution].
He said, "Simply go, and you shall understand it naturally. Once Pei arrived at his post, there were the Marquis Wang Houping, the Marquis Shi Hou, and the Marquis Dong Hou among his attendants.
Pei realized in his heart, "These are what are called 'various marquises' (zhuhou).

He then distanced himself from them and lay down, contemplating the meaning of the phrase "releasing the elder brother's robe" (fang boqiu), yet he did not know what it signified. After midnight, something came and settled upon Pei’s blanket. Pei...
He woke up and found that he had been robbed. The object [of his possession] leaped about, making a loud *hong-hong* sound.
Hearing it, a man outside entered with a torch, intending to kill him. The spirit then said, "I truly have no ill intent; I merely wished to test you, my Lord.
Grant me one pardon, and I shall repay your kindness deeply. Chen Pei asked, "What thing are you, that you have suddenly presumed to offend the Grand Master?"
The Guardian said, "I was originally a hundred-year-old fox who has now transformed into a *mei*.
I was on the verge of transforming into a deity when I encountered the wrath of the Magistrate; I have suffered great misfortune. Please grant me my release. My name is Boqiu.
If the Magistrate ever faces an emergency or difficulty, he need only call my name, and he will be liberated. Pei then said joyfully, "I shall release Boqiu."
This was indeed the meaning [of the dream]. He immediately released the dog. He slightly opened the coverlet, and suddenly a crimson light, like a flash of lightning, issued from the door.
On the following night, there was someone knocking at the door. Pei asked, "Who is it? The reply was, "Boqiu. He asked, "For what purpose have you come?
The reply was, "To report a matter. He asked, "What matter do you report? The reply was, "There is a thief in this district who has escaped as a slave. Pei—
When cases were brought forward, they were verified; he would always first inform Pei before taking action. Consequently, within his jurisdiction, there was not even a hair’s breadth of corruption.
Everyone said that a sage ruler had appeared. Later, after more than a month had passed, the Court Scribe Li Yin secretly consorted with Pei’s maidservant.
Filled with alarm and fear, and apprehensive that Boqiu might come to report the matter, he then plotted with several officials to murder Pei. He then claimed that no one else was present.
He then ordered his feudal lords to enter directly with clubs, intending to strike him down and kill him. Pei was terrified and immediately called out to Boqiu, "Come to my rescue!
At once, there appeared an object like a roll of one *shen* of vermilion silk, which then produced a sound. The lords prostrated themselves on the ground, their souls lost.
Thereupon, they were bound one after another and interrogated regarding their intentions; consequently, they all confessed.
More than a month later, Qiu took leave of Pei, saying, "I have now attained the status of a deity and shall ascend to heaven. I shall no longer come and go to visit you, my Lord of the Prefecture.
Thereafter, he departed and was never seen again. (From the *Sou Shen Yi Ji*).

Empress of Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty. Her surname was Xi. At her birth, a crimson light shone through the chamber, illuminating all the vessels and utensils. As she grew up, she was naturally intelligent and wise;
she was skilled in clerical script and calligraphy, and there was no matter of history, biography, or female handicrafts with which she was not proficient. During the Song and Qi dynasties...
Various kings sought her hand in marriage, but her father, Ye, refused them all. Later, she was given in marriage to the Emperor. She bore him three daughters.

When the Emperor served as the Governor of Yongzhou, the Consort passed away. Her nature had been cruelly jealous; during the Tianjian era, she transformed into a giant python and entered the inner palace.

He had a dream concerning the Emperor. When the Emperor’s health was about to become unstable, the python would suddenly stir up the water so that it surged upward, or manifest in the form of a dragon, its radiance shining brilliantly.
At times, the python spoke in human speech and addressed the Emperor, saying: "While I was alive, I was envious of both the great and the small;
my nature was cruel and venomous, harming things and injuring people. After death, I became this python body, lacking food and drink, and tormented by hunger and distress. Furthermore—
Within her scales were many insects that bit and gnawed at her flesh; her suffering was most intense.
Moved by the Emperor’s past affection for her, she revealed her plight to him and prayed for a single meritorious act to bring about her deliverance. Upon hearing this, the Emperor was deeply moved.
Consequently, he erected a pavilion over the exposed well, provided a vast store of clothing, installed a silver pulley, and set out golden jars filled with the hundred flavors [of food and drink].
He performed a sacrifice for him. The Emperor then assembled a great multitude of śramaṇas in the palace hall and inquired what virtuous practice could effectively liberate him from his suffering.
Master Zhìgōng replied, "One must pay homage to the Buddha and perform repentance; then his transgressions may be removed.

Thereupon, the Emperor, together with Master Zhìgōng and śramaṇas of renowned virtue, searched through the texts of the Great Canon and extracted the words of the Buddha. Moved by the appearance of Maitreya’s name inscribed therein, they compiled this Rite of Repentance.
The text consists of ten fascicles. While performing court rituals within the palace, the Emperor suddenly smelled a most fragrant and pervasive incense.

Looking upward, he beheld a celestial being of exquisite and dignified appearance, who said to the Emperor: "By virtue of Your Majesty’s merit, I have already cast off my snake body and attained rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
I now manifest this celestial form as proof. Having offered his sincere thanks, the being vanished upon finishing his words. (From the *Tong*)
[Included in the Preface to the *Zhàibìng Chàn*].
At Longyuan Monastery in Shu Commandery, there was the śramaṇa Huishao, surnamed Chen. He was originally a native of Taichou in Yingchuan.

Possessing few desires and great wisdom, he was exceptionally intelligent and stood out from his peers. At the age of fifty-four, he passed away at his home monastery. At that time, there was a commoner in Chengdu surnamed...

He should have been named Shifeng. Due to illness, his breath ceased, yet his heart remained warm. On the fifth day, he regained consciousness and said: "I was led away to the abode of King Yama. I heard the verdict being pronounced:
'Go to welcome Dharma Master Shao. In an instant, he arrived. The King descended from the hall, joined his palms, and prostrated himself with his head at the Master's feet;
he said nothing further, but merely wrote a document consisting of the single character *zheng* (大政). Shao then went outside and sat down."
Under a tree by a desolate road, he saw a young boy holding a lacquered willow basket containing a *kāṣāya* robe, which he told Shao to put on.
Dozens of monks came to welcome them; Feng recognized the two Dhyāna Masters, Huihe and Huaci, who departed through the air amidst canopies and banners lining the path.
Furthermore, at the end of that night, a nun from Anpu Temple, who had been suffering from a long illness and was unconscious, awoke and said, "They have sent Shao."
The Dharma Master, together with five hundred monks, ascended a staircase made of the seven precious gems and reached the celestial palace. Within the lecture hall, the ground was like crystal;

the couches and mats were elegantly arranged, and there were also fly-whisks, desks, tables, and lotus ponds. Sào took his seat and spoke for a short while, then rose and bid farewell to those who had come to see him off.
Such were the subtle and auspicious signs of his birth and passing, which moved and inspired others in this manner. By means of the heavens...
He passed away on the third day of the seventh month in the second year of the Jianyuan era (as recorded in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Lènà, whose name means "Ratnamati" in Chinese, was a śramaṇa from Central India during the Northern Wei dynasty; he was a native of the Western Regions and was thoroughly versed in the Tripitaka.
Miaoru (Wondrous Entry) was a master of *dhāraṇī*. At the beginning of the Yongping era of the Wei dynasty, he came to travel in the Eastern Xia (China).
Emperor Xuanwu frequently invited him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and [Miaoru] would examine its profound meanings without neglecting it for even a single day.

While he sat upright upon the high seat, suddenly there appeared a man holding a ceremonial tablet and bearing a name-list, appearing like a high official, who said: "I have come by the command of the Heavenly Emperor to invite the Dharma Master to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka*."
Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, his intention was: "This Dharma assembly has not yet concluded; wait until the recitation of the scripture is finished, and I shall comply with your command.
When the religious service was about to end, he again saw the former messenger say: "By the command of the Heavenly Emperor, I have come down to welcome you.

Thereupon, with a smile and a joyful countenance, he addressed the assembly to take his leave and suddenly passed away on his Dharma seat. The four officials, including the *Dujiang* (Chief Lecturer), [were present].
He also passed away at the same time. When the monastics and laypeople within the borders of the Wei heard of and witnessed this marvel, there were none who did not sigh in admiration.

Later, while the monk Śramaṇa Xuánjǐng of a temple in Yèxià, Xiāngzhōu of the Sui dynasty—whose mastery of the profound and subtle was comprehensive and who exclusively lectured on the Mahāyāna—was lying down...
After being ill for three days, he told his attendants: "Xuanjing wishes to see Maitreya Buddha; why then have I become the Lord of the Yāma Heaven?

He further said, "The guests are exceedingly numerous, and they must be attended to. When asked the reason for this, he replied, "How can the perceptions and thoughts of an ordinary person be scrutinized?
Just now, a host of devas arrived, wishing to invite me forth. Thereafter, extraordinary fragrances filled the air.
The entire community heard this together. He further said, "I wish to depart; may I be reborn in this world as a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend).

He then passed away at his residence on the sixth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Daye era. Throughout his life, he had constantly maintained the vow to have his remains submerged in water.
After his death, in accordance with his prior intent, he was buried in the deep waters of the Zibo River. Three days later—
They went to observe the place where [the image] had sunk; instead, it had become a sand mound, exceedingly high and steep, with the waters branching off around it.
Both the clergy and the laity regarded this as an auspicious omen of refinement, and its traces have been transmitted to the present day. (The two preceding entries are from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).

In Luzhou, the Regional Inspector (Cishi) Xin Yanzhi constructed a fifteen-story pagoda. A local man named Zhang Yuan died suddenly and then revived, saying that his spirit had traveled to the heavens.
There he saw a hall of extreme magnificence and beauty, where a celestial being said, "Regional Inspector Xin has performed great meritorious deeds; this hall was built to await him."
In Silla, a country to the east of the sea, there was the Zen Master Xuanguang. He visited Nanyue and realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra.
The Master then took his leave of Nanyue and returned to Jiangnan with his monk’s staff. There he encountered a merchant ship from his own country and managed to board it.

Just as they reached the vast ocean, he suddenly beheld clouds of various colors dazzling his eyes, and elegant music filling the sky; crimson ceremonial staffs and rainbow-colored banners arrived, accompanied by the sound of proclamations. From the void—

The *Zhongsheng* (Record of Central Sounds) relates: The Heavenly Emperor invited the Chan Master Xuanguang from海东 (Haidong). The Master folded his hands and declined with humility; consequently, the boat halted and would not proceed.

Immediately, he saw a person in green robes respectfully escorting him into the great palace. There, he beheld a display of celestial guards arrayed in formation, with fish and shell creatures interspersed in profusion.

In the intervals between sessions, spirits and deities all looked up with reverence and said, "The Celestial Emperor has descended to our dragon palace and requested the Dharma Master to expound the dharma-gates he has already realized;
we have received no small benefit. Once they had ascended the hall, they requested him to mount a high platform, whereupon the Celestial Emperor questioned him.
The Master expounded [the teachings] for him for seven days until it was finished. The Emperor personally escorted him to his departure point;
as the Master stepped back onto the boat he had previously been using, the vessel drifted away. (The above two accounts are from the *Tongji*).
In the capital of the Tang dynasty, at Dà'ān Guó Monastery, there was the Dharma Master Zǐlín. When he was young, he suddenly felt a longing to return and visit his parents.
His father had lost his sight, and his mother had been deceased for three years. Consequently, he went to a mountain shrine to seek knowledge of his mother’s abode in the afterlife. Immediately—
She spread out her sitting mat and recited the Lotus Sūtra, vowing to see the King of Mount Tai as her appointed goal.

That night, the King of Mount Tai indeed summoned his neighbor and asked, "For what reason do you suffer so grievously? The neighbor replied, "My mother, Lady Wang, has already completed the mourning period since her death;
I venture to ask the Great King, where is she now? The King looked to his registrar official, who answered, "Lady Wang is currently detained in prison, undergoing suffering."
The neighbor said, "What crime has my mother committed? The King replied, "When she gave birth to the Monk, she ate chicken eggs and took the pus from a white-footed leech's head;
for this reason, she has become your teacher. The neighbor wailed in grief and exhaustion, entreating the King to grant her release. He said, "I am bound by my lot and have no way to escape.
However, for the sake of the Dharma Master, I pray that you allow me to go to Mount Mao to pay homage to King Aśoka."
The King’s Stūpa may perhaps be traced to this origin. The following morning, Ling set out on his journey and arrived at Mount Moshan Temple in Nanyin, Kuaiji.
He prostrated himself, wailing with grief until his five limbs touched the ground. Having completed his prostrations, he cast down his staff some forty thousand times.
Suddenly, he heard a voice calling out to him, as if from the void. Looking up into the clouds, he saw his mother, who thanked him, saying: "By your power, I have been delivered."
"I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; therefore, I have come to inform you. Having spoken, he suddenly vanished.
The site where she had previously performed her prostrations is now the base of the thatched hut on the verdant slope of the rear peak at Yǔwáng Temple on Mount Mào. The pond still remains there.

(If people of old, even after giving birth, could receive such a heavy reward for eating chicken eggs, what must be the retribution for those who kill living beings in abundance after childbirth? Those who act as mothers or children should not fail to know this. Mount Mào is located approximately forty li southeast of the city of Ningbo Prefecture in Zhejiang. [This was told by] Aśoka.)
Stūpa. For details, see the fourth fascicle. ○ *Zhì* (pronounced as in "zhí") means a tether; *mí* (pronounced as in "mí") means to bind. Shouzhou. Mount Zijin.
Chan Master Xuangong was a native of Yongjia. Upon seeing Mount Zijin, his heart was filled with joy, and he remained there to practice meditation and contemplation.
Previously, this mountain had been plagued by many fierce tigers; they would sometimes devour traveling merchants or injure woodcutters. [To avoid them...]

As for the tyrannical administration, the mourning for his wife was exceedingly sorrowful. He consulted his clan to choose a place to dwell; thereafter, tigers and beasts vanished from sight, and those entering the mountains from nearby areas felt no more fear.
One day, a crowd of Zen practitioners gathered, and they saw an old man who hurried before the master’s seat, bowing and kneeling with diligent reverence.
The master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I was originally a tiger. I lived in these mountains, devouring many people."

"Born [in heaven], I was transformed by the Great Master’s teaching; his subtle influence turned my mind, and I attained liberation from this karmic body. Having been reborn in the heavenly realm, I have come to express my gratitude.
Yet, in the brief moment it took to turn and walk away, I vanished without a trace. (The above two accounts are from the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*).
At Ximing Monastery in Chang’an, there was Vinaya Master Daoxuan. His virtue mirrored the profound currents of the Dharma, and his practice was pure and lofty.

He devoted his life to asceticism and sincere cultivation until his final breath. Wandering tirelessly in search of the Way, he resolved to serve as a presiding master and compiled over two hundred scrolls of ritual protocols;
these collected high standards possessed profound significance. During the Zhenguan era, he once lived in seclusion at Yunshi (Cloud Chamber) in the Qin region.
At Mount [Name], people saw a celestial youth attending at his left and right. While walking the night path at Ximing Monastery, his foot slipped on the front steps;
a being supported him, allowing him to tread upon the air without harm. Looking back closely, he saw it was a young man. The Vinaya Master immediately questioned him.
"Who is it that stays here in the night? The youth replied, "I am no ordinary person; I am Nanda, the son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North.
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, I have guarded the Upādhyāya for a long time. The Master said, "In my practice of cultivation, there is no need for the Prince’s assistance.
Your majesty possesses sovereign spiritual power; in the Western Regions, there are matters where Buddhist rites may be performed."
"Please procure it for me. The Prince said, "I possess a tooth relic of Śākyamuni Buddha. Although my precious hands have long been [at your disposal], I would still sacrifice my head and eyes;
how could I dare not offer this? He then presented it to the Master, who preserved and venerated it with offerings.

On the occasion of the middle spring month in the second year of the Qiánfēng era, while residing in the capital at Jìngyè Temple south of the city, he was pursuing tranquility and cultivating the Way. At that age...

When he reached his twilight years, his physical strength was beginning to fail. He focused his mind on the four modes of birth and contemplated the three assemblies. Suddenly, due to past affinities, a spirit from the netherworld appeared to him.
His illness gradually subsided, and as he redoubled his efforts in reverent devotion, he was moved by a response from the unseen realm. At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings arrived.

He inquired after the health of the Vinaya Master and extensively recounted matters such as the appearance of the four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa in the world and the traces left by their parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, various devas and the ministers and subordinates of the Four Heavenly Kings arrived at the door of the Vinaya Master’s room; their movements resembled those of humans, and they made sounds as they stepped.
The Vinaya Master asked, "Who is there? They replied, "We are disciples, surnamed Zhang and named Qiong. The Master asked, "Which donors are you from? They replied:
He said: "This is the fifteenth son of the Heavenly King of the South. The King has ninety-one sons, all of whom possess heroic strategy and divine martial prowess, each governing their own capital.
The lands they administer, whether sea or land, are divided by distinct territories; the boundaries of what is upheld and what is transgressed are clearly demarcated.

All have personally received the Buddha’s teachings and protect both the good and the evil, ensuring that the Bequeathed Dharma flourishes once more. Having accumulated and cultivated these merits, they constantly provide protection."
"It is merely a formal gesture. The Master said, "Since you, donor, have already bestowed your virtue upon me, I have come to visit you. For what reason do you not enter through the gate?

He replied, "Your disciple, lacking the Master’s instruction, does not dare to enter rashly. The Master said, "I wish for you to enter and take your seat. Having entered, he paid his respects and sat down.
The Master asked, "Donor, since you have deep faith in the Triple Gem and have received the Buddha’s entrustment to protect and uphold it—"
"Welcome to visit me. Why do you not manifest your form? He replied, "My disciple’s *saṃbhogakāya* is distinct from that of others, and its radiance and color are also different.
It would disturb the minds of the multitude; it is sufficient to converse with you, Master, without the trouble of manifesting my form.
He asked, "Since spring began, my strength has gradually weakened. Medicine has been ineffective, and I do not know whether the duration of my life will be long or short. He replied:
The Master replied, "My life is nearing its end; there is no need for medicine. He was asked, "On what day will your karmic retribution conclude?

He answered, "Why must you ask for the time? You should simply know that my life will soon come to an end. I shall be reborn in the fourth heaven, in the presence of Maitreya Buddha. He was further asked, "Who are your companions?"
The disciple replied: "My third elder brother, Zhang Yu, was exceptionally talented and possessed transcendent insight; he held the Buddhist tradition in profound faith and reverence.
He compiled the *Qihuan Tujing* (Illustrated Scripture of Jetavana) in more than one hundred fascicles. Its splendor towers like a celestial palace, while its fame has not yet reached the underworld.

Having received this report from my teacher, I have applied my thoughts and sought to record it in order to enlighten both the clergy and the laity. Furthermore, another person came to the Master’s abode, paid his respects, and performed the rites of homage."
After exchanging greetings regarding the weather, the Master asked, "Where are you from, lay devotee? What is your name? He replied, "Your disciple’s surname is Wang and my given name is Fan.
I am a minister at the Lan-tai (Palace of the Orchid Terrace) of the Great Wu. I am currently a messenger under General Wei, the Heavenly King of the South.
The General has extremely many affairs; he protects the Buddha-dharma of the three continents. There are disputes and transgressions..."

Whenever there were matters of peril, he would personally go to mediate and persuade them until they reached an understanding. Now, having joined in the salutation (*vandana*), he will arrive shortly.
Furthermore, another man came and said, "My surname is Luo; I am a native of Shu. He spoke with the accent of Shu and explained the characteristics of the Vinaya in great detail.
When they first met, they followed secular etiquette and recounted their circumstances in great detail with many formalities.
Furthermore, there was a deity surnamed Fei who paid homage as before and said: "In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I was born in the First Heaven (Cāturmahārājika) under the command of General Wei.
While the other devas were intoxicated by sensual desire, I, by the power of my past vows, did not engage in celestial lusts. It was pure.
He purified his holy life and devoted himself exclusively to the Vinaya. General Wei maintained the celibacy of a youth and did not accept celestial desires.
Beneath each of the Four Great Kings are eight generals; thus there are thirty-two generals for the four kings who patrol the four continents, coming and going to provide protection and assistance.
Among all those who have left the household life within the four continents, the Dharma of the Buddha exists only slightly in the northern continent;
in the other three continents, the Buddha-Dharma is widely propagated. Nevertheless, many people violate the precepts, and few act in accordance with the Dharma.

In the eastern and western continents, people lack wisdom, and their afflictions are difficult to transform. In the southern continent, although many commit offenses, they can be transformed to follow what is good, for their minds are easily disciplined.

I prostrate. When the Buddha was on the verge of entering *nirvāṇa*, he personally entrusted me with his teachings and commanded that I protect them all, so that Māra would not cause them disturbance.

He said, "If I do not protect [the Dharma], who will there be to practice my teachings when they are thus broken by those who violate the precepts? Therefore, I have dared not fail to follow the Buddha’s admonitions.

Although I see those who destroy the prohibitions, I pity and protect them; when I see them perform even a single good deed, I do not dwell upon their ten thousand transgressions, treating the matter as if it were forgotten.
