Faults! Do not dwell upon past failures. Furthermore, the stench of human beings rises into the void for four hundred thousand *li*.
All the pure devas are without exception weary of it; they do so only because they have received the Buddha’s entrustment to protect the Buddha-dharma and thus must cohabit with humans.
The various devas dare not fail to come. Among the thirty-two generals of General Wei, he is the one who most diligently provides great protection.
There are many sons and daughters of Māra who mock and toy with bhikṣus; those whose power of the Path is slight are all deluded and disturbed by them.

When the General hastens there in urgent pursuit, he eliminates and cuts down [the demons] according to the occasion. Thus, when business arises, he must go to the abode of the Four Heavenly Kings, whereupon the Kings, upon seeing him, all...

[The Buddha] rose and said, "It is General Wei. Because he has cultivated the practice of perpetual youth and protects the True Dharma, my disciple—who by nature delights in the Vinaya—has all the *vinaya* rules established throughout the Tathāgata’s lifetime present within this assembly. Listen as you receive these precepts.

He then asked, "As for the many stone Buddhas in Chengdu, the capital of Yizhou, in what era were these images made? Why have they emerged from the earth? [The Buddha] replied, "This is the primordial foundation of Shu."
On Mount Qingcheng, in present-day Chengdu, lies a site that was once the land of Mahāsamudra.
In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a person constructed it by the West Ear River (Xier) to serve as a likeness of the entire body of Prabhūtaratna Buddha.

To the northwest of this place, it is over two thousand *li* from Kuizhou; it is said that it is not far from India, and there have been those who have traveled there repeatedly. During the Jin dynasty, there was...
The monks saw an earthen mound at this site; though they removed it as soon as it appeared, they could never level it.
Later, seeing it split open, they dug down more than a *zhang* deep and discovered a statue and human bones within a boat. The skull, elbows, and shins were all exceptionally large.
It was several times greater than that of people today; this was during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, when the lifespan of those in Jambudvīpa was twenty thousand years.

At present, the kalpa is in decline; lifespans are shortened, and people are small. It is certainly not always thus, so it should not be considered strange. When it first emerged, it was difficult to pull out;
a disciple transformed himself into an old man and, through skillful direction, [the image] reached Zhou by the end of the day.

The Dharma was briefly obscured, but it was revived during the Sui dynasty and brought forth once again. The people of Shu knew only that it had emerged from the earth through its spiritual power, yet they could not fathom its origins.
Upon seeing that its lotus pedestal bore many characters of the *Prabhūtaratna* (Many Jewels), it was consequently named after them. Furthermore, [the interlocutor] asked:
"Those *lièshū* (clerical) characters originated in the era of the fallen Qin; how could they have already existed during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha?"
"Do you have books from this country? He replied, "The clerical script (lìshū) of Li Si from the fallen Qin dynasty is a recent development.

However, the origins of this clerical script trace back to the rise of the ancient Buddhas. Currently, throughout the four directions of Jambudvīpa—among the more than one thousand islands that adorn this single region of Jambudvīpa—and within the more than one hundred countries, the written characters and spoken sounds are identical to those of the present Tang state; it is only because of the sea..."

The roads are vast and distant, spanning hundreds of thousands of *li*. Because the translations have not been transmitted, people in this region remain bound to their old ways like those guarding a stump;
this is not to be wondered at. Have you not heard of Gu Yewang of the Liang dynasty? He was the Grand Tutor of the Imperial Academy.

When he extensively investigated the origins of characters, their appearances were inconsistent. Thus, the preface to the *Yupian* states: "There was one who opened the tomb of Lord Chunshen and obtained its inscription."
The script is entirely in the *li* (clerical) style. Upon examining the record of Chunshen, this *li* script was contemporary with the six states during the reign of King Wu of Zhou;
thus, it was not from the day of the annexation. Regarding the various scripts of this country, both *zhuan* (seal) and *li*, they still remain obscure;

how then can one know of events from the time of Kāśyapa Buddha? The histories are not based on what was heard or seen by their own ears and eyes. Furthermore, he asked: "Now, to the west of the Western Capital, there is a high..."

Regarding the four earthen mounds: popular tradition claims these were the platforms where Cang Jie created writing. How can it be said, then, that the *lìshū* (clerical script) characters already existed in ancient times?
The answer is: it is not without basis to say that Cang Jie piled up earth on these platforms to create heights in order to observe bird tracks.
Furthermore, regarding the lineage of Cang Jie, its origins are rarely known in this land; some say he was a minister of the Yellow Emperor, while others...
It is said that this refers to the ancient emperors. As for the script of bird tracks, its forms have changed over time along various paths;

such things as these are now completely obsolete, and there is no need to labor over useless talk regarding them. Furthermore, there was a celestial being named Lu Xuanchang who came to visit the Vinaya Master and said:

"Your disciple lived during the time of King Mu of Zhou and was born in the First Heaven. Originally, during the era of Kāśyapa Buddha, I was a celestial being who served as a medium for transformation."

Therefore, it appeared briefly during the Zhou dynasty. As for the high four-sided terrace you asked about, its origin lies in Kāśyapa Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma at this site during his third assembly to save sentient beings.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: When a person is about to die, they will personally perceive the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Those who have performed evil deeds see themselves suffering in the three evil realms, or see Yama holding various weapons as he arrests and leads them away, or hear sounds of suffering.
If one has performed good deeds, they see the palaces of the devas, adorned with celestial maidens, and experience the joy of playful recreation; such are the superior matters they perceive.
Therefore, Chan Master Yongming Shou said: "If the mind is pure, one is born by transformation in a pure land of fragrant terraces and jeweled trees;
if the mind is defiled, one takes form in a foul land of hills, mounds, pits, and ravines. These are all fruits of equal nature."
*Liùdào jí*, Scroll One, Phonetic Explanations:

*Dìshì* (帝釋) is a term from the Sanskrit *Śakra Devānām Indra*. In the language of China, it means "Capable Lord of Heaven" (*néng tiānzhǔ*). This refers to one who is capable of [ruling] the thirty-three [gods].
The Lord of Heaven, in his former life as a human being, was surnamed Kauśika. He constructed a stūpa for the relics of Kāśyapa Buddha, with thirty-two people assisting in its construction;
they were all reborn together in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where Śakra became their lord. Collectively, this realm is called the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

The seven wholesome karmas of body and speech consist of: refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct with the body; and refraining from false speech, frivolous chatter, divisive speech, and harsh speech with the mouth.

Regarding the ten unwholesome and ten wholesome karmas: the three of the body are killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the four of the mouth are false speech, frivolous chatter, [divisive speech, and harsh speech].

Regarding speech, there are two: double-tongued speech and harsh speech; regarding the mind, there are three: greed, anger, and delusion. To refrain from these actions is called the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*).

Tiantai says: "The ten wholesome paths are of two kinds: first, abstention (*saṃvara*); second, practice (*caryā*). Abstention means merely refraining from the aforementioned evils so as not to harm others.
Practice means cultivating superior virtues to benefit and bring joy to all. These two are collectively termed 'wholesome' because they are good."
To accord with principle is what constitutes "righteousness" (yi). To cease perversions and return to the True is why it is called "accordance with principle.

Cessation (śamatha) means to bring to rest the evils of profound perversion; cultivation (bhāvanā) means to gradually return to the goodness of the supreme path. Therefore, both cessation and cultivation are termed "good."
Alternatively, it may be designated by the name "Way" (*dharma*), for it is able to lead one through to the fruit of supreme bliss.
Regarding the term *shen-zhi* (埏埴): the upper character is pronounced *xiān* and refers to kneading; the lower character is pronounced *shí* and refers to sticky clay.
Laozi said, "Knead clay to make vessels," which refers to shaping pottery.
Qià (pronounced like qiā) refers to a cap.
Jǔnqún (the first character is in the third tone) means to be distressed or in a difficult situation.
Lùlú: the upper character is pronounced lù and the lower is pronounced lú; it refers to the circular wooden device used for drawing water from a well.
*Hào* (with the third tone) is the name of a district located in Changshan. During the reign of Emperor Guangwu of the Han dynasty, the character *Hào* was divided to form the name Gaoyi.
*Yú* (pronounced *yú*) means to lift up together; it refers to being carried by two people.
There are three distinctions regarding the *yojana*: the large is sixty *li*, the medium is forty *li*, and the small is thirty *li*.
[Question: "In the teachings, it is always said to be eighty-four thousand; why is this so? [Answer: "This..."
As for the great number: within the human body there are eighty-four thousand pores, and the mind possesses eighty-four thousand defilements and afflictions;
therefore, the Buddha taught eighty-four thousand Dharma gates to counteract them.

Question: Furthermore, why is it commonly said that there is a period of seven times seven days? Answer: When a person is in the womb, the physical form is fully developed over seven periods of seven days;
at the time of death, one will certainly undergo rebirth by the end of the seventh seven-day period. The rest is as explained later.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Small Sections* (Xiaopin) is in ten fascicles;
the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra in Large Sections* (Dapin) is in thirty fascicles.
The term "gong" (犎) is pronounced "feng" (風) and refers to a breed of ox. It originates from the kingdom of Kaśmīra; its shape is like that of a camel, with its back rising high and prominent.
Twenty-five: first, the four continents—east, west, south, and north; second, the four evil destinies—*asura*s, *preta*s, animals, and hell-beings;
third, the six heavens of the desire realm; fourth, the Brahmā kings; fifth, the heaven of non-perception; sixth, the five *anāgāmin* heavens.

There are seven heavens of the Four Dhyānas and eight heavens of the Four Emptinesses. These twenty-five states of existence are all subsumed within the six realms of rebirth, wherein there is both birth and death.
The Brahmā King, the Heaven of No-Thought, and the Anāgāmin (Non-returner) heavens are all included within the Four Dhyāna heavens.
This is because non-Buddhists claim that the Brahmā King is the sovereign who gives rise to all things, and they regard the state of no-thought as nirvana due to the absence of mental activity. Five.
The Anāgāmin is true liberation; therefore, this category is established separately by name.
The eight classes of beings are: first, the devas; second, the nāgas; third, the yakṣas; fourth, the gandharvas; fifth, the asuras.
Sixth, the garuḍas; seventh, the kiṃnaras; eighth, the mahoragas.
There are four groups of those who have left the household life and two groups of householders:
the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and the upāsakas and upāsikās who all receive the five precepts.
The first character of "quianzhe" (譴謫) is pronounced qiān (first tone) with a falling intonation; the second is pronounced zé (second tone). It means to reprimand or punish.
"The food of dharma-joy and dhyāna-delight" refers to loving and delighting in the Great Dharma.

By attaining the Dharma, one nourishes the seeds of the Path and the mind gives rise to joy, not craving worldly flavors, while constantly maintaining right mindfulness; this is called the food of dharma-joy. Because one has attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), [one...]
This sustains and nourishes the life of wisdom. As the factors of enlightenment become perfectly clear and bright, right mindfulness manifests before one.
The mind gives rise to joy and bliss, no longer craving worldly flavors; this is called the food of dhyāna-joy.
The pronunciation of Xi is like Hei. Formerly, Chen Zhen was the elder brother of the Great Master Zhizhe. He served as the Military Aide (Zhongbing Canjun) to Prince Jin’an of the Liang dynasty.
At the age of forty, the immortal Zhang Guo prophesied of him, "Your death shall occur within one year.
The Master ordered him to perform the Vaipulya Repentance. Zhen saw a signboard at the gate of a heavenly palace that read: "The Hall of Chen Zhen. Fifteen... [days later].
In the year [of the cycle], she was due to give birth. After the delivery, she saw a needle and asked in astonishment, "What medicine have you been taking?

She replied, "I have merely been practicing repentance. She said, "If it were not for the power of the Way, how could one transcend death? In the end, her life was extended by fifteen years before she passed away.

When Emperor Wu performed repentance rites on behalf of Lady Xi, she was still reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; yet as for Zhen, who personally practiced the methods of repentance, how much more so!
Is it not already established in the heavenly realms?

Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is also called dependent arising (*idappaccayatā*) and also called causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). That is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations;

volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions sensation; sensation...

Conditioned by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*) arises; conditioned by grasping, becoming (*bhava*) arises; conditioned by becoming, birth (*jāti*) arises; conditioned by birth, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) arise. This is called the law of the cycle of cause and effect across the three periods of time.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the two causes of the past. Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—these five—are called the effects of the present.
Craving, grasping, and becoming—these three—are called the causes of the present. Birth and old age and death [are the effects of the future].
2. This is called the future fruit. The details are as found elsewhere.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoxiang Forest in Nanhai, Guangzhou, while residing at Jiqi. *Liu Dao Ji*, Volume 2.
The term for the human realm (*manuṣya*) is *narā-mānuṣa* in Sanskrit; this is translated here as "human. A "human" (*nara*) means "endurance" (*kṣānti*).

This is because one's mind is able to endure with equanimity amidst the favorable and adverse conditions of the world. The *Lokasthiti-śāstra* states: "For what reason is it called the human realm? There are eight reasons for this."
1. Intelligent; 2. preeminent; 3. subtle in intention; 4. perfectly awakened; 5. possessing superior wisdom; 6.
able to distinguish between the false and the real; 7. a fit vessel for the Noble Path; 8. born from the karma of intelligence.

Furthermore, because one has previously performed and accumulated intermediate wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, one goes there, is born there, and causes that birth to continue; therefore, one is called a "human."
They proceed [to rebirth] and are also full of pride; therefore they are called "humans. Among the five destinies, none possess such great pride as humans do.
Furthermore, they are able to quiet the mind; therefore they are called "humans. Among the five destinies, none are able to quiet the mind as humans are.

However, a human body is difficult to obtain, and the True Dharma is difficult to hear. Now that you have obtained a human body and heard the True Dharma—if you do not hear the True Dharma, you will remain entangled in worldly views and how could you know of the saṃsāra of the three periods of time and the six realms? You must cultivate the causes for human and celestial rebirth and construct the path to Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, time passes with such rapidity, like a white horse glimpsed through a crack; if you do not plan to practice early, when else will you wait?
The turning of the breath is itself the next life; how can one be certain of the direction of rebirth? Since wholesome causes have not yet been established, evil fruits now manifest.

Once the human body is lost, it is not a matter of mere kalpas. Thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fu-fa-zang jing) says: "The human body is not solid; it is subject to decay, corruption, danger, and fragility."
It is like a mass of foam that changes and perishes in an instant. Once impermanence arrives, who can remain?

When the breath no longer flows and the body becomes swollen, blue-black, and putrid, the hair, fur, nails, and teeth lie scattered upon the ground. Thus one knows that the human body is nothing but suffering and impermanence.

Furthermore, there are various inequalities among beings—whether foolish or wise, poor or wealthy, noble or lowly—all of which arise from the differences in the wholesome and unwholesome karma created in previous lives;
thus, their karmic retributions are not uniform, and the places they inhabit likewise differ.

There are the four great continents (*caturmahādvīpa*), the eight intermediate continents (*aṣṭamadhyadvīpa*), and the various divisions of lesser continents; yet none of them escape the three calamities (*trividha-vipatti*).
Regarding the eight sufferings: when the wise contemplate them, it is logically appropriate that they give rise to revulsion and swiftly seek liberation.
To trace their origin: when this world was first formed, the great earth was a single ocean of water. Stirred and agitated by the winds, it condensed into a single mass, like boiled milk.
Once it had cooled, solidification occurred; subsequently, the ocean waters gradually became earth, upon which [the world] arose.

The essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) was fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor. At that time, some of the gods from the Ābhāsvara heaven of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), whose merit had been exhausted, were reborn there;
others descended out of a desire to behold the new land. Being by nature fickle and impulsive, they tasted the essence of the earth with their fingers.
As they did so three times, they found it to be sweet and delicious. Eating it incessantly, they gradually became coarse and corpulent, losing their celestial splendor.
The light of the divine power of form was then utterly extinguished in great darkness.

Subsequently, a black wind blew upon the waters of the ocean, causing the sun and moon to emerge and be placed at the edge of Mount Sumeru, established within the solar path to revolve around Mount Sumeru and illuminate the four continents.

At that time, the people rejoiced when they saw them emerge and were filled with dread when they saw them enter. From this point onward, there were days and nights, waning and waxing moons, spring and autumn, and years.
The cycle ends and begins again. At the time when the kalpa first forms, the various devas descend to become humans;

they are all born by transformation (*upapāduka*), their bodily radiance is sovereign, and they travel through the air by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). There is no distinction between male and female, nor between noble and base; as they arise together in the world, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).

Those who consume much of the "earth-flavor" (*pṛthivī-rasa*) have coarse and withered complexions, while those who consume little have radiant and lustrous complexions; thus, [the former] eventually give rise to [the latter].
As they vied with one another over these causal conditions, disputes arose. The essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) gradually diminished, and all were filled with distress.
Then a crust of earth appeared, resembling thin pancakes; when that crust also vanished, a layer of earth-skin (*pṛthivī-tvac*) appeared.
When the earth-skin disappeared, natural earth-fat (*pṛthivī-meda*) appeared. When the earth-fat ceased to grow, two-stalked grapes appeared, which were likewise sweet in flavor. After a long time...
They ate much and mocked one another. Grapes ceased to grow, and then wild rice appeared; it grew spontaneously without being sown, free from husks or chaff, reaching a length of four finger-widths.
They harvested it morning and evening, and as soon as the stalks were cut, they grew back again. By morning and evening, the grain was already ripe.
Even though they harvested it repeatedly, it showed no sign of depletion. Sustaining themselves on this, they lived for a long time. At that time, they...
Because sentient beings possess impurities within their bodies due to solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), they develop two channels in order to expel them;

consequently, the male and female organs arise. Thereupon, they give rise to defiled attachment and thus draw near to one another, whereby they commit unrighteous acts. As for all other sentient beings...
When they saw this, they vied with one another to cast away dung, refuse, earth, and stones, refusing to dwell together and banishing them from their midst.
In the present day, when a girl is married off, people cast gold, silver, hemp, and beans; all of this originates from the ancient practice of casting away dung and soil.
Because those people of that time drove them out and banished them, those who delighted in committing evil subsequently gathered together.
They constructed dwellings to cover their bodies and committed unrighteous acts; this was the first time houses were established, and thus families came into being.
At that time, when evening fell or when morning dawned, the sentient beings would gather rice to eat because of hunger.

Every day they took enough rice so that nothing remained over. There was one being who, out of laziness, rose in the morning and took the rice for both the morning and the evening, bringing it along with him. When evening came, a companion called out to him to go together and take rice.
That person replied, "You go and take it yourself; I took rice in the morning and have already finished taking provisions for two meals. At that time, he...
Having heard these words, his companion praised them in his heart, saying, "This is also very good. When I go to gather [the rice], I shall bring back enough for two days' provisions.
In this way, they took turns emulating one another, gathering enough for two days, three days, seven days, and even for half a month or a full month;
thus, the amount gradually doubled from the previous quantity. Because of this greedy mind, it increased and grew ever more intense day by day.
Consequently, husks and impurities grew within the rice. At the time of the first harvest, it would not grow again; even when it did grow, its grain gradually deteriorated.
Thereupon, people vied with one another to gather and reap it. Because they accumulated it out of greed, the husks and impurities increased further, and the rice lost its vitality.
Once harvested, it would no longer sprout, though some remnants might remain. Seeing this, the people began to speak to one another...
He said, "Let us divide the boundaries of the land," and so they each divided it among themselves.

For this reason, the cultivation of fields in the world first began, and thus boundaries were established. At that time, one being, although he possessed his own field, privately stole another's grain, doing so repeatedly without ceasing.
They then brought him before the assembly and recounted the matter. He, in turn, spoke with resentment, saying, "It was for the sake of a little."
Because of this matter, he humiliated me before the assembly. For this reason, the great multitude gathered together and said to one another:
"We do not know which of these two persons is guilty. We wish to select from among the assembly a single being who is handsome in appearance."
Endowed with perfect physical characteristics and possessing penetrating wisdom, he was established as the Lord of the Fields (*kṣetrapati*).
He punished those who transgressed and nurtured those who were faultless. Regarding the fields sown by us, the multitude, each according to the law, gave him one-sixth of their produce.
At that time, from among the assembly, a person of complete virtue was selected and immediately established as the Lord of the Earth (*bhūmipati*). He then...
He governed according to the Dharma and nurtured the multitude of people. Once the population had grown large, they established him as their lord of the earth.
For this reason, there arose in the world the Kṣatriya royal lineage. At that time, a certain being thought to himself:
"All the family ties and worldly possessions in this world are like thorns, boils, and sores; it is now fitting to abandon them and enter the mountains to practice the Way in a place of stillness."
He reflected. Then he entered the mountains and meditated beneath a tree. Day after day he left the mountains to enter the village for alms.

When the villagers saw him, they honored and made offerings to him with increased reverence, and the multitude together praised him, saying: "This man is truly able to abandon his domestic burdens and enter the mountains to seek the Way.
Because he is able to distance himself from evil and unwholesome dharmas, guarding the Path and abiding in integrity, his conduct is pure and white. On account of this—
They are called *brāhmaṇas*. For this reason, there are *brāhmaṇa* castes in the world.
Among those beings, some practice various occupations, migrating and pursuing profit to sustain themselves;

because of this, there are *vaiśya* castes (*vaiśyas* being merchants) in the world. Furthermore, among those beings, some exert themselves in the fields and cultivate various arts to support their livelihood.
Thus, because of this, there are the Śūdra castes (the agricultural people) in the world. Due to these causes and conditions, there are four social classes, with the Kṣatriyas foremost.
They dwell together for a long time, for immeasurable years. When the lifespan decreases to eighty-four thousand years, the height of a human body is eight *zhang*.
After every hundred years, it decreases by one year [in lifespan]; thus it decreases until the lifespan is ten years, at which point the height of a human is [also reduced].
One foot. Again, after a hundred years have passed, it increases by one year. In this manner, it increases until it reaches eighty-four thousand years.
This single cycle of decrease and increase is called a *kṣudra-kalpa* (minor kalpa), totaling one million six hundred and eighty thousand years.
Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease constitute a *madhyama-kalpa* (intermediate kalpa), which amounts to thirty-three million six hundred thousand years. However, [there are] eight kalpas...

That has already passed. Now we are in the ninth *kalpa* of decrease (*apakarṣa-kalpa*). Human lifespan will be between sixty and seventy years, and human height will be six or seven feet (measured by the Zhou standard).
Thus they shall remain for a full twenty minor *kalpas*, at which point the time for the *saṃvarta-kalpa* (the kalpa of destruction) will arrive. First, there will be the calamity of fire.

Next comes the calamity of water, followed by three calamities of wind. In this manner, twenty minor kalpas of destruction pass, during which the mountains, rivers, the great earth, Mount Sumeru, and the Iron Ring Mountains are all ground to dust. Then, for another twenty minor kalpas of empty space, the kalpa of formation begins;
after further twenty kalpas have passed, the world is finally established. Thus it cycles again and again, with each eon proceeding inexhaustibly. (The Ābhāsvara Heaven...)

It is the second dhyāna heaven of the form realm (rūpadhātu). Because humans descended from the Brahmā Heaven, their speech is the Brahmā language and their script is the Brahmā script. Thereafter, as people moved according to their locations, their spoken sounds became diverse; now, it survives only in India (Tianzhu).
"Brahman" (婆羅門) is translated here as "Pure Conduct" (淨行), similar to the Confucians of this land.
In the Song dynasty, the scholar of Jingzhai, Liu Mi, wrote the *Sanjiao Pingxin Lun* (A Balanced Discourse on the Three Teachings), stating:
"Zhang Hengzhu did not believe in the doctrine of rebirth, asserting that the Buddha’s claim that consciousness undergoes death and transmigrates through rebirth was a failure of reflection.

This is precisely the view of Zhuangzi regarding 'resting oneself through death. His intention was that death is simply a state of rest, after which nothing further remains. This is quite different [from the Buddhist perspective].

If one does not realize that birth and death are boundless and that the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) never ceases—wherein beings within the four modes of birth and six realms receive retribution according to their karma—can it be said that there is no such thing as *saṃsāra*?

The *History of the Southern Dynasties* records that Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty dreamed of a monk with squinting eyes who entered the palace holding an incense burner, intending to take rebirth in the royal household.
Upon waking, a son was born to the ladies of the harem; from his youth, the boy suffered from eye disease, and medical treatments were administered.
He did not succeed; in the end, he became blind in one eye. This was Emperor Yuan.

The *Record of the Speeches and Deeds of Illustrious Ministers* records that before Fan Zuyu was born, his mother dreamed of a magnificent man standing beside her who said, "I am the Han General Deng Yu.
Upon waking, she gave birth to a son, and thus named him Zuyu. Because Deng Yu’s internal conduct was pure and complete, he was given the courtesy name Chunfu.
Based on this evidence, it is clear that the books of the Confucian school already contain the doctrine of saṃsāra.
To then claim that the Buddhist doctrine of saṃsāra is false is a failure of the utmost scrutiny.

Cheng Mingdao did not believe in the doctrine of hell, asserting that the Buddha devised this deceptive teaching for those of inferior capacity to frighten them into doing good. This is precisely what a petty person [would say].
To regard minor evils as harmless is a mistaken view. It implies that one may commit transgressions while alive, thinking, "Once dead, who will ever investigate or punish me?

Yet little do they realize that Heaven and Earth, along with the divine spirits, are manifest and arrayed everywhere; their rewarding of the good and punishing of the evil follows one like a shadow follows a form.
Can it be said, then, that there are no hells? The *Biographies of the Deeds and Words of Illustrious Ministers* records that Wang Jinggong’s son was named Pang.
His conduct was not virtuous; indeed, most of the matters in which Wang Jinggong acted contrary to principle and harmed the Way originated with Pang.
After Pang died, Wang Jinggong had a vision of him standing by the side of his gate wearing an iron cangue. Thereupon, he abandoned his residence.

Ban-shan is Zhong-shan Temple. It was established for the purpose of cultivating merit for the deceased. Judging by this evidence, it is clear that the Confucian classics already contain doctrines concerning hell.
To claim, therefore, that the Buddhist doctrine of hell does not exist—is this not a failure of reflection?
If one were to say that the doctrine of cause and effect is not to be trusted, then [the fact remains that] when one performs good deeds, a hundred blessings descend upon them.

Xiang said: "To perform unwholesome deeds brings down a hundred calamities; to accumulate goodness will surely result in abundant blessings, while to accumulate unwholesomeness will surely result in abundant calamity.
Confucianism certainly teaches people through the principle of cause and effect. How could it be said that its teachings are insufficient to practice?

To claim that violence is harmless—is this truly to understand the Way? If you say that the doctrine of ritual purity and purification is not worth adopting, then [you must] refrain from eating [forbidden things]."

Regarding "pungent foods" (hun): Confucius held them to be prohibited during the purification rites for sacrifices. As for the three days of intensive purification (*zhāi*), the *Liji* regards it as the virtue of clarity and purity.

It is clear that the Confucian school teaches people through such ritual purity; how could those who hang meat like forests and spend ten thousand coins daily on food be considered paragons of beauty?
If you claim that the precept against killing is not the way, then consider the prayer of King Tang.

The netting [of fish] and Zhao Jianzi’s release of living creatures were both acts of this same intent. When King Xuan of Qi could not bear to kill a single ox, Mencius called it a "method of benevolence" (*ren-shu*).
When the Duke of Song rescued the ants on the outskirts of his domain, the gentleman considered it a praiseworthy tale.

How has the Confucian school ever failed to regard the protection of life as a matter of supreme virtue? If one were to claim that the precept against drinking alcohol is not of this nature, then even the Great Yu...

King Tang’s abhorrence of fine wine and Emperor Guangwu’s abstention from drinking were both rooted in this principle. Intoxicating liquor that leads to disorder was the reason for the punishments meted out by the former kings;
drunken clamor at the banquet was the cause of the satirical critiques found in the *Shi*. How could the Confucian school ever have failed to regard excessive indulgence as the root of calamity?
If one were to say that the warning against theft is not a concern of the Confucian school— [the text here appears incomplete].
This is what is esteemed. It is as Yi Yin said: "If it is not the Way, and if it is not the Righteousness, one shall not take even a single straw from another.
And as Dongpo said: "Between heaven and earth, every thing has its own master; if it is not that which belongs to me..."
"Though it be but a single hair, one must not take it. What, then, is the meaning of this?
If you say that the teaching against false speech is not a priority for the Confucian school, then Sima Guang’s study of utmost sincerity would naturally begin with non-falsehood.

Furthermore, in his composition of the *Zizhi Tongjian*, he stated that Duke Xiao of Qin did not abolish the reward for moving the wooden pillars, and that Duke Wei of Qi did not go back on his word after the covenant at Cao Mo.
In that alliance, Duke Wen of Jin did not covet the profit of attacking Yuan. What, then, was his intention?

If one were to say that the precept against illicit lust is a mere fabrication, then consider that the praise for rectifying what is wrong and the censure of licentiousness are found in the odes of the *Shijing*;
thus, the Confucian school has never permitted people to engage in illicit lust. If one were to say that the doctrine of giving is a delusory claim, then consider [the case of] Ci...

Regarding poverty, one should provide relief for those who are destitute; this is recorded in the *Dai Li* (The Ceremonies of Dai). Thus, the Confucian tradition has never prohibited people from practicing almsgiving.

As for the claim that death entails eternal extinction and no further consciousness, the *Xici* (Appended Phrases) states: "The wandering soul undergoes transformation. The *Classic of Filial Piety* says:
"They are honored by ghosts. The *Zuo Zhuan* records: "Ghosts still seek food. And Zhang Suiyang said: "In death, I shall become... [a deity].
If one uses a fierce ghost to kill a thief, this implies that even after death, there certainly exists the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

If it were said that although there is consciousness after death, one no longer incurs retribution for sin, then it would contradict the *Book of Documents*, which says: "The Way of Heaven blesses the good and brings calamity to the licentious"; the *Book of Changes*, which says:
"The ghosts and spirits harm the full and bless the humble"; and the *Zuo Zhuan*, which says: "Should anyone change from this oath, the manifest deities shall strike them down. — *Zhuangzi*...

It is said: "If one does evil in the seclusion of darkness, ghosts will find and punish them. Thus, within the profound obscurity, there are indeed matters of rewarding the good and punishing the wicked.
In the world, there are those who expose the treacherous and uncover the hidden as if by divine power; they certainly do not allow the guilty to go free so as to foster villainy and evil.
How much more so when the weighing of merits and demerits, and the granting or withholding of judgment, are truly presided over by the divine spirit!
Indeed, those who are intelligent and upright cannot be obscured, nor can they be deceived.
They do not comply with the private sentiments of worldly people, nor do they fear the power and influence of the living. Thus, how could those who have committed offenses escape punishment?
The discourse on the hells has already been addressed previously. As for the transformation into animals after death, there are numerous instances recorded by the Confucianists.

The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: The Buddha told the elder Śāṇakavāsin, "Good son, there are four kinds of karma created by sentient beings.

Second is karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*): when one creates karma in this body, one receives it in the body immediately following.

Third is karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*): when one creates karma in this body but does not receive it in the next, but rather receives it from the second or third lifetime onward, this is called karma to be experienced in subsequent lives. third, that which is fixed in both retribution and time (because since the karma is fixed, the time of its maturation is also fixed); and fourth, that which is not fixed in either retribution or time (because since the karma is not determined, both the retribution and the time are also not fixed).

Furthermore, there is that which is "complete performance" after having acted, where both the action and the time are fixed. Furthermore, there is that which is "incomplete performance" after having acted.

Such is the correspondence between cause and effect. Yet the principle of karmic retribution is subtle; even those of penetrating insight remain dim-sighted regarding it, for it lies beyond the reach of discursive thought. To regard it otherwise is a false view.

This refers to the accumulation of immeasurable defilements and afflictions, whereby one undergoes the suffering of the cycle of birth and death.

Even by the supernatural power of a Buddha, one cannot prevent them from going, for their karmic force is fixed. Thus, when they perceive their parents in union at a place where there is a karmic connection—specifically at the moment of the "fire-light of desire"—they immediately enter the womb.

The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body then ceases, and seizing the semen and blood of the parents, it forms the subsequent physical aggregate known as *kalala*. This is the "flesh-ball" (*māṃsapiṇḍa*), which is the initial consciousness-mind; it is the name for the fusion of the parents' semen and blood with that mind. If they do not unite after seven days, the intermediate state being dies and is reborn again, waiting for a second week, a third week, and so on, up to seven weeks. Immediately, one is reborn among the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals. If the retribution for prior karma has already been fixed such that one is to be born in hell, as a ghost, or an animal, the intermediate state body (antarābhava) proceeds directly to that place of birth.

Just as with oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, and other such livestock, which have a specific time for gestation—if that time is not met—they will instead enter the womb of a mountain-dwelling ox, horse, pig, sheep, or similar creature. If they have already been born among humans or devas, through the power of this merit, their blessings and lifespans will both increase within those realms.

In these degenerate times, the vulgar do not understand the meaning of the "seven sevens" (the forty-nine-day period). If the blood flows out without ceasing, the male seed does not remain but flows out together with it. If [the blood] has been completely discharged, then—
The male seed returns to its original place, and only then does the embryo form. Thus, once the blood has ceased, the male seed can remain, and an embryo is immediately established.
The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: The Buddha told Nanda, "I shall preach to you the Sūtra on Entering the Mother’s Womb; you should listen attentively."
Nanda, although there is a mother’s womb, there are cases where one enters it and cases where one does not. How is birth received? As for entering the mother’s womb:

if the father and mother possess defiled minds and engage in sexual desire together, and the mother’s womb is pure, and her menstrual period has arrived, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) manifests—know that at such a time, it is called "entering the mother’s womb.
Within this, the form of the intermediate state has two types: first, those whose physical appearance is handsome...
Correct. Second, regarding the ugliness of appearance: the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of those in hell has an appearance as ugly as a charred stump.

The intermediate state of animals (*tiryagyoni*) is smoke-colored. The intermediate state of hungry ghosts (*preta*) is water-colored. The intermediate states of humans and devas have forms like the color of gold.

The intermediate states of those in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) have forms that are bright white. As for the heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is fundamentally no intermediate state.
Because they lack form, sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) may have two hands and two feet, or four feet, or many feet, or be footless;
the intermediate state they experience takes on a form corresponding to the place where they are to be reborn according to their prior karma. (As for the gods of the formless realm...)

Since there is no physical body, there is no intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). However, according to one's prior karma, in order to be reborn in whichever realm one is destined for, one experiences an intermediate existence that takes on the form of that destination; thus, "intermediate existence" is so called. (For example, *tiryag-yoni* refers to animals. If one is to be born in the intermediate existence of the heavens...
The head is directed upward; humans, ghosts, and animals travel horizontally, while those in the intermediate state of hell have their heads directed straight downward.
All beings in the intermediate state possess supernatural powers and travel through the air as if by means of the divine eye, observing their place of rebirth from afar.
Regarding the phrase "the arrival of the menstrual period," this refers to the time of conception.

Nanda, there are some women whose menses arrive after three days, or five days, or half a month, or even a full month; some must wait for specific conditions before their menses finally arrive after a long duration.
Furthermore, if a woman lacks physical vitality, undergoes much hardship, has an unattractive appearance, or lacks wholesome food and drink, her menses may [not arrive as expected].
"Come, it shall quickly cease. It is just as when water is sprinkled upon dry ground; it dries up immediately.
If there is a woman who possesses physical power, constantly enjoys peace and happiness, has a beautiful appearance, and receives excellent food and drink, her menstrual flow will not cease quickly.
It is just as when water is sprinkled upon moist ground; it is difficult for it to dry. Why is this so?"

Entry [into the womb] occurs as follows: if the father’s semen is emitted but the mother’s is not, or if the mother’s semen is emitted but the father’s is not, or if neither is emitted, entry into the womb does not occur.
If the mother is impure while the father is pure, or if the father is impure while the mother is pure, or if both are impure, conception likewise does not take place.
Furthermore, if the mother’s reproductive organ is afflicted by wind-disorders (*vāta*), or by jaundice, phlegm, or other such ailments, [conception does not occur].
There may be those with blood-gas fetal knots; or those with fleshy growths; or those who have taken certain medicines; or those with the "barley-belly" disease or the "ant-waist" disease;

or those whose birth canal is like the mouth of a camel; or whose interior is like a multi-rooted tree, or like the head of a plow, or like a wagon-pole, or like a climbing vine, or like tree leaves, or like barley awns; or those whose abdomen is deep below, or those whose [abdomen] is above.
It may be deep; or it may not be a suitable vessel for the womb; or blood may flow constantly from it; or it may be like the mouth of a crow, perpetually agape and never closing;
or its upper and lower parts, or its four sides, may be uneven in width; or it may be high in some places and low in others, or undulating; or it may contain worms that devour the fetus.
It is putrid and impure. If the mother possesses such defects, conception does not occur.

Or, if the parents are noble while the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is lowly, or if the intermediate state being is noble while the parents are lowly—in such cases as these, conception is likewise not achieved.
If both the parents and the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) are noble, yet their karma does not coincide, the conception of an embryo will not occur.
If the intermediate state being lacks the two-fold passion for male and female toward the prospective realm, it will likewise not undergo rebirth.

Nanda, how does the intermediate state being enter the mother’s womb? If the mother’s womb is pure and the intermediate state being appears before it, seeing [the parents] engaged in sexual union, [it enters]. If not...
As explained above, there are many faults and afflictions. Only when there is karma of mutual affinity between the parents and the child does one enter the mother’s womb.

Furthermore, when that intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) is about to enter the womb, its mind becomes inverted: if it is male, it conceives desire for the mother and aversion toward the father;
if it is female, it conceives desire for the father and aversion toward the mother. This occurs regarding what was created in a past life.
Due to various karmas, they give rise to deluded thoughts and form erroneous perceptions, conceiving notions of coldness, great winds, heavy rains, and clouds and mists;

or they hear the clamor of a great multitude. Having formed these conceptions, according to the superiority or inferiority of their karma, they further give rise to ten kinds of false and illusory thoughts.
What are these ten? "I am now entering a house," "I wish to ascend a tower," "I am mounting a terrace or palace."

"Nanda, at that time, the intermediate state being, having formed these thoughts—'I am ascending a bed,' 'I am entering a grass hut,' 'I am entering a leaf shed,' 'I am entering a thicket of grass,' 'I am entering a forest,' 'I am entering a hole in a wall,' or 'I am entering between the fence-posts'—immediately enters the mother's womb.
You should know that what is called the *kalala* consists of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood, and nothing else; it arises from the father..."
The union of the mother’s semen and blood serves as the object-condition for consciousness, upon which it depends and abides.
Just as when one relies on curd, a vessel, a churning stick, and the continuous application of human effort, butter can be produced, whereas it would not arise otherwise;
you should know that the kalala body formed from the impure semen and blood of the parents is likewise so. Furthermore, Nanda, there are four similes for you—
Listen well. Just as when relying on green grass, insects are able to arise; the grass is not the insect, yet the insect does not exist apart from the grass.
Nevertheless, through the conjunction of causes and conditions based upon the grass, the insect is able to arise, its body appearing blue.

Nanda, you should know that the *kalala* body formed from the father’s semen and the mother’s blood is also like this: through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise as roots. It is just so.

Worms arise depending on cow dung; the dung is not the worm, yet the worm does not exist apart from the dung. Nevertheless, through the harmony of causes and conditions based upon the dung, the worm is born, its body becoming yellow.
Nanda, you should know that the *kalala* body formed from the father’s semen and the mother’s blood is likewise so:

through the harmony of causes and conditions, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*) arise. It is like a worm arising depending on a jujube fruit; the jujube fruit is not...
This worm does not exist apart from the jujube fruit; rather, it arises only through the conjunction of causes and conditions based upon that jujube.
Its body is red in color. Nanda, you should know that the *kalala* body formed from the father’s semen and the mother’s blood is also like this:

through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise as its roots, just as a worm arises based on curd and its body becomes white in color. [The same applies] in detail, even unto... the cause.

Through the conjunction of conditions, the great elements arise from the root. Furthermore, depending upon the impurity of the parents—the *kalala*—the earth element manifests, having solidity as its nature;
the water element manifests, having moisture as its nature; the fire element manifests, having warmth as its nature;
and the wind element manifests, having lightness and motion as its nature. Nanda, if there is the impurity of the parents—the *kalala*—...
Body. If there were only the earth element and no water element, it would immediately dry up and completely disintegrate, just like a handful of dry flour or ash.
If there were only the water element and no earth element, it would immediately scatter and dissolve, like a drop of oil on water.
By means of the water element, the earth element does not disperse; by means of the earth element, the water element does not flow. Nanda, Kaṭa...
In the *kalala* stage of the body, if there is the earth element and the water element but no fire element, it will rot and decay.

For example, Nanda, like a lump of flesh kept in the shade during the summer months. In the *kalala* stage of the body, if there is only the earth, water, and fire elements but no wind element, it will be unable to grow and expand.
All of these are caused by prior karma as the primary cause, acting together with one another as conditions.
Through mutual attraction and response, consciousness is able to arise. The earth element is able to support; the water element is able to cohere; the fire element is able to mature;

and the wind element is able to expand. Nanda, it is further like a person or his disciple who, having refined sugar, blows upon it with their breath to cause it to increase in volume while remaining hollow within, like the core of a lotus root. Within the body, there are likewise the great elements of earth, water, and fire.
The wind and the growth through the power of karma are also like this. Nanda, it is not from the impurities of the parents that the *kalala* body arises;
nor is it from the mother’s womb alone, nor is it from karma alone. It is neither cause nor condition by itself;
only when these various conditions come together does the embryo first come to be. It is like a fresh seed that has not been damaged by wind or sun, being firm and solid.

A hole. When the storage and planting are appropriate, and it is sown in fertile soil that is well-moistened, then through the convergence of these causes and conditions, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will arise and grow in succession. Nanda, you should know this:
the sprout and the rest do not come into being apart from the convergence of conditions. It is not produced by the parents alone, nor by karma alone, nor by other conditions alone.
Conception occurs only through the causal condition of the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood; it is only then that there is an embryo, Nanda.

Just as a person with clear vision, seeking fire, places a sun-crystal gem in the sunlight and sets dry cow dung upon it, whereupon fire is produced—so too should it be understood that [conception] occurs by virtue of the union of the causal conditions of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood.

Only then does there arise birth from a womb. From the impurities of the father and mother, the *kalala* is formed; this is designated as "form" (*rūpa*). Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) constitute its "name" (*nāma*);
these together are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). (Name refers to the mind—namely feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; form refers to the body.

This aggregation of the aggregates, this loathsome name-and-form, which takes rebirth in the various realms of existence—even for a mere fraction of a moment—I do not praise. Why? Because it is birth.

Within all states of existence, this constitutes great suffering. Just as even a small amount of excrement is foul-smelling, so too should it be understood that birth within any state of existence is called suffering, even in its slightest form.
These five aggregates of clinging—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all possess arising and abiding.
Growth, as well as decline and decay—birth itself is suffering, staying [in the womb] is sickness, and growth, decline, and decay are old age and death.
Therefore, Nanda, out of a craving for the flavors of existence within the ocean of becoming, you lay within your mother’s womb and undergo such intense suffering.
Furthermore, Nanda, you should know this: generally speaking, there are three types of those who enter the womb.
The eighteenth week: during the first week, the embryo resides in the mother’s womb like a wedge or an abscess, lying amidst filth as if within a cauldron.
The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) dwell together in one place, scorched by a fierce fever and undergoing extreme suffering.

It is named *kalala*, appearing like rice gruel or curdled milk. Within seven days, it is boiled and cooked by internal heat, and only then do the solid nature of the earth element, the moist nature of the water element, the warm nature of the fire element, and the mobile nature of the wind element manifest.
(From the twenty-second week until the thirty-seventh week, each has its own wind, as well as the positions, forms, and names within the womb; these details are numerous and not recorded here.
Nanda, during the thirty-eighth week, there arises within the mother’s womb a wind called *Nīlotpala*.
This wind causes the fetus to turn head-downward, stretch out both arms, and move toward the birth canal. Next, there is another wind called *Adhogama* (Going Downward), by which—
Due to the power of karma, the wind blows the fetus downward, causing the head to face down and the two feet to point upward as it approaches the birth canal.

Nanda, if that fetus, in a previous life, had committed various evil deeds or caused the destruction of human embryos, by reason of these causes and conditions, when it is about to emerge, its hands and feet will be crossed and disordered;
unable to turn or shift its position, it will lose its life within the mother’s womb.
In the end, because of this, the mother experiences dissatisfaction and extreme, agonizing suffering;
she dies as a result, or even if she survives, it is no different from death. Nanda, if that embryo is the result of wholesome karma, even if it is positioned inversely, it will not harm the mother;
it will emerge safely and without experiencing such suffering. Nanda, in ordinary cases, there is no such calamity.
When the thirty-eighth week arrives and she is about to give birth, the mother undergoes great suffering; her very nature is nearly extinguished before she can finally emerge from the womb.
Nanda, you should observe this carefully and seek liberation. Nanda, for any being born from a womb, it is a state of extreme pain and distress.
At the moment of birth, whether male or female, the infant falls into human hands or is wrapped in cloth and placed [upon them].

Whether in the sunlight, or in a shaded place, or placed in a cradle, or situated on a bed or mat, or within the embrace of one's arms—for these reasons, they all experience stinging pain, bitter agony, and extreme suffering.
Nanda, it is like a flayed cow standing near a wall and being eaten by the insects of the wall;
or if it stays near trees or grass, it is eaten by the insects of the trees and grass; or if it dwells in an open space, various insects [devour it].
They are devoured and all undergo suffering and affliction. It is the same at birth:

they are washed with warm water and experience great suffering and affliction, like a leper whose skin is溃烂 (ulcerated) and from whom pus and blood flow profusely, further subjected to the lash of whips and clubs, undergoing extreme agony.
After being born, they drink the dregs of their mother’s blood and thereby grow large; by "dregs of blood," Nanda, it is meant her breast milk. Nanda.
Since there is such boundless and extreme suffering, not a single thing therein is worth delighting in.

What wise person would give rise to attachment for this ocean of suffering, wherein they are constantly transmigrating without rest? (The details are as found in the Vinaya texts; if one wishes to know them extensively, one should consult that Vinaya.)
In the Sanskrit language, *Nanda*; here it is translated as "Joy" (the Buddha’s own younger brother).
The *Old Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables* states: Formerly, Śākyamuni Buddha went to the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, to preach the sutras for his mother.
At that time, there was a deva whose lifespan was nearing its end; seven signs were about to manifest: first, light from the nape of his neck...
1. His body withers; 2. the floral ornaments upon his head fade; 3. his facial complexion changes; 4. dust settles upon his robes; 5.
sweat breaks out from beneath his arms; 6. his physical form becomes emaciated; 7. he leaves his seat. Thereupon, he reflects within himself.

After his life ended, he was to abandon the pleasures of heaven and descend to be born in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, where he would become a son within the womb of a sow afflicted with scabies and leprosy.
He was filled with great anxiety and distress, not knowing what means he might find to escape this retribution. Then a deity spoke to him:
Now the Buddha is here preaching the sutra for his mother. The Buddha is the savior of all beings throughout the three periods of time;

only the Buddha can deliver you from your grave transgressions. Why do you not go to take refuge? Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, she prostrated herself in worship. Before she had even had the opportunity to ask a question, the Buddha spoke.
The Buddha told the devaputra: "All things in the universe ultimately return to impermanence; this is something you have long known. Why, then, do you grieve?
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "Although I know that celestial blessings cannot be maintained for long, I regret that upon leaving this seat, I shall fall into the womb of a pig."

He regarded this as poison; though he had received a body in the human realm, he did not dare to act out of fear. The Buddha said, "If you wish to escape this pig's body, you should take the three refuges, saying:
'Namo Buddha, Namo Dharma, Namo Bhikṣusaṃgha. Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, take refuge in the Bhikṣusaṃgha.
Thus, following the Buddha’s teaching, the pig took the refuges three times each day and night.
Seven days later, his life span ended by the decree of fate, and he arrived in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, where he became the son of an elder.

While still in his mother’s womb, he took refuge [in the Triple Gem] three times daily; upon being born and falling to the ground, he likewise knelt and took refuge. When his mother gave birth, there was no foul discharge.
The mother’s attendant maidservant, terrified, abandoned him and fled. The mother, too, was deeply perplexed that her child had fallen to the ground and spoken;
she regarded it as an omen of ill fortune and intended to kill him. She then reflected to herself: "I have few children; if I were to kill this son, my husband would surely punish me."
He immediately said to the elder, "Stop, stop! This child is no ordinary person. Though a man may live a hundred years, he may still not understand self-refuge;
yet this child, upon being born, was able to call himself a Buddha. You should raise him with care and not allow him to be treated with contempt.
The child then grew up, and at the age of seven, while playing with his peers by the side of the road, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana happened to pass by.
The child approached. The child said, "I am the Śramaṇa. Śāriputra and the others were astonished that a small child could pay homage to a bhikṣu.
The child said, "Does the ascetic not recognize me? When the Buddha was preaching the sūtra for his mother in the heavens, I was then a deva;
later, I fell to become a pig, where I received instruction from the Buddha and took the Three Refuges. Now I have obtained a human body. Śāriputra immediately entered [samādhi].

Through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he perceived this through contemplation and immediately offered a prayer of blessing. He then invited the Buddha and the Sangha, and after the offerings were completed, the Buddha preached the Dharma for them.

At that moment, the parents, their son, and all their internal and external kinsmen attained the stage of *avaivartika* (this is translated as "non-retrogression," meaning the stage of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva). This is the merit of taking refuge. (Kauśāmbī is the same as the kingdom of Kuśinagara; Vaiśālī is the same as Viśalā.)
[These regions] are all within the borders of Central India).
The *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* and the *Paritappa-sūtra* state: At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder whose wealth and treasures were beyond counting.
He had an only son, twenty years of age, who had recently married. Not even seven days had passed since the couple...
They respected one another. Desiring to go to the rear garden during the third month of spring, they went to play within the park. There was a pear tree there, tall and large with beautiful blossoms.

The wife wished to have some flowers, but as there was no one to pluck them for her, her husband climbed the tree. He reached even the smallest branch, which then snapped, causing him to fall and die.
The members of the household, both old and young, rushed to where their son lay; they cried out to heaven and wailed. Among those who heard this, there was none whose heart was not moved by grief.
The child was encoffined and returned home; the family’s weeping did not cease. The World-Honored One, pitying their ignorance, went to inquire after them.
When the elder’s household, both great and small, saw the Buddha, they were moved by grief and paid him homage. The Buddha said to the elder, "Cease your weeping and listen to the Dharma.
All things are impermanent and cannot be preserved for long. Where there is birth, there is death; sin and merit follow one another. This child has three sets of parents."
At that time, they wept and wailed, their grief overwhelming them as they wondered, "In the end, whose son was he? Who was his kinsman?
The Elder Forgetting-Grief knelt before the Buddha and said, "What sins did this child commit in his past lives that his flourishing and beautiful life should thus come to an untimely end?"
"I only pray that you will explain this. The Buddha told the householder: "In the distant past, there was a young boy who entered a sacred tree with a bow and arrows to play.
There were three other people nearby watching him as well. A sparrow was perched in the tree, and the boy wished to shoot it."
The three men urged him, saying, "If you can hit the sparrow, you are a hero of this world. The boy was delighted at heart; he drew his bow and shot it, and the sparrow died immediately.
The three men laughed together and rejoiced with him, then each went their separate way. Thus he passed through birth and death.
Throughout many kalpas, wherever they met, these three individuals suffered together in retribution for their sins. Among them, one possessed merit and now dwells in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
another was born in the ocean as a nāga king born by transformation; and the third is this present elder.
As for the young child, he was previously born in heaven as the son of a deva; having fallen from a tree and ended his life there, he was immediately reborn in the ocean.
He was born as the son of a dragon king, and on the very day of his birth, the King of the Golden-Winged Birds (Garuḍa) seized him to devour him.
Today, in these three places, his distress and weeping are beyond words. Because he had assisted others in their joy in past lives, these three people now receive this retribution of anguish.
As for the young boy, because in his previous life he delighted in giving and respected others, he has been born into a wealthy family.

He delighted in hunting and harming living beings; therefore, his life was short. When the elder attained understanding, both the great and the small rejoiced, and all attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (this is translated as "entering the stream," meaning one who has entered the stream of the noble path, i.e., a person of the fruit).

The Vinaya states: Once, while the Tathāgata was sitting in a grove with the bhikṣus, a monkey came down from a tree, took the Buddha’s bowl, climbed up, filled it with honey, and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha did not accept it. The monkey immediately understood the Buddha’s intention;
he carried the bowl to the water’s edge, sprinkled water upon it to purify it, and presented it to the Buddha. The Buddha then accepted it and instructed Ānanda...
He distributed it among the community of monks. The monkey was filled with joy; he leaped and danced about, fell into a pit, and died.

He was reborn into the household of the elder Śreṣṭhin Sārthavāha, with a handsome and upright appearance. He left the household life and realized arhatship, becoming known as Madhuvāsika (translated here as "The Elder Who Offered Honey").
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*) and the *Sūtra on Requiting Kindness* (*Bà'énjīng*) state:

In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a young bhikṣu who saw an elderly bhikṣu who constantly delighted in chanting. Although the elder’s voice was dull and muffled, the youth considered his own voice excellent and said, "Your voice now is like the barking of a dog.
At that time, the old bhikṣu asked him, "Do you know me? I have now already attained arhatship..."
Upon hearing this, Han Dao was filled with terror and self-reproach; he immediately confessed his transgression before the elder bhikṣu, who granted him absolution for his error.
Although he was spared from falling into hell, because of those evil words, he underwent five hundred lifetimes constantly taking birth as a dog.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants who, accompanied by a white dog, traveled together to another country. While resting midway on their journey, the dog stole some meat.
The merchants cut off the dog's four legs, threw it into a pit, and departed.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing from afar with his divine eye the dog’s body convulsing on the ground, emaciated by hunger and on the verge of death, immediately took his alms-bowl and food.
He flew to where the dog was and, with a heart of compassion, gave the dog food, thereby saving its remaining life. Once the dog had eaten, he rejoiced and further preached the Dharma for it.
Seven days later, the dog’s life ended, and it was reborn in the house of a brāhmaṇa in Śrāvastī. His name was Kuṇḍika.
When he reached the age of seven, Śāriputra transformed him, leading him to leave the household life. Śāriputra preached the sublime Dharma for him, and he immediately realized arhatship.

Having fully attained the six supernormal powers, he beheld his own previous existence as that of a starving dog. Having received the grace of his teacher Śāriputra, he has now obtained a human body and attained the fruits of the Path.
He thought to himself: "I shall serve my teacher with all that is required for his needs for the remainder of my life, remaining forever a śrāmaṇera."

He did not receive the full precepts because he had previously left the household life while maintaining pure discipline; thus, having now encountered Śākyamuni Tathāgata, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
The *Dugou jing* (Sutra on Saving the Dog) says: Long ago, there was a śramaṇa who saw a butcher holding a puppy, intending to take it back and kill it.
The śramaṇa said to him, "The sin of killing living beings is most unwholesome.

I pray that you will trade this dog’s life for the food in my bowl, so that its life may be spared and you may obtain immeasurable merit. Despite his earnest and repeated exhortations, the butcher would not consent.
Following the words, the śramaṇa immediately fed the puppy with rice, stroked it with his hand, and offered prayers of blessing. Weeping, he said:
"By what transgression did you come to this state, obtaining this canine body, lacking self-mastery, and being killed and eaten by others?

I pray that in every lifetime your sins may be extinguished and merit may arise, so that you may leave this canine body behind, be born as a human, and encounter the Three Jewels. Thus the puppy was [granted]...
As he ate, a virtuous mind immediately arose within him; he leaped for joy and, knowing he had found refuge, felt great delight.

The butcher led him back to slaughter and eat him, but when the dog’s life ended, he was reborn into the family of a great elder. At that time, a śramaṇa went begging for food and arrived at the elder’s gate.

The son saw him and, filled with joy, prostrated at his feet and offered him food of a hundred flavors. He then followed him into the monastic life, deeply understood the meaning of the sūtras, and soon attained the three [knowledges].

They shall attain non-retrogression and transform all beings, causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta. If even animals can thus attain the Way, how much more so for humans—how could they fail to obtain the fruit?
In India, on the shores of the South Sea, there was a withered tree. Within it lived five hundred bats, making their home in its hollows. A caravan of merchants halted beneath this tree;
as the weather turned cold and windy, everyone was suffering from hunger and frost. They gathered firewood and clarified butter (*ghṛta*), piling them beneath the tree and kindling a fire.
As the smoke and flames gradually grew fierce, the withered tree caught fire. At that time, among the merchants, there was one trader who, during the night—

After the distribution was finished, they recited the Abhidharma Piṭaka. Although those bats were distressed by the fire, out of their love for the sound of the Dharma, they endured it and did not emerge.

When their lives ended there, they took rebirth according to their karma; all of them obtained human bodies, left home to practice and study, and—driven by the sound of the Dharma they had heard—became intelligent and sharp-witted, collectively realizing the fruits of sainthood and becoming fields of merit for the world. They lived near Kaṇiṣka...
King Kaniṣka and the Venerable Pārśva convened five hundred sages in the kingdom of Kaśmīra to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
These were all, as it were, five hundred bats among withered trees. (From the *Xiyu ji*: "Nanhai" refers to the coast of South India;

the kingdom of Kaśmīra is a kingdom of North India. The *Abhidharma-piṭaka* refers to the great *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra-piṭaka*. In the south, bats are called 'flying rats'. Even the common people of today do not yet believe in humans.)

They die to become six kinds of domestic animals; how much more so those who possess faith among the wriggling and sentient beings! Little do they realize that these wriggling and sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-nature. Because their evil karma is heavy, they gradually become dull and ignorant until their forms become minute.

If their karmic retribution gradually diminishes, they gradually become sentient and grow larger until they regain a human body. This is why our Śākyamuni Tathāgata, throughout many kalpas in the past, was once a deer, a goose, a swan, a fish, a turtle, a louse, and so forth. Thus, the Buddha frequently recounted to his disciples the deeds he performed in his various previous lives.
The tenth patriarch, the Venerable Pārśva, appeared five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the reign of King Zhengding of the Zhou dynasty.
Yáng Yòu (courtesy name Shūzǐ), the Grand Tutor of Tàishān in the Jìn dynasty, was a renowned minister of the Western Jìn whose reputation surpassed that of all within the realm.
When he was five years old, his wet nurse was once asked to retrieve a finger-ring he had previously played with. The wet nurse replied, "You originally did not have this."
"What did you take it? Huìyù replied, "I was playing by the eastern wall in the past, and it fell into the midst of a mulberry tree.

My wet nurse said, 'You must find it yourself. Huìyù said, 'This is not my former residence; the child does not know where it is. Later, while he was wandering and looking about after going out the gate, he walked straight toward the east.
His wet nurse followed him until they reached the house of the Li family. There, he entered and found it beneath a tree at the eastern wall."

"Little Huan. Li Shi said with shock and regret, "My son once possessed this ring and used to fondle it. He died suddenly at the age of seven, and after his death, I knew nothing of where the ring was.
This is the property of my deceased child; why do you take it away? Xu You held the ring and ran off. Li Shi then questioned him.
Once the wet nurse had related Xu You’s words, Li Shi was filled with both grief and joy, and she immediately sought to find Xu You.
He returned to being his son's father; only after the villagers offered explanations and persuasion did he desist. When Sengyou grew up, he constantly suffered from a head ailment.
A physician wished to treat it with aggressive measures, but Sengyou said, "When I was three days old, my head was facing north toward the door.

I felt a wind blowing against the crown of my head and suspected this would cause me trouble, though I could not yet speak. Since the source of the illness is so ancient, it cannot be cured. Later, Sengyou served as the governor of Jingzhou.

As Governor-General, he was stationed at Xiangyang. He provided the Wudang Monastery with extensive resources, far exceeding those given to other monasteries. When someone asked him the reason for this, Sengyou remained silent.

Later, during a session of repentance, as he recounted the workings of cause and effect, he said: "In my previous life, I incurred various transgressions. It was by virtue of building this monastery that I was able to receive salvation.
This is why my feelings of devotion toward making offerings have been so exceptionally profound. (By mentioning his "previous life," it is implied that this refers to more than just one lifetime.)

Furthermore, unless one has attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), how could one know the events of many lifetimes? Those who have come from the human realm and obtained a human body may be able to remember the events of their previous births; however, those who have come from other realms are unable to remember them.
This is what is meant by the statement that "one cannot return to restore the original verification."

Wang Lian of Langya, courtesy name Xuānmíng, was a *shìzhōng* (Grand Master for Attendant) under the Song dynasty. His father, Wáng Mǐn, courtesy name Jìyán, had been the *Zhōngshū lǐng* (Director of the Imperial Secretariat) under the Jìn dynasty.

He was acquainted with a certain foreign *śramaṇa*, whom he admired for his dignified bearing; every time he beheld Mǐn’s refined presence, he felt profound respect and joy, and would frequently say to his fellow students: [He was like this...]
"If in a future life I may become the son of such a person as this, my immediate wish would be fulfilled.
When Min heard this, he teased him, saying, "The Master’s conduct and talent are such that you could only be the son of a disciple. Shortly thereafter, the śramaṇa fell ill and passed away.
More than a year after his death, Lian was born. As soon as he was able to speak, he understood foreign languages and the wonders of distant lands.

Rare were the silver vessels, pearls, and shells he encountered—things he had never seen in his life and whose very names he had not heard. He immediately gave them names and identified their origins.
Naturally, he received offerings from various Brahmans that surpassed those of the Han people; they all addressed him as "Śramaṇa.
Having examined his former lives, [the Emperor] bestowed upon him the title "Ālán" (A-lien). Consequently, this became his great name, and so forth.
