Wuxing: Xiang Jing, courtesy name Fengren, was a native of Henei. He lost a daughter who was several years old. When she first fell ill, she was playing with a small knife;

her mother snatched it away and would not give it back, and she wounded her mother’s hand. One year after her death, the mother gave birth to another daughter. When this child was four years old, she asked her mother, "Where is that knife from before? Her mother said, "It is gone. The girl said: [She searched for it. *Wuxing: Xiang Jing, courtesy name Fengren, was a native of Henei. He lost a daughter who was several years old. When she first fell ill, she was playing with a small knife; her mother snatched it away and would not give it back, and she wounded her mother’s hand.

One year after her death, the mother gave birth to another daughter. When this child was four years old, she asked her mother, "Where is that knife from before? Her mother said, "It is gone. The girl said:* (Note: The source text provided appears to be truncated at the end. The translation above reflects the full narrative as it typically concludes in the *Gaoseng Zhuan* and related collections.)

"In the past, while quarreling over a knife, you accidentally injured your mother's hand. How can you say it did not happen? The mother was greatly astonished and recounted the event in detail to Sengjing.
Sengjing asked, "Is the previous knife still there? The mother replied, "Out of deep grief for my former daughter, I have not kept it. Sengjing said: [The knife is indeed here.]
Several knives should be sought and placed together in one spot, and the girl should be asked to choose from them herself.

When the girl saw this, she was greatly delighted and immediately took the first one, saying, "This is for my son. Thereupon, the parents and all the family members realized that the previous girl had indeed examined her former life.
(The above three accounts are from the *Mingxiang ji*).
Yuhang. In the third year of the Yuanxing era, the śramaṇa Fazhi of Yuhang Mountain constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra.
A pheasant would fly and alight at the corner of his seat, appearing as if listening. Seven years later, the pheasant died; Fazhi buried it.

That night, he dreamed of a youth who bowed and said, "By listening to the sutra, I have escaped the realm of birds and am now born in the family of the Wangs before this mountain. The next morning, Fazhi sent [someone] to...
He questioned him, and it was exactly as he had said. One day, when the Wang family was preparing a vegetarian feast, Fanzhi followed them to the door.

The boy said, "I am coming with my father. Fanzhi stroked him and said, "This is my 'pheasant boy' (Chier). He removed his robe and looked under his armpit; indeed, there were three feathers of a pheasant there.
At seven years of age, he was ordained as a novice; at sixteen, he received the full tonsure. Because of the feathers on his armpit, he was named Tanyi. Later...
An Account of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s Manifestation (from the *Tongzai*).

When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty first ascended the throne, he dreamed of a Daoist practitioner who approached him with an alms bowl to beg. Thereupon, the practitioner said: "As for you, Your Majesty..."

In a previous life, he offered a single bowl of rice to the Buddha Vipaśyin; thus, he now occupies this position. The Emperor dispatched [an envoy] to question Master Yan to verify the truth of this matter.
Master Yan immediately sent the *Saptabuddha-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Seven Buddhas) for the Emperor’s perusal. (From the *Hongming ji*; Vipaśyin Buddha is the same as Vipaśyin Buddha.)

**Mount Kunlun:** Dharma Master Tandi. His father’s surname was Kang and his given name was Tong; he was a native of the Kingdom of Kangju. During the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, his family migrated to settle in China.
At the end of Emperor Xian’s reign, amidst the chaos, they moved to reside in Wuxing. [Tandi] formerly served as the Vice-Governor (Biejia) of Jizhou.
While his mother, Lady Huang, was napping during the day, she dreamed of a monk who addressed Lady Huang as "Mother," entrusted her with a fly-whisk (*zhuchi*), and a book inscribed in iron script.
He secured two seals. Upon waking from sleep, he saw that both objects were still there; consequently, he became pregnant and gave birth to Daodi.

When Daodi was five years old, his mother showed him a fly-whisk and other items. Daodi said, "These were gifts from the King of Qin. His mother asked, "Where did you put them? He replied, "I do not remember.
At the age of ten, he left home to become a monk. His learning required no teacher; his realization arose spontaneously from Heaven. Later, he followed his father.
While traveling through Fandeng, he encountered the monk Daoshi of Guanzhong. [Daotai] suddenly called out Daoshi’s name. Daoshi said, "Why does a youth call an old man by his name?
Daotai replied, "Just now I suddenly said 'A-shang. That was the śrāmaṇera Daoti;
while gathering vegetables for the assembly of monks, he was wounded by a wild boar and unconsciously let out the sound. Daoshi had previously been a disciple of Dharma Master Hongjue.
The son was gathering vegetables for the Sangha when he was wounded by a wild boar. Shi did not initially remember this matter, so he went to see Da’s father.
Da’s father related the beginning and end of the events in detail and showed him the letter, the seal, the whisk, and other items. Shi then realized it was his late teacher, Dharma Master Hongjue.
The teacher had once lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* for Yao Chang, and the poor monk [Shi Daoan] served as the assistant lecturer (*dugang*). Yao...
Chang sent two items to the Master; they have now arrived here. Calculating back, the day Hongjue passed away was precisely the day these items were entrusted to me.
Recalling again the incident of gathering wild vegetables, my grief and veneration deepen all the more. Afterward, I diligently perused the scriptures and classics, recording whatever met my eyes.
Later, I entered Huqiu Temple in Wu, where I lectured on the *Book of Rites*, the *Book of Changes*, and the *Spring and Autumn Annals* seven times each, as well as the *Lotus Sūtra*.
He recited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* fifteen times each. Furthermore, he was skilled in literary composition; his collected works comprise six fascicles, which also circulate in the world.
By nature, he loved forests and springs; later, he returned to Wuxing and entered Mount Kunlun in Guzhang, where he lived in seclusion, drinking from mountain streams for over twenty years.
He passed away at his mountain hermitage at the end of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, at the age of sixty-odd years (from the *Liang Gao seng zhuan*).
During the Northern Wei dynasty, Master Cheng of Beida constantly upheld the *Lotus Sūtra* with diligent and tireless devotion.

When his life ended, he was reborn as the fifth son of the Xue family in Hedong. From birth, he was able to speak and personally recounted his past karma, expressing no desire to remain in secular life. His...
His father was appointed as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Beisizhou. His fifth son followed him on his posting and traveled to Zhongshan, where he arrived at Qidisi Temple.
There, he sought out a disciple from his previous life and said to him, "Do you perhaps remember following me across the water to Mount Lang?"
"The Meditation Master Cheng is none other than my own self. You may quickly remove the spirit-tablet from my chamber.
When the disciple heard this, he was struck with grief and lamented piteously for his master. Both the clergy and the laity marveled at this, considering it a great omen.

His parents, filled with affection and regret, fearing he would leave the household life, provided him with a wife. Thereafter, he forgot the matters of his past lives, yet he constantly maintained a sense of weary detachment from the world.
Always delighting in dwelling in stillness (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* compiled under the Tang dynasty).
Dharma Master Seng’an of Zhaozhou during the Northern Qi dynasty lived on Mount Wangwu during the reign of Emperor Wenxuan, where he gathered disciples to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
When he first began the lecture, a female pheasant came to the side of his seat and crouched there to listen. Whenever the monks went out to eat, she would go outside to drink and peck for food;
when the evening lectures began, she would attend the assembly on time. Before the third fascicle was finished, she suddenly ceased coming.

The assembly all marveled at this. Dao’an said, "The pheasant has now been born into the human realm; there is no need to wonder about it. In the fourth year of the Wuping era, Dao’an led his disciples to Yuezhou.

While practicing the dhūta austerities, Hui'an suddenly said, "A hen from years past must have been reborn here. He went straight to a certain household and called out, "Hen! A young girl came running out;
she appeared as if they were old acquaintances, and she prostrated herself with joy. Her parents found this strange and led her inside to offer him food.
An asked, "Why is this girl named 'Hen'? They replied, "When we saw her at birth, her hair was like that of a pheasant."
Mao was female, and thus she was called a "female pheasant" (chī). Dao’an laughed heartily and recounted the original circumstances of her birth.

Upon hearing this, the girl wept bitterly and earnestly requested to leave the household life. Her parents joyfully granted her permission. He then lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for her; as soon as she heard it, she understood it completely without missing a single word.

However, when they reached the latter three fascicles, she was utterly bewildered and could not comprehend them. At that time, she was only fourteen years old, yet she immediately proceeded to lecture upon them herself.
Those far and near all listened and marveled at his past cultivation. Because of this, he personally exhorted others, and those who followed him were numerous (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Emperor Xuan [reigned]... Upon ascending the throne, he once visited Master Sengchou. Sengchou remained seated on his mat and did not rise to welcome him.
When his disciples urged him to rise, Sengchou said: "In the past, when King Udayana came with a malevolent mind, the Venerable Piṇḍola descended from his seat and walked [to meet him]."
He went out seven paces to welcome him. Seven days later, the king lost his throne and was captured by a neighboring state, where he was shackled at the feet and imprisoned for twelve years.
"Although I am now of meager virtue," [Sengchou] said, "I hope that Your Majesty may obtain merit. Shortly thereafter, he was slandered on this account, and the Emperor harbored a grudge against him.

When the Emperor was about to enter the monastery again to suppress him for his lack of respect and execute him, Sengchou already knew of it. Upon the Emperor's arrival at the monastery, he [prepared...]
After traveling about ten *li*, he waited for him there. The Emperor asked in astonishment, and Sengchou replied, "I feared that my own blood would defile the monastery;
therefore, I have come from afar to meet the blade. The Emperor was struck with awe and repented, apologizing. He said to his minister Yang Zun, "I was not enlightened;

I nearly recklessly insulted a holy master. He then treated him with the same respect as before. The Emperor asked about his previous life, and Sengchou replied, "Your Majesty’s previous life was that of a *rākṣasa*. Now..."

[His] fondness for killing was merely a residual habit. The Emperor asked how he knew this. Sengchou requested that a basin be filled with water and that he perform a mantra over it, then commanded the Emperor to observe from above.
[The Emperor] saw his own reflection clearly in the form of a rākṣasa, followed by a swarm of rākṣasas. The Emperor was greatly alarmed.
From then on, he abstained from meat and spent his days in seated meditation, prostrating to the Buddha and practicing the Way with the vigor of a whirlwind. (From the *Tongzai*).
Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty was the seventh son of Emperor Wu. His name was Yi, and his courtesy name was Shicheng.

Initially, Emperor Wu dreamed of a monk with one eye missing who held an incense burner and said, "I am to be reborn in the royal palace. Subsequently, the Emperor's mother dreamed that the moon fell into her breast, and she then gave birth to the Emperor.

The Emperor suffered from an eye ailment from his youth; despite medical treatment, it was ineffective, and he ultimately lost sight in one eye. He was first enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiang and ascended the throne at Jiangling.
There, he donated his palace to establish Tiangong Monastery and Tianju Monastery. He frequently lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* and expounded upon the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
He lived to the age of forty-seven (as recorded in the *Liang Shu*).

Cui Yanwu of Boling during the Sui dynasty served as the Prefect of Wei Prefecture during the Kaihuang era. While on an official tour of inspection, he arrived at a certain district and was struck with both astonishment and joy.
He said to his attendants, "In the past, I once lived in this very district as the wife of another man; now I recognize it."
While staying at home, he happened to ride his horse into Xiu Lane. As the lane wound its way, he arrived at a certain house and ordered the gate to be knocked.

The master of the house was elderly; he came out to pay his respects. Yanwu entered the house and first ascended its hall. Looking toward the eastern wall, he saw a high protrusion about six or seven feet above the ground.
He then said to the host, "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and the golden hairpin that I read in the past [are here]."
"These are the five pairs [of scrolls] hidden high up within this wall. As for the last sheet of the seventh fascicle of that scripture, its characters were lost to fire.
Whenever I recite this scripture now and reach the end of the seventh fascicle, I always forget it and cannot remember it.

Consequently, I had my attendants excavate the wall; indeed, they found the scripture case. Upon opening the end of the seventh fascicle, both [the missing text and] the golden hairpin were recovered."
It was exactly as she had said. The host wept and said, "During the lifetime of my deceased wife, she often recited this sutra. These hairpins were also her belongings.
Yanwu said, "The locust tree in front of the courtyard—when I was about to give birth, I untied my own hair and placed it in a hollow of that tree.
Please have someone search inside the tree. When they searched, they indeed found the hair. Thereupon, the host was both grieved and overjoyed, and Yanwu left behind her clothing.
He provided the host with generous provisions and departed.
During the Daye era of the Great Tang, a traveling monk arrived at the Temple of Mount Tai and wished to stay overnight. The temple manager said:
There was no separate hall here; one could only stay beneath the eaves of the shrine. However, recently those who had stayed there as guests had all died. The monk said, "It matters not.
Having no other choice, he followed his advice and prepared a bed beneath the eaves. When night fell, the monk sat upright and recited the sutras.
After about one watch, he heard the sound of tinkling jade ornaments from within the shrine curtains. In a short while, the deity emerged and prostrated before the monk. The monk...

The Master said, "I have heard that many who stay overnight here die; could it be that you, O Dānapati, are harming them? I pray that you will protect them. The spirit said, "Those who meet death are already approaching.
Upon hearing the voice of the disciple, they become terrified of dying themselves; it is not I who kill them. I pray that the Master has no cause for concern."
The monk invited him to sit and they conversed for about the duration of a meal. The monk asked, "I have heard it said among the people that Mount Tai governs the ghosts;
is this indeed so? The spirit replied, "As a disciple of meager merit, such a place exists. Do you wish to see those who have passed away?
The monk said, "There were two fellow students of mine who died before me; I wish to see them. The spirit asked for their names and then said, "One of them has already..."

He was reborn among humans. One person, however, was in prison with such heavy offenses that he could not be summoned. "If you, Master, would go there to see him, it would be well," [the official] said.
Upon hearing this, the monk was greatly pleased; he rose and went out, and before long arrived at a certain place where he saw many shrines and prisons ablaze with fire, the flames most intense.
A divine general led the monk into a courtyard, where they saw a man from afar amidst the fire, wailing and unable to speak.
The physical form had changed beyond recognition, and the stench of the scorched flesh and blood was heart-wrenching. The deity said, "This is it. Do you not wish to examine it closely?
The monk, filled with grief and pity, sought to depart. Suddenly, he arrived at the temple and sat with the deity once more.
He then asked whether there was a way to save his fellow student. The deity replied, "It can be done. If you can transcribe the Lotus Sūtra for him," [he will be saved].
Thus he was spared. As dawn approached, the spirit took leave of the monk and entered the hall. At daybreak, the temple superintendent saw that the monk had not died;
finding this strange and extraordinary, the monk explained what had occurred. Thereupon, he immediately transcribed a copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Once the scripture was completed and its adornments finished, the monk again stayed overnight at the temple with the sutra. That night, the spirit appeared as before, joyfully prostrating itself and offering greetings.
He explained his purpose and informed him of the matter. The deity said, "Disciple, I already knew this. It was for your sake that I transcribed the scripture;
as soon as I began writing the title, he was already delivered and has now been reborn as a human being. However, this place is impure and unsuitable for housing the scripture."
"I pray that you, Master, will return and deliver [the scriptures] to the temple. After they had conversed for a long time, dawn approached; he took his leave and departed.
He subsequently delivered the scriptures to the temple. Zhang Deyan, the Vice Governor of Hangzhou, who previously served as the Governor of Yanzhou, was fully aware of these events.

(The above two accounts are from the *Mingbao ji* [Records of Miraculous Retribution], a work in two volumes compiled by Tang Lin, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel during the Yonghui era of the Tang Dynasty.)
Xu Ling: Chan Master Zhìwēi was, in his previous life, Xu Ling, the Minister of the Interior during the Chen dynasty.

Having listened to Great Master Zhìzhě lecture on the sutras, he made five vows: first, to maintain right mindfulness at the time of death; second, not to fall into the three miserable realms; third, to take rebirth among human beings;
fourth, to leave the household life as a celibate youth; and fifth, not to become a monk who conforms to worldly customs. Later, he was born into the Zhū family of Jìn-yún.
At the age of eighteen, as he was about to take a wife, he encountered a Buddhist monk on the road who said to him, "Young man, why do you intend to violate your former vow?

He then showed him his five vows. Having heard this, Wei no longer returned home; he went immediately to Guoqing Temple and sought out Dharma Master Zhang’an to inquire about and receive the essential points of the mind. Thereupon, he realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra.

At Tiantai Guoqing Monastery, the monk Zhihuan served as the *zhisui* (steward). He lent ten bolts of monastery cloth to Li Yiji, the County Magistrate of Shifeng, but after a long time, they were not returned.
Zhihuan died and was reborn as a slave of the monastery, with the characters "Zhihuan" inscribed on his back.
Subsequently, the Magistrate also died and likewise became a slave of the monastery, with the characters "Li Yiji" inscribed on his back. (The above two accounts appear in the *Fozu Tongji*).
Ji [Prefecture] (Tiantai County; known as Shifeng during the Sui and Tang dynasties).
Liu Shanjing of Fenzhou, a native of Xicheng, was orphaned at a young age and was raised by his mother. Throughout her life, his mother...
She constantly studied the Buddhist scriptures and practiced asceticism with diligent devotion. She passed away in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era.
Shanjing grieved for her beyond the bounds of propriety, weeping without ceasing. In the following year, within a state of blurred vision, Shanjing saw her mother appear to her and said:
"I cultivated merit during my previous life, which allowed me to receive a male body. I am now born here in this county, in the Song family of Shizhao Village to the south.
If you wish to see me, you may go there at once. Having spoken these words, she vanished. Shanjing went there exactly as she had said.
Before long, he arrived. On that very day, a son was born into the Song family. Shanjing consequently presented him with clothing and goods, explaining the full circumstances of the matter.
This boy is still living today, and Shanjing has always treated him with the etiquette due to a mother.
The śramaṇa Shanfu of Xizhou, who was an old acquaintance of Shanjing, heard what Shanjing and his fellow villagers had said and related it to me.
In Fuyang County, Xiangzhou, at Zili Temple, there was a monk named Yan Gao, whose secular surname was Zhao.
His nephew had previously been born as a son in the Ma family of the same village. When this son of the Ma family died at the end of the Zhenguan era, at the moment of his death—
He looked toward his mother and said, "I have a karmic affinity from a previous life with the Zhao clan; after my death, I shall become their grandson.
The Zhao family lived in the same village as him. His mother did not believe him, so she marked his left rib with ink to create a large black mole.
Later, the wife of the Zhao family dreamed that this child came to her and said, "I shall be your son," and consequently, she conceived.
While pregnant, she saw in a dream that it was clearly the son of the Ma family. After the birth, she examined the black mole [on the child's body] and found it still in its original place.
When the boy reached the age of three, without anyone leading him, he went of his own accord to the Ma family’s home and said, "This is my former residence;
it still exists today. He is now fourteen or fifteen years old. At Zili Temple in Xiangzhou, there is the monk Huiyong. Dharma... [text ends].

Thus it was truly and equally stated (the two items above are from the *Mingbao Shiyiji*. This record consists of two fascicles and was compiled during the Longshuo era by Lang Yuling of Zhongshan in the Tang dynasty; his courtesy name was Yuanxiu).
In Qizhou was the Great Master Hongren of the Fifth Patriarch at Huangmei. He was the son of the Zhou family; from birth he was precocious and remarkable.
In his childhood, a strange monk sighed and said, "This child lacks seven of the marks [of a Buddha] and thus does not equal the Tathāgata.

The *Linjian Lu* states that when the Great Master of the Fourth Patriarch resided at Mount Poutou, there was an unnamed old monk living on the mountain who did nothing but plant pine trees; people called him...
The practitioner Cai Song once requested of the Patriarch, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch said, "You are already old;
even if you were to hear it, would you be able to propagate it widely? If you could come back again, I might still wait for you.
Cai Song then departed and went to the water's edge, where he saw a woman washing clothes. He bowed to her and asked, "May I stay the night? The woman replied, "I have parents and brothers who..."
She went to seek him. He replied, "Yes. The woman nodded her head in agreement. The old monk turned his staff and departed. Upon returning home, Lady Zhou immediately became pregnant.
Her parents were greatly appalled and drove her away. Having nowhere else to go, she worked at spinning in the village for her daily livelihood.
Soon after, she gave birth to a son; deeming him an ill omen, she cast him into the water. The next day, she saw him swimming upstream against the current, his physical form fresh and radiant.

Ming was greatly startled and subsequently took him up. When he had reached the age of a young boy, he followed his mother in begging for food; the people of the village called him "The Child Without Surname.
The Fourth Patriarch saw him on the road at Huangmei and asked him in jest, "What is your surname? He replied, "I certainly have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one.
The Patriarch asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Patriarch said, "Are you then without a surname? He replied, "Nature is empty."
Thus, there was none. Wuzu converted his mother and caused her to leave the household life when he was seven years old.
He departed for Mount Pòtóu; while he stood gazing from afar, the Daoist’s physical body remained there. Alas! The Fifth Patriarch’s coming and going within birth and death was merely his sport.
Were it not for a sage who has attained the fruit of enlightenment, who could act in such a manner? (From the *Tōngzǎi* and the *Línjiān lù*).
At Shibi Temple in Bingzhou, there was an elderly monk whose practice consisted of meditation and recitation. He was diligent and refined in his conduct.
Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, a dove built a nest upon the pillar of his room and raised two fledglings. Whenever the old monk had leftover food, he would always go to the nest to feed them.
Although the dove chicks later grew somewhat larger, their wings were not yet fully developed; as they attempted to fly together, they both fell to the ground.
They died, and the monks buried them together. Ten days later, the monks dreamed at night that two young boys said to them:
"We, because of a minor transgression in our past lives, received the bodies of pigeons. Recently, we heard the Dharma Master reciting the Lotus Sūtra and the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Having heard this sublime Dharma, we have now attained human bodies. We are currently [at a place] ten paces to the side of this temple..."
In another village, in the family of such-and-such a person in such-and-such a hamlet, [the soul] had taken rebirth as a male; beyond ten months, he was due to be born.
The monk went to visit according to the appointed time and saw that a woman in this household was giving birth to twin sons at the same time.
He then performed the *pūrṇamāsa* (full-moon) feast for them. The monk called out, "Pigeon boy! and both boys responded in unison, saying, "Yes. After one had responded—

More than a year later, he finally spoke [of this matter] (*from the *Mingbao Shiyi*: "Formerly, in the fourth year of the Yongping era of the Wu dynasty, the Indian śramaṇa Jīvaka arrived in Luoyang. He displayed many divine wonders;

he pointed to the śramaṇa Zhu Fayan and said, 'This bodhisattva has come from among sheep,' and he pointed to Zhu Faxing and said, 'This bodhisattva has come from among devas'; both were verified. Now these two children have come from among pigeons; it is truly not false").
Zhuanghui: Prince Zhuanghui was shown by Empress Wu Zetian to the divine monk Wan Hui. Wan Hui said, "This is a tree-spirit from the Western Regions;
you should raise him as your brother. Princess Anle, relying on Empress Wei, plotted treason.
Wan Hui encountered her on the road, spat at her from afar, and said, "Her stench is unbearable; she must not be approached. Later, Anle was indeed executed. (From the *Tongjian*).
(Ji). Wengeng County, Dengzhou. During the Kaiyuan era, Wang Shi, the wife of Guo Xing, gave birth to a daughter with a crane-like beak.
Later, as she was about to die, she said of herself: "I have manifested this to people merely to show them the reward for the vegetarian fasts my ancestors once observed."
The śramaṇa Shi Niuyun was a person of the Kaiyuan era. In his youth, he was not particularly intelligent. Consequently, he traveled to Mount Wutai to pay homage to the Great Being Mañjuśrī.
Upon first arriving at the Eastern Terrace, he saw an old man who asked him, "For what purpose have you come? He replied:
"I wish to see the Great Sage; I seek one of keen wisdom. The old man said, "Mañjuśrī dwells on the Northern Terrace.
Yun immediately headed north, and the old man was also to the north. Yun thought this must be Mañjuśrī himself, and so he prostrated himself incessantly.

The old man said, "In your previous life, you were an ox. Because you once carried the scriptures, you have obtained the retribution of being a bhikṣu. Your nature is dull and deluded; within your breast..."
"There is some clotted flesh remaining. Close your eyes and do not open them; I shall dig it away for you.

He then used a hoe to excavate his chest, which did not cause much pain. He felt his mind suddenly become clear and expansive. When he opened his eyes, he saw the old man manifesting the body of Mañjuśrī, who said to him:

"I have bestowed intelligence upon you. From then on, Huiyun possessed total retention (*dhāraṇī*) and eloquent realization, becoming a teacher to the world. (The above two accounts are from the *Tong*.)
[Recorded]. In the twenty-sixth year of the Xuanzong era, the śramaṇa Fashou dreamed of a strange monk who exhorted him to provide five hundred cassocks to be offered to Huixiang Temple.
Upon waking, he found this strange; he subsequently begged for funds to have them made. When they reached the required number, suddenly—

One day he encountered a monk who said, "I shall lead you to enter Huixiang Temple. Following him, they entered Zhongnan Mountain, where they saw a lofty vermilion gate halfway up a cliff with a signboard reading "Huixiang.
They hurried inside and paid their respects to the elder Upāli (Shàngfāng lǎsù). The other monks were all extraordinary and magnificent; they greeted him with inquiries after his well-being.
Xiu took off his *kāṣāya* and distributed it throughout the temple. The elder led him into an empty room and called out—
The attendant took the *shichibashiku* (flute). When the attendant arrived carrying the jade flute, the old master said, "This was the former residence of the Emperor of Tang.
He once lived here; because he loved music, he descended to become the ruler of men. After a long time, he shall surely return.

He then handed over the flute along with the *kāṣāya* (robe) and instructed Xiu, saying, "Take these back and present them to the Emperor of Tang. Xiu returned to the capital and submitted them via a memorial. The Emperor took them.
She played the *xiāo* flute with such skill that it was as if she were a former imperial consort (details appear in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
In the first year of the Xingyuan era of the Shouzhou [reign], there was a commoner named Mao Han in Anfeng County, Huaixi, Shouzhou; his wife was Zhou.

He was born with the head of a pig, the ears of an elephant, the feet of a mule, and the gills of a fish, though his body was human. His parents wished to drown him, but he then spoke in human speech:

"In a previous life, because I did not believe in cause and effect, I borrowed five thousand coins and two bolts of hemp cloth from the monastery’s permanent assets at Kaiyuan Temple in Luzhou but failed to repay them. Therefore, I have suffered this retribution. I hope my parents will take me in and raise me. Wait—
When he grew up, he was sent to the monastery to repay his debt. By the age of seventeen, he was sent to the monastery to sweep the floors;
from time to time, he would whip himself with an iron staff, crying out that he was returning the debt. Because he relied on repaying this debt, he was named Lai-zhai (Reliant-on-Debt).
During the Xingyuan era, when Wei Gao—then Grand Marshal and Chief Secretary of the Secretariat—was first born, his father offered a meal to the monastic community to pray for blessings.
Suddenly, a holy monk arrived. When the meal was finished, the wet nurse took the infant in her arms and requested a blessing.
As the monk rose, he said to the assembly, "This child was formerly Zhuge Wuhou. In the future, he shall bring about a period of excellent governance in Shu; you should name him 'Wu'. Thus he spoke.

Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished. Subsequently, Gao Youguan’s conduct in public and private life, his integrity, and his achievements were generally comparable to those of Zhuge Liang (Wuhou).
He governed Sichuan for twenty-one years and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nankang. His virtue remained with the people; even today in Sichuan, he is venerated with offerings.
He had a profound affinity for Buddhism; when the stone statue at Jia Prefecture was first completed, Gao composed a commemorative inscription for it.
At Longhuai Monastery, Chan Master Tanshang spoke to his disciple Hui at the time of his death, saying:

"My karmic conditions dictate that I shall be reborn in the Yang family on the mountain peak of Mianzhu in Guanghan. Seven years hence, you shall come to see me. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
Yang was a Daoist priest. He first had a daughter named Xinsiang, who knew the Way from birth. Next, he had a son named Huikuan;

when the boy was five or six years old, Yang would converse with him daily, discussing matters entirely beyond worldly affairs. His parents recorded these conversations, but later they were mostly forgotten.
One night, Yang dreamed that [the child] rebuked him for breaching their agreement. Startled awake, Yang immediately set out for the mountain peak and knocked at the door.
Huikuan asked, "Who is knocking at the door? Huì hurriedly replied, "I am your disciple, Huì. Huikuan smiled and said, "How do you know it is me, that you call yourself my disciple?
Huì said, "Hearing the Master's voice, it is just as it was in the past. They then met face to face. Huì brought out the records his father had compiled and showed them to him;
they were treatises on the *Mahāvyūha* and other works. Huì immediately offered these to Huikuan and returned once more to Longhuai.
He shaved his head at the temple; from this point on, his spiritual wonders became manifest daily, and the common people called him "Venerable Saint" (Sheng Heshang).

His sister also followed him into the monastic life. Once, she entered the water for contemplation; the entire room became serene and still, and her physical form could no longer be seen, as only water was visible everywhere.
She was also titled "Saint Nun" (Sheng Ni). The tenth generation of the Kuan family became a *bhikṣu*, and the record of his tenth rebirth still exists today.
At Mount Heng Monastery, there was the Dharma Master Zhibian. His realization and understanding were peerless, and he composed many works. Yet, he had few disciples;
whenever he read his own writings, he would invariably sing them aloud once and sigh three times, lamenting that he had not yet met one who could appreciate his music.
One day, an elderly monk arrived and borrowed his compositions to read them. He remarked, "Your insight is supreme and accords well with the Buddha’s intent. Now, you are..."

"Your followers are merely lacking the necessary karmic conditions. You may provide food for birds and beasts; twenty years hence, you shall naturally have a following. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Hui Bian then sold his robes and bedding to exchange for rice, which he cooked and scattered outside the city walls.

A great flock of birds was moved to gather there, seizing the rice before flying away. He made this vow: "May those who eat my food become my dharma companions twenty years from now. Twenty years later...
He traveled to the city of Ye to open a lecture hall, where there were over a thousand people in attendance, all of whom were young bhikṣus.
At Huilin Temple in the Eastern Capital, there was the śramaṇa Yuánzé, who was on intimate terms with the hermit Lǐ Yuán. Huilin was the former residence of Lǐ Yuán;
his father, Lǐ Chéng, had been killed by Lù Shān while serving as the governor of the Eastern Capital. Consequently, Lǐ Yuán did not take office and lived as a recluse. He constantly...
While residing in the monastery, he spent the entire day in conversation and laughter with Sengze. By chance, they set out together to travel to Mount Emei;
Huiyuan intended to go by traveling upstream from Jingzhou through the Gorges, whereas Sengze wished to take the Xiyu pass from Chang’an.

Huiyuan felt that since he had long since severed ties with worldly affairs, he did not wish to enter the capital again. Unable to persuade him, Sengze eventually departed from Jingzhou. As his boat reached Nanpu, he saw a woman.
A man wearing a brocade apron was carrying a water jar on his back to draw water. Zé looked at him and wept, saying, "That which I did not wish for has come from this.
Yuán asked him the reason for this. Zé said, "My wife has been pregnant for three years; she has been waiting for me to be her son.
If we had not met, it would have been that, but now that we have met, there is no way to escape it. You should use divine incantations to assist me so that [the child] may be born quickly."
When the child was born, [Seng]yuan made a vow: "I pray that you, Master, will visit on the third day and take a smile as my token of faith.
Thirteen years hence, at the exterior of Tiantzhu Monastery in Hangzhou, I shall meet you there. Yuan wept with grief; he prepared a bath for the child, and by evening, Zhe had passed away.
After three days, the mother’s milk flowed. Yuan went to see him; when the boy saw Yuan, he indeed laughed joyfully. Yuan immediately related this to the family, and they buried him.
Having finished his business, Yuan returned to the temple. Later, as had been agreed, he traveled from Luoyang to Hangzhou to fulfill their appointment.
When the appointed time arrived, by the side of Ge Hong’s Well, he heard a cowherd boy tapping on the horn of his cow and singing:

"The ancient spirit upon the三生 stone— Discussing moon-gazing and wind-reciting need not concern us. I am ashamed that my lover has come from afar to visit; Though this body is different, its nature remains forever."
Yuan asked, "Is Master Ze well? He replied, "Master Li is truly a man of faith. However, his worldly ties are not yet exhausted; do not approach him for now.
Only when you have practiced diligently without indolence shall we meet again. He then sang this song: "The affairs before and after the body are vast and dim;
To speak of their causes and conditions would break one's heart. I have searched the mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue; Now I turn my smoke-shrouded oars back home."
He ascended the Qutang Gorge and then vanished, becoming invisible. Huìyuǎn returned once more to Huílín Monastery; by the beginning of the Chángqìng era, he was eighty years old.

Emperor Mùzōng issued an edict appointing Yuǎn as Palace Counselor (Jiànyì Dàfū), but he did not go to serve. Shortly thereafter, he passed away at the end of his natural life. (The above five accounts are from the *Tōngzǎi*. As for Master Zé’s foreknowledge of three lifetimes:

this may have been a noble one who had attained the first fruit of the *srotāpanna*, reaching the limit of seven births and seven deaths to exhaust all afflictions and outflows (*āsrava*), realizing the state of an *arhat* and attaining the fruit of non-arising to transcend the triple world.)

One undergoes birth and death once again. Now, having already passed through three lifetimes, there remain three or four more lifetimes ahead; hence it is said, "before the body and after the body. Yet, one has not yet found the place of rebirth; hence it is said, "having already searched everywhere."

In Wu Commandery, there was a man named Qi Junzo. Being poor, he encountered a foreign monk who gave him a jujube to eat. Immediately, he realized that his previous life had been as a monk who lectured on the sutras.

Thereupon, he extensively explained his past lives and his lapses regarding the precepts at the lecture seat. He subsequently entered the monastic order at Lingyin Monastery, taking the name Jiankong (as recorded in the *Tongji*).
Emperor Renzong of the Song Dynasty was the late-born son of Emperor Zhenzong. On the night of his birth, he cried incessantly. There was a man of the Way who could stop such crying;
when summoned, the man said, "Do not cry, do not cry! Why is it not as it was when you first did not laugh? Upon saying this, the crying ceased. This was indeed the truth.
Zong once prayed to the Supreme Deity for an heir. The Deity questioned the various immortals as to who should go [to earth], but none answered.
Only the Barefooted Great Immortal smiled; he subsequently descended to become his heir. His fondness for being barefoot while in the palace was the verification of this (from the *Gangjian*).

In Chuzhou, Provincial Vice-Governor Zhang Fangping was dispatched to serve as the Prefect of Chuzhou. Upon arriving at a monastery, he saw that the handwritten manuscript of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* remained perfectly intact.

He thus knew that his former life had been that of a monk who transcribed scriptures (Elder Xun; his subsequent life was as Minister Li. Senior Seat-holder Yan; his subsequent life was as Wang Shipeng—all of which are recorded in the biographies).
**Gongliang:** Prime Minister Ceng Gongliang’s previous incarnation was the Chan master Qingcaotang.
**Dongpo:** Su Dongpo’s younger brother, Zhe, styled Ziyou, was exiled to Gaoyao County in Guangdong.
At that time, Chan Master Yun’an of Dongshan and Chan Master Cong shared a dream one night that Chan Master Wuzu Jie had arrived clearly; they then [conversed] with him.
They went out of the city to welcome him. Shortly thereafter, Dongpo arrived. The three men recounted their dreams.

Dongpo said, "When I was eight or nine years old, I often dreamed that my body was that of a monk traveling back and forth through Shaanxi. Furthermore, when my late mother was pregnant with me, she dreamed of a one-eyed monk seeking lodging.
Yun'an was startled and said, "Master Jie is a man from Shaanxi and has one eye that is squinted. Calculating backward from the end of his life, it has already been five..."
Ten years later, when Dongpo was forty-nine, he frequently referred to the Preceptor Jie (the three instances above are from the *Tongji*).
Regarding Huang Shanggu: while Huang Shanggu was exiled to Fuling, he dreamed of a woman who said she was his previous incarnation.

Because termites had hollowed out the coffin, they were attached to both armpits; consequently, Shanggu suffered from a condition known as "armpit odor" (*yixi bing*). The woman therefore instructed him to open her grave.
When the reburial was performed, the illness was cured; it was indeed just as he had said (as recorded in the *Monthly Ordinances*).
At Qingshou Temple in the capital of Yan lived the monk Shijiao Heng, whose courtesy name was Xuming. He was the son of Wang Shi of Rencheng in Jizhou.

Formerly, there was a monk named Fú'ān from Cíjì Temple in Bìnjīng. Having resided in Rènchéng for many years, he cultivated pure deeds with such diligence that both monastics and laypeople held him in high esteem.
One day, while attending a vegetarian feast at Mángshān Village, he leaned against a tree and passed away.
That evening, he appeared in a dream to his younger sister, Féng Zìpéng, saying, "I have been reborn in Western Chen. When the village saw this, they beheld him descending upon a white horse.
In the village was the home of Wang Guangdao. Feng Jue spoke with his mother; thus, the three of them all had the same dream.
At dawn the next day, they went to Guangdao’s house to inquire about it. His mother, Lady Liu, had also dreamed the previous evening that Master An sought lodging there.
That night, indeed, a son was born who clenched his right thumb as if unable to extend it; he only blinked his eyes and did not smile. On the following day, there was...
The fellow monks Fuguang and Fu Jian heard of this and came to visit. Upon seeing him, they called out, "Brother An, are you well?

An looked at them intently, raised his hand and extended his fingers, and smiled. His mother used to lie in the master’s room whenever there was the sound of someone reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Because of this, everyone called him Master An; thus, the village of Mangshan was named after him.
The stele was inscribed upon stone to record these wonders. At the age of seven, he left the household life; at fifteen, he attended upon Master Puzhao Bao.
One day, suddenly hearing the sound of the wooden board being struck, he attained realization with vast clarity. Later, he appeared in the world and presided over five monastic seats.
The Ming dynasty, Xiangshu era: Baolin Monastery. The monk Datong, whose courtesy name was Yiyun and whose pen-name was Biefeng, was the son of the Wang family of Shangyu in Yue.
His father was Youqiao and his mother was of the Chen clan. Ten months after his mother conceived him, while his father was sitting in the hall during the day, he suddenly—
He saw an extraordinary monk with a thick, white beard entering while shaking his mendicant’s staff. The father rose and bowed, asking, "Where have you come from, O Monk?

He replied, "From Mount Kunlun," and then proceeded straight through the door into the inner quarters. The father hurried after him and heard the sound of a child crying in the room. The father smiled and said, "Could it be that my son is one who has returned to this world?

The Master was exceptionally bright and spirited from childhood; whenever he read a book, he immediately grasped its profound mysteries. Initially, he practiced the composition of literary works, moving with graceful ease.
His movements were grand and worthy of admiration. Thereupon his father sighed and said, "This son possesses the seeds of *prajñā*.
How could he be allowed to remain entangled and submerged in the toil of worldly defilements? He then ordered him to enter Chongsheng Temple in Kuaiji to shave his head.

Hearing that Dharma Master Chungu was lecturing on the essential tenets of the Qingliang school, he went to rely upon him at Jingde Temple in the prefecture and mastered his transmission entirely. Later, hearing of the Dharma of Zhongfeng of Tianmu...
The Way was flourishing there; upon his arrival, he felt a sense of intending to remain there for the rest of his life.

One day, Zhongfeng summoned him and exhorted him, saying, "The school of the Worthy Head (Xianshou) is daily receding and becoming ever more obscure. Your capacity is sufficient to restore it. Do not linger here for long.
He then specially wrote a verse in praise of the image of Qingliang and presented it to him as he sent him on his way. The Master rejoiced greatly and said, "Only now do I truly understand."

All phenomena originate from the one mind. Without realizing this, who can distinguish what is Chan and what is Teaching? He returned to Baolin Temple and again attended upon Chonggu, reporting the intent behind his visit to Zhongfeng.
Chonggu immediately ordered him to share the seat and lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and so forth.
(The above two accounts are from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming Dynasty*.)
During the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, in Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, there was a man named Guan Chun who, together with his wife, sold straw sandals in Jinling.

They had no children. Every day, whatever money or silver they earned, they took only what was necessary for their subsistence; the remainder they threw into a well. As years passed, they did not consider this practice particularly strange.
At one time, a monk came to beg for a hundred pieces of gold. Chun said, "I make my living by weaving straw sandals every day..."
"To fill my belly, how could I have silver? The monk said, "If you are willing to give it up, then it shall be yours. Chun said, "There is nothing I am not willing to do.
The monk then hired someone to dig a well, and by chance, they found a hundred pieces of gold, which the monk took and departed.
Later, Guan Chun was struck dead by lightning. There was a scholar named Zhu Yuanjia who wrote in vermilion upon his back: "The Buddha is not benevolent; three..."

Jia later became the first-ranked graduate (zhuangyuan) of the imperial examinations and rose to the rank of Minister of the Ministry of Rites. By imperial decree, he was sent to Goryeo to confer the title of King upon the crown prince. The king’s surname was Li and his name was Zhong. The king said to Jia, "I have fathered a son who is now eight years old, yet he has been unable to speak or smile. On his back, there are vermilion characters; I do not know what kind of omen or portent they signify. Jia ordered the boy to be brought forward, and upon seeing the characters, he said: [The characters read: "Born from the womb of a woman, He shall become a great man. In the year of the Dragon, He shall ascend the throne. Jia said, "This is a most auspicious sign. He then had the boy brought out and showed him the characters. Upon seeing them, [the boy] immediately began to speak. The king was overjoyed and bestowed gifts upon Jia. Subsequently, the boy ascended the throne and ruled for many years. It was because of this that Jia was granted the posthumous title of Duke of Huaiyin. His descendants continue to this day. This account is recorded in the *Song Shi* (History of Song), in the biography of the Minister of Rites, Wang Jia. It is also found in the *Wenxian Tongkao* (Comprehensive Examination of Literature and Institutions), in the section on the "Five Classics," as well as in the *Jinshi Cuibian* (Categorized Compilation of Imperial Histories). Furthermore, it appears in the *Xin Tang Shu* (New History of the Tang), in the biography of the Minister of Rites, Wang Jia, and in the *Tang Shu* (History of the Tang), in the biography of the Minister of Rites, Wang Jia. It is also cited in the *Lidai Sanbao Ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Ages), in the section on the "Sutra of the Great Decease," and in the *Fayuan Zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma), in the section on the "Sutra of the Great Decease. It is also mentioned in the *Shishi Yaolan* (Essentials of Buddhist History), in the section on the "Sutra of the Great Decease," and in the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks), in the biography of the monk Daoyue. It is also recorded in the *Song Huiyao* (Institutional History of the Song), in the section on the "Ministry of Rites," and in the *Song Shi* (History of Song), in the biography of the Minister of Rites, Wang Jia. Zhan recounted the circumstances of the matter to the King, explaining that he had personally heard it when he was young while living outside the secular world; however, he had forgotten the names of the two individuals involved.
In the nineteenth year of the Kangxi era, at the age of seventy, Zhan traveled to Jinling to pay homage at the Baoyun Pagoda. There he met the hermit Zhou Hunyuan of Henan, whose father—
During the Ming dynasty, the ancestors of Guan Chun all held office at court. Yuan Xiang heard this account and saw the official letter sent by the King of Goryeo to Guan Chun;
its paper was lustrous, firm, and thick, as heavy and precious as a jade tablet. Those who understood the matter remarked that these were the blessings resulting from Guan Chun’s past deeds.
Because he committed evil in his previous life, he has now repaid it with a single lifetime; yet, having been born as a crown prince, is this not a source of joy?
At that time, Han Yunjia,
the Magistrate of Dong’an County in Qingluo Dingzhou, addressed Tieqiao in the year of Jiyou of the Kangxi era, saying:
In a previous life, I was a monk at a certain hermitage on Mount Taiyue. He came seeking lodging at my home; my father provided him with vegetarian food and kept him there.
When he went out to receive [the guest], he was no longer to be seen, yet he had already made a sound like a clap of thunder upon the ground. (Zhang Mu Zhi of Dongguan, whose pen-name was Tieqiao.)
In Huizhou, at Boluo County, there was Han Ersu, the second son of Duke Wenque. He was a friend of Zhang Mu Zhi and Liu Liangcheng.
At the beginning of the Great Qing dynasty, he died in the suppression of the rebellion and was reborn as the son of Liu Liangcheng. Before his birth—
Liang Cheng was merely a dream; Shu entered the room, and she subsequently gave birth. When the child was able to speak, Liu had an aunt who teased her, saying, "Who are you?
She immediately replied, "My father is an official, my elder brother is a monk, and I have been harmed by people for five years now, so I no longer remember.
Mu, because of this, rejoiced at the continuation of their karmic bond across three lifetimes and sent a poem to Liang Cheng, saying: [Poem omitted per instructions]

Wandering on, why does it never end? To return once more is truly lamentable. How could I forget the words spoken that day? Yet I rely upon seeing this moment of rebirth. In dreams and illusions, what is truly fixed?
Let us cease being deluded by enmity and affection. I am ashamed to dwell in this world in vain;

yet these are still the beard and brows of my former self. (My elder brother entered the monastic life, taking the name Zuxin and the pen-name Shengren. His mother observed the vegetarian fast during the late Ming dynasty. At the time of her death, she said to her family: "I am going to the home of Kuang Xusheng, a Confucian scholar in Guangzhou. Later, when the family went to visit, they indeed found him there.)

At dawn, he passed away. He was the fifth son of Xu, born to Lady Cui of Foshan. This was because Lady Cui had once visited the Han residence and recounted how the entire family of the Kuang clan had placed their faith in the Triple Gem. Some say that after a person’s life ends, the consciousness immediately goes to seek rebirth in a womb.

"Now, why was it that she gave birth while inside the room? He replied: "As the celestial deities above have said, humans receive seven consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and each consciousness has its own deity. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the principal one. Although the principal one has already departed, the remaining deities continue to guard [the body], which is why her physical form is seen.

Alternatively, there may have been someone already in the womb who, due to evil karma, was destined to die within the womb; yet because of the mother's virtuous karma, another person came to take their place. Furthermore, there are those who die suddenly before their natural time has ended, and upon reviving, they see themselves undergoing punishment in hell."
The Elder Lianyin of Huguang resided at Falun Temple in Duanzhou. He said to Xiangqiao:

"A certain elder brother of mine lived in seclusion on a mountain, reciting the Lotus Sūtra daily. There was always a pheasant that would come to listen to the sutra, and once it had finished, it would fly away.
For several days afterward, it did not appear. About ten li from the mountain, there was a local gentleman who sent a messenger to the mountain, saying..."
The Master said, "In a dream last night, my disciple was entrusted to be born as the son of the householder; he has now sent me here to inform you, my teacher.

However, lately he has cried incessantly day and night. I request that you come once to see him. The Master looked about and saw that he had no disciples, save for a single pheasant that used to come to listen to the sutras.
Having not been seen for several days, it may be that this pheasant has ascended [to a higher realm] through the merit of the sutras.
"Could he have become a human being? He then went to that man's house. The man came out carrying his child; the child immediately ceased crying and was filled with joy.
[The monk] took this as proof.
Master Wang, the Prefectural Instructor of Chaozhou, served as a Professor in Fujian. There was an old man who mended buckets, who received silver coins every day.

He then took one-third [of his earnings] to purchase incense and candles as offerings to the Buddha. When he died and had no wealth for his funeral, Wang Jiaoshou lamented that there was no karmic retribution for him.
In the midst of his ritual fast, he took up his brush and wrote on paper: "For three days a week I made bamboo buckets;

I burned incense regardless of my poverty. The sky is vast and the Buddha is not seen; when dead, I shall question the Lord of Yama. Upon hearing that the local magistrate had fathered a son, Wang Jiaoshou went to [congratulate him].

The local official congratulated him, saying, "The birth of your son is most extraordinary; there are several characters upon his back. When asked what the characters said, he replied, "Three coins per day for carrying a water bucket.
The King said, "I wrote those myself. Why have they appeared here? He ordered an attendant to go to his desk, retrieve them, and examine them again.
By the time they returned, the characters on the boy's back had already vanished. The principle of *parinirvāṇa* (rebirth) can thus be clearly demonstrated. This is similar to—
I, the Magistrate of Wuan County, Shu Yinglongzi Tanhua Hongzhi, have inscribed these characters upon his back. His vow was to be reborn as Hongci.
That man still exists today at over fifty years of age in the Wushen year. (The above four accounts are from the Tieqiao ji).
Shu Yinglong was a native of Guangxi. His son, Hongzhi, won the third-place jinshi degree at the age of twenty, but died shortly thereafter.
Yinglong wrote characters in vermilion on his back, praying that he might be reborn into his family. Later, the boy was indeed conceived in the home of Yinglong’s tenant farmer;

when the characters were discovered, he was sent to Yinglong to be raised and named Hongci. He passed the provincial examination and, while traveling to the capital by carriage through Guangdong, arrived at Dongguan, where he paid respects to his biological father.
[Memorial Tablet]. Supplementary Account of Tan Jingsheng.
At the beginning of the Southern Tang dynasty, there was a recluse named Tan Jingsheng, who was a friend of Chen Tuan. He authored the *Huashu* (Book of Transformation).
One hundred and ten chapters. Song Qiu composed the preface for them. Among the sixty-six chapters, one states:

The Lord of Zitrong said, "I have received the retribution of my karma and am a dragon of the Yangchi Pond. Trapped beneath the accumulated waters, a severe drought has persisted for years, and the water has turned to mud.
My body is vast and immense, yet there is no hole large enough to contain it. As the scorching sun descends upon me, I suffer from burning heat both within and without. Various...
Within his scales, small insects had each grown, biting and gnawing him with great suffering. One morning, when the air was cool, the light of heaven suddenly broke forth;
five-colored clouds drifted across the sky, containing within them auspicious signs: azure hair coiled in spirals and a golden countenance as clear as the moon.

The mountain spirits and the Lord of the River, along with the myriad multitudes, bowed their heads in prostration, praising and rejoicing with voices that shook heaven and earth. Celestial incense swirled about, following [the apparition].
It was springtime when I was born there. I then looked up and wailed piteously, entreating for deliverance. The myriad spirits and various sages all said to me:
"This is the Great Sage of the West, the Perfectly Awakened World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha.

Now that his teachings are circulating in the Eastern Land, he has manifested a transformation body in accordance with the Dharma and is about to go to the Middle Kingdom. Since you have encountered him, you may be liberated from your past karma. I—

He then leaped up with joy and entered into the celestial light, where he fully recounted the principles of karmic retribution from his past lives. The World-Honored One said, "Excellent, O Son of Heaven!
You have been filial and loyal to the state in the past, and furthermore, out of compassion for the world, you have given rise to a mind of protection and sustenance.
Yet, as cause and effect were not yet complete, enemies contended with one another; through the perception of self and other, they indulged in cruelty and transferred their anger [upon others]."
All things are karmic debts that must be repaid; now I repent of my own accord, desiring liberation.
At this time, do you still harbor thoughts of enmity or kinship, or notions of anger and delusion? Having heard the ultimate truth, my mind has become clear and enlightened.
Internally and externally all was utterly empty, abiding like space. Looking back at his own body, it vanished as soon as he thought of it.

He was then reborn as a man, attaining the wisdom of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). This is my place of return and reliance. (From the *Record of the Shrine of Lord Zitrong of Shu*. Because he beheld the golden countenance of the Buddha with joy, he spontaneously experienced auspicious signs;
because he attained the wisdom of empowerment, he became intelligent and sagacious, serving as Wenchang.)
Biàn Hào of the Southern Tang: When he was first born, his parents dreamed that Xiè Língyùn entered their room; thus, his childhood name was Kānglè.
He served the Southern Tang as a Commandant of the Capital (Dūyúhòu) and followed Chá Wénhuī in the conquest of Jiànzhōu.

Sà. Subsequently, when he served as a military governor (jièdùshǐ), he established vegetarian feasts and extensively performed Buddhist rites.
The people of Tán called him "Master Biān" (as recorded in the Wǔdài Shǐ).

Phonetic gloss:
*yú* (渝) has the sound *yú*; it means "to change.
*jí* (殛) has the sound *jì*; it means "to execute."
Gǔn (鯀) is the same as Gǔn; its pronunciation is gǔn. It is the name of Yu’s father.
Huángnéng (黃能) has the final sound of dài (乃帶切), pronounced nài. It refers to a three-legged turtle, which is called néng.
*Tíjué* (the first character pronounced *tí*, the second *jué*): another name for the *ziguī* (cuckoo). *Hú* (pronounced *hú*):
the yellow crane (*huáng-hú*) or the great white crane (*hóng-hú*); it may also be pronounced *gǔ*, referring to a small bird.
Yuan (黿): Pronounced like "yuan. It resembles a turtle but is larger.
Zhang (麞): Pronounced like "zhang. The *mi* (麋) is larger than a deer and has antlers; the *zhang* (麞) resembles a *ji* (麂) but is smaller and lacks antlers.
Ji (麂): Pronounced like "ji. It belongs to the species of the *mi*.
The *ju-ying-xin* (a type of hawk) is also called *chen-feng*. It is yellow in color with a swallow-like jaw; it flies swiftly and strikes and eats doves and pigeons.
"Luò" (雒) is pronounced "Luò" (洛). It refers to the horned owl (*gǎoqī*) of today; it is also known as the *xiūliú*.

The five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Form is the body; the other four are the mind. The mind is what is called "name" (*nāman*).
The character for "xiè" (榍) is pronounced as xiè;

the character for "chí" (雉) is pronounced as chí with the fourth tone. It is also called the wild pheasant (*yējī*). The male has a crest and a long tail, its body is adorned with variegated patterns, and it delights in fighting.
Qíyì (岐嶷): The first character is pronounced qí; the second is pronounced yì (with the initial *n-). This refers to a small child possessing intelligence and discernment.
Huì (喙): Pronounced huì. It refers to the beak of a bird. Jué (钁):
Pronounced with the rhyme qiú and the final bō. It is a voiced consonant (*k*). It refers to a dog’s hoe. Kuāng (匡): A final consonant sound. It refers to a dog’s plowshare.
Biàn tóng biàn (辯同辯): A vulgar character. Qù (噱):
Pronounced with the initial of jí (極) and the final of xuè (虐). Jiāng (彊): The entering tone.
It means to laugh. Yù (龥): Pronounced yù (豫). It means to call out while bowing one's head.
*Miao* (眇) is pronounced *mǎo*. It means "one-eyed" or "small.
*Ālán* (阿練), in Sanskrit, is fully *āraṇya*; this is translated here as "tranquil seclusion" (*jìjìng*). This refers to the dwelling place of the *saṃgha*. *Sù* (泝) is pronounced *sù*.
To go upstream against the current is called *sù*. *Huí* (洄) also means "toward. When water wishes to flow downward, to go against it is... [the text ends].
This is the highest [state]. The eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) are: first, the hells; second, the animal realm; third, the hungry ghosts; fourth, the long-lived heavens;
fifth, the continent of Uttarakuru; sixth, being blind, deaf, or mute; seventh, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence; and eighth, being born before or after a Buddha. These—

Regarding these eight places: although the retributions of suffering and pleasure differ among them, they are all obstacles that prevent one from seeing the Buddha or hearing the Buddha’s True Dharma.

As for the Heaven of Long Life (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*), their lifespan is five hundred kalpas; non-Buddhists who cultivate the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) are born in this heaven.
In the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*), the lifespan is one thousand years; because they are attached to pleasure, they do not receive instruction. Therefore, [the Buddha's] Dharma...
They do not attain it. "Worldly wisdom and eloquence" refers to those whose worldly, heterodox intelligence is sharp and keen;
they merely indulge in the study of external texts and do not believe in the Buddha's teaching on cause and effect. This constitutes an obstacle and hindrance.
The Three Jewels are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. "Buddha" means awakening. During the long night of birth and death, people do not awaken for themselves;
only the Buddha has attained awakening. Over three great incalculable eons, he practiced the six perfections and myriad deeds until his merit and wisdom were perfected.

Therefore, he is called the Greatly Awakened One (*Mahābuddha*). "Dharma" refers to all the scriptures of the Tripiṭaka spoken by the Buddha, which cause people to abandon evil and cultivate goodness, to leave behind desire and transcend the world, and to attain the state of non-arising and non-ceasing. "Saṃgha" refers to the pure and harmonious assembly.
These are bodhisattvas, arhats, and even those who have received the Buddha’s two hundred and fifty major precepts;
because they commit no transgressions, they are said to be "pure. Because they are equal and harmonious in the six points of concord, they are said to be "united."

The Pratyekabuddha is also called the Solitary Realizer (*Pratyekabuddha*). Appearing in an age without a Buddha, they awaken by themselves to the twelve links of dependent origination without a teacher and thereby transcend birth and death.
They are the noble ones of the Middle Vehicle; in Sanskrit, they are called *Pratyekabuddha*.
Arhat is here translated as "Birthless," meaning that one will not undergo birth and death in future lives.

It is also called "Unattached," because one is no longer attached to afflictions or birth and death. It is also called "Worthy of Truth" (Yingzhen); these are the noble ones of the Śrāvaka vehicle of the Hīnayāna.
*Zèn* (pronounced *zān*, departing tone): to slander and defame.
*Kuì* (pronounced *chuī*, departing tone): the soft and fine hair of an animal.
*Gū*: to bind an object with bamboo strips (*miè*).
The *liǎoyīn* bird is that which suspends objects.
*Diéyīn* means layered, doubled, thick, fallen, accumulated, and piled up.
The three calamities refer to the minor three calamities: first, weapons; second, pestilence; and third, famine.

The eight sufferings are: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age; third, the suffering of illness; fourth, the suffering of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from what is loved; sixth, the suffering of encountering what is hated;
seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and eighth, the suffering of various calamities and misfortunes, both great and small.
