Regarding the path of the asuras:
in Sanskrit it is called *asura*, also *asura* (阿素洛), and again *asura* (阿須倫); in the Chinese language, it means "Non-Gods" (非天). Its...
The palaces and gardens are all composed of the seven treasures; they resemble those of the heavens, yet are not truly heavenly.

It is further said that there are no "handsome" beings, meaning that while the men are ugly, the women are beautiful. Alternatively, it is said that although they do not drink alcohol, there are ghosts and animals within this heavenly realm.
Those subsumed under the heavenly path dwell within jeweled cities in the open spaces of Mount Sumeru, while those subsumed under the ghostly path dwell in the great ocean.
On the edges, or within the rocky walls of great mountains. Those categorized as belonging to the realm of animals dwell at the bottom of the great ocean, with the seawater above them;
there is a wind that sustains it like a cloud, so that it does not enter their palaces, just as a person gazes up at the heavens. The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states:
"One thousand yojanas east of Mount Sumeru, King, beneath the great ocean, dwells the Asura King Vemacitra."
The land is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Within the great city, the palace is named Śvetaketu; it is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
It is adorned with seven tiers of railings, seven layers of golden and silver bell-nets, and seven rows of trees.
The sevenfold city walls are all composed of the seven precious gems. There are gardens, ponds, flowers, and fruits, where various birds sing in harmony. Extensive...

As it is stated in the sūtras, these details need not be recorded here at length. One thousand yojanas south of Mount Sumeru, beneath the great ocean, lies the palace of the Asura King Vala, measuring eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
One thousand yojanas west of Mount Sumeru, there is the palace of the Asura King Śambara, with dimensions as previously mentioned. [Mount Sumeru...]
To the north, beyond a thousand yojanas beneath the great ocean, lies the palace and dwelling place of Rāhu, the Asura King.
It is vast, exquisite, and similar in its splendor to those described before. His female attendants and retinue are beyond calculation;

they enjoy themselves together, indulging in their mutual affection and pleasure. His other ministers, concubines, and servants are even more numerous, as fully described in the sūtras. It is not [to be omitted].
It can be fully described. The lifespan of the Asura Kings is incomplete; it is mostly diminished and rarely reaches its full extent.

Their natural bodies are one hundred *yojana* long, up to seven hundred *yojana*. Their transformed bodies are sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojana* tall, standing at the bottom of the great ocean level with Mount Sumeru.
Possessing great illusory arts, they constantly battle with the Trāyastriṃśa devas. The sun and moon emit...
The light struck their eyes, and they shielded them with their hands. When the people of the world saw this, they said that the sun and moon were eclipsed.
Because their merit was not equal to that of the devas, they were constantly defeated in battle; they then led their troops and fled into the pores of lotus fibers.

This was the retribution for having maintained the precepts and delighted in superior giving in previous lives, yet being motivated by a mind of inferior-grade ten wholesome deeds. Their minds were mostly...

Due to flattery and arrogance, and an inability to practice forbearance, they receive this body. Because they maintained the precepts and practiced giving, their palaces are composed of the seven treasures;
yet because they lacked forbearance, their physical appearance is ugly and hideous. Due to their flattery, arrogance, and love of victory, they constantly fight with the devas.
The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states that by possessing ten types of karma, one receives the retribution of an asura. First, their bodily conduct is subtle...
1. Evil. 2. Subtle evil in verbal conduct. 3. Subtle evil in mental conduct. 4. Arising of conceit (*māna*). 5. Arising of the "I-am" conceit (*asmimāna*). 6.
Arising of overweening conceit (*adhimāna*). 7. Arising of great conceit (*mahāmāna*). 8. Arising of false conceit (*mithyāmāna*). 9. Arising of conceit regarding conceit (*mānātimāna*). 10.
Directing all roots of goodness toward the realm of the asuras. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that the asuras dwell in...

There are five dwelling places. The first is on the earth, within Mount Cakravāḍa (the mountain of various peaks), [including the seven mountains of gold and among the various rocky cliffs]; their power is the weakest.
Second, twenty-one thousand yojanas into the sea to the north of Mount Sumeru, there is an asura named Rāhu, who commands an immeasurable host of asuras.
Third, another twenty-one thousand yojanas beyond that, there is an asura named Śūraṃjaya.
Fourth, another twenty-one thousand yojanas beyond that, there is an asura named Puṣpa.
Mālā. Five times more than twenty-one thousand yojanas further, there is an asura named Vemacitra.
From within this place, a sound issues forth that penetrates beyond the sea, saying: "I am Vemacitra, the Asura. (Vemacitra means "High Resonance.
The first is Rāhu, the King of the Asuras, who has four jade-like daughters born from his mere thought. The first is named... [as above]... like... (The remainder of the name follows).
Shadow; second, All Fragrances; third, Wondrous Forest; and fourth, Supreme Virtue.
Each of these four daughters has twelve nayutas of handmaidens as her retinue, all of whom surround the Asura King.
They enjoyed themselves together, indulging their passions and pleasures beyond all description. The Asuras of Courageous Prowess possessed superior majesty;
the Asuras of Flower Garlands possessed even greater majesty; and the Asura Vemacitra possessed double the majesty and retinue, which was further beyond calculation.
The remaining ministers, ladies-in-waiting, and attendants were likewise beyond description.
One should know that there are vast differences in status between them; they cannot be discussed as a single uniform category. The life spans of the asuras vary:
some have a lifespan of five hundred years, where five hundred human years constitute one day and night for them;
some have a lifespan of six thousand years, where six hundred human years constitute one day and night for them; and some have a lifespan of seven thousand [years].
One human year is equivalent to one day and night for them. The sizes of their palaces vary; each is different.
Furthermore, they can transform their bodies, manifesting various forms at will. It is also said that the food and clothing of the asuras appear spontaneously.

Their crowns, sashes, and garments are made entirely of the seven treasures and are pristine and pure. Their food and drink appear according to their thoughts, complete with a hundred flavors, equal to those of the devas.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, although their clothing and food surpass those of humans, [they are still subject to change].
If one eats in such a manner, then one is not equal to humans. This means that whenever they eat, at the very last mouthful, they must transform it into green mud;
just as the Dragon King, though he may consume a hundred flavors, must at the very last mouthful transform them into a frog.
Therefore, the Sūtra says they are not equal to humans. The Āgama Sūtra states: "The Asuras have great..."
Possessing such majestic power, he gave rise to this thought: "The King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the various devas of the sun and moon pass over my head;

I vow to seize the sun and moon to fashion them into earrings. Upon seeing him, the Sun and Moon Devaputras each harbored terror and could not remain at ease in their respective abodes, for his form was fearsome.
The Sun and Moon possess great majesty and virtue, and they dwell for the duration of one intermediate kalpa.
Furthermore, this eon is a time of blessing and protection for the sentient beings of the world; the sun and moon are not troubled by the asuras.

At that time, the asuras became increasingly enraged and immediately commanded the two asura kings Śambara and Vemacitra, along with their various ministers, each to prepare weapons and go forth to battle the devas. Then Nanda and Upananda...

The Great Dragon King’s body encircles Mount Sumeru for seven circuits. As the mountain shakes and clouds spread, he strikes the waters with his tail, causing the great ocean's waves to crest over Mount Sumeru.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven say, "The asuras wish to wage war! and all the nāgas, spirits, and deities likewise perceive it.
Each holding weapons, they engage in combat one after another. If the gods are defeated, they all flee to the palaces of the Four Great Kings.
They prepare their chariots for an offensive and first inform Śakra. Śakra then informs the gods of the Suyāma Heaven, and so on, up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Surrounded by countless hosts of devas, as well as nāgas and spirits, Śakra commanded them, saying:
"If my army is victorious, bind Vimalacitra the asura with the fivefold bonds and bring him back to the Sudharmā Hall; I wish to behold him."
The asura also said, "If my host prevails, I shall bind Śakra with the fivefold fetters and return to the Hall of Seven Leaves; I wish to observe this.
Then a great battle broke out at once, yet neither side inflicted injury upon the other; they merely made physical contact, which gave rise to pain and distress.
Thereupon Śakra manifested his true form, possessing a thousand eyes and wielding a vajra-pestle from which smoke and flames issued from his head. When the asura saw this, [he was struck with fear].
They were thus defeated. They immediately captured the asura Vemacitrin, bound him, and brought him back.
Seeing Śakra from afar, he immediately unleashed foul language. Śakra replied, "I wish to discuss the meaning of the Dharma with you;
why must you speak such foul words? The *Buddhadarśana-samādhi-sūtra* states: "When this asura king Vemacitrin’s son grew up, he saw the various..."
Surrounded by celestial maidens, she addressed her mother, saying, "All people have spouses; why am I alone without one?
Her mother replied, "On Mount Gandhamādana there is a deity named Gandharva. This deity has a daughter whose beauty is exquisite and whose complexion surpasses white jade.
From every pore of her body, she emits wondrous sounds that are most pleasing to my heart. I shall now betroth her to you; she will fulfill your wish."
"No. Your words are excellent, most excellent. I pray that you, Mother, will go and seek her. At that time, the mother went to Mount Gandhamādana and addressed the musical deities:
"I have a son whose power and sovereignty are such that there is no equal to him in the four continents.
You have a daughter who may be wedded to my son. When the girl heard this, she joyfully consented to follow him. Then the son of the asura—
After she had been taken as his wife, before long she became pregnant. After a thousand years had passed, she gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was upright and extraordinary;
among all those above and below heaven, there was none to compare with her, and her facial features were exquisitely beautiful.
There were eighty-four thousand on the left side and eighty-four thousand on the right side; it was the same for the front and back.
When the asuras saw this, they considered it extraordinary, like the moon among the stars—it was truly marvelous.

Śakra, the Lord of Devas, Kauśika, heard of this and sought her hand in marriage. The asura rejoiced at hearing this and gave his daughter to him as a wife. Śakra established her name, calling her Rati (Delight).
When the gods, including Śacī, saw her, they marveled at such an unprecedented sight; looking east, they forgot the west, and looking south, they forgot the north.

Even down to a single hair, everyone felt a surge of joy and delight. When Śakra reached the Nandana Grove and entered the pool with his celestial maidens to sport therein, Manoharā immediately became jealous.
She dispatched five yakṣas to inform her father, the King, saying: "Now this Śakra..."
Śakra was no longer favored; he sported with his own retinue of celestial maidens. When his father heard these words, anger arose in his heart.

He immediately mobilized the fourfold army and went to attack Śakra. Standing upon the great ocean waters and crouching atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, he simultaneously extended nine hundred and ninety-nine hands to shake the city of Sudarśana and rock Mount Sumeru and the four great oceans.
At that moment, the waters surged with waves. Śakra was struck with terror and did not know where to turn. Then a deity in the palace addressed the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Do not be so greatly terrified. The Buddhas of the past have taught the Prajñāpāramitā; Your Majesty should recite and uphold it, and the host of spirits will shatter of their own accord.
Thereupon, Śakra sat in the Sudharmā Hall, burned various famous incenses, and made this great vow: "Prajñāpāramitā..."
Pāramitā. This is the great vidyā-mantra; this is the unsurpassed mantra; this is the unequaled mantra. It is true and not false.
By upholding this Dharma, I shall attain the Way of the Buddha and cause the asuras to naturally retreat and disperse.
As these words were spoken, a wheel of swords descended spontaneously from the void and hovered above the asuras; at that time, the ears and noses of the asuras—
Their hands and feet fell off all at once, causing the waters of the great ocean to turn as red as mother-of-pearl beads. At that moment, the asuras were struck with terror;
having no place to flee, they entered into the pores of lotus fibers.
In the western regions of India, there was the Master Bhāviveka. His magnanimity was vast and profound, and his supreme virtue was deep and far-reaching.

Outwardly he wore the robes of the Sāṃkhya school, yet inwardly he propagated the teachings of Nāgārjuna. In quiet contemplation, he thought to himself: "If not Maitreya attaining Buddhahood, who else can resolve my doubts?"
Thereupon, before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he recited the *Svacittadhāraṇī* while abstaining from grain and subsisting only on water.
After three years had passed, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifested a body of wondrous color and said to the master of treatises, "What is your aspiration?"
He replied, "I wish to remain in this body until I may behold Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said, "The human body is fragile and precarious;
the world is fleeting and illusory. You should cultivate supreme goodness and aspire to be born in Tuṣita Heaven, where you will be able to pay homage to him more swiftly.
The Master of Śāstras said, "My resolve cannot be diverted, and my mind cannot be divided. The Bodhisattva said, "If that is so, then it is fitting..."
He traveled to South India, to the country of Mahānanda. Not far from the southern city, there was a great mountain crag, the abode of the Vajrapāṇi deity.
It is said that those who recite and maintain the Vajrapāṇi Dhāraṇī with utmost sincerity shall have their vows fulfilled.
Thereupon, the Master went there and recited it. After three years, the deity spoke to him, saying: "What is your wish? You have been so diligent."
Lì said, "I wish to retain this body until I may behold Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva pointed him out, saying, "He has been sent here to make this request;
shall he not fulfill my vow? It rests with you, O Spirit. The Spirit then bestowed upon him the method and said to him, "Within these rocky cliffs lies the palace of the Asuras.
If you perform the invocation according to the ritual, the stone wall shall open. Once it opens, enter within; you may [proceed]."

"I await the sight [of him]. The Master of Śāstras said, "Dwelling in seclusion, I have nothing to behold; how could I know when a Buddha appears? The deity said, "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you.

Having received this command, the Master devoted himself single-mindedly to recitation and retention. After another three years had passed, without having entertained any other thought, he took mustard seeds and struck them against a stone wall;
it opened up suddenly and completely. At that time, hundreds of thousands of millions of people gazed upon it, so captivated that they forgot to return home.
The Master of Treatises stepped across the threshold and addressed the assembly, saying: "For a long time I have prayed and waited to behold Maitreya.

Now that the holy spirit has granted its protection and my great vow is fulfilled, you should enter here and together witness the Buddha’s arising. Those who heard this were struck with terror and none dared to step upon the threshold;
they claimed it was a den of venomous serpents, fearing for their lives. Although he spoke to them repeatedly, only six people followed him.
He entered. The master of the treatise looked back and took leave of the assembly, then proceeded with composure. Once he had entered, the stone wall closed back together.
The assembly all lamented with resentment, regretting the error of their previous words. (From the *Xiyu ji* of the Tang Dynasty; Maitreya is the same as Mili; Nāgārjuna was formerly called Longshu.)

[Section on] Central India. Master Xuanzang said: "In the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era, while I was at Nālandā Monastery in the kingdom of Magadha in Central India, I saw a layman say: 'There was once a man who was fond of beauty.

He had long heard it said in the scriptures that when asuras give birth to sons, they are extremely ugly, but their daughters are beautiful. He heard that within those mountains there were asuras...'"
In the cave there is a separate palace, exceedingly refined and exquisite, as magnificent as that of the gods.

That person, desiring to see an asura maiden to become her consort, constantly maintained the dhāraṇī with diligent application for three years. As the three years were nearly complete, his prayer was fulfilled.
Before departing, he summoned a disciple who was a close friend to accompany him; the disciple—
At that time, she also accompanied him. Since the incantation had shown its efficacy, they eventually arrived at the palace gate. The guards at the entrance were extremely stern;
with utmost sincerity, she requested the gatekeeper to announce her presence to the lady. The gatekeeper announced her, and she explained the purpose of her visit in detail.
The asura woman was delighted and asked the gatekeeper, "How many people have come? He replied, "Two. The woman then said to the gatekeeper, "Recite..."
The mantra-reciter arrived and entered; his companion remained outside the gate. A gatekeeper came to announce him, and the reciter led him inside.
Once the disciple saw himself being led in, he suddenly found himself standing at the southern gate of his own home, having reached it without even realizing it.
From that time on, he had no further news of that man. Because of this, the disciple resolved his mind to leave the household life and practice the Way, making this vow:
While making offerings to the Triple Gem at a monastery, that person related the circumstances in detail to Xuanzang. (India is Tianzhu.
In the kingdom of Campā in Central India, within a rocky ravine on a mountain to the southwest, there is a cave of an asura.
A man, while wandering the mountains to practice the Way, encountered this cave and entered it. Inside, he saw the palace of an asura, exquisitely refined and wondrous.
The flowers and plants resemble those of a celestial palace; its gardens, ponds, groves, and fruits are beyond description.
When the asura hosts saw these people—beings rarely encountered here—they asked, "Can you dwell here for long? They replied, "We wish to return to our own abodes."
Seeing that [the Buddha] was not there, the asura offered him a peach. After he had finished eating it, the asura said, "You should leave quickly;
I fear your body is too large for this cave to contain you. Having spoken, he rushed out, whereupon his body began to grow. His form became coarse and massive;
his head had just emerged when his great body blocked the opening, so that he could not get entirely outside. From that time until now, many years have passed.

There were one hundred [such beings], each possessing only a massive head like a three-shi jar. When people saw them, they would converse with them, and the beings would relate their circumstances in full detail.
People took pity on them and said, "We shall bore through the rock to bring your bodies forth; what do you think of this? They replied, "It is a great favor.

The people reported this to the King, recounting the matter in its entirety. The sovereign and his ministers deliberated together: "These are no ordinary men; their strength rivals that of a thousand warriors. If we bore through the rock..."

He emerged. "Had there been any unforeseen intent [to harm], who could have resisted it? For this reason, he remained as before; people of the time called him the "Great-Headed Immortal" (Dàtóu Xiānrén).
The Tang envoy Wang Xuancè visited him three times; he rubbed the man's head with his hand and conversed with him clearly and distinctly.
Recently, in the mountains, a wildfire scorched his head until it was charred black, yet his life did not end. To the west...

The *Guozhi* (Records of the Kingdoms) consists of sixty fascicles, compiled by the state. By imperial decree, various scholars were commissioned to produce illustrations, which were collected in the Central Secretariat (*Zhongtai*).
There is also another forty-fascicle version, which began in the third year of the Linde era and was completed at the end of summer in the first year of the Qianfeng era.
When I met Xuance, he recounted these matters in detail (as recorded in the *Xiguo zhi*).
(Question: Why are those in the asura realm so few? (Answer: Those born into the asura realm have no [human] retribution;
therefore, humans cannot know of them. By examining the preceding scriptural passage, one will know for oneself that they are not few.
*Liùdào jí*, Scroll Two, Phonetic Explanations:
Rāhula; here it means "Seizer of the Sun."
*Cuàn* (pronounced as *cuàn*): to flee; to hide away. *Nà yóu tā*:
translated here as "ten thousand billion.
*Xiā máo* (upper tone *xiá*, lower tone *má*; commonly written as *máo*): a frog; colloquially called a *háguì*.
Nanda and Upananda. Nanda means "Joy" (in Chinese). Upananda means "Near-Joy.
*Kànglì* (the first character pronounced *kàng* with the second tone, the second character pronounced *lì*): this refers to a husband and wife; it denotes a marital couple.
Gandharva is translated here as "Fragrance-Body" (xiāngyīn). They are the musical deities of the Heavenly Emperor.
The fourfold army consists of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
The character *hàn* (written with the radical for "mouth" and the phonetic *hán*, pronounced in the third tone) means to shake or move.
The character 儅 (dāng) is pronounced with a departing tone; it means "exactly" or "in the center.
帀 is a vulgar form of 匝 and is incorrect.
When Song Jiao was young, he accompanied his father while serving in Yingshan to study there. He saw a dog being swept away by water, and ant nests reaching as far as the city walls.
He waded across by means of a bridge woven from bamboo. Later, he became the provincial examination head (zhuangyuan) through the power of his hidden virtue (*yin-de*).
The site of the Ants' Bridge where he crossed still exists today to the south of the administrative seat of Yingshan County in Hubei.
*The Collection on the Six Realms*, Volume Three.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoxiang Forest in Nanhai, Guangzhou, while residing at Sui.
The Realm of Ghosts and Spirits.

Question: What is meant by the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*)? Answer: Because they have committed excessive acts of stinginess and greed through body, speech, and mind, they go there and are born there;

thus, they experience the karmic retribution of hunger and thirst for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, during which time they do not even hear the names of water or food, let alone see them or obtain them.
For this reason, it is called the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Furthermore, they are called "ghosts" (*preta*) because of their constant longing and hope.
That is to say, within the six realms of existence, they constantly seek food and drink from humans. Furthermore, "preta" means "fearful";
this is because they are characterized by timidity and great dread. Question: Upon what do they dwell? Answer: Either in hells, mountains, oceans, or wildernesses.

Within the ancestral temple, in the streets, alleys, and villages of the human world, in latrines, trees, flowers, fruits, roots, stalks, and medicinal herbs—everywhere they were present, yet people did not see them.
Even when people walked through their palaces and houses, the rooms did not collapse; it was as if ghosts passed through a person’s walls without piercing or damaging them.
A "spirit" (shen) is one who possesses power. Those of great power can move mountains and fill the seas; those of lesser power [can do the same].
Those who can conceal or manifest themselves and undergo transformations possess fortune; those who are majestic and numinous are called *shen* (spirits).

Those without fortune, who are base and possessing only a haunting presence, are called *gui* (ghosts). Furthermore, there are various distinctions such as poverty, wealth, nobility, and meanness, not limited to one kind, as listed below.

In the past, when I first resided at Mount Dinghu, several years prior, there was a man from Di Village at the foot of the mountain who went up the mountain to gather firewood and approached the front of my hermitage.
It was not far away; it was entirely composed of reeds and rushes. When that man first brought his blade down to cut one stalk, the sound was like a peal of thunder.
Terrified, he fell to the ground and implored the deity for forgiveness of his offense. The voice then ascended into the air, gradually fading away until it vanished.

Thus one knows that among plants and trees, regardless of their size, spirits and deities all dwell; they must not be recklessly felled, lest one invite calamity upon oneself. Therefore, the Buddha established these prohibitions.

"O Bhikṣu, you must not destroy any grasses or trees. If there is a necessity for their use on behalf of the Triple Gem, you should perform a sacrifice beneath the tree, recite verses from the Buddhist sūtras, and praise the merit of giving. You must wait until the middle of the night;
only when no unusual signs appear may you dispatch someone to cut them down the following day."
In the "Treatise on Resolving Doubts," Mouzi was asked: "The teachings of Buddhism state that when a person dies, they shall be reborn.
I do not believe this statement to be certain. Mouzi replied: "When a person is at the point of death, their family members climb onto the roof and call out to them.

Once they have died, whom are you calling? The questioner said: "I am calling their *hun* and *po* souls. Mouzi said: "If the spirit returns, one lives; if it does not return, where has the spirit gone?"
[The interlocutor] said: "It accomplishes the spirits and ghosts. Mouzi replied: "That is so. The soul-spirit is certainly not extinguished; it is only the body that decays and rots.
The body is like the roots and leaves of the five grains, while the soul-spirit is like the seeds and fruit of the five grains.
Roots and leaves must inevitably die, but how could the seeds and fruit ever come to an end? When one attains the Way, it is only the body that perishes. Laozi said: "What I..."
"It is because there is great affliction: it is because I have this body. Someone asked, "Whether one practices the Way or not, all must die. What difference is there?
Mouzi replied, "This is like someone who has not performed a single day of good yet asks for a reputation lasting a lifetime.

Those who possess the Way, though they die, their spirits return to the Hall of Blessings; those who do evil, once dead, their spirits shall suffer the calamity thereof. This is the distinction, O foolish man!"

Those who are ignorant are blind to accomplished matters, while the worthy and wise anticipate them before they have even sprouted. The difference between the Way and what is not the Way is like comparing gold to grass;

the difference between good and evil is like contrasting white with black. How could they not be different? Yet why do you say they are the same? (Mouzi, a contemporary of Emperor Xian of the Han dynasty, during the Chuping era).

The *Sūtra on the Original Arising of Heaven and Earth* states: At the time when the kalpa was first formed, there was a prince of a certain Brahmā-deva who was the father of the various spirits such as Maheśvara.
He practiced the austerities of a brahmacārin for twelve celestial years;
during six days of this period, he repeatedly cut his own flesh and blood and placed them into the fire. After the twelve years had passed, the Heavenly King descended and spoke to him.
The Son of Heaven asked, "What boon do you seek? She replied, "I seek to have a son.

The Heavenly King said, "The dharma for making offerings to a rishi consists of burning incense, sweet fruits, and the like. Why do you place meat and blood into the fire as if it were a sinful practice?"
"You have destroyed wholesome dharmas and delighted in committing evil deeds; therefore, you shall give birth to evil offspring who eat flesh and drink blood.
At that moment, eight great ghosts emerged from within the fire; their bodies were black as ink, their hair was yellow, and their eyes were red, emitting a great radiance.
The deities such as Maheśvara and others are born from these eight spirits;
for this reason, during these six days, the deities such as Maheśvara possess great power and afflict sentient beings. Among all the spirits, Maheśvara is the greatest.
Within each month, there are portions belonging to the sun; of Maheśvara’s month, there are four [such portions].
The solar divisions (*divasa-bhāga*) refer to the eighth, fourteenth, twenty-third, and twenty-ninth days. The remaining deities have two lunar-day divisions (*tithi-bhāga*) each:
the first day and sixteenth day of the month for one deity, and the second day and seventeenth day, as well as the fifteenth day, for the other.
The thirtieth day belongs to all deities; Maheśvara is the king of these divine kings.
Furthermore, because he receives many days, four days are counted as days of fasting (*upoṣadha*). The remaining days belong to all deities, and these too are counted as days of fasting.
For this reason, malevolent spirits and ghosts possess power on these six days. However, within the Buddha-dharma, there is no distinction between good and bad days.
In accordance with the temporal conditions of the days, the Buddha teaches sentient beings to observe the fast and precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*) in order to eliminate their afflictions.

(According to the sutras, observing the Eightfold Precept of the Fast on these six days brings merit that surpasses that of gods and humans, even leading to the attainment of Buddhahood; its blessings are inexhaustible. If one seeks the blessings and joys of the mundane world, among devas or humans, they too shall be accomplished. How could it merely be for the sake of escaping present calamities?

Therefore, it is said that in accordance with the temporal conditions of the days, he teaches the fast and precepts so that one may escape disasters and afflictions in the present, while ultimately perfecting the fruit of Buddhahood.)

The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "There are three kinds of hungry ghosts (*preta*): those without wealth, those with little wealth, and those with much wealth. Those without wealth are further divided into three:

those with flaming mouths, those with needle-mouths, and those with foul-smelling mouths. As for the hungry ghost with a flaming mouth: from within this ghost’s mouth, fierce flames constantly erupt, burning incessantly;

its body is like a scorched *tāla* tree. This is the bitter fruit summoned by extreme stinginess. Regarding the needle-mouthed [hungry ghost]: [the text continues with the description of the needle-mouthed preta].
As for the "Mouth-Demon" (Mukhakaṭapūtana): this demon has a belly as vast as a mountain, yet its mouth is like the eye of a needle.
Although it sees various kinds of exquisite food and drink, it cannot consume them; its hunger and thirst are unbearable. As for the "Stinking-Mouth Demon" (Pūtimukha):

from within the mouth of this demon, there constantly issues an extremely foul, putrid stench worse than excrement overflowing from a latrine door; its own malodorous breath permeates itself, and it is constantly vomiting into empty space.
They are perverse. Even when they encounter food or drink, they are unable to receive it. Tormented by hunger and thirst, they cry out wildly and run about in confusion.
There are also three types of those with little wealth: namely, Needle-Haired, Foul-Haired, and Great-Tumored. As for the Needle-Haired ghosts, the hair on their bodies is rigid, sharp, and piercing;
one cannot approach them. It drills into their own bodies and shoots outward through many others, like a deer struck by a poisoned arrow, trembling in terror.
When they run, if they encounter impurities, it slightly relieves their hunger and thirst. As for the "Foul-haired Ghosts" (Pūtimukha), the hair on these ghosts' bodies is exceedingly foul-smelling;

they are constantly defiled by putrid stench and rot. Their flesh and bones are steaming with filth, and as their entrails and bellies gush toward their throats, they vomit up bitter poisons that are difficult to endure as they afflict the body.
They pluck out their hair, wounding and tearing their skin, which further intensifies their suffering. When they encounter impurities, they obtain a small measure of relief from hunger and thirst.
As for the "Great Goiter Ghosts," it is said that due to the power of their evil karma, a great goiter grows upon the ghosts' throats like massive swellings.

Burning with fever, terrified, and afflicted by piercing pain, they tear at one another's flesh until putrid pus wells forth; they scramble together to eat it, obtaining only a small amount to satisfy their hunger. Those with many possessions suffer most.
There are also three types: those who seek sacrifice (*yajña*), those who seek abandonment (*utsarga*), and those of great power (*mahānubhāva*). Regarding those ghosts who seek sacrifice:

these ghosts constantly go to places of sacrificial offerings to partake of the offerings made by others. It is their natural state that they travel across different regions like birds soaring through the air, moving to and fro without obstruction.
Due to their former resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), they form this hope: "When my life comes to an end, my sons, grandsons, and descendants shall surely..."

They worship me with requisites and food through the power of their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), having been born among these hungry ghosts due to past virtuous causes and thereby eliciting this sacrificial offering.
Alternatively, there are those who in previous lives were by nature fond of their kin and acquaintances;

desiring to provide them all with abundant requisites, they accumulated precious wealth in an improper manner, harboring a heart of stinginess and being unable to practice generosity. By virtue of such evil karma, they are born here.

Among the hungry ghosts, while dwelling by the side of their former homes or in places of excrement and filth, they see their kinsmen and acquaintances who, out of remembrance, invite śramaṇas, brahmins, and the destitute to provide offerings for the sake of cultivating merit.
Upon seeing this, those ghosts develop the perception that the kinsmen and the wealth belong to themselves;
furthermore, clearly perceiving the present manifestation of the fruit of their own stinginess, they give rise to pure faith toward the field of merit, which continues in succession.

They are born and grow with a mind associated with renunciation (*tyāga*). By this, it becomes karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Through the power of this, they obtain an abundance of requisites.
As for those who desire to discard, these ghosts constantly wish to collect what others have discarded, such as vomit and leftover excrement, to serve as their food;
they too obtain an abundance. This is because, due to the fault of stinginess (*mātsarya*) in their previous lives, whenever they see a place where there is food and drink...

Impurity or emptiness: those who delight in impurity perceive emptiness, while those who delight in purity perceive impurity. This also arises from present merit; according to what is appropriate, each obtains an abundance of food, drink, and requisites.
These are the natural laws of their respective birthplaces, which differ from one another and cannot be logically deduced.

As for the reason why, it is as in the realm of hell, where the matter born of karmic maturation (vipākaja-rūpa) continues even after being interrupted; this is not the case in other realms. Regarding the [matter of]... (Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be incomplete in the source text.)
Within the human realm, there exist superior mindfulness, wisdom, the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and so forth, which do not exist in other realms.

For example, in the celestial realm, all requisites appear according to one's desires; such matters are the natural law (*dharmatā*) of those birthplaces, and one cannot seek a fixed measure within them.

Regarding the "powerful" hungry ghosts (*preta*), as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: among the hungry ghosts, those who are excellent are like the hungry ghosts possessing majestic power (*prabhāva*), whose forms...

Their appearance is upright and handsome, no different from that of the devas. Furthermore, all the deities of the five sacred peaks, the four great rivers, the mountains, and the seas are for the most part handsome;

this is what is meant by "beautiful. Among the ghosts, those who are ugly are the spirits lacking majesty and virtue; their forms and features are so base and loathsome they cannot be fully described.
Their jaws are like those of starving dogs, their hair is as disheveled as flying tumbleweeds, and their throats are as narrow and small as—

Their bodies are pierced by needles; their legs are like withered, rotten wood; their mouths constantly drool; their noses perpetually flow with tears; pus forms within their ears, and blood flows from their eyes.

All such conditions as these are called "great ugliness. Furthermore, regarding the sufferings among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), those ghosts who lack majesty and power are perpetually hungry and thirsty;
for many years they have not even heard the names of broth or water, so how could they ever encounter such sweet delicacies?

If they encounter a great river and wish to drink, it immediately transforms into a blazing torch; even if they manage to get it into their mouths, their bellies are instantly scorched and withered. For those of such a kind, how could it not be suffering?
As for the pleasures within the realm of ghosts, these belong to those possessing majesty and power: they are wealthy and abundant, with food and clothing provided spontaneously;
they wear celestial garments upon their bodies and partake of heavenly provisions; their forms are elegant and dignified, and they ride upon celestial carriages.
They gallop lightly, sporting at will; how are they any different from the gods? For such as these, how could it not be joyful? Question:
Since they possess such pleasure, they must be superior to humans. Why, then, do the sutras state that humans and ghosts belong to different realms (*gati*)?

Answer: The sutras state that ghosts and spirits are not equal to the human realm. Briefly stated, there are two reasons. First, regarding the manifestation of their karmic retribution, they do not equal humans. This is because...
Those ghosts and spirits lie hidden by day and roam at night; thus they do not equal humans. Second, being empty, timid, and full of fear, they do not equal humans.

Although they possess majestic power and virtue, because their retribution is base and inferior, they are constantly afraid of humans. Even if they encounter humans by day or night, they always yield the path and hide themselves in private. Question:
Since they are inferior to humans, how can they obtain such majestic power and virtue, and have a retribution equal to that of the heavens? Answer: Indeed.

Because in a previous life they practiced great acts of giving, they receive this majestic retribution; because in a previous life they were sycophantic, crooked, and insincere, they have entered this realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Furthermore, there are distinctions between the noble and the lowly: those who possess majestic power are called noble, while those who lack majestic power are called lowly.
Moreover, those who serve as kings of the ghosts are called noble, whereas those who are subject to their command are called lowly.

[They are] lowly. Question: What is the distinction between the wealthy and the poor? Answer: Those who possess majestic virtue (*vaibhava*) and have an abundance of food and clothing, with servants at their command, are called wealthy.
Those whose bodies are constantly in distress, who are perpetually subjected to forced labor, who do not even hear of coarse food, and for whom tattered clothing is hard to obtain, [are the poor].
Those of such a kind are called poor. Furthermore, there are those with majestic power who dwell in mountain valleys, or in mid-air, or by the seashore;
all possess palaces adorned with the seven treasures. They wear flower garlands upon their heads and are clothed in celestial garments;
they partake of ambrosial food and, like the sons of gods, ride upon elephants, horses, and chariots, each sporting at will. Their karmic rewards surpass [those of the former].
Among humans, all mountains and rivers, and all Buddhas, possess dwellings upon which they rely for their abode.

Those without majesty and virtue—such as wandering ghosts and those tormented by hunger and thirst—possess no dwellings at all; they either rely on burial mounds or take up residence in thickets and forests.
They dwell among grasses and trees, in rocky caves, or rely upon impure filth; they reside in secluded latrines or old cesspools. None possess houses or dwellings.
Their hair is disheveled and matted; they go naked without clothing; their complexions are withered and haggard, as they cover themselves with their own hair.
Carrying earthen vessels, they go about begging. These beings of inferior retribution are for the most part human in form, though some are lateral [animals].
Some have faces resembling pigs, while others resemble various kinds of evil birds and beasts, just like those depicted in murals on walls today.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* (*Zhuangyan lun*) states: The Buddha said, "In the past, there was a son of a great merchant leader named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, who went to sea to gather..."
Having returned from his journey, Ratna stayed apart from his companions.

Distraught at having lost them and tormented by hunger and thirst, he saw a city in the distance and, thinking there must be water there, went to its edge intending to seek a drink. However, this city was a city of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Upon entering the city, at a crossroads where many people would gather, he saw nothing at all; he cried out for water.
Water. When the various classes of *preta* heard the sound of this water, they all gathered there like clouds. "Who is compassionate enough to give us water?
cried these *pretas*, their bodies like charred pillars and their hair wrapped around them; they all came together with palms joined and spoke thus: "We pray you, grant us water.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said, "I too am driven by thirst and have come seeking water. At that time, the *preta*s—

When the hungry ghosts heard that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was tormented by thirst, they went of their own accord to seek water; their hopes were completely extinguished, and each let out a long sigh, saying: "Do you not know? This is the city of hungry ghosts.
Why do you seek water here? [Among hungry ghosts, there are two modes of birth: those born from a womb and those born through transformation.

As for those with "maturation-born" (*vipākaja*) form—that is, bodies produced as the fruit of karmic retribution—this is according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle) compiled by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, who annotated the Buddha’s sutras. Regarding the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they possess only great majesty.]

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "As for the great number of hungry ghosts (*preta*), there are thirty-six kinds. Because their causal actions were not equal, they differ."

The retributions they receive are each distinct: 1. The *pota* (cauldron) hungry ghosts: (This is because they were hired by others to kill living beings, and thus receive the retribution of being boiled in cauldrons of boiling water; or because they received deposits from others and refused to return them, hence they receive this retribution. 2. The needle-mouthed hungry ghosts:

(Because they hired people with wealth to carry out slaughtering, their throats are like the point of a needle, such that not even a drop of water can pass through. 3. The vomit-eating hungry ghosts: (These are those who urged their wives to give alms [to others].)

1. The Ghost Who Regrets Its Words: Because it was stingy with its wealth, it constantly eats its own vomit. 2. The Ghost That Eats Excrement (4): Because a woman deceived her husband and ate all the food and drink for herself, she is now a wicked wife to her husband and must constantly eat excrement and vomit.

3. The Ghost That Eats Food (5): Because it withheld grain from people, causing them to die, it now suffers the agony of being burned by fire and crying out in hunger and thirst. 4. The Ghost That Eats Breath (6): Because it consumed fine foods without sharing any with its wife or children, it now constantly suffers from hunger and thirst, obtaining only foul odors.

5. The Ghost That Eats Dharma (7): Because it sought wealth and profit while preaching the Dharma to others, its body is perpetually hungry and thirsty until its flesh is completely wasted away; only through receiving the Dharma from the Sangha does its life survive.

8. The *āśiviṣa* (Water-Drinking Ghost): Because they sold wine and defiled water to delude foolish people and caused them to fail in observing the precepts and fasts, they constantly suffer from parching thirst.

9. The *ākāṅkṣin* (Hope-Ghost): Because they engaged in buying and selling while disputing prices and used deception to take property, they constantly suffer from hunger and thirst; however, if offerings are made to their ancestral spirits, they immediately obtain food. 10. The *niṣṭhīvana-bhakṣaka* (Spittle-Eating Ghost): Because they deceived monastics with impure food, their bodies constantly suffer from hunger and thirst.

Constantly subjected to boiling and burning, they seek human saliva and also eat impurities. 11. Garland-eating Ghosts (*Mālā-bhakṣa*): In past lives, these beings stole flower garlands from Buddhas to adorn themselves. When people encountered misfortune, they offered such garlands as sacrifices; consequently, these ghosts obtain food by eating garlands.

(A "garland" [*mālā*] refers to flowers strung together. 12. Blood-eating Ghosts (*Rudhira-bhakṣa*): Due to killing living beings and consuming their blood, and failing to provide for their wives, they receive this retribution. Their bodies are smeared with blood, and only after a sacrifice is performed can they eat. 13. Flesh-eating Ghosts (*Māṃsa-bhakṣa*):

Because they cut the flesh from the bodies of sentient beings into pieces, weighed them, and engaged in deceitful buying and selling, they receive this retribution. They are full of guile and hideous, such that people loathe the sight of them.

14. The Fragrance-Eating Ghosts (*Gandharva*): Because they sold foul-smelling incense and took excessive payment for it, they now eat only the smoke of incense and subsequently suffer the retribution of poverty. 15. The Fast-Walking Ghosts:

If there are those who violate the precepts yet wear the Dharma robes, deceiving others to take their wealth under the pretext that it is for providing care to the sick, yet ultimately fail to give anything and instead consume it themselves; by receiving this retribution, they constantly eat impurities, which burn their own bodies. 16. The Opportunity-Watching Ghosts:

Because they plotted and deceived others to take their wealth and failed to cultivate meritorious deeds, they receive this retribution: fire issues from the hair on their bodies, and they subsist by consuming the vital energy and impurities of human beings.

17. The Ghosts of Darkness (Because they perverted the law to seek wealth and imprisoned people, their eyes could see nothing and their voices were constantly piteous; thus they undergo this state in dark places filled with venomous snakes, suffering as if cut by knives). 18.

The Ghosts of Great Power (Because they stole the property of others and gave it to evil associates instead of bestowing it upon fields of merit, they receive this retribution: possessing great power and supernatural faculties, they are nonetheless subject to much affliction). 19.

The Blazing Ghosts (Because they breached cities to plunder and slaughtered the common people, they receive this retribution: wailing and crying out with fire blazing from their entire bodies; after death they fall into hell, and if later they obtain human form, they are constantly robbed and plundered).

20. The Ghost Who Waits for the Vulnerabilities of Infants (Because of killing infants, they gave rise to a mind of great rage; consequently, they receive this retribution, constantly waiting for human vulnerabilities and being able to harm infants). 21.

The Ghost of Lustful Desire (Because of coveting wealth through lust and failing to bestow it upon fields of merit, they receive this retribution; they roam among humans, engaging in sexual union with them and falsely manifesting as monsters in order to seek their livelihood). 22.

The Ghost of the Ocean Islands (Because of traveling through wildernesses and seeing those suffering from illness, yet deceiving people to fraudulently seize their property, they are born on ocean islands to undergo the sufferings of cold and heat, which are ten times greater than the sufferings of humans). 2.

13. The Ghosts of the Staff-Bearers of King Yama (Because in a previous life they attended upon kings and ministers and exclusively practiced violence and evil, they receive this retribution; they serve as the king’s attendants and act as staff-bearers). 24.

The Ghosts that Eat Small Children (Because they used incantations and arts to deceive and plunder people’s wealth, and slaughtered pigs and sheep, they fell into hell after death. Subsequently receiving this retribution, they constantly eat small children). 25.

The Ghosts that Eat Vital Essence (Because they feigned themselves friends, saying "I shall protect you," yet caused others to lose their lives in battle, failing to provide protection at all, they therefore receive this [retribution]).
26. Rākṣasa Ghosts: (Because they killed living beings for great feasts, they receive this retribution of being scorched by the fires of hunger. 27. Fire-Eating Ghosts:

(Because they gave impure food to practitioners, they fall into this retribution, constantly eating filth. 29. Wind-Eating Ghosts: (Because when they saw renunciants coming to beg, they promised...)

30. The *Kukūla* (Charcoal-Eating) Pretas: Because they formerly presided over prisons and denied food and drink to those incarcerated, they now receive this retribution, constantly suffering from hunger and thirst as if in the torments of hell.

31. The *Visha-bhakṣaka* (Poison-Eating) Pretas: Because they formerly administered poisoned food to cause people to lose their lives, they fell into hell; subsequently, having emerged as pretas, they are perpetually hungry and constantly consume poison.

32. The Ghosts of the Wilderness (*Āṭavika*): Because they constructed lakes, ponds, and wells in the wilderness for others, yet later maliciously breached them to leave travelers parched and exhausted, they receive this retribution;

they constantly suffer from hunger and thirst, and fire burns their bodies. 33. The Ghosts Who Eat Ashes and Soil in Cemeteries (*Śmaśānabhasmabhakṣaka*): Because they stole flowers belonging to the Buddha, sold them to sustain their lives, they receive this retribution.

34. Ghosts dwelling under trees: Because they saw people planting trees to provide shade for others, yet with an evil mind they cut them down to take the wood for their own use, they fell into the midst of trees and undergo the suffering of cold and heat.

because they partake of offerings made at crossroads, they obtain food to sustain themselves. 36. Māra ghosts: Because they practiced deviant paths and did not believe in the true and correct [Dharma], they fell as demon-ghosts and constantly destroy the wholesome dharmas of others. If...

They are constantly tormented by hunger and thirst, enduring great suffering; they may only drink the rain from heaven, catching it with their upturned beaks, and are not permitted to drink anything else.

first, slight evil in physical conduct; second, slight evil in verbal conduct; and third, slight evil in mental conduct.
Fourth, they are stingy and full of greed; fifth, they give rise to improper evil; sixth, they are sycophantic, crooked, and envious; seventh, they give rise to false views;

Due to these karmic causes, they are born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are some hungry ghosts who, in previous lives, were malicious in speech and delighted in..."

The Dharma Master An Qing (styled Shigao) of Luoyang, China, was the son of the principal consort of the King of Anxi in South India.
He was the Crown Prince. From his youth, he was renowned for his filial conduct. His intellect and aspirations were sharp and keen; he applied himself with diligence to learning.

Whether it be foreign scriptures, the seven luminaries and the five elements, medical prescriptions and esoteric arts, or even the languages of birds and beasts, there was nothing he did not master and comprehend.

Once, while traveling, he saw a flock of swallows and suddenly said to his companions, "The swallows say that someone will soon arrive with food. Shortly thereafter, someone indeed arrived. The assembly all marveled at this;

Later, his nature became prone to anger; after his life ended, he was destined to receive an evil form. "If I had the power," he thought, "I would certainly have delivered you.

In his anger, he was thus the manifestation of his former intention. He then extended his neck to receive the blade, his countenance showing no sign of fear.
The bandits then killed him. Spectators filled the road, all of whom were struck with awe at this extraordinary marvel.

This divine consciousness returned as the crown prince of the King of Anxi—this is none other than the present-day Shigao. After Shigao had traveled through China to propagate the teachings of the sutras, his work was complete.

During the final years of Emperor Ling’s reign, when the Guanzhong and Luoyang regions were in turmoil, he took up his monk’s staff and traveled to Jiangnan, saying, "I shall pass through Mount Lu to deliver my former fellow student.

Dharma Master Tansui of Baima Monastery in Heyin, Jin, once heard a voice at midnight suddenly knocking at his door, saying, "I wish to invite the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma for the ninety-day retreat.
Tansui did not consent; however, when the invitation was pressed, he finally agreed. Yet, he remained in the midst of sleep.
Upon waking, he realized that his body was within the shrine of the White Horse Mound deity, together with a disciple.
From then on, he went there in secret every day, and no one else knew of it. Later, when a monk from the monastery passed before the shrine, he saw two high seats; Sui was seated on the northern one.
The disciples were in the south. They heard the sound of someone preaching and also smelled the fragrance of a wondrous incense.
Consequently, both monastics and laypeople spread the word, some claiming it was a divine marvel. At the end of the summer retreat, the deity bestowed upon them one white horse and five white sheep.
There were ninety rolls of silk. When the prayers for blessings were finished, they each departed.
