Looking back, she sighed and said, "The waters of the sea may run dry, and Mount Sumeru may be toppled, but that superior person maintains a will as firm and steadfast as ever. Later, [she returned]...
In the third year of the Long’an era, he traveled to the Western Regions together with Faxian.
The Dharma Master Tanyong of Mount Lu stood eight chi tall and possessed a heroic bearing that surpassed ordinary men. He retired to Mount Lu to serve Huiyuan as his teacher;
he had extensively studied both Buddhist and secular scriptures and was devoted to the propagation of the Dharma, undaunted by fatigue or hardship. Thereupon, at...
To the southwest of the mountain, he established a separate thatched dwelling where he and his disciple Tanguo cultivated their thoughts within the gates of dhyāna.
Once, at one time, Tanguo dreamed of a mountain deity who requested to receive the five precepts. Tanguo said, "My master is here; you may go to him to seek and receive them."
A short while later, Daoyong saw a man wearing a single-layered garment, whose bearing was upright and elegant, followed by about thirty attendants.
The man requested to receive the five precepts. Because Faguang had previously received a dream, Daoyong knew he was a mountain deity. He then preached the Dharma and conferred the precepts upon him.

The deity offered foreign-style spoons and chopsticks as a religious gift (*dakṣiṇā*), prostrated himself, took his leave, and vanished in an instant. (The above two accounts are from the *Liang Gao seng zhuan*).
Zhu Tansui. During the Taiyuan era, when he was over twenty years old, he was fair-skinned and handsome.
He was a common secular-style śramaṇa who once passed before the temple of Qingxi and entered the shrine to look around.
That evening, upon returning home, he dreamed of a woman who came to him and said, "You shall come to serve as the deity within my temple. Tansui asked, "Who are you? The woman replied, "I am..."
Qingxi Zhonggu died after being ill for about one month. As she was dying, she said to her young fellow-disciples, "I have no merit, yet I have committed no great sins.
After death, I shall become the deity of the Qingxi Temple. When you pass by, you may go to visit me."
After he had died, when the young men arrived, they greeted him with inquiries after his well-being; their voices sounded just as they had in the past.
Upon parting, he said, "I have not heard the chanting of the scriptures for a long time; I long to hear it once more. His companion, Huijin, then performed a chant for him.

As he continued to sing praises, [the deceased] spoke again, saying, "At a parting on a crossroads, there is still a sense of sorrow; how much more so this separation, where body and spirit are divided!"
He sighed deeply over the profound darkness [of his fate]. How can such feelings be described?
Thereupon, he sobbed uncontrollably, and all the youths present likewise shed tears (from the *Xu Soushen ji*).
Shifeng: Mount Chicheng. Dhyāna Master Tamlan (also known as Tanyou) traveled to Shan during the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty and stayed at Mount Shicheng.
Later, he rested at Mount Chicheng in Shifeng. Seeing a place where the woods and springs were pure and expansive, he took up residence there.
Dozens of fierce tigers crouched before Lan, yet Lan continued to recite the sutras as usual. One tiger fell fast asleep; Lan—
He struck the tiger’s head with his *ruci* (wish-fulfilling) staff and rebuked it, saying, "Why do you not listen to the sutra?
After several days had passed, he suddenly saw a man several *zhang* tall who called out to Lan, ordering him to leave. He also encountered various strange birds and beasts who tried to frighten Lan;

however, seeing that Lan remained serene and self-possessed, they knelt and paid him homage, saying, "Since the Dharma Master possesses such great majesty and virtue, you have come to dwell upon this mountain."
The disciple reasoned from this point and offered himself [to the Master]. Zhūqī was the maternal uncle of the King; he had now gone to Mount Wēixiāng to join him.
Huìlán said, "I, a poor monk, have been searching the mountains and hope to meet you. Why do we not dwell together? The spirit said, "It is not that I, your disciple, am unwilling to do so.
However, my subordinates have not yet become familiar with the transformation of the Dharma and are difficult to control at present. When people from afar come and go, they might perhaps..."

[The deity] intruded upon [him]. "The ways of humans and spirits differ," [the deity] said, "and for this reason I am departing. Lan asked, "Who were you originally? How long have you resided here? And where do you intend to go?
The spirit replied, "I am the son of the Emperor of Summer. I have dwelt on this mountain for over two thousand years.
As they parted, he took Lan’s hand and presented him with three caskets of fragrant incense. Thereupon, sounding drums and blowing horns, he ascended upon the clouds and departed.
He departed. Three years later, he suddenly heard the muffled sound of chariots and cavalry, with attendants filling the mountain peaks.

Suddenly, there appeared a man wearing a *zhè* (cap), who announced himself as King Zhūqī. He was followed by twenty-three people, including his wife and children, all of whom were of upright appearance, surpassing anything seen in the world.
Upon arriving at Hui-lan’s dwelling, they exchanged greetings; Lan then asked, "Where does the *dānapati* reside?"

"Where do you reside? he asked. He replied, "In Weishang Mountain, Anle County. Having long been familiar with your reputation through hearsay, I have now come with my family to seek refuge and request the precepts of returning home (the *śaraṇa-gamana*).
Senglan immediately conferred them upon him. Once the dharma had been received, [the donor] offered a reward of ten thousand coins and two jars of honey, then took his leave and departed.

Immediately, the sound of whistling flutes and blowing horns was heard, their resonance shaking the mountains and valleys. Senglan’s assembly of over ten meditation practitioners all [witnessed this].
[According to] the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*:
She was the wife of Wang Ningzhi of Langya and the daughter of Lady Xie, the consort of the Jin General of the Left.
She had frequently lost two sons; her grief was so excessive that she wept for many years as if dwelling in the midst of the ultimate calamity. Later, she suddenly saw the two...
The sons returned together, all bound in shackles and fetters. They consoled their mother, urging her to be patient and self-restrained, saying, "We are both guilty;

if you will show us compassion, you should perform meritorious deeds on our behalf. Thereupon, her grief subsided somewhat, and she applied herself diligently to virtuous works (*from the Mingxiang ji*).
Hu Maohui of Huainan was able to see ghosts; though he did not like seeing them, he could not stop himself from doing so.

Later, while traveling to Yangzhou, he returned to the east of Liyang City. There was a shrine there, and it happened that the local people were about to perform a sacrifice with a shaman and a priest.
In a mere moment, a group of ghosts shouted to one another, "The high official is coming! Each of them fled the shrine in haste. As they looked back, they saw [Hu Maohui].

Two śramaṇas entered the shrine. The various ghosts, two by two and three by three, embraced one another and waited from within the grass beside the shrine, spying upon the śramaṇas with great trepidation.
After a short while, once the śramaṇas had departed, the ghosts all returned to the shrine;
they were moved to faith and subsequently served the Buddha with sincere devotion (from the *Xu Soushen Ji*).
Qin II:
Yao Chang. Yao Chang was a Qiang of the Western Rong. Following the defeat of Fu Jian, Chang—having been a veteran general—led his own tribesmen in rebellion.
When Jian fought him and was unsuccessful, he was subsequently strangled to death by Chang. Chang then usurped the throne.

He established the capital at Yongguan and changed the name of Chang’an to Cháng’ān. After he had reigned for eight years, Fu Jian led a host of ghost-soldiers that entered the palace during broad daylight;
they pierced his private parts, and after he bled several pecks of blood, he passed away (as recorded in the *Tongzai*).
At Gaoping, Li Xian’s domestic slave Jian was traveling to Shitougang when he suddenly encountered a man who said, “My wife had an illicit affair with another man and was subsequently killed by him.
I now wish to take revenge; can you assist me? The slave followed his instructions.
Indeed, a person appeared, and the ghost seized him by the head and called out to the slave for a hand, causing the victim to fall to the ground. That person died on the way.
The ghost gave the slave one thousand coins and a piece of dark-blue silk *zǒngpáo* robe, instructing him:
"This robe was given to you by Ding of the West Gate Market; you may wear it yourself, but do not sell it. (From the *Míngxiáng jì*).

Sima Wenxuan of Henei in the Song dynasty was a considerable believer in the Buddha-dharma. In the ninth year of the Yuanjia era, while observing the mourning period for his mother, he also lost his younger brother.
On the morning of the full moon, he suddenly beheld his brother’s physical form upon the spirit seat, appearing no different than on ordinary days; he looked around in distress and sighed.
"Alas! He was begging for food and drink. Wen then attempted to speak with him, saying: "During your lifetime, you practiced the ten wholesome deeds.
If it is as the sutras say, you ought to have been reborn in heaven. If you were in the human realm, why have you been born among these hungry ghosts?

He looked up and down in deep reflection, remaining silent and without reply. That very evening, Wen saw his younger brother in a dream, who said: "The merit of the good I cultivated during my life..."

He was reborn in heaven. "The ghost at the spirit bed is merely a demonic apparition; it is not my true self. Fearing that you, my elder brother, might be suspicious or alarmed, I have come to inform you.
The next morning, Prince Wenxuan invited monks to recite the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* and ordered men to strike and bind the entity.
The ghost then fled beneath the bed and further ran outside the door, its form becoming somewhat hideous and loathsome, causing the entire family to be struck with terror.
Terrified, he scolded and drove him away. The ghost said, "I am merely a hungry beggar. After several days had passed, he finally departed.

Shortly thereafter, by the head of his mother’s spirit-couch, there appeared a ghost with reddish skin and a very tall, robust body. Wenxuan’s eldest son, Xiaozu, conversed back and forth with him, answering all questions exhaustively.
At first, Wenxuan was afraid, but in the end he gradually became accustomed to it; the ghost, in turn, grew increasingly familiar with him.
They were so familiar with him that in their daily lives and comings and goings, they were almost like members of the same family. At that time, the news spread throughout the capital;

those who came and went to see them filled the streets and alleys, their tracks overlapping one another. At that moment, there was a monk at Nanlin Temple who was conversing with a śramaṇa from Lingwei Temple about ghosts;
they spoke with great intimacy, and the ghost said: "In a former life, I was once a person of noble rank, but because I committed many evils, I have suffered [this retribution]."
Before his report was finished, he was indeed reborn as this ghost. In the Year of the Tiger, four hundred classes of ghosts were spreading a great pestilence;

those who were destined to suffer the calamity were spared from harming the practitioners of the Way. However, those who met with untimely deaths were extremely numerous, and many innocent, virtuous people were wrongly implicated.
Therefore, I have come to oversee this matter. The monks offered him food, but the ghost said, "I already have my own provisions; I cannot accept it."
"This is food. She said, "The spirits possess much knowledge. From where did I come when I was born? For what reason have I become a practitioner of the Way?
He replied, "I came from among humans. The causes and conditions for my leaving the household life are due to my original vows. She asked about the various states of existence, death, and rebirth;

he answered her briefly on all points, and his responses were consistently verified by spiritual efficacy. As the details are numerous, I shall not record them here in full. She said, "The paths of humans and ghosts are distinct."
"Since you do not seek food, why have you stayed so long? The ghost replied, "In this place there is a woman who ought to be captured;
however, because she is diligent in observing the precepts, she is difficult to obtain. It is for this reason that I have delayed these past days.
I feel no small amount of shame for having disturbed my host. From now on, I shall not appear before you very often. Later, when someone went to look, they heard only [her voice].
He spoke thus. It was the tenth year of the Yuanjia era. On the twenty-eighth day of the third month, he said to Wénxuān, "I have come for a brief stay.
Since you have mobilized your entire household to cultivate merit, and your fear is so great, how can I remain long? Xiàozǔ said:

"I grant you permission to stay as a guest. Why have you taken over the spirit altar of one who has already passed away? He replied, "The deceased in your household each belong to their own respective altars.

This seat is set out empty; therefore, I am merely staying here temporarily. Thereupon, he took his leave. In the third year of the Tianqi era, when Zhan was thirteen years old, there was Liang Nianbin in Magang Village, Shunde County.

He lived together with his younger brother and son-in-law in Dingwu Lane within the city walls of Yangjiang. They all served as naval soldiers. At that time, several hundred pirate ships from Fujian approached the mouth of the Yangjiang River, and the troops of the five counties were mobilized.

He led an expedition by ship. Having lost discipline, he was killed along with several thousand others who drowned. On the following day, the army returned, but Bin and his companions were missing. Bin’s wife immediately requested a Daoist priest to take a ritual banner-pole out of the city to the riverbank to summon their souls.

As the wife held the banner-pole, she said it felt exceedingly heavy. The Daoist priest said, "The souls should return on the first seven-day period. Bin’s daughter sifted ashes beneath the spirit altar, enclosing the area tightly with mats to verify the truth of the matter. Early the next morning at dawn, I went to observe; I saw that the ashes were entirely goat tracks.

The traces [of this] were as follows: A Daoist said, "He has been cast down into the realm of animals. The following year, the three men, including Bin, returned from Fujian, begging for food along the way. From this, one can verify that ghosts are often deceitful and flattering, falsely manifesting various transformations of form in order to seek food and drink.

However, once a person has died, their spirit enters the six realms of existence. Those born in the heavens possess clothing and food provided spontaneously; yet, they hear the foul vapors of the five grains and mixed foods of the human world, which rise and permeate them for four hundred thousand *li*.

Those born as humans or animals have their physical form and spirit separated upon entering the womb, so how could they return? Only those in the single realm of ghosts can come and go, yet even they are subject to supervision and cannot act with freedom. Even when the place of rebirth has not yet been fixed, their intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body sustains itself only through fragrance and does not consume solid food;

furthermore, they do not know where they are headed. Only when the retribution of karmic conditions is determined do they proceed to the place of birth and take up residence in a womb. Nowadays, when the secular world establishes spirit tablets, these are mostly ghosts seeking food who falsely assume the forms of their kin, or perhaps spirits that follow Daoist practitioners.

Shamans and spirit-mediums are *chil-liang* demons who seek only their own sustenance; they cause wives, children, and relatives to experience either joy or terror, giving rise to groundless grief and suffering.

In Chang’an, there was a man named Wang Hu. Several years after his uncle had died, in the twenty-third year of the Yuanjia era, the uncle suddenly manifested his form and returned home to reprimand Hu for his lack of filial diligence and for neglecting the management of the household affairs. He punished Hu with five strokes of the cane. Onlookers and neighbors—
The villagers all heard his voice and the sound of his staff, and they even saw the marks left by the staff, yet they could not see his form;
only Hu was able to approach him directly. Shu said to Hu, "I ought not to die; the Way of the Spirits requires me to calculate the registers of the various ghosts."
"I am now accompanied by a great multitude of officials and soldiers; I fear they might alarm or harm the villages and hamlets, which is why I have not brought them forward.

The Hu man also saw a vast multitude of ghosts, clamoring and bustling as if outside a village. Suddenly, the uncle took his leave and said, "I shall return briefly again next year on the seventh day of the seventh month.
I wish to take you with me to travel through the dark paths, so that you may know the retribution of sin and merit. There is no need for [further concern]."

"It is a waste of effort. If your intention does not cease, it will simply result in your coming for tea. When the appointed time arrived, he indeed returned and said to Hu’s family members, "I have now finished my tour of the Hu lands;
I shall soon send you back. There is no need for worry. Hu then immediately lay down upon his bed.
Everything became indistinct, as if vanishing. At this, the barbarian intended to travel north to tour the various mountains and witness all manner of spirits and monsters.

Finally, he arrived at Mount Songgao, where the various spirits encountered him and prepared a feast for him. The other flavors were no different from those of the mundane world, but the ginger was exceptionally crisp and delicious.
The barbarian wished to break off some to take back with him, but the people around him laughed at him and said, "You may eat this here; you must not take it away."
Upon his return, Hu saw a place where the buildings were magnificent and spacious, and the curtains and mats were exquisitely arranged; two young monks resided there.

Hu approached them, and the two monks provided him with various fruits, betel nuts, and other refreshments. Hu wandered through the site for a long time, fully observing the retributions of sin and merit, as well as suffering and joy.
He then took his leave and returned home. His uncle said to Hu, "Since you have already realized that goodness is worthy of pursuit..."
He said, "It would be more appropriate for you to practice while remaining at home. The Venerable Baitu (Pindola) is of such refined and lofty conduct that he is worthy to be served as a teacher.
After Hu received this advice, he went to the monastery and saw a young monk from Mount Song who was among the assembly of traveling students.
Hu was greatly astonished, as he had been separated from his uncle for a long time; he asked when he had arrived. The two monks replied, "We have resided in this temple since our youth."
"I do not recall ever having known you in the past. Why, then, do you speak of our meeting at Mount Song? The two monks replied, "You are mistaken; how could such a thing have occurred?
The next day, the two monks departed without further ado. Hu then informed the various śramaṇas of the matter, recounting what he had seen at Mount Song in the past.
The assembly was all struck with wonder and immediately went in search of the two monks, but they were nowhere to be found.

Wherever he was, people realized he was a divine monk. Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, a monk from Chang’an named Tanshuang came to travel in the Jiangnan region and recounted these matters in full detail.

(The śramaṇa Tanshi walked barefoot through mud and water without being soiled; because the color of his feet remained exceptionally white, people of the time called him "Bai-zu Ālán" [the White-footed Hermit]. He was held in great reverence by the Wei barbarians.)
In the fourth year of the Yuanjia era, Zheng Xianzhi, the Palace Secretary (Shangshu Poye) of Yongyang, followed the Imperial Carriage on a tour of the capital and arrived at the capital city.
That evening, he died suddenly. He then leaned against his funeral couch and spoke to his family members, saying: "My lifespan has long since been exhausted, and I should have passed away long ago.

However, thanks to my respectful faith in the Buddha-dharma during recent years—releasing living beings and practicing almsgiving—I have been able to extend my life for several [years] through this merit."

It has been many years. Now, the retribution for deeds in the hidden and manifest realms is as certain as a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound. You ought to cast aside worldly affairs and elevate your mind toward the Great Teaching.
At that time, many of the eminent and noble heard this (the above three accounts are from the *Mingbao ji*).
At Waguan Temple in the capital was Dharma Master Huiguo, a native of Wuzhou. At the beginning of the Song dynasty, he traveled to the capital and resided at Waguan Temple.
Once, in front of the latrine, he saw a ghost who paid his respects to Huiguo and said: "In the past, I served as the *karmadāna* for the assembly of monks.

Because I was slightly lacking in accordance with the Dharma, I fell into the realm of the dung-eating ghosts. Your Reverence’s virtue has always been lofty and brilliant, and you are also compassionate."
I pray that you will provide a means to rescue me. Formerly, there were three thousand coins buried beneath the roots of a persimmon tree;
I pray that you take them for the sake of merit. Guo immediately informed the assembly and had them excavated, whereupon they indeed obtained the three thousand coins.

He used them to commission a copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and to provide offerings for a vegetarian feast. Later, he saw this ghost in a dream, who said: "I have already attained rebirth as a superior being. Great!
This was superior to [the accounts of] former days (as recorded in the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan*).
Wang Wenming, during the end of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, served as the Magistrate of Jiang’an. His wife had been ill for a long time.

One day, his daughter prepared rice gruel for her mother outside; when it was nearly finished cooking, it turned into blood. She discarded it and made it again, yet it was just as it had been before. This happened twice.

3. Shortly thereafter, his mother passed away. Later, while his children were weeping before her shrine, they suddenly saw their mother lying upon the funeral couch, her appearance as if she were alive.
The children wailed with deep emotion, and she vanished instantly. Previously, Wenming had favored a handmaid of his wife’s household;
when she became pregnant and was about to give birth, he sent her to guard the house on the day of his wife’s burial, while the rest of the people all went to the cemetery.
As the military units were just setting out, his wife manifested her form and entered the house to beat a maidservant.
Later, when his daughters had finished preparing a meal for their father—having slaughtered a chicken and finished cleaning it—the chicken suddenly leaped up, held its head high, and crowed loudly.
Wenming died shortly thereafter, and his sons followed in succession in death (from the *Shuyiji*).

He Donghai (styled He Dazhi) was a Grand Minister of Agriculture during the Song dynasty. He did not believe in the scriptures and teachings of the Dharma and frequently committed acts of cruelty and harm.
During the Yongchu era, he fell ill and beheld a ghost of immense stature and vigor, with the head of an ox and the body of a man, holding an iron fork in its hand and guarding him day and night.
Distraught and terrified, he had Daoist masters perform incantations, talismans, seals, and registers, and employed every means of exorcism and protection; yet [the affliction] persisted.
He saw [the apparition] as before. Having heard that the śramaṇa Huìyì was ill, he went to visit him.
Tánzhī recounted what he had seen. Huì said, "This is the ox-headed *āpāra* (attendant of hell). Sin and merit are never obscured; they are summoned only by the actions of men.
If you can turn your mind toward the Dharma, this ghost will vanish of its own accord. Tánzhī remained stubborn and unrepentant. Shortly thereafter, he died (*from the Míngxiáng jì*).
Zhang Yi was whipped during the Taishi era; his wounds were so painful that someone instructed him to burn the remains of a ghost from a dead person and apply them as an ointment.
He hired a young boy from the same household to climb a ridge and fetch a skull, which he burned and applied to his sores.
That night, there was a fire in the hearth inside the room that burned the boy’s hand; furthermore, something in the air pressed down on the boy’s head and thrust it into the fire, shouting at him.
He said, "Why did you burn my head? Now I shall repay you with this fire. The boy cried out loudly, "Zhang Yi burned you!
He replied, "If you had not taken it and given it to Zhang Yi, how could Zhang Yi have burned it? He pressed down on the boy's head for a long time.

The hair was completely consumed, and the skin and flesh were scorched and rotted away before he finally abandoned it. Yi was greatly terrified; he took the remaining bones, buried them back in their original place, and offered wine and meat as libations.
Thereafter, no further calamities or anomalies occurred. (From *Shuji ji*. [Question]: When a person dies, their soul enters one of the six realms of existence.

How can it remain to guard these withered bones? [Answer]: This [soul] has already fallen into the realm of ghosts. Having received no offerings from humans and having no other place to rely upon, it guards the withered bones out of resentment. How could it possibly burn the ghost [who buried it]?)
In Xiangcheng, there was a man named Li Yi. His father was a person who did not believe in demons or the occult. There was a residence that had long been considered ominous and unfit for habitation;
anyone who lived there invariably died. The father nevertheless purchased it and moved in. For many years he enjoyed peace and security, and his descendants flourished.
He was appointed as a Second-Rank Official (*erqianshi*) and was about to move his household to his post. Upon his departure, he requested a banquet for his relatives, both internal and external.
Just as he was about to set out, his father said to him: "Does the world truly have such things as fortune and misfortune?

This residence has long been said to be ill-omened, yet since I lived here for many years, all was peaceful and auspicious, and I have even attained this official promotion. Where, then, are the ghosts? From this day forward, it shall be..."
"This is an auspicious dwelling. Those who reside here have no cause for dissatisfaction in their hearts. Having finished speaking, he went to the latrine.
After a short while, he saw something within the wall, about the size of a rolled mat and five feet high, which was a brilliant white.

He returned, took a knife, and struck it, cutting it in two. It immediately transformed into two people. He struck them again crosswise, and they became four people. They then snatched the knife away and turned to strike him back.

Li was killed. [The executioners] brought him to his seat and slaughtered his sons and younger brothers; anyone with the surname Li was inevitably put to death, while those of different surnames suffered no harm.
Yi was still an infant in his mother’s arms. When the household realized the danger, the wet nurse carried him out through the back gate and hid him in another family’s home;
thus, he alone escaped with his life. Yi’s courtesy name was Jingzhen, and he rose to the rank of Governor of Xiangdong (as recorded in the *Xu Soushen Ji*).

In Qi, there was the Dharma Master Hongming of Kuaiji. During the Yongming era, he resided at Yunmen Temple, making the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the performance of prostrations and repentance his primary practice.
Every morning, his water jar would fill itself; these were truly celestial youths serving as his attendants. He also moved a tiger [to leave].

He entered the room and prostrated himself before the bed; after a long time, he departed. Later, he saw a young boy come to listen to the sutra, who said: "In the past, I was a śrāmaṇera at this monastery.
Because I stole food from the monks' kitchen, I have now fallen into a latrine. Hearing you, Venerable Sir, reciting the sutra, I have exerted myself to come and listen.

I pray that you will provide a skillful means to help me hope to escape this karmic burden. The next day, [the Master] preached the Dharma for him; once he had attained understanding, the boy vanished. Afterwards, on the mountain...
The spirit came to cause him distress; Ming then seized it, bound it with his waist-cord, and the spirit, having offered its apologies, was released.
Consequently, the affliction was forever severed (from the *Liang Dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Master Chanchao of Lingyuan: Toward the end of the Jianyuan era, he resided at Mount Lingyuan in Qiantang.

One night, he suddenly heard the sound of wind and thunder and saw a man approach holding a ceremonial tablet, identifying himself as Yan Zhen and Chen Tong. After a short while, another person arrived;

his appearance was exceptionally dignified, and he was accompanied by a retinue of attendants. He descended from his seat to pay respects and introduced himself as a disciple, stating that he resided at...
Seven *li* away, Master Ren was governing this region. When Master Cheng arrived, he was granted the blessing of sustaining all living beings by the Master.

However, the people of Fuyang had, without cause, excavated the foot of Lushan Mountain to make bricks, thereby destroying the dragon’s dwelling. The dragons were collectively incensed and vowed not to send rain for three hundred days;

more than one hundred days have now passed, and the planting of crops has been permanently abandoned. Since your virtue and Way already penetrate the divine, I entreat you— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly. This translation reflects the available portion.)
The Master went to the dragon’s abode to bring moisture and nourishment to the common people. Sengchao said, "To raise clouds and send down rain is the power of this donor;
what can I possibly do? The spirit said, "I and my followers are only able to raise clouds, but we cannot send down rain. That is why I have come to invite you. Sengchao consented.
He then traveled five li to the south, reaching Mount Chiting, where he recited incantations and offered prayers for the dragon from afar.

The Dharma. When night fell, a group of nāgas took human form and came to pay their respects to Hui-chao, requesting to receive the Three Refuges. At the hour of *bū* (the late afternoon), it suddenly began to rain heavily.
He immediately went to Linquan Temple; hearing of his arrival, the Magistrate of Lin sent a boat to welcome him.
That very day, Hui-chao fled back to Lingyuan (as recorded in the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan* and the *Tong Dai*).
At the White Stupa Temple (Baitasi) in Yangzhou, the śramaṇa Daochang was in charge of the monastic property. He misappropriated these goods for his own personal use.

Suddenly, several officials from the underworld entered his room during the day, dragged Daochang to the ground, and were about to cut off his neck. Startled, Daochang cried out and begged for his life.

The official spoke in a stern voice, saying, "If you return all the assets and wealth belonging to the monastery to the Sangha, we shall release you and let you live. Daochang knelt and struck his head in prostration.

He replied, "I dare not disobey your command. He immediately struck the bell to assemble the congregation; they all gave up their robes and clothing to fashion an image and prepare a vegetarian feast.

Three days later, the official from the underworld arrived again and, seeing that Daochang possessed only a single bowl and a single robe, departed without speaking. From then on, Daochang exerted himself in diligent cultivation and ultimately achieved both clarity of insight and virtuous conduct.
At Mount She in Langya, there was the Dharma Master Fadu. Toward the end of the Song dynasty, he traveled to the capital.

There was a man of high virtue from Qi Commandery named Sengshao, who maintained his traces beyond the mundane world and lived in seclusion on Mount She. He held Fadu in esteem, treating him with the courtesy due to a teacher or a friend. When [Sengshao] passed away...
He donated his residence to establish Qixia Temple and invited [Seng]du to dwell there. Previously, there had been Daoist practitioners who wished to use the temple grounds as a retreat;

those who stayed there invariably died. Even after it was later converted into a temple, it remained frequently haunted by terrors. Once [Seng]du himself took up residence, all the malevolent spirits ceased their disturbances.
After about a year had passed, there suddenly arose the sounds of men, horses, drums, and horns. Suddenly, a person appeared holding a paper name-card.
The messenger said, "Jin Shang’s appearance is most elegant and his retinue is strictly disciplined. Once he has completed his formal salutations, he will speak:

'I, your disciple, have been the master of this mountain for over seven hundred years. The Way of the spirits follows its own laws; no worldly things can interfere. All those who have previously sought refuge here...'"
"Perhaps it was not truly authentic; thus death and illness followed one after another, which was also his fate. The Dharma Master is one to whom all turn for his moral virtue.
I respectfully offer this [temple] to serve him, and I pray that he will receive the five precepts so that we may forever establish a karmic bond for future lives.

Sengdu said, "The paths of humans and spirits are distinct; there is no room for them to be mutually compromised. Furthermore, your blood-offering sacrifices are strictly prohibited by the five precepts. Shangdang replied, "If I were to prepare..."

The disciples went ahead to clear the way of obstacles. Thereupon, Sengdu went his way. At dawn the next day, he encountered a man who presented him with ten thousand coins, incense, candles, and a knife.
The note read: "Your disciple Jin Shang respectfully offers this provision. On the fifteenth day of the month, Sengdu held a religious assembly for him.
Jin Shang returned once more to join the assembly in prostrations and the practice of the Way; having received the precepts, he departed. A shrine medium at Sheshan dreamed of a deity...
He informed [the deity], saying, "I have already received the precepts from Master Du; therefore, you must not slaughter animals for sacrifices.

From then on, the offerings at the shrine were restricted to vegetables and dried meats alone. Once, while Du was resting on the ground after a fit of illness, he saw Hui Shang coming from outside, who stroked his head and feet with his hand before departing.
A short while later, Shang returned carrying a lapis lazuli bottle filled with water, which he offered [to Du].
His *dudu* [medicinal herb] was sweet in taste and cold in nature; such were the signs of his spiritual resonance.

Prince Ziliang of Jingling and Prince Shian of Qi, among others, all paid him remote homage with the reverence due to a teacher, providing for his four requisites without fail throughout the six periods of the day. (The above two accounts are from the *Liang Gao seng zhuan*).
In Nanyang lived Song Dingbo. When he was young, he was walking at night when he encountered a ghost. The ghost asked, "Who are you? Dingbo then asked in return, "And who are you?
The ghost replied deceptively, "I am a ghost. The ghost asked, "Where do you wish to go? He answered, "I wish to go to the market in Wan.
The ghost said, "I also wish to go to the market in Wan. They traveled together for several li, when the ghost said, "Walking is too slow."
"It is late; we may carry each other by turns. Ding Bo said, "Very well. The ghost then carried Ding Bo for several li.
The ghost said, "You are too heavy; are you perhaps not a ghost? Ding Bo replied, "I have only recently died, so my body is naturally heavy.
Ding Bo then carried the ghost behind him, yet the ghost was hardly heavy at all. This happened two or three times. Ding Bo spoke again, "I have only recently died..."
He realized they were ghosts. He asked them, "What do you all fear or avoid? The ghosts replied, "We only dislike human saliva. Thereupon they traveled together. On the way, they encountered water.
Ding Bo ordered the ghosts to cross first; he listened, and there was not a sound at all. When Ding Bo crossed himself, he made a splashing noise. The ghosts asked, "Why did you make a noise?
Ding Bo said, "I have only recently died and am not yet practiced in crossing water; that is why it is so. Do not take me as strange."
As they were traveling toward the market in Wan, Dingbo placed the ghost upon his head, gripping it tightly.
The ghost let out loud, piercing shrieks, demanding to be set down, but he paid no heed. They proceeded directly to the market in Wan, where he set it on the ground;
it immediately transformed into a sheep. Fearing it might change back, he spat upon it repeatedly. He sold it for fifteen hundred coins and departed.
At that time, Shi Chong said, "Dingbo sells ghosts for fifteen hundred coins" (from the *Lieyi zhuan*; Shi Chong was a person of the Jin dynasty).
In Fenzhou of the Wei, at Xuanzhong Temple, there was the Śramaṇa Tanluan. His home was near Mount Wutai, where divine traces and numinous wonders abound; later, he went [there].
In Jiangnan was the dwelling of Tao the Recluse (Tao Yingju), where [Luan] sought the recipes for immortality. Tao joyfully bestowed upon him ten scrolls of these recipes.
Upon returning to the Zhejiang River, he encountered the deity of Baolangzi, who had surged forth waves for seven days with a single drumbeat.

This coincided exactly with the onset of the tide, leaving no means by which to cross. Luan then went to the temple and prayed with his true feelings, vowing that if his request were granted, he would...

The temple was being constructed. In a brief moment, the deity manifested his form; he appeared like a man of twenty years of age and said to Lü An-luan, "If you wish to cross over, you shall succeed tomorrow morning.
I pray that you do not break your word. When dawn arrived, the waves were still surging and raging; only after he had just stepped into the boat did they subside.

He remained serene and tranquil, attaining realization through these means. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty held him in high esteem and consequently issued an imperial decree to construct a new spirit temple for the River God.
Later, as he took his leave of the Emperor and returned to the territory of Wei, he arrived at Luoyang where he encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci from Central India.
Sengluan went to inform him, saying, "In the Buddha-dharma, there are methods for longevity and immortality that surpass those of the immortals here in this land."

The Master asked, "Is this a sūtra? Zhi spat on the ground and said, "What kind of talk is this? It is not comparable [to the Dharma]. In this region, where is there a method for longevity and immortality?
Even if one were to attain a long life, one would not live forever; in the end, one would still revolve through the three realms of existence (trisaṃsāra).

He then presented the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* to him, saying, "This is the method of the Great Sage. If you practice according to it, you shall surely attain liberation from birth and death and forever sever [the cycle of rebirth]."

He wandered through saṃsāra. Later, he moved to reside at Xuanzhong Temple on the northern mountains of Fenzhou. With single-minded devotion, he followed the sūtras to cultivate the practices of the Pure Land.
On the day of his death, banners, flowers, and canopies rose high, reflecting upon the temple buildings, while fragrant smoke billowed forth; the entire monastic community witnessed this together.
He passed away in the fourth year of the Xinghe era of the Wei dynasty (as recorded in the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan*).
Wang Yanwei of Henan, Zhou, was by nature cruel and wicked and took pleasure in hunting. His parents had raised him alone and loved him with extreme tenderness.
They repeatedly admonished him not to associate with evil people and did not allow him to go hunting, fearing it would cost him his life. [Yet] he did not heed them.
Regarding the succession of the lineage: Wei did not follow his father’s instructions and constantly hunted without ceasing, while also pursuing and harassing wicked people.
When his parents saw that he would not stop his violent conduct, they punished him with fifty strokes of the cane. His body was so scarred that he could not leave his door.

Out of resentment toward his parents, he waited until they were asleep at night and secretly used a sack of earth to press down over their mouths, sitting atop them so that no breath could escape, intending to kill them.
Upon his death, there were no scars or sores upon him. As he was about to pass away, he did not doubt that it was I who had done this.

Suddenly, he saw a ghost come into the hall, causing the entire house to tremble; everyone, both old and young, became aware of it. The ghost overturned the bed before Wei, and Wei lay down on his back; the sack of earth was already upon Wei’s belly.
His parents woke up and tried to pull the sack off their son’s abdomen, but they could not remove it from his body. Wei saw it again.
He was pressed down by a ghost upon a sack of earth. Extremely exhausted and on the verge of death, he cried out for help.
His entire family, both young and old, as well as his neighbors, joined forces to pull him up, but in the end they could not move him. He could not produce a loud voice;
he could only strike his head with his hands and join his palms before passing away (as recorded in the *Li Guixin Lu*).
Sui Renqian of Zhaojun in the Tang dynasty was a native of Handan. In his youth, he devoted himself to the study of the classics and did not believe in ghosts or spirits.
He often wished to test whether they existed or not, so he went to visit the dead and studied their ways for over ten years, yet he could not succeed in seeing them. Later, he moved his family.

He was heading toward the county seat when, on the road, he saw a man who appeared to be a celestial official. His robes and cap were most magnificent, and he rode a fine horse followed by more than five thousand riders.
He looked at Ren Qian but did not speak. Ren Qian saw him several times afterward, always in this manner. Over ten years, they met dozens of times.
Later, the man suddenly halted his horse and called out to Ren Qian, saying, "I have seen you frequently lately, and my heart has come to cherish and admire you."
"I wish to be your companion. Qiàn immediately bowed to him. He asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am but a ghost. My surname is Cheng and my given name is Jing.
Originally from Hongnong during the Western Jin dynasty, I served as a Provincial Aide (Biejia). Now I hold the office of Senior Secretary (Changshi) to the State of Hu."
Renqian asked, "Where is that country located? What are the names of its king and people? He replied, "To the north of the Yellow River, all together constitute the kingdom of Linhu.
Its capital is in the sandy desert to the northwest of Loufan; this is it. Its king is none other than the former King Wuling of Zhao, who now governs this country.
It is entirely under the jurisdiction of Mount Tai. Every month, the high ministers each send an envoy to pay court at Mount Tai."
"Shan, it is for this reason that I have frequently come to this place to meet with you.
I am able to benefit you by allowing you to foresee calamities and misfortunes so that you may avoid them in advance, thereby escaping untimely harm.

However, only the destiny of life and death, and the retribution of great fortune or disaster, cannot be altered. Renqian followed his advice. Jing then ordered his attendant Chang Zhang to [inform him].
He presented these items as gifts and sent him along with Sui Qian. He instructed him, "Should there be any matters, you must inform me beforehand;
whatever you do not know, you shall come and tell me. Thereupon they parted. The attendant followed him constantly, like a personal servant.
Whenever he was questioned, there was nothing he did not know in advance. At the beginning of the Daye era, Lingcenxiang served as the Magistrate of Handan, and his son was Wenben.
Before he had reached the age of twenty, Zhi Xiang requested Ren Qian to instruct him in the classics and books at his home.
Ren Qian informed Wen Ben of this matter and further said to him: "Cheng Changshi told me there is one thing about which I am ashamed to speak to you;
yet, since I have become your friend, I cannot help but tell you. The way of ghosts and spirits also has food, but they can never eat their fill. They constantly...
He suffered from hunger and thirst. If he could obtain human food, he would be satiated for a year.
Many of the ghosts frequently stole people's food, but because I was of high status, they were unable to steal mine. I request a single meal from you.
After Zhanqian informed Wenben, Wenben immediately prepared a meal, setting out various delicacies. Zhanqian said, "The ghosts do not wish to enter human dwellings; we may eat by the water outside."
Canopies were erected and seats were arranged; wine and food were set out upon them. Wenben followed his instructions exactly.

When the time arrived, Renqian saw that two guests of the Duke of Jing had come and were seated, accompanied by more than a hundred horsemen. Once they were seated, Wenben bowed twice toward the table and apologized for the lack of refinement in the meal.
Renqian conveyed the Duke of Jing’s intention and offered his own apologies on his behalf. Initially, when Wenben was about to set out the food, Renqian had requested that he provide gold and silk.
He presented it to him as a gift. Wenben asked, "What kind of object is this? Qian replied, "The objects used by ghosts are all different from those of humans.

Only gold and silk can be used interchangeably [with their human counterparts], yet even these are not as good as the artificial versions. By coating large tin with yellow pigment to make gold and using paper to make silk, one achieves what is most precious and superior.

Wenben followed his instructions and made them. When the time came... [the ghost appeared].* *Note: The source text ends abruptly at "及景" (and when the scene...). The narrative likely continues with the ghost's appearance and reaction to the gifts.*
When the meal was finished, he ordered his attendants to take turns sitting and eating with him. Wen Ben presented the gold coins and silk he had made to him as gifts.
Jing Shen thanked him with great joy, saying, "Because of Master Sui, you have troubled yourself with providing for me, noble sir.
Do you perhaps wish to know the length of your own lifespan? Wen Ben declined, saying, "I do not wish to know. Jing Shen laughed and departed. Several years later, Ren Qian fell ill.
He was not severely ill, yet he did not recover for over a month. Baoqian questioned the administrator in charge, but the administrator did not know.
He then questioned the Chief Secretary (Changshi), who replied, "No one in the country knows.
Later that month, while traveling to pay homage at Mount Tai, the Chief Secretary came to report the news, saying: "A man named Zhao from your hometown has become a spirit of Mount Tai."
"Registrar. There is a vacancy for one registrar; I have recommended you for this office and am therefore summoning you for the preparation of the legal documents.
Those who complete the documents shall face death. Zhiqian asked to be allowed to take the documents out. Jing said, "Your longevity should reach over sixty years, yet you are only forty now.
You have been summoned only because Registrar Zhao has acted arbitrarily. I shall petition on your behalf. He then spoke as follows:
"Libationer Zhao inquired after Elder Sui: 'In the past, we were fellow students, and our bond of affection was profound. Now, by good fortune, I have become a Libationer of Taishan.

It so happens that there is currently a vacancy for an official post, and the Magistrate is now selecting a candidate. I have already petitioned the Lord of the Prefecture, and he has granted permission for me to employ you.
Since you, elder brother, cannot achieve eternal life and your destiny is such that you must die, meeting with this opportunity at the time of death is not necessarily [without merit].'"
"Since you hold office, why begrudge a life of twenty or thirty years of mere existence to prolong the time? Now that the official documents have already been issued, they cannot be stopped.
I hope you will resolutely carry out what I intend and have no further doubts. Qiàn became filled with anxiety and fear, and his illness grew even more severe.

Jing said to Qiàn, "If Assistant Magistrate Zhao truly intends to bring you to justice, you may go to Mount Tai yourself to lodge a formal complaint at the prefecture; then it may be possible [to avoid this]."
To avoid this, Zhiquan asked, "By what means may I see the Prefect? Jing replied, "As for ghosts, they can indeed be seen. Go to the east of the Taishan Temple;
crossing a small ridge, there is a level plain which is his capital. When you go there, you shall naturally see him.
Zhiquan reported this to Wenben, who prepared a full set of travel provisions for him. After several days, Jing told Zhiquan again, "The official documents are about to be completed."
The official accused him. Fearing he could not escape punishment, [Zhang] Qian hastily fashioned a Buddha image, and the incriminating document vanished of its own accord.
Qian informed Wen Ben that he had spent three thousand coins to have a seated image painted on the western wall of the temple.

When Jing arrived and told him, "You are cleared," Qian—who personally did not believe in Buddhism—still harbored doubts. He therefore asked Jing, "The Buddha-dharma speaks of the three periods of time."

[The interlocutor asked: "Regarding cause and effect, is this [the state of being a ghost] real or illusory? He replied: "It is entirely real. Zhu Qian said: "If that is so, when such people die, they ought to be distributed among the six realms of existence.
How can it be that they all become ghosts? Are Zhao Wuling Wang and you yourself still ghosts even now?

Jing said: "How many households are there within your commandery? Qian replied: "More than ten thousand households. Jing asked again: "How many prisoners are in your jails? Qian replied: [The number of prisoners was stated.]

[The Emperor] asked, "How many people are there usually in your household? [Zhen] Qian replied, "Twenty or fewer. He asked again, "Within a district of ten thousand households, how many hold the rank of the fifth grade or above?
Qian replied, "None. He asked again, "How many hold the rank of the ninth grade or above? Qian replied, "A few dozen.

The Emperor said, "The principle of the six realms of existence is divided exactly like this. Those who attain the heavenly realm are not one in ten thousand, just as there is not one such person within your district."
Among those who attain the human path, there are tens of thousands; they are like the several dozen people of the ninth rank within your district.
Those who enter hell are likewise tens of thousands; they are like the prisoners within your jail. However, ghosts and animals are by far the most numerous;
they are like the households subject to corvée labor within your district. Within this path, there are further gradations, as [he] pointed out.
His attendant said, "That man is not as good as I am; those who fall short of him are still many. Zhiqian asked, "Do ghosts die? He replied, "Yes.
Zhiqian asked, "When they die, into which realm do they enter? He replied, "I do not know, just as a person does not know [the destination] of birth."

Yet they do not know what occurs after death. Qian asked, "Is the performance of Daoist *zhāojiào* (incantations and offerings) of any benefit? Jing replied, "The Heavenly Emperor presides over the six realms of existence;
this is called the Celestial Bureau (*Tiān-cáo*). King Yama is like the Son of Heaven of the human world. The Lord of Mount Tai is like the Chancellor (*Shàngshū-lìng*).
The spirits who record the five paths are like the various Ministers (*Shàngshū*). Our own country is like a great [kingdom]."

Whenever the prefectures and commanderies adjudicated human affairs, the Daoists would submit petitions (*shangzhang*) on behalf of the people to seek blessings, as if seeking the grace of the deities.

The Celestial Office (*Tiancao*) would receive these and issue an edict down to King Yama, stating: "On such and such a day of such and such a month, we received a petition from so-and-so, which said... and so forth.
"You ought to exhaust the principles of justice. Do not allow for wrongful or excessive punishment; Yanluo, receive this with reverence and carry it out as one would obey an imperial decree.
Where there is no principle, one cannot seek exemption; where there is injustice, it must surely be redressed. What benefit is there in [failing to do so]?
Qian asked, "How does the Buddhist tradition cultivate merit? Jing replied, "The Buddha is a Great Sage; he does not issue written edicts. As for those who cultivate merit, Heaven..."

If one serves the gods with reverence, they will often grant pardon. If one’s merit is thick, even if there are records of one’s offenses in the registers of the underworld, they cannot be summoned or seized.
This is not something I understand, nor do I know why it is so. Having finished speaking, he departed immediately. Within one or two days, Zhiquan was able to rise and recovered.
When Wang Ben’s father passed away, he returned to his hometown. Zhiquan sent him a letter, saying: "The spirits and ghosts are certainly real."

He was greedy and deceitful. Formerly, when he desired food and drink from you, Master, he was so earnest; now that he knows there is no further profit, his manner upon meeting you is utterly cold and indifferent.
His usual attendant still follows him about. His home county has been overrun by bandits, and those who died were nearly all of them.
I was guided by an official in charge of affairs; though I frequently encountered bandits, I did not see them and thus remained safe throughout.

On the eighth day of the ninth month in the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era, an archery contest was held at Xuanwu Gate for civil officials. At that time, I, Wenben, served as the Vice Director of the Secretariat.

He sat facing me together with my elder brother, the Minister of the Imperial Treasury (Taifu Qing), along with Ma Zhou, the Censor-in-Chief for Administrative Affairs (Zhishu Shiyushi), and Wei Kun, the Palace Aide (Gongzhongshi).
Wenben spoke these words himself to others. (From the *Mingbao ji*. [Note: Although there are many beings in the hells hereafter, how do they compare to ghosts and animals?

Ghosts and humans cannot be seen, whereas animals—those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation, including minute insects—pervade the world across water, land, and air. Thus, it is said that they are the most numerous.)

Huozhai County: In the sixth year of the Wude era, Li, the Clerk, died. After seven days had passed, he appeared invisibly and said to his wife, "I calculated that I still have six years remaining in this world; however, the Lord of Destiny came to take me by error.
I have already petitioned King Yama, who granted me leave to roam among humans for another six years. I am currently in the realm of ghosts. He further said, "The life of man is impermanent."
"Why do you not cultivate merit? You should go to the Dharma Master Xuànjiàn to listen to the Dharma. He then entered the lecture hall with his wife and engaged in conversation with others.
Someone asked him, "Why do you not manifest your form? He replied, "The bodies received in the realm of hungry ghosts are extremely hideous;
I cannot bear to look at them myself, much less for others to see. He later went to Jǐngyè Temple to listen to the Dharma Master Yú lecturing on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Another asked, "Now that you are preaching this sutra, what kind of beings have been moved to listen? He replied, "From human beings upward, there are spirits and ghosts;
above them, the various heavens are filled in successive tiers. Yet, seeing that the devas smelled the fragrance of the Dharma Master’s wine, they all turned their faces away to listen.
It is not only at this assembly that the various devas are thus moved; whenever there is a Dharma service, there are none who do not descend. Another asked, "..."
Upon hearing this, he immediately repented his transgression and thereafter never drank again (as recorded in the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).

Although others may have committed the offense of drinking alcohol, if they possess right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) and their wisdom and understanding are free from error, they will move devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts to listen to them together.

This is what is meant by "breaking the precepts but not breaking the view. To hear [the teaching] and immediately repent is something that none but the wise could achieve; had it not been for such [wisdom], it would not have been possible. If one were to speak otherwise...

This contradicts the intent of the scriptures; one thus incurs the sin of slandering the Dharma. Ghosts and spirits will seize the opportunity to rebuke such a person—how could they possibly move the ears of Heaven?

Emperor Wu was the son of Emperor Muzong. He abolished Buddhism and Daoism, ingested cinnabar elixirs, and received talismanic registers. The elixir caused an abscess on his back, which became parched and painful.
He lost his composure and fell ill; for ten days he was unable to speak, and then he passed away at the age of thirty-four. He had occupied the throne for six years.
The *Baoying zhuan* (Account of Retribution) states: On the fifteenth day of the first month, someone walking at night reached the foot of Emperor Muzong’s tomb and suddenly heard human voices.

This was said to be the theft of a horse. While [the thief] was hiding within a withered thicket, suddenly a man in crimson robes appeared holding a tablet and proclaimed: "Where is the Director of the Imperial Treasury? Two officials came forth and replied, "He is here. The man in crimson robes asked, "Has the envoy from the Lord of Haisi arrived yet?
