Li Yan sat in judgment and destroyed the Buddhist teachings; he was deprived of his longevity and removed from his position. He was destined to have his soul summoned along with that of the Lord of Haisi.

At that time, there were merchants who heard the sound of bells coming from the east; two officials in vermilion robes suddenly vanished. A few days later, Emperor Wu indeed passed away (*from the Tongzai:

Prime Minister Li Yan, courtesy name Deyu, assisted Emperor Wu in destroying the Teachings; he was subsequently demoted to the post of District Magistrate of Yizhou and died of a malignant disease. See details in the Tongji and Taiping Guangji*).
Recorded). In the first year of Longshuo (661 CE), during the reign of [Emperor Gaozong], a bhikṣuṇī named Xiuxing of Jingfu Temple had a maidservant named Ren Wuniang die in her quarters.
Later, while Xiuxing was performing rites for Wuniang’s spirit, more than a month passed; then her elder sister and younger brother [arrived].
In the middle of the night, he suddenly heard groaning from the spirit seat. At first, his younger brother was greatly terrified;
later, he questioned it, and the voice replied: "During my life, I ate meat at this monastery. Because of this, I suffer great agony. There is a wound upon my body."
"I fear it will soil the bedding. You should place a great deal of ash upon the bed. Her younger brother followed her words and placed the ash there.
Later, when he looked at the bed, he saw a great deal of pus and blood. She spoke to her brother again, saying, "I am too ill to sew clothes; you are wearing very tattered rags.
You should bring some cloth, and I will make a shirt and socks for you. Her brother placed the cloth upon the funeral couch. After [a period of time] had passed...
That night it was accomplished. He then said to his sister, "When I was young and afflicted by an illness, I killed a crab and applied its juice to my wound, which healed me.
Now I have entered the Hell of the Blade Forest; there are currently seven broken knives within my flesh.

I pray that you, my sister, will let your compassion flow and perform meritorious deeds on my behalf to rescue me. I know you are pressed by distress and may not be able to manage the arrangements, but please use only the clothing you are wearing."
"These garments will be of no benefit to the deceased; they have not yet been damaged, so please accept them for use. Before his sister could reply, he said, "I shall take them myself.
After a long while, he spoke again, "The clothes have arrived; they are currently on the bed. His sister went to inspect them and found they were the very shrouds used for his enshrouding.
She then sent them to Jōdo-ji Temple to the Master Hōken, requesting that he transcribe the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* [for her].
Each time he finished copying one fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he would announce, "One blade has been drawn.

When he had completed seven fascicles, he said, "Seven blades have all been drawn forth; now, through the assistance of merit, I shall immediately go to take rebirth together with my elder sister and younger brother."
They wept their farewells and departed. Shen Xuangfa of Wuxing and the monk Zhizheng of Jingtu Monastery recounted the same account (from *Mingbao Shiyi*).

During the Liang dynasty, the Magistrate of Wangcai killed an ox for food and drink; while lying upon the floor of a Buddha hall, he was stricken with white leprosy and died. During the Tang dynasty, Emperor Xuanzong issued an edict that on the days of national mourning, incense must be offered in the prefectures and kingdoms, and no wine or meat may be carried into the monasteries.

During the Song dynasty, Emperor Taizong issued a decree that on the days of national mourning, from the Chancellor downwards, incense must be offered at temples and observatories, and the consumption of raw meat and alcohol was strictly prohibited (from *Tongji*). When people of the secular world reach the end of their lives, they do not know to perform meritorious deeds for the deceased, yet they still lavish effort on the funeral rites. Once the realms of the living and the dead have been separated, the existence and non-existence [of the deceased]...

Their physical bodies are different; therefore, it is said that there is no benefit for those who have died. How could one know that by performing merit on their behalf, they will have clothing and food provided for themselves, and eventually be reborn among humans or devas? As the *Mingxiang ji* records:

After the monk Miaoyi of Longhua Monastery in Jiangling, Song Dynasty, passed away, he returned to his room one night before his spirit-tablet and spoke to his disciple Kezong. Zong asked, "Where has the Upadhyaya been reborn this life? Miaoyi replied, "It is quite tolerable. However, I was due to undergo a minor retribution for two years, which I have now avoided. I wish to appeal to the authorities, but because I lack a *kāṣāya*, you must hurry [to provide one]."

He prepared [the funeral rites], invited monks to receive offerings, and bestowed the robe upon them. I immediately obtained it. Zong followed these instructions to provide food for the monks and offer the robes as *dakṣiṇā*. When this was finished, the bhikṣu Daomeng suddenly saw the deceased’s wondrous body wearing the robe, entering the hall and sitting according to the monastic order. He listened to the sutra until the assembly dispersed, after which he could no longer see him.

This proves that by giving a robe one receives the retribution of obtaining a robe, and by giving food one receives the retribution of obtaining food; this is truly not a falsehood. Master Zhipan said: "The Vinaya clarifies the three robes of the deceased, permitting only that they be given to the Sangha to be shared among them. I have never heard of the Buddha commanding [otherwise]."

One should don it upon one’s deceased body and follow it into cremation. In this degenerate age, the ignorant frequently commit unrighteous acts; even those with discernment must clarify this matter. If the body remains intact after passing away and is enshrined in a stupa for burial, it may still be appropriate to don it upon the true physical form.

If one follows the method of cremation by fire, then it is improper to wear [the robe]; to do so would incur the transgression of violating the Vinaya by taking up a garment intended for burning. As for the claim that a deceased monk has no robe and thus should act according to the *Mingxiang ji*, I have personally heard of this error.

My nephew Zhen-shi, Zhen-gao, and Zhen-kang unfortunately died young. On the day their shrines were cremated, they were all not wearing *kāṣāyas*, but only plain cloth shirts and skirts. Prior to the offering of the vegetarian feast (*zhāi*), the seven-strip robe (*qītiáo*) he had worn during his lifetime was used for a method of drawing lots (*niānjiū*) to be bestowed upon the monks.

Furthermore, he instructed his descendants that they must personally practice this even at the moment of their own demise. I venture to inform my acquaintances to together honor this dharma. *Fàn-yǔ* (Sanskrit) *kāṣāya*; *huá-yán* (Chinese) "robe of ruined color. It belongs to the five major colors.

It is not something worn for performing official temple duties (*yingfù*). As for the five-colored [robes], there are those today who, being unacquainted with the Vinaya teachings, hang the robes of the deceased on trees; this is deeply contrary to the Dharma. (The pronunciation of *jiū* is like *jiū*; *niānjiū* means to draw lots).
Yáo Míngjiě (解) was originally a śramaṇa of Puguāng Temple. He was by nature intelligent and quick-witted, possessed literary elegance, and was skilled in calligraphy and painting.
As for playing the *qín* lute, he was also peerless among his contemporaries. Yet, he always took pleasure in the mundane world and found no joy in the gates of the Way.

In the first year of the Longshuò era, he was selected to respond to an imperial edict and traveled to Luoyang; upon ascending the examination ranks and returning to lay life, he became quite prosperous.
He spoke thus. Not long after, he passed away. Later, he appeared in a dream to his acquaintance, the monk Chijung of Jingtu Temple, saying:
"Mingjie lacked merit in his past lives and did not follow the Inner Teachings; now he suffers great punishment and is in extreme hunger and deprivation.
If you still feel the affection of an old friend, could you perhaps grant me a single meal? Chijung promised him this within the dream. Upon waking, he then...
He prepared a meal. When night fell and he had just fallen asleep, he saw Mingjie arrive and apologize for his conduct, saying...
[and so forth]. Cui Yü of Boling was the son-in-law of Wang Zhihong. During the Zhenguan era, Zhihong served as the Magistrate of Hechuan County in Qinzhou.
He gave his daughter in marriage to Yü. While in Hechuan, Yü fell ill and died. After he had been dead for several dozen...

One day, his family suddenly heard the voice of Yu speaking in the middle of the night. At first, the entire household was struck with alarm and fear; later, however, they came to regard it as a regular occurrence.

They heard him say, "Yu is my son-in-law. Although it is not appropriate for him to have a spirit tablet established at his wife's family home, since he has no other place to rely upon, I shall simply set one up for him.
His wife followed this request and provided food morning and evening, though she did not permit the establishment of a formal memorial altar.

Meat. He only ordered that vegetarian food be served and constantly exhorted him to pay homage to the Buddha, forbidding any negligence. Furthermore, he spoke in detail about the matters within the hells, saying:
"In a person's life, one can never avoid killing and filial impiety; all other sins are merely minor by comparison. He also said:
"Although Yu has no sin, it would be of great benefit to provide him with merit. For Yu’s sake, frequently establish offerings of vegetarian feasts and..."
He transcribed copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, and others, totaling three or two volumes each.

Combined with his previous meritorious deeds, he was as if he had attained the state of an Arhat. From that time forward, he did not return again. The royal family followed his instructions exactly, transcribing scriptures and providing offerings.
Suddenly, Tuo returned once more to express his gratitude and apologized. He then said, "I shall now take my leave. The entire household wept as they saw him off. Tuo—
There was a posthumous child already four or five years old, who said, "Wang Yu, this child will certainly hold official rank; I pray you raise him well.
After this, he did not come again. This was related by Wang Zhihong himself (the above two accounts are from the *Mingbao ji*).
Yin Anren of Jingzhao was a man of great wealth who had long supported the monks of Cimen Temple. At the beginning of the first year of the Yining era, a traveler stayed at his home;
this guest stole another’s donkey and slaughtered it within the house, leaving the donkey skin behind at Anren’s residence.
In the third year of the Zhenguan era, Anren encountered a man on the road who said to him, "I have come to summon you."
The messenger said, "Tomorrow you shall die. Anren was terrified; he went straight to Cimen Temple and sat beneath the Buddha hall, remaining there overnight without coming out.
The next day, indeed, three riders and dozens of foot soldiers, all bearing weapons, entered the temple.
Seeing Anren from afar, they called for him to come out. Anren did not respond, but his recitation of the scriptures proceeded with even greater intensity. The ghosts said to one another:
"Yesterday you did not take it immediately; today you cultivate merit in such a manner—how could you possibly obtain it?
Because of this, they went together, leaving one person behind to guard [the site]. The guardian said to Anren, "In the past you killed a donkey, and that donkey now accuses you.
We have been sent to seize you. You must face him together; what is the use of not going? Anren replied from afar, "In the past..."
"Others stole and killed my donkey themselves; they merely gave me its hide. It was not I who killed it, so why do you pursue me?
I beg you to go back and say to the donkey for me: 'I did not kill you, but now I am also performing merit for you;
this will be of benefit to you, so you should let me go. The man consented, saying, 'If the donkey does not agree, I shall come again tomorrow.'"
"If you agree to this, he will not come. Having finished speaking, he departed. The next day, [the man] indeed did not arrive.
Thereupon, Anren performed merit-making rituals for the donkey on its behalf, and his entire family observed the precepts and ate only vegetarian food. Lu Wenli recounted this story;
Anren is still living today. (From *Mingbao Shiyi*).

At Xianju Monastery on Mount Song, Chan Master Yuangui was building a hermitage in the Pang Valley within the mountains. At that time, a man arrived with a retinue of many attendants wearing tall caps and trousers tucked into their boots;
he walked with light steps and a composed gait, announcing his arrival to visit the Great Master. Upon seeing him, Guī observed that his appearance was majestic.
His spirit was sharp and his demeanor extraordinary. [The deity] said to him, "Welcome, O benevolent one! Why have you come? He replied, "Do you, Master, recognize me?
Guì said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all with a single eye. How could I distinguish or recognize any one of them?
The deity responded, "I am a mountain deity of this peak. I can bring benefit or harm, life or death, to people. How can you, Master, view me with a single eye?"
"Alas! Gui said: 'You can bring life and death to others, but I am fundamentally unborn; how then could you kill me?
I regard my body as equal to empty space, and I regard myself as equal to you. Can you destroy empty space and yourself?
If you could indeed destroy empty space and yourself, then I would be neither born nor extinguished. Since you cannot even do this, how much less can you bring life and death to me?'"
"Yes," the Spirit of Mount Yue replied, bowing his head twice. "I am also intelligent and upright among other spirits, yet how could I possess the vast wisdom and eloquence of the Master?
I pray that you grant me the true precepts so that I may transcend the world and assist in your majestic blessings.
Guī said, "Since the spirit has requested the precepts, he has already received them. Why is this? Because there is no precept apart from the precept itself."
"What precepts are these? The deity said, "These are the principles. What I have heard is obscure and dim; I seek only the Master’s precepts. I am your disciple.
Guī declined, but could not refuse him. He immediately prepared a seat, burned incense, lit the censer, and facing the altar, said:
"I confer upon you the five precepts. If you can uphold them, say 'I can'; if you cannot, say 'No'. The deity said, "Wash your ears and listen attentively."
With an open mind, he received the instruction. Kui asked, "Can you refrain from sexual misconduct? The spirit replied, "I am married. Kui said, "That is not what I mean;
I mean that you have no lustful desires. The spirit replied, "I can. Kui asked, "Can you refrain from stealing? The spirit replied, "Why would I lack for anything?
How could I ever steal? Kui said, "That is not what I mean; I mean that you do not enjoy blessings for your licentiousness, nor do you suffer calamity for failing to provide offerings."

"Good," [the Master] said. "The spirit replied, 'I am able. [The Master] asked, 'Are you able not to kill? The spirit replied, 'The power of governance rests with me; how could I say I do not kill? [The Master] said, 'I do not mean this.
I mean whether there is any excess, error, confusion, or doubt. The spirit replied, 'I am able. [The Master] asked, 'Are you able not to be deceitful?
The spirit replied, 'I am fundamentally upright; how could I have deceit? [The Master] said, 'I do not mean this. I mean whether there is anything before or after [that is inconsistent].'"
"This does not accord with the Will of Heaven. The spirit said, "I can. [Zhou] Gui asked, "Can you avoid being ruined by wine? The spirit said, "I have the strength to do so.
Gui said, "The above constitutes the Buddha's precepts. He further said, "To uphold them with a conscious mind, yet without a mind of restrictive attachment;
to regard external things with a conscious mind, yet without a mind that clings to the body—if one can act thus, then one will exist prior to heaven and earth. Not...

It is for the sake of purity. Though it dies after heaven and earth, it does not age. Though it undergoes transformation all day long, it does not move. Though it reaches ultimate stillness, it does not rest.

To awaken to this is to realize that though one marries, it is not for the sake of a wife; though one feasts, it is not for the sake of taking; though one holds office, it is not for the sake of power;
though one is intoxicated, it is not for the sake of delusion. If one can be without a mind toward the myriad things, then even if ensnared by desire, one will not be bound by it.

Lust. To bring blessings to the licentious and calamities to the virtuous. Not to commit theft through excess, error, or confusion. Not to commit killing when the sequence of actions violates the Way of Heaven.

Not to commit falsehood through delusion, negligence, or inversion. Not to become intoxicated through stupor or disorientation. This is called being "without mind. Without mind, there are no precepts;
without precepts, there is no mind. There is no Buddha and no sentient beings; there is neither you nor me. When there is neither me nor you, who is able to [act]?
"Be cautious! The spirit said, "My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha. Zhi Gui replied, "Regarding your ten supernatural powers, five can be exercised while five cannot.
The Buddha’s ten powers, however, have seven that can be exercised and three that cannot. The spirit was struck with awe and withdrew from his seat; kneeling with great reverence, he said:
"May I hear it? [The other] replied, "Can you cause the Supreme Deity to turn eastward in his course and cause the seven luminaries to move westward?
He said, "I cannot. Kui said, "Can you seize the Earth-Spirit, melt the Five Peaks, and bind the Four Seas?
He said, "I cannot. Kui said, "These are the five things you cannot do. Kui then said, "The Buddha can empty all phenomena and perfect the wisdom of the myriad dharmas."

One cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma (*niyata-karman*). A Buddha can know the natures of all beings and exhaustively comprehend events across billions of eons, yet he cannot transform or guide those for whom there is no karmic affinity (*apratyaya*).
A Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot exhaust the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*).

These are the three things that cannot be done. Furthermore, fixed karma is not eternal; even those without affinity are limited to a single lifetime; and the realm of sentient beings is fundamentally non-existent.
Increasing and decreasing—vastly, there is not a single person who can preside over the existence of dharmas. That dharmas have no presiding subject is called the non-existence of dharmas.

That there is no dharma and no presiding subject is called the absence of mind. As I understand the Buddha, he likewise possesses no supernatural powers; he is able to act solely through the absence of mind.
"It is because he has thoroughly realized all dharmas that his activity manifests mysteriously before sentient beings.
If there were a mind or an act, his activity would necessarily not be universally pervasive. The mountain deity said, "I am truly shallow and ignorant; I have not heard the meaning of emptiness.

You, Master, now bestow the precepts upon me, and I shall reverently practice them. What further karmic cause could bind me to this mundane realm? I wish to repay your compassionate virtue. [He then] offered...

"I am capable of this," [the deity] said. Guī replied, "I observe that the body is without substance and that all phenomena are impermanent; I have seen this clearly. What further desire could I have?
The deity said, "The Master must surely command me to perform a worldly task to display my modest divine powers, so as to cause those who have already resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment]."

There are five types of people: those who have first resolved their minds [for enlightenment], those who have not yet resolved their minds, those who lack faith, those who will certainly gain faith, and those who possess the divine spirit within themselves.
These individuals know that there is a Buddha and there is a divine spirit; they know there is capability and incapability, and there is that which is spontaneous and that which is not spontaneous.

Guī said, "Non-action is it! Non-action is it! The Spirit said, "Even the Buddha causes spirits to protect the Dharma. How could you, Master, abandon and rebel against the Buddha? [He] followed accordingly.

"I have already received your instructions. He further stated, "I shall certainly appear amidst the wind and thunder of a dark night, tossing and shaking with a great resonance; I pray that you, Master, will not be startled.
