(The character *zhuan* in the phrase "one transmission" [hòiyī zhuanzì] was originally circled and pronounced as an oblique tone. If it were truly an entrustment through transmission, then...

The characters erroneously interspersed throughout the preceding and following sections should all be laboriously corrected; furthermore, it would be especially excellent to revise any instances where the level and oblique tones (*pingze*) do not accord with the rhyme scheme (and so forth).
Once the ritual proceedings were concluded, I saw off the various venerable monks as they returned by boat. On the fourth day, my friends deliberated on recording these events;
the record was completed at noon, and we continued drinking joyfully until the second watch of the night. During this gathering, I composed a poem.

One note says: Since we parted, the Heavenly Emperor has commended me for not seeking revenge against my enemies. Three months hence, I shall be born into the human world so that I may allow you to fully realize your unreached talent.
Wait until the ninth month, then respectfully compile your poetry and prose and send it to me for inclusion in this transmission, thereby fulfilling the noble intentions of you gentlemen.
I hope you will not laugh at me as one would at the "Madman of Feng" (Fengfu). This would be a great favor.
"How profound this is! (Appended below is the autograph of the Immortal Lady). [Ning said:
"I have often witnessed matters concerning immortals and ghosts; I have frequently obtained accounts of them through written records or oral traditions.
There are many who have heard their voices, and many who have seen their deeds. Yet, in the end, none has been able to..."
In his calligraphy and brushwork, he responded to questions with the fluency of a flowing stream; whenever there was a sound, he would answer as if conversing face-to-face. Such was he.
Moreover, he was able to endure resentment without the slightest trace of a haughty or aggressive air. He was frugal in receiving benefits and invariably faithful in keeping his promises.
The verses she bestowed upon me were mostly admonitions and warnings; they were upright, dignified, and entirely devoid of feminine affectations.
How could she be spoken of on the same day as demons and goblins? Therefore, I honor her by calling her a "Celestial Lady" (*xiányuán*).
Now that her letter states that the Heavenly Emperor has commended her, it further proves that blessings for goodness never fail. I dare not utter even half a word regarding her traces.
I have adorned [this collection]. As for these poetic slips, I did not dare to add or subtract even a single character.

Although there were errors and scribal mistakes, I retained them as they were, merely to record the anomalies rather than out of a fondness for such things. Every character in the Immortal’s writings is consistent from beginning to end; I have respectfully preserved them.

I shall wait until September to see how the poems and prose turn out, at which point I will compile them for binding and publication. This concludes the *Biographies of Immortal Ladies*. [This is] what was previously bestowed.
There were several dozen sheets of poetic correspondence; now only three or five have been carved, while the remainder are all contained in the *Xianyuan zhuan* (Biographies of Immortal Ladies).

Although the lady came as a karmic creditor, she ultimately did not speak of the reason for her grievance. Master Hu likewise refused to clear himself of his own fault, doing nothing but remaining in a state of awe and trepidation.
That a grievance remains unavenged perfectly accords with the mind of the Great Being (the Bodhisattva); this is especially so in these degenerate times.
Fools are so resentful over even minor grievances that they seek retribution; how much more so would those who possess power and influence fail to forget a slight?

As stated in the *Śīla-sūtra*, one does not seek revenge even against an enemy with whom one shares the same sky. Thus it is said: "To kill and be killed in turn—what benefit is there in this cycle of life after life?
This is precisely what is meant. I only regret that you, Madam, though possessing the wisdom and sharp faculties of this world, have not deeply penetrated the distinction between good and evil.

This is the source of cause and effect; yet one does not yet know there is a further point beyond it. Should one at some time encounter a true master of the school, one will immediately cast away the ladle and the bag.
*Liùdào jí*, Scroll Three: Phonetic Explanations.
*Yīng*: Pronounced *yīng*. To touch, press, or approach closely. *Yǐng*: Pronounced *yǐng*. A goiter or tumor on the neck.
The upper character (利-禾+皮) is pronounced *pī*; it means to split with a knife. The lower character (罩-卓+齊) is pronounced *jì* in the third tone; it means to extract juice with the hand.
*Xié* (with the initial *hú* and final *jié*) is pronounced like *xiè*.
It means a stiff neck. *Ōu* is pronounced like *ōu*. It means a grave; it also refers to a heap of sand.
*Cǎn* is pronounced with the third tone like *cān*. It means sorrow; it also means pain; furthermore, it means cruel or toxic.
*Ti* (pronounced *ti*) refers to nasal mucus; that which issues from the nose is called *ti*, while that which issues from the eyes is called *ti* (pronounced *ti*).
*Gong* (pronounced *gōng*) refers to the hair ornament worn by women in the state of Fan.
[The character for] *zhé* (折) is pronounced *zhǐ* (志). *Mùguāng* (目光) means "eye-glance. [The character for] *shàn* (剡) is pronounced *shǎn* (閃). It is the name of a commandery located in Kuaiji.
*Fǔ* (脯) is pronounced *fǔ* (府); it refers to dried meat. *Suíqiàn* (眭蒨):
the upper character is a surname; the lower character is pronounced *qiàn* (倩), with the phonetic component *cāngdiàn* (倉殿) as its initial.
"Hán-dān": the upper character is pronounced *hán*; the lower character is pronounced *dān*.
It is the name of a commandery of Zhào. "Qiàn" (qìng): the initial is *qìng* with the departing tone;
it means to borrow someone for service. "Suì" is pronounced *suì*.
Páng (upper tone *páng*, lower tone *ǔ* with rising intonation);
huī (tone *huī*);
wēiyí (upper tone *wēi*, lower tone *tuó*).
*Jìn*: the first character is pronounced with the rising tone (*shǎngshēng*). *Lè pǐ*: the first character is pronounced as *qì*, and the second as *pǐ*.
*Gèn*: pronounced as *yǎo*; it means to look into the distance.
*Jī*: The sound of "chicken. A beautiful epithet for women.
*Jǐ*: The sound of "jǐ. A small table. It refers to something set out that is not leaned against.
*Làn*: Same as *dàn*. Pronounced *jiàn*. *Lù*: The sound of "liù. The foot of a mountain.
*Zào cuǐ*: the upper character is pronounced *cáo*; the lower character is pronounced *cuī* with the third tone.
The *tāla* tree has no branches or joints; its trunk resembles that of a palm tree.
"Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term, fully rendered as *bodhisattva*. This is translated here as "Awakened Being. [They] seek the Buddha-way above.

They transform sentient beings below; hence they are called "Awakened Sentient Beings" (*bodhisattva*). They are also called "Opening Beings" (*kaishi*), meaning they are able to awaken all sentient beings.
They are also called "Great Beings" (*mahāsattva*), meaning they seek the supreme above and transform those below, thereby establishing the Great Task.
Jin (pronounced jin) was a great officer of the state of Chu, surnamed Jin and named Shang.
He resided at West Lake. [There was also] the Dharma Master Zhenguang of Nantianzhu, who constantly lectured on the Lotus Sūtra and fully possessed the five qualities of a Dharma master.
As for his karma: while he was washing his hands, not a single drop fell to the ground. The Dragon King transformed himself into an old man and came daily to listen to the sutras.

Because of a prolonged drought, the Master requested that it rain. The King sought the precepts on behalf of the dragons; the Master performed the ritual to summon them and conferred the precepts upon them. Immediately, rain fell.
The Dragon King, wearing a high crown and crimson robes, came at night to pay his respects. The Master asked him the reason for the prolonged drought.

The Dragon replied, "People lack correct faith and frequently commit evil deeds. Consequently, the celestial moisture and the earth's fertility have flowed deep into the ground; the five grains provide no nourishment for the skin.
There is indeed a cause for this parched drought" (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
In Gusu, the lay practitioner Cao Luchuan told me that his daughter was staying with her husband’s family.
During the summer retreat, she was sitting in her room when a snake came down from the wall chasing a pigeon and fell into the center of the courtyard. When the family members saw it, they killed it.
Several days later, the snake possessed the girl and spoke. When Luchuan went to visit her, she said, "I was formerly the Governor of Jingzhou. When Gao Huan rebelled, he pursued me..."
"I reached the riverbank and subsequently died in the river. My parents, wife, and children do not know whether I am safe or well.
Lu Chuan said in astonishment, "Huan was a person of the Six Dynasties; now we have passed through the Sui, Tang, Song, and Yuan to reach the Great Ming.

You ghost, realize that you have been dead for a long time, and furthermore, learn that you were a snake. The ghost further said, "Since I have become a snake, I have no regrets about my death. However, please perform a ritual for me for the Liang dynasty."
"I shall perform one volume of the *Huangchan* (Imperial Repentance). I am going now. He then invited the monk Dingkong of Sizhou Temple to perform the repentance ritual.

When the repentance was completed, he requested a vegetarian meal and offered a single altar of *hu-shi* (rice-bowl food) for the hungry ghosts. The next day, the girl recovered as she had been before.
How great indeed is the power of repentance! (From Master Yunqi’s *Zhuchuang Suibian*).

*Sou Shen Ji* (Records of Searching for the Divine; compiled by Yu Bao of the Jin dynasty. Having died and returned to life, he witnessed the phenomena of ghosts and spirits within heaven and earth, and subsequently compiled accounts of divine beings and spiritual anomalies from antiquity to the present, titling it *Sou Shen Ji*).
Shi Fachong: He preached the Dharma in Suzhou, Hangzhou, and Jiaxing County in Western Zhejiang. There was a deity named Gao Wang.
The deity sent down a message, saying: "On my behalf, request Dharma Master Cong to come and receive the Bodhisattva precepts. The resident followed these words and made the request.
Once the ordination was completed, the deity again sent down a message, saying: "From this day forward, you must completely abstain from alcohol, meat, and the five pungent vegetables.

If you wish to pray for blessings in the future, you may invite the assembly of monks to the temple to perform the *zhai* (fasting) and practice the Way. This continued for two years. [At that time,] Xiu...
The deity of Haiyan County in the prefecture was known as the Lord of Poyang. During a regular sacrificial rite, he descended and addressed the officiant, saying:
"On my behalf, request Dharma Master Cong to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The assembly then welcomed the Master to deliver the lecture. The deity again descended and said:

"In the way of spirits, there are many karmic obstacles and sufferings. Since I began listening to the Dharma, the tiny insects that used to devour me within my scales and shells have ceased their torment. I pray that..."
He requested his teacher on his behalf to lecture once more on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. The teacher lectured upon it again, whereupon a deity descended;
he offered prayers of thanks (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
On the fifteenth day of the first month in the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, Dharma Master Huileng of the Tang dynasty had a vision while at Gantong Temple.

He said that he had dreamed of King Yama inviting him to lecture on the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises), while Dharma Master Chang was lecturing on the *Fahua* (Lotus Sūtra). He asked Master Chang whether this was appropriate.
Master Chang replied, "Excellent. Huileng then made a vow: "May I always dwell in hell to teach and transform sentient beings, and to lecture upon the Great [Vehicle]."

Since there was already this omen in the *Shengjing*, this vow was now fulfilled. At the end of the ninth month, Prince Jiang Jianleng, seeing that [the Master’s] physical strength was weak, sent him some stalactite from Shaozhou and pressured him into taking it.
That night, he dreamed of a person in official robes who said, "Do not take this milk;
King Yama has already completed the adornment of his ritual arena, and there is a great abundance of medicinal milk there. This occurred at dusk on the fifteenth day of the tenth month.
At that time, he finally realized that his illness was not healing. He told the temple master Baodu, "I recall when I was eight years old, going to Longquan Temple to pay homage to Avalokiteśvara.
Before I had even reached Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, I had already recited [the scripture] three times; it was as clear as if it were before my eyes. Having finished speaking, [he passed away].
From outside, a loud voice announced: "The Dharma Master has risen early and burned incense; the messenger has arrived. Baodu asked, "Who are you?
The reply was, "We are messengers of King Yama, here to welcome Master Ling. He immediately rose, burned incense, bathed, and completed his repentance and prostrations before the Buddha.
Returning to his room, he took the private notes he had kept on the essential meanings of the sutras throughout his life and burned them, saying, "These private notes were for others."

He read it, yet he could not grasp its profound meaning. When it was time for the small meal, a strange fragrance suddenly wafted forth; Sengleng composed his countenance and passed away (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
A certain villager of Haichang had an old woman who died and spoke of her life’s affairs and the retributions of the underworld in great detail to her family members.
The family gathered around to listen; among them was the villager, who suddenly focused his mind to recite the Buddha’s name.

The woman said to him, “If you were always like this, why would you worry about not attaining the Way of Buddhahood? He asked why she said this, and she replied, “Because your mind was reciting the name of the Buddha.”
"Because of Amitābha Buddha. [The monk] asked, "How do you know this? He replied, "I see that your body possesses radiance.
A village dweller who could not recognize a single character, upon a mere fleeting thought, still caused the ghosts to show him respect; how much more so for one who has practiced for a long time?
Therefore, the merit of reciting the Buddha's name is inconceivable. (From *Zhuchuang Erbi*)
King Yu Liao of Yue established Longce Temple and invited the monk Ke Zhou to the Tianbao Hall. There, he expounded the sutras for the underworld authorities during the night;

ghosts and spirits manifested their forms to listen to the Dharma. He also offered them ritual food (dharmāhāra). In recognition, King Liao bestowed upon Ke Zhou a golden bowl and purple robes, and conferred upon him the title "Zhengzhi Tongming" (Pure Resolve and Penetrating Clarity).
(From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*). *The Treatise on Protecting the Dharma* asks: Some claim that the Buddhist teachings include the offering of ritual food.
"Mantras can transform the few into the many, as in the saying that seven grains [of rice] can transform into [offerings for] the ten directions. How could such a principle exist?

Wujin said, "Not so. Have you not heard how the single vessel of wine from Goujian caused the entire army to become intoxicated, or how the single spray of wine from Luanba became rain over the Shu region?
When the mind’s spirit reaches its destination, there is nothing it cannot move through resonance. How much more so in this case!"
Relying upon the vast power of the vows of all Buddhas, one expands that virtuous mind so as to transform the few into the many; what cause for doubt could there be?
Thus, Emperor Yuan Shizu asked the Imperial Preceptor Phag mo gru pa: "The food offered in the ritual is minimal; how can it universally succor the immeasurable beings of the netherworld?"
The Imperial Preceptor said, "The power of the mantras of the Buddha-dharma is like the 'horse-quenching pearl.
Someone asked, 'Why do you not now use a single vessel of wine to make the multitude drunk, or a single spray of liquor to cause rain to pour down?

He replied, 'If the mind gives rise to doubt, how can one move the divine response? Only when one has faith and is free of doubt can it be said: "It is still and unmoving, yet it responds and thus acts."'"
A Comprehensive Collection.
Volume Four of the *Liudao ji* (Collection on the Six Realms),
compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoxianglin Monastery in Nanhai, Guangzhou, while residing at Jiqi.

Regarding the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*): "animal" (*tiryak*) is a term from the Sanskrit *tiryag-yoni*. This is translated here as "moving sideways" (*pángxíng*) or "born sideways" (*pángshēng*).

Because their physical form is horizontal, their movement is likewise horizontal; they all move with their heads toward the heavens. Furthermore, because the way they receive their retributive fruits is horizontal, it is so named.
Animals (*tiryagyoni*). Due to having previously committed the ten non-virtuous actions of body, speech, and mind under the influence of predominant ignorance, they go there and are born there.
Being by nature dull-witted and unable to support themselves, they are raised by humans; thus they are called "beasts. They include those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation;
those that move through water, on land, or in the air; and they fill human dwellings, mountains, wilds, marshes, as well as the heavens of the desire and form realms, and the *asura* worlds.

They exist throughout the hells and the realm of hungry ghosts; therefore, they are translated as "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*). This is because those not belonging to domesticated livestock are the majority.
The *Loutan jing* (Sutra of the Burning House) states: "Animals are of three kinds: first, fish; second, birds; third, beasts.
Within these three categories, each is immeasurable in number. The *Zhengfa nian jing* (Sutra of Mindfulness of the True Dharma) states: "Their species are diverse, numbering four billion."
Furthermore, there are those that crawl and those that wriggle, including minute insects too small to be counted; all these are called animals (*tiryag-yoni*).
Their forms vary in size, and their food and drink likewise differ. Among birds, none are larger than the golden-winged Great Eagle (*garuḍa*).
The distance from its head to its tail is eight thousand yojanas, and its height and depth are likewise. Each of its two wings is four thousand yojanas long.
It feeds upon dragons. Zhuang Zhou said: "One does not know how many thousands of li the back of the Great Peng spans. When it is about to fly..."
It strikes the water for three thousand li; its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky. It beats upon the whirlwind and ascends ninety thousand li above the earth before it can finally fly forth.
Its journey is from the Northern Ocean to the Southern Ocean, flying for six months without ever resting midway.
By this standard, it is still but a minor *garuḍa*. Among beasts, none are greater than the dragon. As for the *nāga*...
The two dragon kings, Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Upananda, wrap their bodies seven times around Mount Sumeru; their heads remain at the mountain peak while their tails are in the ocean.
Among large fish, none exceed the makara, which is the whale; its body is three hundred yojanas long.
They may be four hundred *yojana* in size, or even up to seven hundred *yojana*. Their eyes are like the sun and moon; their noses are like great mountains;
their mouths are like crimson valleys; and their teeth are like white mountains. This is what Zhuang Zhou called "the fish that swallows ships.

It is further said that among the aquatic creatures, the largest are like the giant tortoise of Juling, with its head crowning Mount Penglai as it sports in the sea. As for those that are small, their forms...
It is subtler than a mote of dust and cannot be seen by the ordinary eye; therefore, the Buddha did not permit one to observe water with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Rather, if one observes water with the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and finds no insects, it may be used for drinking. Zhuang Zhou said: "Among birds, none is more minute than the *jiǎoliáo*.
It raises its young upon the antennae of mosquitoes; its eggs hatch upon those antennae without falling off. Even so, [the Buddha’s prohibition remains].
How could this be the same as what is seen by the divine eye, which pervades everywhere? As stated in the sūtras, the various species of animals differ from one another;
according to their karmic causes, they receive retributions that are either beautiful or ugly, and these too are each distinct.

For instance, there are those such as the dragon, the steed, the qilin, the phoenix, the peacock, the parrot, the mountain fowl, and the painted duck, which are esteemed by humans and for which sentient beings cherish affection and delight; yet there are also those such as the jackal, the wolf, the tiger, and the leopard.
Monkeys, vipers, snakes, owls, and hawks are detested by people; they do not like to hear their cries.

Yet those whose lifespan is extremely long do not exceed one kalpa, while those whose lifespan is extremely short do not exceed the ephemeral insect that is born in the morning and dies in the evening, not lasting even a single day.
How could the length or brevity of the intermediate lifespans be fixed? If their karmic retribution has not yet...

Exhausted, they cast off their bodies and again receive new ones. Thus, the Venerable Śāriputra observed a single pigeon for eighty thousand kalpas in both its past and future lives, yet it still could not escape its pigeon body.
Furthermore, he saw many golden-colored ants upon a stone in the Jeta Grove;
even since the time of the seven Buddhas, they have been unable to leave their ant bodies. Therefore, one knows that once the human body is lost, [it is difficult to regain].

"Ten thousand kalpas may pass before it can be restored—is this not what is meant by this? (The common world regards Zhuang Zhou as a fabricator of falsehoods and does not believe his account of the *jiaoliao* bird. One might take a Western microscope and observe it;

one will then see the whiskers and eyebrows of a mosquito, its body hairs coarse and long. How could there not be those who breed and hatch the *jiaoliao*? The verification regarding the Great Peng is seen below.)
The *Mahādharmanirdeśa-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "All sentient beings are given names according to their respective forms and categories, such as birds, sparrows, and so forth.
Among these sentient beings, there are no fixed or definitive names for hungry ghosts.
Do not say that a deva is fixedly a deva, a human is fixedly a human, or a hungry ghost is fixedly a hungry ghost; it is just like a single thing."
Above, there are various names, just as for a single person there are various names, or as for a single celestial being (*deva*).
This is likewise true even down to the hungry ghosts (*preta*) and animals (*tiryagyoni*); furthermore, there are many hungry ghosts who have no names at all.
In the space of a single finger-snap, they transform their bodies and manifest in various forms; how could one possibly call out their names?

Because the causes and conditions of their evil karma therein have not yet been exhausted, they manifest various bodily transformations within a single thought-moment. The *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* states:
"Formerly, when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī preaching the Dharma for devas and humans, there was at that time an elder in the city."
His wealth was incalculable, yet he was stingy and greedy by nature and took no pleasure in giving alms. He always ate with his doors closed and disliked having guests.
Whenever it was time for him to eat, he would invariably command his doorkeepers to shut the gates and doors firmly, ensuring that no one should enter the interior without authorization.

Beggars were begging for alms. At that time, the elder suddenly craved fine food and commanded his wife to prepare a meal, instructing her to slaughter a plump chicken, seasoned it with ginger and pepper, and boil it until cooked. When it was immediately ready, he ordered the outer gate to be closed.
The husband and wife were seated together with a young boy sitting in the center, and they ate their meal as a group.
The couple took pieces of chicken and placed them in the boy’s mouth, doing so repeatedly without ceasing for even a moment.

The Buddha, knowing that this elder possessed the merit from past lives to be delivered, transformed himself into a śramaṇa. While they were seated and eating, he appeared before their seats and offered a blessing. And...
He said, "Give a small amount in alms; you shall obtain great merit. The elder raised his head and, seeing the transformed śramaṇa, immediately reviled him, saying, "You are a man of the Way;
how can you have no shame? Your family members sit and eat together; why do you intrude upon them?
The śramaṇa replied, "It is you who are foolish and do not know shame. As for me, a mendicant, why should I feel ashamed? The elder asked:

The elder said, "I am with my wife and family; we enjoy ourselves together. Why should I feel shame? The śramaṇa replied, "You have killed your father and taken your mother as your wife, yet you provide for an enemy.
You know not shame or disgrace, yet you call yourself a 'beggar' (bhikṣu). How can you be so devoid of shame and modesty?
Having heard this, the elder was startled and asked, "Why do you, O practitioner, speak such words? He replied, "The chicken on the table—that is you."
In a previous life, your father was constantly reborn among chickens due to his stinginess and greed, and was eaten by you.

This young child was formerly a rākṣasa, while you were a great merchant who boarded a ship to go out to sea; the vessel repeatedly lost its way and drifted into the land of the rākṣasas, where you were eaten by them.
After five hundred such lifetimes, when his life there ended, he was reborn here to serve as your attendant.
"Son, because your remaining karmic retribution is not yet exhausted, he has come wishing to harm you. As for this wife of yours, she was your mother in a previous life;
because the bonds of affection were so deep and firm, she has now returned to be your wife. Now you are foolish and do not recognize your past lives;
you have killed your father and nurtured an enemy, taking your mother as your wife. Thus you revolve through the cycle of birth and death in the five realms of existence, wandering without end."

Regarding the five paths of rebirth, who is able to know them? Only those who follow the Way perceive this; seeing that the foolish do not understand, how could they not feel a growing sense of shame?
Thereupon, the elder’s hair stood on end and he appeared as if struck with terror. The Buddha manifested his majestic spiritual power to cause him to recognize his past lives.
Upon seeing this, the elder immediately recognized his former existence; he then repented and apologized for his transgressions, and straightaway received the five precepts.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. (Because asuras encompass gods, ghosts, and animals, it is called the "five paths. If asuras are included, it is termed the "six paths.
Since there are three evil paths, there should likewise be three good paths; however, the translator has omitted this.)
The Venerable Aśvajita of India went into the city to beg for alms and saw a crow; he then smiled.
His disciples asked him about it, and the Venerable said: "In a past kalpa, I wished to leave the household life, but my parents would not permit it.
They forcibly betrothed me to a wife, and when I had a son who was six years old, I again desired to depart. My parents then instructed their son to embrace my feet and weep."
He said, "Father, if you abandon me, upon whom shall I rely for my livelihood? You must kill your son first, and only then may you depart;
because of this child, you will not be able to leave the household life. From that time on, for ninety-one kalpas, he transmigrated through the six realms of existence and never again saw him.
Now, observing with the eye of the Path, he sees that the crow is none other than his former son. Out of compassion for his ignorance and his long dwelling within birth and death, [he speaks thus].

One should smile with joy. If one obstructs another from leaving the household life, it will not only result in rebirth in the evil realms, but even if they later obtain a human body, they will likely be born blind for many lifetimes.

Therefore, when a wise person sees someone seeking to leave the household life, they should use skillful means to bring it to fulfillment and must not create obstacles. (From the *Dharmapada-śāstra*).
Du Yuan, courtesy name Yongping, was a native of Fuyang in Zizhong during the Jin dynasty. His family was immensely wealthy. He had an only son named Tianbao, whom he doted upon.
When the boy was ten years old, he died of a sudden illness in the third year of the Taiyuan era. Several months passed.
The pig raised by the family had given birth to five offspring; one was the fattest.

Later, when a new magistrate arrived in office, he wished to present it as a ceremonial gift and seized it to have it slaughtered. Just then, a bhikṣu suddenly appeared before him and said, "This pig is your own child.
Have you forgotten it after these past hundred-odd days? Having finished speaking, he vanished instantly. [The magistrate] looked around in all directions to search for him.
He looked and saw [the figure] departing through the air toward the Western Heaven, while the fragrance filled the marketplace and did not dissipate until the end of the day.

The śramaṇa Zhi Dun (style name Daolin) was a native of Chenliu. His spiritual presence was exceptionally brilliant, and he was a preeminent master of the elegant traditions of both Daoism and Buddhism.
He once debated his teacher regarding the nature of things, arguing that it would be insufficient to slaughter a chicken egg for immediate consumption.
[The Master] was punished together with all the crawling and flying insects. The Master soon passed away. Suddenly, he appeared before [Zhi] Dun, holding a chicken egg in his hand.
He threw it to the ground and broke it open; a chick was seen emerging from its shell and walking about. Dun immediately realized this and regretted the error of his previous words.
In an instant, both the Master and the chick vanished without a trace. (The two preceding accounts are from the *Mingxiang ji*. [The egg was already within the hen’s belly.]...)
There is a conscious spirit that enters it, just as a person in the womb [is one with it] and there is no duality.
Over forty li to the southeast of ○ City in Yizhou during the Sui dynasty, there was a family surnamed Huangfu. Among the brothers living in the household...
There were four brothers: the eldest and the youngest both diligently attended to their livelihoods and were benevolent, loyal, and filial. The second brother was named Qian;

he associated with evil friends and did not attend to his work. In the eighth year of the Daye era, while their mother was inside the hall, she took sixty coins, intending to have them used for market purchases, and placed them upon the bed.
The mother then went toward the back of the house, and Qian entered the hall from outside.

He looked around to left and right; seeing no one, he stole the money and took it out for his private use. When the mother returned and could not find the money, she did not know her son had taken it.
She then questioned all the members of the household, both free and servile, but they all said they had not seen it.

The mother, resentful that the matter was not cleared, proceeded to whip the entire family, young and old. Both the adults and the children harbored resentment. In the following year, she passed away and was reborn as the mother within the household.

Within the belly of a pig, after three or five months had passed, a single piglet was born. When the animal reached the age of two years, in the eighth month during the autumn *she* (community festival), money was required.
It was sold to a household participating in the *she* in a distant village for six hundred coins. The *she*-official took it away.
At the beginning of the first watch of the night, the entire family, both old and young, saw the pig; it first touched its wife with its snout and appeared in her dream, saying: "I am your husband."
For the sake of taking sixty coins from the village headman, my entire family was unjustly subjected to needless torture, which caused me to be reborn as a pig. Now I have come to repay this debt;
I have already been sold to the village butcher, who has bound me, intending to kill me. You are my wife; how can you bear to remain silent and not let our sons and daughters redeem me?
At first, his wife dreamed of this; she suddenly woke up with a start, yet she still did not believe it and fell back asleep.

The dream was thus. The pig again touched the woman with its snout; she started in alarm and put on her clothes. She went to the hall to inform her mother-in-law, who had already risen and was sitting up.
Her dream was identical to that of the woman. The children all likewise saw the same dream. That night, she packed her belongings and sent her son and her elder brother to move away.
He also took twelve thousand coins with him. His mother told her son, "If the village official refuses to release him, we must seek to pay double the price;
I fear he will be executed at dawn. She urged him to ride away quickly. Having traveled thirty *li* from his home, the son arrived at that place.

He did not say that it was his own relative, fearing it would bring disgrace upon his family name; he merely said, "There is no need to kill it. I now wish to redeem this pig. The head of the village shrine refused.
"The time for my sacrifice to the earth god has arrived," he said, "and I will not give the pig to you. Though [the brother] pleaded with him repeatedly and most earnestly, he would not let go.

The elder brother’s son grew terrified and anxious, fearing that the pig would be killed. He privately relied upon a man of knowledge and faith who had once served as a county magistrate, and related the matter in full detail.
The circumstances were indeed true. Later, he finally ransomed the pig. Once he had obtained the pig, he drove it toward the wild fields.

The elder brother said to the pig, "If you are truly my younger brother, you should quickly go forward and return home. The son also said to the pig, "If you are truly my father, you should likewise go forward and return home.
Upon hearing these words, the pig ran ahead and returned to the house. After a long time had passed, his relatives...
They all knew [the truth]. The children felt ashamed and humiliated, and their neighbors, harboring mutual resentment, mocked and reviled them by calling them pigs.

The children spoke privately to the pig, saying: "Father, because you performed unwholesome deeds in this life, you have received this body as a pig; we, your sons and daughters, cannot even show our faces.
During your lifetime, Father, you were always on very close terms with the Venerable Xu (Xiuxian). You used to send us, your children, to the Xu family to deliver food."
"I am offering this to my father. Upon hearing these words, the pig shed tears and galloped toward the Xu family home. The Xu residence was more than forty *li* from his own dwelling.
In the eleventh year of the Daye era, the pig died at the Xu household. One can truly know that karmic retribution does not discriminate between kin and stranger;
it is as clear as something before one's eyes. How can one not be cautious? At Hongfa Temple in Chang’an, there was the Dharma Master Jinglin, who was a descendant of [the aforementioned lineage].
In the neighborhood, people personally witnessed this pig. The Dharma Master recounted it to me.
There was a man named Bian Shuyu of Yangzhou; his father served during the Sui dynasty and was granted the rank of Yitong for his merit in the conquest of Chen. However, he was miserly and stingy.
Once, he hired people to build a house for him but did not pay them their wages. When the laborers demanded their money, Zhou Yu’s father whipped them.
The workers said in anger, "If you truly owe us this, we shall become oxen to work for you when we die. A short while later, Zhou Yu’s father died.
That same year, the builder’s wife gave birth to a yellow calf with black markings across its waist, encircling it completely like a person's belt. To the right...

A white mark spanned across it, slanting through from side to side; its size was exactly like that of an official’s ceremonial tablet (*xianggu*). The owner of the ox called out, "Gentleman Bian, why do you wrong me?
The calf immediately bent its front knees and placed its head upon the ground. Yu then ransomed it for one hundred thousand coins.
The owner of the ox did not permit it; only after [the ox] had died was it collected and buried. Yu merely spoke of this upon approaching it.
During the Daye era of Luoyang, there was a man surnamed Wang who constantly observed the five precepts and would occasionally speak of events yet to come.
The people of his village respected and trusted him. One day, he suddenly said to others, "Today someone will bring me a donkey.
At noon, a man indeed arrived leading a donkey and wept as he spoke, saying, "I lost my father early in life."
He had been raised by his widowed mother as an only son and daughter. Two years had passed since the daughter was married and his mother died.
On the day of Cold Food Festival, he took wine and food to offer at her tomb. As he rode toward the burial site on a donkey, intending to cross the Yi River, the donkey refused to wade across.

They whipped his head and face until they were wounded and bleeding. Upon reaching the burial site, they unyoked the donkey to perform the sacrifice; shortly thereafter, the donkey vanished, and they returned to their original location.
That day, the sister was sitting alone in her brother’s house when she suddenly saw her mother enter, with blood flowing from her head and face.
Her appearance was haggard and emaciated. Wailing and weeping, she told her daughter: "In my lifetime, I avoided your brother and gave you five *sheng* of rice.
Because of this, I incurred this transgression and have been reborn as a donkey. I have been repaying your brother for five years. Today, I wish to cross the Yi River."
"The water was deep and I feared it. Your brother whipped me until my head and face were completely broken, yet he still expected me to return home and beat me even more severely.
I fled here to inform you that my debt is now nearly repaid; why do you treat me with such irrational cruelty?
Having said this, she went out, but her mother could not be found. When the brother finally returned, the daughter first observed that the donkey’s head and face were mangled and broken.

Blood flowed from the wound, appearing exactly as if his mother had been injured. The girl took him in her arms and wailed. Her elder brother, surprised, questioned her; she told him what had happened.
The brother also said that at first he had refused to cross the river, and that it was only after he was lost and recovered that he spoke of the circumstances, which matched exactly.
Thereupon, the brother and sister embraced one another and wept bitterly; even the donkey shed tears and would not eat grass or water. The brother and sister knelt and pleaded with him. If...
"This mother wishes to eat grass. The donkey immediately began to eat. After a while, it stopped again. The brother and sister were at their wits' end;

they then prepared some millet and sent it to the place where the King of the Five Precepts was, whereupon the donkey ate and drank once more. Later, the donkey died, and the brother and sister collected its remains for burial.
In Linyang County, Jizhou, there was a man named Geng Fusheng. His family possessed a modest amount of property.
In the eleventh year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, Fusheng’s mother, Lady Zhang, borrowed two bolts of silk from her husband to provide for their daughter.
Several years later, the mother passed away and was reborn as a sow within the family home. She subsequently gave birth to two piglets; Fusheng [raised] both of them.
Having finished eating it all, she subsequently ceased to conceive. Fu Sheng then summoned a butcher to sell her.
While he had not yet taken her away, a traveling monk arrived with a young boy, seeking alms from Sheng. He paused for a short while at Sheng’s house, and the boy entered the pigsty to play.
The pigs spoke to him, saying, "I am the mother of Fu Sheng; because I avoided him in former days..."
"My father’s eyes! He took two bolts of silk and begged for me as a bride. Because of this sin, I have been transformed into a sow.
I gave birth to two piglets, but they were devoured by their mother. Now that my debt has been repaid and I owe nothing more, the butcher wishes to summon me to sell me;
please report this to him. The youth related all of this to his teacher. The teacher then said in anger, "You are utterly deranged! How could a pig understand such things?"
Having said this, he immediately went to sleep. After another day had passed, the pig saw the youth and spoke again, saying, "The butcher is coming;
for what reason do you not inform him? The youth spoke to his master once more, but the master did not permit it. A short while later, the butcher arrived to take the pig.
The pig leaped over its pen and ran out, heading toward the bed beneath the monk's seat. The butcher then reached the monk's quarters. The monk—
He said, "A pig came to me; I shall now redeem it. He then took out three hundred coins to redeem the pig.
Later, he spoke privately to Fu Sheng, asking, "Has anything ever been lost from your home, such as silk? Sheng replied to the monk, "During my father's lifetime, two bolts were once lost.
He then asked how many sisters there were. Sheng replied, "There is only one elder sister, who was married to the official north of the county."
The monk then related in detail what the youth had said. Upon hearing this, Fu Sheng wept uncontrollably with grief.
He thereafter redoubled his efforts to provide offerings for the sow’s mother. After several days had passed, the pig suddenly died of its own accord.
It appeared in a dream to the girl and said, "Having now settled my debt, I have been reborn in a favorable realm. It further exhorted the girl to diligently cultivate merit.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, Wei Qingzhi, the Chief Secretary of the Prince of Wei, had a daughter who had previously died.
The couple grieved for her deeply. Two years later, Qingzhi was about to gather his relatives and guests to prepare a feast; his family purchased [a girl]...
Before the sheep had been slaughtered, at night, Qingshi’s wife dreamed of her deceased daughter.

She was wearing a green skirt and a white shirt, with a pair of jade hairpins atop her hair—the very ones she had worn during her lifetime. She came to see her mother, weeping as she said, "I have previously used certain items."
She did not tell her parents. Due to the retribution of this karma, she has now received the body of a sheep to repay the lives of her parents;
she is due to be slaughtered tomorrow morning. The one that is a blue sheep with a white head is she. She specifically prays for your compassionate grace and begs for her life.
Her mother woke up in alarm and went to observe the sheep herself at dawn. Indeed, there was a blue sheep whose neck and shoulders were entirely white, with two white spots upon its head.
It was shaped like a jade hairpin. The mother wept bitterly before it and forbade her family from killing it, waiting for Qingshi to arrive before releasing it.

Shortly thereafter, Qingshi arrived and urged that they eat. When the cook informed him that the lady had forbidden the slaughter of the green sheep, he became enraged and immediately ordered its killing.
As the butcher hung the sheep up to slaughter it, several guests had already arrived and saw one [sheep] hanging there.
A young woman, of upright and handsome appearance, pleaded with the guest, saying, "I am the daughter of the Regional Inspector Wei;
I beg you for my life. The guests were struck with astonishment and stopped the butcher. Fearing that Zhi would be angry, and seeing only the bleating of the sheep, they proceeded to slaughter her.
Subsequently, the guests sat without eating. Zhi questioned them in wonderment, and the guests related the matter in full. Zhi was overcome with grief and fell ill, eventually passing away.
It began. Among the common people of the capital, many were well-acquainted with this matter. Minister Cui Dunli recounted it in detail when he visited me.
Regarding the customs of the marketplace in Chang’an: every year, from the first day of the new year onwards, people take turns preparing food and drink to invite one another.
This was known as the "Transmission of Seating. Zhao Da, a calligrapher from the Eastern Market, was next scheduled to provide the meal.

A guest arrived early, and later he saw a young girl on the pestle, about thirteen or fourteen years old, wearing a blue skirt and a white shirt, with a water-drawing rope tied around her neck fastened to the pestle’s pillar.
She wept and said to the guest, "I am the daughter of my master. In years past, before I died—"
At that time, she had stolen one hundred coins from her parents intending to buy cosmetics, but died before she could use them.
Those coins are now inside the kitchen building, within the wall at the northwest corner. Because of this crime of theft, she must now repay her parents' lives.

Having finished speaking, she transformed into a white-headed green sheep. The guest was startled and informed the host; when the host questioned her physical appearance, it was revealed to be his young daughter.
"Two years have passed since his death. I found a hundred coins in the kitchen wall, appearing as though they had remained there for a long time.
Thereupon, I sent the sheep to the Sengsi Temple, and my entire family no longer eats meat. Lu Wenli related this account to Lin. (The above seven accounts are from the *Mingbao ji*).
Emperor Wenzong: While the imperial kitchen was preparing a meal, an egg was being cooked. Suddenly, a very faint sound was heard coming from within the cauldron.

Upon listening, it was found that the eggs were collectively calling out to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva with profound lamentation. The supervising cook reported this to the Emperor, who dispatched someone to investigate.

As expected, the Emperor sighed in admiration and said, "I did not know that the spiritual power of the Buddha-way could be such as this. He issued an edict that from now on the use of chicken eggs was forbidden.

On another day, while eating clams, there was one that could not be pried open; he burned incense and prayed for it, and it opened. Suddenly, it transformed into the image of a Great Being (Bodhisattva).
The Emperor summoned the Chan Master Weizheng of Taishan and questioned him about the matter, saying... [and so forth]. Immediately—
An imperial edict was issued to all monasteries throughout the realm to establish images of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara and offer them worship (as recorded in the *Tongji*).

In the northern section of the West Market in the capital, there was a master artisan named Wang Hui; his mother had previously passed away, and he had already completed the period of mourning for her.
In the second year of the Xianqing era, a dog with greenish-yellow fur was born into the family.
It happened that the master’s wife beat it several times with a staff because it had stolen some food. The dog then spoke in human speech, saying: "I am your paternal aunt.
For you, my daughter-in-law, to strike me with a staff is a great error. Because I was excessively cruel to my own family members, I have received this retribution. Now that I have been..."
He struck her and said, "I am ashamed to go to your house," and she immediately ran away. When Huìshī heard of this, he wept and carried her back home, but she left again.

This happened four or five times in total. Seeing that her resolve had ceased, Huìshī invited her to the main street north of the market, specifically behind the large northern wall of his own shop, where he built a small hut for her and provided food daily. The people of the market...
Travelers and onlookers gathered there in great numbers; those who threw cakes to it were beyond counting.

This dog never left this house, yet after the time for the midday meal had passed, it refused to eat. After one or two years, no one knew where it had gone. (The phrase "after the time for the midday meal" refers to the period following noon.)
Li Xin of Bingzhou was a native of Taipingli in Wenwater County. He served as a guard in the Longzheng government office.
In the winter of the Xianqing era, he traveled to Shuozhou for the military census according to custom, riding a chestnut horse and leading a foal.
At that time, late in the year, the cold shadows and wind and snow were thick and severe; after traveling some dozen li, the horse suddenly refused to move forward.
Xin waited for the appointed time. When the time drew near, he hurriedly beat [the horse] several dozen times. The horse then spoke in human speech and said to Xin:
"I am your mother. Because I avoided your father during my lifetime and begged for over a stone of rice for you, I have received this retribution."
"This colt is none other than your younger sister. Since she has repaid the debt through her labor, why do you continue to suffer?

Why do you press me so urgently? When Xìn heard this, he was struck with astonishment; his tears flowed uncontrollably as he prostrated himself in gratitude. He then personally took up the saddle and bridle, saying:
"If you are indeed Xin, you should go home yourself. The horse then proceeded forward; Xin took up the saddle and bridle and followed it back to his home.

When Xin’s brothers and others saw him, they wept together in sorrow. They separately prepared a spacious stall for him to keep and feed him. His mother also invited monks to perform a vegetarian feast;
the entire family was diligent in their practice, and both the laity and clergy of the local community all marveled at this extraordinary event. At that time—
Wen Wuyin, Vice Minister of Works, and Zhang Jinping, Judicial Official of Qizhou, were both at home observing the period of mourning for their parents.

Upon hearing of this, they found it extraordinary and went to visit him with sincere interest. Seeing that the horse was still there, they inquired into the details of how it had come to be, and everything was exactly as had been reported.
Lü Boda of Xiaoyi County, Fen Prefecture, borrowed one thousand coins from a man of the same county during the Yonghui era.
Later, he breached the contract and refused to acknowledge it. When the creditor produced the contract to demand repayment, Lü Boda made a vow before a Buddha together with the money-lender, saying:
"If I do not repay you, I pray that after my death, I shall become a beast of burden for your household. He spoke thus.
He died before a year had passed. When he reached the age of two, a cow belonging to the owner of the money gave birth to a red calf with white hair on its forehead;
the hair formed the three characters "Lù Bódá. His son and nephew were ashamed of this and offered five thousand coins to redeem it, but the owner refused to give it up.
He then donated it to Qifu Temple in Xicheng County, where the monk Zhen [took charge of it].
Thus, he assisted in the construction of a fifteen-storied stupa. Anyone who saw it would resolve to cease from evil and ultimately offer money and goods as alms.
(The above three accounts are from the *Mingbao Shiyi*).
Record of Ming Dynasty Shaozhou, Qujiang County, Liucun Village. The Liu family kept a male dog for several years until the end of the Chongzhen era.
One day, the dog entered the kitchen; fearing the dog would steal food, the wife struck it on the head with a wooden ladle, whereupon it died. Its—
At night, the dog appeared in a dream and said to its master, "I am your nephew. Because I owed you eight cents of silver, I acted as your guardian for your household.
Now that my debt has been repaid, I depart. Upon waking, the uncle did not believe it; he fell back asleep, and the dream was exactly as before.
The next morning, he buried the dog on the mountain behind his house. That night, the dog again appeared in a dream and said to the uncle, "I have received your great kindness in burying me..."
"I had a dog in the mountains behind my house that was recently stolen by someone from our village. He has not yet finished eating it; there is still one leg hanging over the kitchen stove to smoke.
Early the next morning, the owner went to the mountain to look for it and found it had indeed been stolen.

When he went to the thief’s house to question him, the thief at first refused to admit it. The owner said, 'There is still one leg remaining hanging over the kitchen stove to smoke,' and he described the dog."

Because of these causes and conditions, the man was struck with terror and apologized incessantly. [His son] Qín heard this firsthand and recorded it. The Sūtra states that all sentient beings, as they transmigrate through the five realms of existence, have been mutual relatives to one another.

These words are not empty. Among the six domestic animals raised by people today, some come to repay debts, while others come to be born out of love for their homes. To those with ordinary eyes, this is invisible; who would know that these are not their own kin? That one should then kill and eat them—how can one not feel sorrow at heart?
In the Qing Shaoxing era, Wang Han-chong reported that in the city of Shaoxing, during the Gengzi year of the Shunzhi reign,

there was a fifty-year-old woman at the East Gate who habitually used the pretext of soliciting donations for Buddhist services to deceive people. She suddenly fell ill for several months and gradually transformed into [a beast].
The pig has long hair on its snout, prefers to lie down with other pigs, and its voice resembles that of a pig as well.
At the Bridge and Prince Pan’s residence in Yangcheng (Guangzhou), [Wang] Qiao and the Prince Pan were feasting in the guest-house tower of Ye Mingqi.
There were four turtles intended for cooking and serving to the guests; Qiao and the Prince Pan spoke at great length about how extraordinary they were and that it was improper to kill them. Mingqi—
[The author] said: "I once saw within a turtle a creature resembling a Hui-zi, with its head, face, and folds of clothing all complete.

Qiao said: "For a Hui-zi to be inside a turtle is also most extraordinary. Furthermore, I have often heard of turtles entrusting their dreams to people to beg for help, yet humans, for the sake of food, suddenly lose their heart of compassion.
Alas! (The above two accounts are from the *Tieqiao ji*. Early Qing Dynasty. The marketplace at the Four Archway Gate in Yangcheng.)

In the midst [of the proceedings], a large turtle was presented as a sacrificial offering; within its belly were four dead children. People saw this and questioned me about it. I said, "This is called the 'Turtle Treasure' (Kūrma-ratna). It can speak for humans; it is not a malevolent spirit. When the turtle is born, they are born; when the turtle dies, they die with it, just as the eighty thousand families of worms within a human's pores die when the person dies.

If anyone wishes to see them, one should keep the turtle in a basin and observe from a secluded place. Every time the moon reaches the full phase and rises to the midpoint of the sky, the turtle raises its head to gaze at the moon, and the treasure emerges from the crown of the turtle’s head.

The upper part [of the dance] is sung; its head resembles that of a *huíhuí* (Persian). People desire to obtain it and wish to master its method. A common saying goes: "If one obtains it, one shall slit open the belly of a tortoise to store it within. When encountering treasure beneath the earth, it will immediately inform the person. In my youth, I once heard of someone boiling a turtle.

As it cried out for its life within the cauldron, the man opened the vessel, only to find the turtle already dead. He simply called it a "tortoise-ghost" (*bièguài*). How could he have known that it was a treasure that deserved to be killed? Formerly, when I lived in seclusion at the White Elephant Grove on Mount Xilai in Yíngdé County, there was a monk...

His mind was filled with compassion. Planning to go to the market the following day to buy living creatures to release, that evening he dreamed of forty-five people begging for their lives. The next morning, when he went to the market, he encountered a cage of field crabs; upon counting them, there were exactly forty-five. He then purchased them and released them back into the wild.

Yet all sentient beings cherish life and dread death; in their hunger for food and their need for rest, as well as in their experience of suffering and joy, they are no different from humans. Although their forms differ across ten thousand species, their nature is one and the same. People are all conditioned by long-standing custom and fail to perceive this;

whether killing or eating [them], they collectively bind themselves to enmity for ten thousand generations. When retribution arrives all at once, what can be done to avoid regret? *Tián há* (Field Clam), also called *tián jī* (Field Chicken) and specifically named *xiā mó* (Toad), is commonly eaten in the regions south of the Ling Mountains.
The *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance) states: "Sins and blessings accumulate one upon another, their heavy counts clearly distinguished;

hereafter, one shall receive the retribution of these sins and blessings, each without fail. A virtuous thought leads to receiving a body among devas or humans; an evil thought leads to receiving a body in the three evil realms."
In a single day and night, the evil thoughts of greed, hatred, and delusion are incalculable; they plant the roots for future birth and death.
Hereafter, one shall receive eighty million and five hundred thousand bodies of various kinds. Within a hundred years, the calamities sown for future lives are exceedingly difficult to enumerate.
The soul follows these seeds to receive form, pervading the three thousandfold great chiliocosm. (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)
It is said: Those who are fond of killing are not welcomed by any living being. If one does not take pleasure in killing, all sentient beings will joyfully seek to rely upon them.
Therefore, when the life of one who upholds the precepts is about to end, their mind is peaceful and joyful, free from doubt and regret.
Whether they are reborn in the heavens or among humans, they shall always attain long life. This constitutes the causal condition for attaining the Way. Thus it is said.
Until one attains Buddhahood, one dwells for an immeasurable lifespan. Those who take life will experience various forms of physical and mental suffering in both this life and future lives;
those who do not kill shall be free from these manifold sufferings. The *Dìchí jīng* (Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra) states:
"The sin of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, a short lifespan; second, [sickness]."
Such people suffer many illnesses. Thus, these ten non-virtuous actions are each fully present, resulting in five kinds of retributive fruits.
First: for what reason does one who kills receive the suffering of hell? Because by killing, they cause suffering to sentient beings;
therefore, when the body perishes and life ends, the various sufferings of hell all come to press upon them. Second: for what reason does one who kills emerge as an animal? Because of killing...
Lacking compassion and acting contrary to human ethics, one exhausts the retribution for hellish offenses and receives the body of an animal.
Third, why does killing lead to rebirth as a hungry ghost (*preta*)? Because such killing necessarily stems from a mind of stinginess and a greedy attachment to flavors, one becomes a hungry ghost.
Fourth, why does killing lead to birth among humans with a short lifespan? Because of that killing and its violence...
By harming the lives of sentient beings, one obtains a short lifespan. Fifth, for what reason does killing result in contracting many illnesses?

Because killing violates the natural harmony of things, various afflictions converge upon the perpetrator; thus, one contracts many illnesses. One should know that killing involves such suffering as this:
to kill another is, in fact, to kill oneself. What wise person would willingly kill themselves? (The remaining nine unwholesome actions are detailed as in the sūtra. [From the] Canon.

As recorded: In a past kalpa, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was once a lion, an elephant king, a deer, a monkey, a goose, a sparrow, a *saṃjīva* bird, and even a rat or a louse. Long ago, there was a female tortoise who became pregnant and fell ill;
she said to her husband, "I wish to eat the heart and liver of a monkey, and only then will I recover. Her husband replied, "The monkeys are in the mountains. He said: [and so forth].
"How can we obtain it? the wife said. "If we do not obtain it, we shall die. The husband went into the mountains and saw a monkey upon a tree.
He said, "I will be your friend. If this mountain has no fruit, I can carry you across the water to another mountain where there is good fruit;
would that not be delightful? The monkey agreed. On another day, the monkey rode on the back of a tortoise across the water, and when they reached the middle...
The turtle said, "My wife longs for your heart and liver to eat; that is why I have become your friend. The monkey said, "Why did you not tell me sooner?
My heart and liver are still hanging from a tree; I have not yet brought them back. You may carry me back to fetch them. The turtle then carried the monkey to the shore.
The monkey immediately climbed a tree and did not come down for a long time. The turtle said, "Good friend, why do you not come down? The monkey replied:
"Who was it that had the leisurely mind to hang from a tree branch? The monkey was Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One. The turtle was Devadatta.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a seer named Kāśyapa who practiced austerities in the mountains.

He said to a louse, "When I enter meditative absorption, do not bite me and cause my mind to become distracted; when I emerge from absorption, you may eat as much as you please. Later, at another time...
The Flea (vulgarly called the "dog louse"). He asked the louse, "Auntie, why are you so plump and white? The louse replied, "I am like the Head Master."
This was because [the flea] would come out of meditative absorption at will to eat his food. At another time, while waiting for the seer to enter absorption, the flea bit him repeatedly.
The seer became angry, lit a fire, and shook his robe; the flea leaped away, but the louse was burned to death.
The louse was the Blessed One, and the flea was Devadatta. Furthermore, in one lifetime, the Buddha and Devadatta were *sahajīvin* birds—birds with a single body.
There were two heads. One was crouching beneath a poisonous tree while the World-Honored One’s head was asleep. Devadatta’s head saw a poisonous flower fall to the ground;
he immediately ate it, wishing to kill the other head with poison, not realizing that both lives would perish together. Thus one knows that people of the present day—
One must not harbor enmity toward others; for throughout successive lifetimes, we shall encounter one another and become mutual adversaries. This was true even before the Buddha attained the Way;
as we wander through the cycle of birth and death within the six realms, there is no type of body among the myriad classes that we have not assumed.

If we do not now abandon evil and cultivate goodness, how can we avoid becoming any of these myriad forms? Those who possess wisdom should reflect upon this for themselves, examining each point in detail.

The Buddhist Canon contains many texts, which cannot be recorded here in their entirety. (The *Tongji* states: "In sacrificing to Heaven and Earth and in offering to the ancestral altars, it is necessary to slaughter animals to prepare the ritual offerings.

From the time of the ancient sovereigns and kings, this has been established as the law. Those who possess a state maintain this as a matter of principle and dare not venture to debate it. Now, those who preside over the transformations of Heaven and Earth are called the Supreme Deity (*Shangdi*) and the August Heaven and Earth; they are the most sagely and divine beings.

How could such a divine and sagely being delight in the slaughter of livestock and sheep, or deign to partake of food that is raw and foul-smelling? This stems from the customs of high antiquity, when people lived by consuming hair and blood; they necessarily used these means to nourish themselves and consequently employed them to serve the spirits. Such a crude and vulgar view fails to realize that sacrificial victims are inherently raw and stinking.")

As for this practice of ritual defilement (*dú*), the common people have long partaken of grain; their customs have not changed. When the sages and worthies taught the world, they took the ancient laws as their model and codified them in the *Liji* (Book of Rites). Subsequently, later kings followed and practiced them, with none daring to debate their merits or faults.

They maintained that nourishing oneself was as it had been in antiquity, yet they failed to consider that serving the deities should not involve such defilement. Now, to be reckless in taking life is inhumane (*bù rén*); to offer raw and foul-smelling things is unrighteous (*bù yì*). If one takes these acts of inhumanity and unrighteousness as the old custom of nourishing oneself, one should still reflect on how to exercise restraint in order to preserve a heart of goodness.

How much less, when serving the spiritual numina of Heaven, Earth, and the ancestral spirits, would one wish to defile them with sacrificial animals and raw, foul-smelling offerings? Since the Buddha-dharma gradually spread to the East, it has encouraged the cultivation of *zhāijì* (fasting and precepts), and the Heavenly Emperor...

If one already knows how to serve the Buddha, how could one serve the heavens while remaining ignorant of serving the Buddha? Once one knows the proper way to serve the Buddha, it becomes clear that it is improper to defile Heaven with sacrificial livestock; this can surely be trusted.

Only Emperor Wu of Liang, and the two emperors of Wei, Xianwen and Xiaowen, issued decrees for sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples not to use oxen and sheep, but to replace them with vegetables, flour, wine, and fruit. This may be called following the Way despite departing from ancient custom; to offer millet and grain and present pure water is precisely the sacrificial method of the Three Dynasties. What need is there for the foul-smelling items of livestock and slaughter?

Emperor Xuan of Qi received the Bodhisattva precepts from Meditation Master Sengchou and never again ate meat. He abolished all five types of hunting preserves and the hawks and dogs used as instruments of life-taking, as well as all slaughter within his realm.

Emperor Wen of the Sui (3rd year: issued an edict that throughout the empire, during the first, fifth, and ninth months, as well as the six days of fasting, it was forbidden to kill living beings). Emperor Gaozu of the Tang (2nd year of Wude:

issued an edict that during the first, fifth, and ninth months, as well as the ten days of fasting, execution, slaughter, and fishing were prohibited, to be made a permanent national custom; in the 1st year of Ruyi, an imperial decree ordered the cessation of slaughter and fishing throughout the empire). Empress Wu (issued an edict ordering the cessation of slaughter and fishing throughout the empire).

Emperor Suzong (issued an edict establishing "Pools for Releasing Living Creatures" throughout the empire, totaling eighty-one locations; Yan Zhenqing composed the inscription). Emperor Taizu of the Song (issued an edict that from the second to the ninth month, the people were not permitted to hunt or shoot; this was codified in the legal statutes).

The True Sect (issued an edict to all provinces and prefectures to restore all fish-releasing ponds; in places where no ponds existed, fishing was prohibited for five *li* around cities in the prefectures along the Yangtze and Huai Rivers.
