In the original text, he was a *jijiu* (libationer) of the Daoist school; wishing to discard his talismans and registers (*fúlù*), he followed the teachings of the Daoist laity (*dàomín*) to offer counsel and restraint, and thus came to practice both traditions.
He constantly exhorted others to observe the Eight Precepts Retreat (the "Jiǔ" [lit. libationer] of Daoists was formerly called the "Jiǔdào";
the term refers to the ritual master). At Sōsì Temple in Yīzhōu was the monk Zhìdá; his conduct was somewhat worldly, yet he was skilled in chanting the scriptures. He was twenty-three years old.
In the sixth month of the third year of the Song Yuanhui era, he died of illness. His body remained warm, so it was not encoffined. After two days had passed, he gradually returned to consciousness.
At dawn on the third day, he was able to speak and look about; he recounted that when he first fell into distress, he saw two men, both dressed in yellow cloth trousers and tunics.
One stood outside the door, while the other went straight to the bedside and said, "The Master should depart. It may be... [text ends]... permitted.
This was a lower realm. Fotuoda said, "I am physically frail and cannot endure traveling on foot. The man replied, "You may ride in a carriage.
As soon as he had finished speaking, a carriage arrived. Once Fotuoda had ascended it, his consciousness became dazed; he no longer saw his family or his house.
As for the carriage he rode, looking out in all four directions as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but wilderness.
The path was arduous and perilous; [the Buddha] showed him the way up the ascent until they reached a vermilion gate. The walls and portals were exceedingly magnificent.

Upon entering and reaching the hall below, there sat upon a haughty couch a nobleman in the hall, wearing a crimson robe and a ceremonial cap. His appearance was stern and remote, possessing great majesty and dignity. He was flanked by a hundred guards on his left and right.

He was granted permission. All around were rows of vermilion pillars and swords standing in dense array. When the nobleman saw Da, he composed his countenance and assumed a solemn expression, saying, "For one who has left the household life, how can you commit so many transgressions?
Da replied, "Since the time I first attained consciousness, I do not recall having committed a sin. The nobleman asked:
Regarding the suspension or continuation of the recitation of the precepts, Zhu Fada said, "When I first received full ordination, I indeed practiced the recitation regularly.

Lately, however, I have been occupied with the fortnightly assemblies and lectures, constantly engaged in the turning of the scriptures; thus, I have occasionally neglected the recitation of the precepts during the *poṣadha*.

He added, "If a śramaṇa does not recite the precepts at the proper time, what fault is there in this? You may simply recite the scriptures for now. Fada then recited three sections of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and then ceased.
The Noble One commanded the recorded messengers of the Dharma, saying, "You may lead him to the place of suffering, but do not cause him excessive pain.

The two men led the Dharma master away. After traveling several tens of li, he gradually heard the sound of thunderous crashing and the roar of boiling fire, while the path ahead grew increasingly dark.
They then arrived at a gate several tens of zhang high, of an extremely hard black color; it was an iron gate, and the walls were likewise.
He realized that this must be hell. Great terror seized him, and he regretted that during his life in the world he had not cultivated his practice.
Upon reaching the entrance of the gate, there was a tumultuous roar; after listening quietly for a long time, he finally recognized it as the sound of people crying out.
Inside the gate it grew increasingly dark until nothing could be seen again. At times the firelight would flicker out and then flare up, revealing several...
The man was led forward with his hands bound behind his back. Behind him followed several men holding spears who pierced him; blood flowed like a spring.

One of these men was none other than his paternal first cousin’s mother. When they encountered one another, he wished to speak with her, but someone dragged him along with such speed that he had no leisure to speak.
After entering the gate for about two hundred paces, he saw an object shaped like a grain storehouse, approximately ten feet high.
The other two men seized Da and threw him onto a granary. Inside the granary was a flame that burned half of Da’s body until it was completely rotted away.
His pain was unbearable, and he fell from the granary to the ground, remaining unconscious for a long time. The two men then took Da away again.
They saw more than ten iron cauldrons, all boiling with sinners; the people inside the cauldrons rose and sank as they boiled. Beside the cauldrons...
People pierced him with forks. Some who climbed out of the cauldrons had their eyes bulging from the boiling heat and their tongues protruding more than a foot;
their flesh was completely scorched and rotten, yet they still did not die. All the cauldrons were full, except for one that remained empty.
The two men said to Da, "Venerable sir, you should enter this one immediately. Upon hearing these words, Da’s heart and gallbladder seemed to be smeared upon the ground; he then made a request.
He said to him, "May you, my lord, listen to this poor monk’s one request: perform a single prostration to the Buddha with a sincere heart, and pray that you may be spared from this suffering.

He prostrated himself on the ground for as long as it takes to eat a meal; his prayers and repentance were exceptionally earnest. When he rose and looked around in the four directions, nothing was to be seen again, except for a level plain and lush trees, the scenery bright and clear.
Yet the two men continued to guide him along until they reached the foot of a tower; the tower was small in height.
Above him was a person who could barely fit to sit. He said to Da, "It is truly a cause for joy that you, a śramaṇa, are currently undergoing such light retribution.
At the foot of the tower, Da suddenly regained consciousness without realizing it. Da still exists today at Suo Temple;

his observance of the precepts has become even firmer, and his practice of meditation and recitation is increasingly steadfast. (Although Da was skilled in chanting the scriptures and lecturing on the precepts, he could not avoid distraction; his mind pursued fame and profit, and he further neglected the poṣadha and the recitation of the Vinaya. Thus, he experienced retribution in the hells. People of today...)

Having left the household life, one should exclusively trade the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure of the Tathāgata for the wealth and profit of this world. Since the precepts no longer concern the heart, how can there be any uposatha? Furthermore, as Da said: "Since the time I first attained consciousness, I do not recall having committed a transgression.
How many people nowadays could truly say this? Please reflect upon yourself: are you not without shame and fear?

At Duobao Monastery, Shi Daoshi resided at the Northern Duobao Monastery. While serving as the superintendent of the halls and pagodas for the assembly of monks, he secretly stole precious ornaments such as curtains and canopies;
what he took was very extensive. Subsequently, he even stole the pearl between the eyebrows of a Buddha image.
He then breached the walls and enclosures as if he were an outside thief, so that the monastic community could not detect him. After more than ten days had passed, he fell ill.

He then saw a strange man who pierced him with spears and lances. This man came and went at intervals; whenever he arrived, [Dao'an] would cry out in alarm, and blood would flow from his body in response to the sound.
At first, this occurred once or twice a day, but later it became more frequent. As the injuries grew severe, the assailant appeared more often until wounds covered his entire body.
He groaned and wailed, unable to stop the sound. The monks of the same monastery, suspecting that he might have committed some transgression, wished to perform a rite of repentance on his behalf.
At first, when questioned, he still avoided speaking; only after two or three days had passed did he fully recount his story. Weeping, he pleaded for mercy, saying:
"I was foolish, perverse, and unprincipled, believing that there were no dark realms of the underworld. In my loss of mindfulness, I committed transgressions and invited this cruel calamity.

While alive, I suffered torture and interrogation; upon death, I was bound to knives and cauldrons. Now that my body has been ground to pulp, I pray only that you grant me compassionate forgiveness. I have nothing else left to offer."
I have only robes, felt mats, and sandals; perhaps these may suffice for a single assembly. Furthermore, I have frequently requested [the opportunity] to perform repentance in full.
In the past, I stole two pearl ornaments from a Buddha image; one has already been given to a woman and cannot be recovered, while the other was pawned for money.
It was with Chen Zhao’s family. It can now be redeemed. Since Daozhi had passed away, the monks gathered together and were able to redeem the *xiangzhu* (divination ball).

They also prepared a vegetarian feast and performed repentance rites. When the artisans first attempted to reattach the divination ball, it shifted and turned back repeatedly, refusing to settle into place.
The assembly of monks again performed prostrations and burned incense, whereupon it finally became fixed. More than a year later, during the darkness of night, his fellow students...
At that moment, he heard voices speaking of emptiness. Listening closely, he recognized them as the voice of Daozhi. Daozhi spoke of himself, saying:
"Since my death, I have been afflicted by every kind of agony for many years and kalpas, with no prospect of release.

It is only by relying on the compassionate protection and salvation of the assembly of monks, who ransomed this statue, its features, and this pearl, that I have found occasional respite amidst such bitter suffering. My gratitude is boundless; therefore, I have come for a brief visit."
He offered his thanks, saying only these words. As he spoke them, the stench of rotting flesh and the agonizing pain were unbearable.
When he finished speaking, the foul odor gradually subsided after a long time. This occurred toward the end of the Taishi era; the temple officials have already recorded it in full.
Regarding the śramaṇa Senggui: he was a monk of Wudang Temple. At that time, Zhang Yu of Jingzhao frequently invited Senggui to his home to receive offerings.
On the fifth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Yongchu era, while free from illness, he suddenly died.
After two days, he revived and said: "On the night of the fifth, during the fifth watch, I heard a clamorous noise in the gate and alleyways. In a short while..."
He saw five men carrying torches and holding banners of faith come straight into the house. They shouted at Cujue, who immediately collapsed onto the ground.
The five men then bound him with red ropes and led him away. They traveled until they reached a mountain that was entirely devoid of grass or trees;
the soil was hard and black, resembling stone or iron. On both sides of the mountain, white bones were piled up in heaps. After traveling several dozen li, they arrived at the third [mountain].
At a fork in the road, there was a man of great height and vigor, clad in armor and grasping a weapon. He asked, "Of the five men, how many are coming?
They replied, "Only one person. The five men then intended to enter through a certain path.
Suddenly, they arrived outside a city containing several dozen houses built of rammed earth. In front of the houses stood wooden posts over ten *zhang* tall, topped with iron beams.
The structure was shaped like a well-sweep (a lever for drawing water). On both sides were troughs for holding soil, and the soil was categorized by quantity;
there were forms as large as ten *hu* (measures of grain) and others as large as five *sheng*. A man dressed in red robes and a red cap spoke to Gui, saying:
"When you were born into this world, what sins or merits did you have? Speak according to the truth; do not speak falsely. Gui was terrified and had not yet replied when the man in red spoke again.

The bureau official said, "We may open the registers to examine your merits and faults. After a short while, the official arrived beneath a tall tree carrying a casket of earth, which he suspended from an iron beam and weighed.
As the scale seemed to tilt, the official said to Rui, "This is the balance for weighing merit and fault.
Your merit is slight and your faults are many; you ought to undergo punishment first. Suddenly, there appeared a man dressed in formal robes and cap.
The man said to Gui, "You are a śramaṇa; why do you not recite the Buddha's name? I have heard that by repenting one may escape the eight difficulties.
Gui then single-mindedly invoked the Buddha's name. The official, seeing his robes and cap, said to the clerk, "You should recite it for this man as well."
"Since you are a disciple of the Buddha, it is fortunate that you may be delivered. The official then weighed him again on the scale, and the scale was perfectly balanced.
Thereupon, they were about to lead Gui before the supervising officer to have the matter adjudicated. The supervisor took up his pen and examined the registers; he hesitated for a long time.

Then another man appeared, dressed in crimson robes and a black cap, wearing a seal and ribbon, and holding a jade tablet. He came forward and said, "There is no record of him upon the registers of calculation."
"This is a human being," [the monk said]. The warden was startled and ordered his attendants to arrest him. A moment later, they saw five people brought in with their hands tied behind their backs.

The warden said, "O executioner-ghosts, why have you brought a human here by mistake? He then whipped them. After a short while, a messenger arrived claiming that the Heavenly Emperor summoned the practitioner.
Upon arriving at the imperial palace, he passed through various halls, all of which were composed almost entirely of gold and jewels.
Its brilliant radiance was so dazzling that one could not gaze upon it steadily. The Emperor’s attendants, dressed in crimson robes and wearing jeweled crowns adorned with precious gems, were there.
The Emperor said, "You are śramaṇas; why do you not apply yourselves diligently to your practice, yet allow these minor spirits to capture you so recklessly?
Gui bowed his head to the Buddhas, praying for grace and seeking blessings. The Emperor said, "Your life is not yet exhausted; you shall now return to life. You ought to be diligent and energetic."
"Do not frequent the homes of laypeople too often. The 'Killing Ghosts' (Śūlika) seize people, and they frequently commit wrongful excesses, just as you have done.
Fanggui asked, "By what means may one escape the calamity of such wrongful excesses? The Emperor said, "To extensively establish meritorious deeds is the most excellent way.
If you cannot manage that, you may observe the Eight Precepts (Aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa). By doing so, you will avoid misfortune while alive and depart from hell after death."
This was the second [instance]. When he had finished speaking, he sent Hui-gui away. Not long after his departure, [Dao-an] saw a monastery with many śramaṇas.
He saw the abbot of Wudang Monastery and the Dharma Master’s disciple Hui-jin; they were all there. The dwellings were grand and orderly, and provisions and attendants were naturally provided.
Hui-gui requested to reside there. A certain śramaṇa said, "This is a land of merit; it is not for you."

This is the place where he was found. The messenger, intending to take him back, arrived at Yu’s house, and [Senggui] revived. (The above five accounts are from the *Mingxiang ji*. As for those monks today who enjoy frequenting the homes of laypeople, let them observe Senggui’s case.

How much more so for those whose observance of the precepts is flawless, yet whose minds engage with worldly passions such that concentration and wisdom are no longer present; thus they are recorded by the spirits of the slain. Had there been no virtuous conduct worthy of praise, how could they have encountered a noble person who instructed them to recite the Buddha’s name and repent, and the Heavenly Emperor who exhorted and encouraged them?)
The Official of Qi: At that time, there was an official surnamed Liang who was extremely wealthy.

As he was about to die, he said to his wife and children, "The slaves, horses, and various attendants whom I have loved throughout my life have served me well for many years and always met my expectations. When I die, they shall be buried with me as funeral offerings."
Otherwise, there would be nothing upon which to ride. When he died, his family members filled a sack with earth and pressed it down to kill the slave;
yet the horse had not yet been killed. Four days after the slave died, he revived and recounted: "I was unaware as I departed, until suddenly arriving at the gate of an official office.
The gatekeeper detained me there, and I stayed at that gate for one night. At dawn the next morning, I saw my deceased master, bound in chains and guarded by soldiers."
He entered the government office and said to the slave, "I thought you were dead, which is why I left instructions to summon you.
Now, each of us must undergo our own suffering; we have no connection whatsoever. I shall now report this to the authorities to have you released. Having finished speaking, he went inside.
The slave peered out from behind a screen and saw the official ask the guards, "How much oil was pressed yesterday? They replied, "Eight *dǒu* were obtained.
The official said, "Press more; take one *hú* and six *dǒu*. The master was then dragged out by the press and could not say anything at all.
When he came again the next morning, his complexion was bright, and he said to the slave, "I shall now speak on your behalf."
The official entered again and asked, "Did you obtain any fat? He replied, "I did not. The official asked, "Why not?

The head official said, "This man died three days ago, and his family invited monks to hold a memorial service. Whenever the sound of the sutras and chants was heard, the iron beam would invariably break."
Thus, he could not obtain it. The official said, "I shall depart for now. The head official informed the magistrate, requesting that the slave be released.
The magistrate immediately ordered his release. They both went out the gate. The master sent the slave to deliver a message to his wife and children, saying:

"I rely upon you all to perform meritorious deeds on my behalf; thus have I been spared from great suffering. Yet I am still not yet free. You must further create scriptures and images to rescue me, hoping thereby that I may attain liberation. From this day forward..."
"In the future, do not perform sacrifices. Since they cannot eat them, you will only increase my transgressions. Having finished speaking, he departed.

The slave was subsequently reborn and related everything in detail to his family. On that very day, they indeed held a memorial assembly; the entire household pursued merit, and the whole clan engaged in ascetic practice. (From *Mingbao Shiyi*).
Those who today practice self-immolation for burial—upon seeing this, they should awaken. To avoid such a violent death and instead incur heavy karmic retribution for oneself!

Zhou Ba Hu. Emperor Wu was fond of eating chicken eggs, consuming several at a single meal. There was an attendant in charge of the imperial cuisine named Ba Hu who was frequently favored for presenting the Emperor’s meals.
After Emperor Wen of the Sui ascended the throne, he continued to serve as the attendant in charge of the imperial cuisine until his death during the Kaishuang era.

He died, yet his heart remained warm. His family members could not bear to enshroud him; after three days, he revived and was able to speak. He first said, "Carry me to see the Supreme Honored One to report this to Emperor Wu.
Suddenly, he saw someone come to call for him, and they went together to a certain place where there was a vast chasm in the earth.
Just as they reached the mouth of the chasm, he saw Emperor Zhou Wu, who performed a ritual prostration before him. The Emperor said, "The King summons you to testify."

"It is my duty. The messenger ordered the Yitong (Minister of Rites) to bow to the king. The king asked, "When you prepared food for the Emperor, how many 'white balls' (*baituan*) did you present in total?
The Yitong did not know what a "white ball" was; he looked to his attendants. His attendants said, "Chicken eggs are called 'white balls'.
The Yitong then replied, "The Emperor ate white balls, but I truly do not remember the number. The king said to the Emperor: "This..."
The people did not remember [this event], but it ought to be recorded. The Emperor rose from his seat, looking dejected and unhappy.

Suddenly, he saw an iron bed in the courtyard, along with several dozen jailers, all with human bodies and ox heads. They laid the Emperor upon the bed, and the jailers used an iron beam to press down upon him.
From the places where both sides of the Emperor’s ribs were split open, whole chicken eggs emerged; in an instant, they reached the level of the bed—there were about ten of them.
The remaining bushels were then exhausted. When the King commanded that the count be completed, the bed and the prison guards suddenly vanished.
Before this, his maternal grandfather, the Duke of Qi, had personally seen the Yitong and recounted the events in detail upon returning home (as recorded in the *Mingbao ji*).

In a district outside the capital of Jizhou during the Sui dynasty, at the beginning of the Kaihuang era, there was a boy of thirteen who frequently stole eggs from his neighbor’s flock to roast and eat.
Later, one morning before the villagers had risen, he heard someone outside knocking on the door and calling out to him.
The child’s voice reached him, and his father ordered the boy to go out and respond. A man appeared and said, "The official summons you. He then led the boy out of the village to the south.
It was formerly a mulberry field that had been plowed but not yet sown with seed. Suddenly, the young boy saw a small city to the right of the road.
The gate-towers on all four sides were painted in vermilion and white with great solemnity. The boy asked in wonder, "When was this city built? The messenger rebuked him, saying, "Do not speak.
They then proceeded to the northern gate of the city and ordered the boy to enter first. As soon as the boy crossed the threshold, the city gate suddenly closed.
Not a single person was to be seen; it was nothing but an empty city. The ground was entirely covered with hot ashes and scattered embers, reaching just above the ankles.
Suddenly, a young boy cried out and ran toward the southern gate. As he was about to reach it, the gate closed. He then ran toward the east and west gates, and the same thing occurred at each.
When he had not yet arrived, it opened; once he had arrived, it closed. At that time, many villagers went out to gather mulberry leaves, both men and women in great numbers.
They all saw this boy in the middle of the plowed field, making sounds like crying as he ran about in all directions. They said to one another, "Is this boy mad?
Since morning he has been playing like this without ceasing. When mealtime came, those who had gone to gather mulberries all returned. The boy’s father—

He asked, "Do you see my son? The man from Sang replied, "The boy is playing and running to the south of the village; he will not come when called. The father went outside the village and saw his son running from afar.
He called out the boy's name once, and the boy stopped immediately. Suddenly, the city ashes vanished. Seeing his father, the boy fell down and cried out as he spoke.
When the father looked at his feet, everything from the mid-calf upward was scorched, the flesh and blood having been consumed by fire.

The lower part of his legs from the knees downward were severely blistered and scorched as if roasted. He carried him home to nurse him, yet while the flesh above the thighs remained as it was, the portion below the knees eventually became withered bone.
When the neighbors heard of this, they vied with one another to come and inquire about the cause. He answered them as before.

When the people examined the place where he had run, the footprints appeared clearly throughout, yet there was no ash or fire at all. This was truly because, due to his karmic offenses, he perceived hell wherever he looked.
Thereupon, the men and women of the town, regardless of their age, all observed the fast and precepts, never failing in them until death.

There was a monk of great virtue, the Dharma Master Daohui, originally from Jizhou, who recounted this in detail, just as his neighbor had told him (from the *Mingbao ji* [Records of Miraculous Retribution]—this shows that hell exists everywhere; it is simply that those undergoing punishment see it for themselves).
In the eighth year of the Kaihuang era, Du Qi of Jingzhao died and revived three days later. He said that he saw King Yama, who asked him, "Do you recognize Zhou Wu?
He replied, "I served as a judicial official in the Left Imperial Guard; I know him very well. The King ordered an official to lead him to an iron house.
From within an iron window, he saw Emperor Wu; his body was extremely emaciated, his complexion was the color of iron, and he wore iron [armor].
Bound in shackles, he wept and said, "Great Lord, for what reason are you so deeply distressed?
The Emperor replied, "I have suffered great distress; that I am here now is a source of great joy. The monk asked, "What sinful karma did you commit to undergo such suffering?

The Emperor said, "Because I believed the words of Wei Yuansong, I defiled and abolished the Buddha-dharma; therefore, I suffer this. The monk asked, "Why did you not cite scriptural authority [to refute him]?"
When Yuansong arrived, the Emperor said: "I once wrote a commentary on it. However, officials have searched everywhere throughout the three realms and have not found it.
If he comes this morning, I shall be released by evening. You must go back and tell the people of the world to perform meritorious deeds for Yuansong's sake."

"Come early to rescue me; if you do not arrive, there will be no time for my liberation. Pray, revive me! Thus he exhorted them regarding matters of the netherworld, urging them to perform meritorious deeds.

(From the *Mingbao ji* and the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*. Yuan Song was a native of Yizhou. He left home to become a monk in his youth; though intelligent and quick-witted, he did not find favor with others. He feigned madness and wandered aimlessly, composing verses upon whatever he encountered. He traveled extensively for over twenty years.)

No one can fathom him. He was likewise a bodhisattva practicing the "inverse course" (*pratiloma-caryā*) of the provisional vehicle (*upāya-yāna*), such as Devadatta and others; who indeed could fathom him?
During the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, Zhao Wenchang, the Vice Director of the Grand Court of Culture (*Wenchang Dafusi Cheng*), suddenly died a violent death.
For several days, only his heart remained warm, so his family did not dare to enshroud him. Later, he regained consciousness and spoke. His kinsmen...
This belongs to the category of strange accounts. Wenchang said: "After I died, a person led me to the abode of King Yama.
The King asked me, 'Throughout your entire life, what meritorious deeds have you performed? I replied, 'My family was poor and I had nothing with which to cultivate merit;
I did nothing but single-mindedly recite and uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Upon hearing these words, the King pressed his palms together, knelt down, and praised me."
He said, "Excellent, excellent! That you are able to receive and uphold the Prajñā is a merit so great it is inconceivable.
The King spoke to the person in charge, saying, "You must investigate thoroughly; do not bring the wrong person.

After a short while, the messenger investigated and realized his error, and immediately reported to the King, saying, "This person is indeed mistaken. Calculating by the breaths of life, he is still some twenty years away from death."
The King, hearing these words, immediately spoke to his messenger: "Lead Wenchang toward the inner scripture repository and fetch the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Following these instructions, the messenger led Wenchang westward for five li until they reached the repository.
There he saw several dozen buildings, exceedingly magnificent and splendid; within them, the scripture scrolls were completely filled. Gold...
The volumes were bound with precious silk covers and were exquisitely adorned. Upon seeing them, Wenchang’s virtuous mind was further inspired.
With single-minded devotion, he joined his palms, closed his eyes, and reached out to draw a scroll at random. Its size was similar to those he had previously recited.

Wenchang became anxious and fearful, suspecting it might not be the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and requested that the attendant exchange it for another; however, the attendant refused. Yet, upon reading the title, it said: "Among all meritorious deeds, this is the foremost."
First, Chang opened it to look; it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Chang was filled with joy and brought it to the king’s presence.
The king ordered one person to hold the scroll on the west side, while Chang stood on the east, facing the scripture.

He sent Chang to recite the sutra, and when the official examined him, not a single character was omitted, and he recited it fluently throughout. At that time, the king released Chang to return home, and further issued instructions.
Chang said, "You must diligently uphold this sutra; do not let it be neglected or forgotten. He then had a man lead Chang out through the south gate.
Just as they reached the gateway, they saw Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou inside an eastern room of the gatehouse, his neck bound with three layers of iron shackles.
The Emperor immediately called out to Chang, saying, "You are a fellow countryman of mine who has come here for a short visit. I must speak with you. Thus it was recorded.
When Chang was summoned, he immediately ran to where Emperor Wu was and prostrated himself before him. The Emperor asked, "Do you recognize me?
Chang replied, "Your servant formerly served as a guard to Your Majesty; I clearly recognize Your Majesty.
The Emperor said, "Since you were my former minister, go home now and speak on my behalf to Emperor Wen of the Sui. I wish to have all my sins fully expiated; only—"
The sin of destroying the Buddha-dharma is grave; it cannot yet be brought to an end. At that time, Wei Yuansong instructed me to destroy the Buddha-dharma.
Although I have pursued Yuansong several times since then, I have not caught him; for this reason, the matter remains unresolved. Chang asked where Yuansong had gone. The King could not find him.
The Emperor said, "At that time, I did not understand Yuansong's intent; I mistakenly destroyed the Buddha-dharma. Yuansong is..."
He is one outside the three realms; he is not subject to the jurisdiction of King Yama. For this reason, they could not find him by pursuing him.
"Tell the Emperor of Sui," he said, "and beg for a small amount of my property to cultivate merit. I hope that through the support of such blessings, I may escape from hell.
Having accepted his charge, he took his leave and traveled for a short while. Upon exiting through the southern gate, he saw a man's head within a large pit of excrement.
A lock of hair emerged. Chang asked the guide, "What is this object? The guide replied, "This is Bai Qi, the General of Qin.
He was buried alive here after massacring the soldiers of Zhao; his retribution for this sin remains unfinished. The guide led Chang back to his home, where he was restored to life.
After three days, Chang’s ailment gradually improved. Chang reported this matter in full to Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty.

Emperor Wen issued an edict that every person within the realm should contribute one coin to have the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* recited for Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, while also observing a three-day fast.
He further commanded that this event be recorded and included in the *History of the Sui* (as found in the *History of the Sui* and the *Records of Miraculous Retribution*).

At Lingyan Temple in Qizhou, during the sixteenth year of Emperor Wen’s reign, the monk Daoxiang died suddenly. He arrived at the underworld and beheld the Bodhisattva Śrī-Ābhāsvara, who led him to tour the hells. There was a notice that read:

"The śrāmaṇera Daohong, while preparing dumplings for the assembly of monks, first stole a bowl of them for himself; he shall fall into the Iron Pellet Hell. However, Hong had suffered from mouth sores for several years.

Upon hearing this, [Daoxiang]... *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment. The final sentence is incomplete, as it ends with "聞相" (heard [this], Xiang), suggesting a narrative continuation regarding Daoxiang's realization.*
Having spoken thus, he prepared offerings for the assembly of monks. Just as he had seen, there were more than thirty people who bore the retribution of their sins.

Within seven days, thirteen of them died; having seen the Bodhisattva point out their karmic retributions, they informed the others, who then each made restitution, and the prison records vanished accordingly.
Furthermore, he saw another record inscribed with: "This person stole a monk’s apricot tree and cut it down."
It was used as material for making combs. A monk of the temple named Daoguo found a piece of leftover wood that was still fit to be made into a comb;
it was worth eighty coins. [The owner] said that [the debt] should be repaid by falling into the Hell of Burning Fire. When Daoguo heard this account, he immediately paid the debt back.
Furthermore, in the second year of the Yangdi era, the monk Daoming passed away. His fellow monk Xu went out into the wilds at dusk and suddenly saw a temple. He went toward it...

He threw it [into the water]. When he encountered Daoming, [Daoming] appeared no different than on ordinary days. However, when he saw the monks' porridge, it was all the color of blood, and his entire body was ablaze with fire.
Xu questioned him in detail, and Daoming said, "This is hell. I once took a bundle of the monastery's firewood to boil dye, but I forgot to repay the cost.
I must suffer these torments for a full year. When he lifted his robes, he saw that everything below his knees was scorched black.
The man said, "I beg you to purchase a hundred bundles of firewood for me and return it to the monastery's permanent endowment, and to copy one volume of the Lotus Sūtra;
then I may be spared from this suffering. Xu agreed. He returned to the temple and prepared everything according to his word.
When he went back to search for the temple, it was silent and nothing could be seen (from the *Sengjing lu*).
In Yongzhou, Zhao Wenruo of Chang’an died during the Daye era. Seven days later, when his family was performing the major dressing and preparing to place him in the coffin, he contracted one leg.
The family members were terrified and did not dare to put him in the coffin. Wenruo then returned to life.
His relatives joyfully asked for the reason, and Wenruo replied: "At the moment of my death, I saw people leading me toward the realm of Yama."
[The King] went to the place of King Yama and asked Mañjuśrī, "During your lifetime, what meritorious deeds did you perform?
Mañjuśrī replied, "I upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King sighed in admiration, saying, "Excellent! This merit is supreme.
Although your merit is virtuous, nevertheless, lead you to the place where you shall undergo retribution. Then, one person led Mañjuśrī northward for ten paces until they reached a wall.
Kongruo entered the hole. A person on the other side reached out a hand through the hole and seized Kongruo by the head, pulling him out with extreme difficulty.
Once he had crossed to the outside of the wall, he saw the great hells and the tortures of the boiling cauldrons, where the sinners were undergoing suffering beyond description.
There were also many pigs, sheep, chickens, fish, geese, and ducks that came crowding forward toward him.
Wenruo said, "I did not eat your bodies; why do you press me so?

Each of the animals replied, "In years past, on such-and-such a day, month, and year, at such-and-such a place, you ate our heads, feet, and four limbs, tearing them apart joint by joint for each person to drink and eat.
Why do you now deny it? Seeing that the animals were citing the truth, Wenruo did not dare to refuse.
[The man] was contrary [to expectations]. He knew only to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and deeply repent for his various sins, uttering no other words.

He then sought out the animals, saying, "When I am restored to life, I shall fully cultivate merit and virtue to repay you. When the animals saw that he was cultivating merit, they all released him at once.
The person who had led Wenruo took him to the king's presence; having finished describing the place where he had witnessed the beings undergoing retribution, the king gave him a bowl of nails.
When Wenruo ate it, he used five nails to pin the text to his head, as well as his hands and feet. Thereupon, he returned home and recovered consciousness.
He recounted the matter in detail, suffering from extreme headaches as well as pain in his hands and feet. After practicing meritorious deeds for a long time, the pain gradually subsided.
From that time forward, he diligently recited and upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, never daring [to neglect it].
Not wasting even a moment of time, he exhorted both monastics and laypeople, as well as those close and distant to him, to receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā.
Later, while on an official mission, he arrived at a post station and rested for a short while upon its veranda;

he felt as though he were about to fall asleep when he dreamed of a woman dressed in blue who came rushing toward him, pleading for rescue and begging for her life. Startled from his dream, he immediately called for the station master and asked him: "You..."
"Is it not for me that you wish to kill this living being? The station master replied, "Indeed, it is for your sake that I wish to kill a small ewe.
Wenruo asked, "What color is that sheep? He replied, "It is a small blue ewe. Wenruo said, "Release it immediately!
I shall provide the price to ransom it and set it free. This was truly due to the power of Prajñā, providing secret assistance through spiritual resonance.

[This is] appropriate. [Question: "Throughout a person's life, the number of domestic animals, fish, birds, and so forth that have been slaughtered for food is difficult to count. Furthermore, the number of people killed by bandits and robbers cannot be calculated. Why is it that we never see a single one of them die a violent death and then return to life? [Answer:

Those people with such heavy karmic offenses cast off their bodies and immediately enter the eight cold and eight hot great hells, where they suffer for long kalpas with no foreseeable end to their release;

therefore, no one is able to see them. Those who now die and then revive again are all merely in the peripheral or minor hells (*prādeśika-naraka*). Even within these minor hells, those whose offenses are particularly heavy are likewise difficult to encounter. This is like the mother of Master Zilin mentioned above, or the fellow student Huirong mentioned below."
At Zhenji Temple in the capital city was the śramaṇa Huiri. From his youth, he had been diligent and practiced asceticism, serving as a disciple of Xinxing.

After Xinxing passed away, Huiri continued to uphold and follow his teachings. During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, while practicing dhyāna and meditative concentration, he remained motionless for seven days.
The assembly all marveled at this, believing him to have entered a state of profound samādhi. Subsequently, Huiri opened his eyes and wept.

As they conversed, the monks asked him in astonishment, "What is this? He replied, "My feet were burned by fire and are in pain; wait until I have finished tending to my sores, and then I will explain.
When the assembly all pressed him for an account, Huiri said, "I was summoned by King Yama to perform rites for seven days.

When the period was complete, the King asked if I wished to see any of my deceased kinsmen or spiritual teachers. I replied that I wished to see two people. The King then sent someone to summon one of them, but I saw only a tortoise."
Huiru came forward to lick [the man’s] feet; tears fell from his eyes as he departed. Another person said, "His offenses are too grave to summon him; let him come to see you.
The messenger led Huiru to the gate of the prison, which was closed very firmly. The messenger called out to the guards, and someone answered.
The messenger told Huiru, "Master, quickly clear the path; do not stand directly in front of the gate. Just then—
As he stepped aside, the gate opened, and a great fire flowed out from it like sparks from a forge. It leaped upon his feet and burned them;
when he raised his eyes to look at the gate, it had already closed, and they were never able to see one another again. The King bestowed thirty bolts of silk as a gift.
He firmly declined, but was not permitted. He said, "I have already sent her to the rear quarters. The monks vied with one another to go to the room and look; there, the silk was on the bed.
On her leg, a burn wound as large as a coin had healed only after more than a hundred days. (The above two accounts are from the *Mingbao ji*.
Zhenji Temple is the present-day Huadu Temple.)
*Liùdào jí*, Scroll Four, Phonetic Explanations:
*wù* (pronounced *wù*), wild duck.

*Chīxiāo*: the first syllable is pronounced *tái*. It is a malevolent bird that eats small birds; the second syllable is pronounced *jiāo*. It is an unfilial bird that, when large, eats its own mother.
*Yù* is pronounced *jù* with a departing tone; it refers to an old woman.
The *Guanfo yufo jing* (Sūtra on Bathing the Buddha) states that when one bathes the Buddha and offers money or treasures, they should be divided into three parts:
the first for making offerings to the Buddha, the second for making offerings to the Dharma of the sūtras, and the third for the use of the Saṃgha.
*Xin* (pronounced as in *xin*) means heat; it also refers to the flourishing of light.
*Jiegao* (upper tone *jie*, lower tone *gao*) refers to a water-lifting mechanism. *Xun* (pronounced as in *xun*):
in antiquity, figures were fashioned from either earth or wood to be buried together with the deceased. In later times, people have become ignorant of this.
This is because humans are buried together.
*Tún* (pronounced like *tùn*) refers to a vessel for gathering rice and grain; it is commonly called a *gǔwéi*.
*Huántún* (the first character pronounced *hón*, the second *tūn* with a departing tone) refers to a rich delicacy made either from wheat flour or rice flour, containing an inner filling.
There is a stuffing. It may be round or flat; it is also called "flat food" (biànshí).
*Bǐ* (pronounced *bēi*) means to supplement, to augment, or to attach.
*Jiào* is the same as *jiào* (to cry out).
Huángyù (晃昱): The first character is pronounced with the second tone of huáng (黃); it means "broad and bright. The second character is pronounced yù (欲); it means "sunlight.
Nìngbō Fǔ (寧波府) includes Mù Xiàn (鄮縣) as its inner district. Mù (鄮) is pronounced mào (茂).
Wushan (Crow Stone Mountain) lies ten *li* southeast of Aśoka Monastery on Mount Mao. Upon the stone there are patterns resembling *kāṣāya* robes, which are distinct and clearly visible.
Among the stone statues from Wuzhong, one is the Buddha Virocana—that is, Vipaśyin Buddha—and another is Kāśyapa Buddha; they arrived by crossing the sea.

Not long after, both Fahui and the artisans passed away. In the nineteenth year, I went to Kaiyuan to offer incense and pay my respects, feeling deep regret.
How lamentable that it has come to this!
"Stūpa" is the Sanskrit term; it is also called *sūtra-dvīpa* (or *stūpa*) or *futu*. In the language of China, it means "accumulated form.

It is a tomb for enshrining the *śarīra* (relics) of the Buddha, signifying that the Tathāgata, throughout three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), cultivated and refined his merit and wisdom.

The remains of all virtues are gathered together to form *śarīra*. At sites such as where the Tathāgata attained enlightenment or preached the Dharma, stupas are erected in all cases to mark these vestiges.
Whether containing *śarīra* or not, they are all termed Buddha-stupas, intended for gods and humans to gaze upon, thereby extinguishing transgressions and generating merit.
Those in this region do not understand this and instead regard them as matters of *fengshui*; this practice began with the Zhejiang region.
The Qiantang River: several times each year, the tide suddenly arrives, with wave crests surging two or three zhang high, drowning boats and destroying houses.
King Zhongyi dispatched strongmen to shoot at it incessantly, but it did not cease. Chan Master Yongming Shou advised the King to build the Six Harmonies Pagoda by the riverbank to suppress it;
consequently, the tide subsided. At present, when the tide arrives, the waves are still high.
It is no more than a few feet in size. Because of this, later generations emulated it as a practice of geomancy (*fengshui*).
It is also due to the blessings bestowed by the Tathāgata’s virtue upon fortunate people; however, it must be kept pure and clean, for only then will there be manifest signs of efficacy.
Śarīra— here translated as "the Buddha’s bodily relics"— refers to the fact that when Śākyamuni Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa,
through the power of his compassionate vows, he emitted the fire of samādhi from his chest, which cremated his golden body and produced śarīra relics in the amount of eight *hu* and four *dou*.

These were as large as beans or as small as sesame seeds, capable of emitting light and manifesting auspicious omens in manifold transformations throughout the heavens, the human realm, and among the *nāgas*.

In the center, a stupa was erected for veneration; it extinguishes transgressions and generates merit. Although it is said to be eight *hu* and four *dou*, it nonetheless transcends the realm of numerical measurement.
All who seek it with a karmic affinity shall obtain it.
The eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) are: first, the hells; second, the animal realm; third, the hungry ghosts; fourth, the long-lived heavens;

fifth, the continent of Uttarakuru; sixth, being blind, deaf, or mute; seventh, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence; and eighth, being born before or after a Buddha. These eight are all obstacles to the Path;
because one cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma, they are called "difficulties."
The Eight Precepts of the Fasting Observance (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*): 1. Not to kill living beings. 2. Not to steal. 3. Not to engage in sexual misconduct.
4. Not to speak falsehoods. 5. Not to drink intoxicants. 6. Not to wear perfumes, floral garlands, or apply scented unguents to the body. 7.
Not to participate in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor to go to see or hear them. 8. Not to sit or lie on high, broad, or large beds. 9. Not to eat at improper times.

The first eight are called the precepts (*śīla*); the last one, abstaining from food after midday and at improper times, is called the fast (*upavāsa*). Together, they are termed the Eightfold Precepts and Fast (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla-upavāsa*).
One is permitted to receive them for only one day and one night, or on the six fasting days (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa-dina*), or on the ten fasting days (*daśa-upavāsa-dina*), or whenever there is leisure.
They must be received from a preceptor (*śīlācārya*) who clearly understands the Vinaya. This is because of their reception and observance.
This precept closes the gates to the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
it is the path for humans and devas, the cause for transcending the world, and the very root of becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch.

Its merits are inconceivable, as detailed in various sutras and treatises, as well as the *Sūtra on the Eight Merits of Nurturing*. Now, these have been collected and arranged into a single volume, titled the *Eightfold Abstinence* (Bā-jiàn-zhāi).

In the first year of the Yongping era of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, the Emperor visited Huālín Garden and established the Eightfold Precepts of the *gāṇḍī* fast.
During the Emperor’s humble years, while seeking refuge in Mount Jiéyáng, he piled stones to construct a stūpa; suddenly, a tree grew beside it.
It appeared like a floral canopy. Later, when the Emperor fell ill, he issued an edict for all *śramaṇas* to pray to the Buddha for seven days; celestial incense filled the hall.
Emperor Wu, the Gaozu of the Liang dynasty, established Guangzhai and Tongtai Temples, and throughout the realm, the people universally observed the six fasts and the eight precepts.

Emperor Xiaozhuang of the Zhou dynasty highly honored the Buddha-sun. He commissioned four niches for plain (unadorned) statues totaling over ten thousand figures and transcribed two thousand scrolls of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
He constantly propagated the practice of the six fast days and the eight precepts without interruption.
Emperor Xiaowu Wen of the Wei dynasty, on his birthday, held an Eight Precepts Retreat at Zhongxing Temple.
When the midday meal was finished, his attendants Yuan Min, Sun, and others further presented fish and meat. The Emperor was enraged and demoted them all from their offices.
He issued an edict that the women of the six palaces must observe the Three Long Fasting Periods of the year and receive the precepts on the sixth day of each month.

In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, there was a drought. An edict was issued for Dharma Master Tanyan to lead the assembly in praying for rain, yet the rain did not fall.

The Emperor asked for the reason, and [Tanyan] replied, "The matter depends on one or two things. The Emperor dispatched Su Cheng, the Governor of the Capital, to inquire about the meaning of "one or two.
Tanyan said, "Your Majesty personally manages the myriad affairs of state, while the various ministers serve as your limbs and arms."

Although their power generally serves as an antidote to the essence [of affliction], both have nonetheless failed in the profound transformation. It is due to these two factors that the rain one desires does not fall.

The Emperor perceived this intent and commanded the relevant officials to select an auspicious day. He established the ritual in the main hall and invited [the Master] to ascend the imperial throne to receive the Eight Precepts.
After the ministers had received them in succession, while the heat was like a burning fire, a great rain poured down copiously.
[Note: The Emperor was delighted. From then on, whenever Yan entered the court, the Emperor would personally serve him with imperial delicacies.

He issued an edict inviting Dharma Master Xing to enter the Taiyuan Hall to confer upon him the Bodhisattva Precepts. Furthermore, he decreed that throughout the empire, during the first, fifth, and ninth months, as well as the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa*), it shall be forbidden to kill living beings.
In the tenth month of winter, the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Great Master Zhi passed through Yuezhou to bestow the precepts upon the Regional Inspector Wang Xuwen.
At the request of the śramaṇa Tanjie and others, he lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. Hearing the Dharma, the local populace was moved and transformed;
throughout the five counties of the prefecture, at more than one thousand locations, everyone abandoned fishing and hunting.
During the reign of Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty, a crow nested in the Taiji Hall. He summoned Qu Anyuan to perform a divination, which stated:
"A female master from the southwest will be able to eliminate this anomaly. At that time, the nun Daorong was residing at Wujiang Temple in Liyang; she was summoned for an audience.
The Emperor placed the flowers beneath his seat to test whether they were ordinary or holy beings; he observed that the flowers where they sat did not wither.
The monk said to the Emperor, "Your Majesty should practice the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa); then calamities and portents will naturally be extinguished.
The Emperor acted according to these words, and the flock of crows carried away their nest. The Emperor then issued an edict to build Xinlin Temple for them to reside in.
Minister Bai Juyi, styled Lètiān, called himself the Layman of Mount Xiangshan.

He once exhorted one hundred and forty-eight people to form the "Assembly for Rebirth Above" at Bótà Temple, where they received the eightfold precepts of the fast nine times under the Great Master Rù.
Jianye is the same as Jinling. When the Qin unified the empire, it was renamed Moling. During the Wu period, it was changed to Jiangning Prefecture. Emperor Gaozong renamed it Jiankang.

He then constructed a stupa, enshrining them on its first tier. Later, it was expanded to three tiers.
The śarīra relics sought by Kang Senghui were also enshrined therein. In the first year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, the Changgan [Stupa] was established.

It was destroyed at the end of the Yuan dynasty and rebuilt in the tenth year of the Yongle era. It was constructed entirely of five-colored glass tiles and bricks, consisting of nine tiers. Each...

its summit is adorned with gold and precious jewels, while its wheel-shaped ornaments, exposed basins, and bells are all made of copper. Nowadays, those who do not know this have replaced them with iron.
At times, the stupa emits light, or lamps, or Buddhas, or sounds that resonate like thunder. Danyang County is located in Zhenjiang Prefecture.

He said, "Since there is no dining hall, we may use the surplus property of the Sangha to build one so that the monks may have their meals. He then had it constructed.
Later, while the abbot, Zen Master Zhi, was sitting in his private quarters at night, he suddenly smelled the scent of burning and heard the sound of shackles and chains.
Looking out, he saw someone carrying a flaming cangue, the end of which rested against the door threshold. Startled, Zhi asked, "Who are you?"

He replied, "The former resident was Dhyāna Master Shouyong of this mountain. It was improper for him to use property belonging to the Saṃgha to construct a refectory; therefore, he undergoes this suffering.

To repay him, one night Huiyong dreamed that Huiming thanked him, saying: "Relying on the Master's power, I have escaped hell and been reborn among humans and devas.

The official replied, "You had your brother slaughter oxen to entertain the *liao* in order to claim the act as a merit for the purpose of seeking office and reward for your own personal gain.

How can you claim it was for state affairs? He then said to Ke’s younger brother, "Because you testified against your elder brother, we detained you for a long time. Now that your elder brother has..."

"I have sent you to kill [them]; you shall thus be without guilt. Let them go free to take rebirth. Having finished speaking, the younger brother suddenly vanished, and they were never able to exchange further words.
The official questioned Ke again: "For what reason did you kill two more ducks? Ke replied, "When I was the former magistrate, I killed ducks to provide for the official guests.
How could this be my crime? The official said, "The official guests already had their provisions; there were no ducks [provided for them]. You..."
He offered them a duck. [The official] said, "This was intended to bring you a good reputation; how can this not be a crime? He asked again, "For what reason did you kill six chicken eggs?
He replied, "In my life I have never eaten chicken eggs. I only remember that when I was nine years old, on the day of Cold Food Festival, my mother once gave me six eggs, and I cooked and ate them.
The official said, "In that case, do you intend to shift the blame onto your mother? Ke said, "I dare not. However, let me explain."
"It is because of that very cause. This was brought about by your own negligence. The official said, "You have taken the life of another; you must suffer for it yourself.
As soon as he had finished speaking, suddenly dozens of men arrived, all seizing Zhi Ke and leading him away. Ke cried out loudly, "The government officials are also being excessively unjust!
Hearing this, the official called him back, asking, "How can there be such injustice? Ke replied, "From birth until now, I have committed sins, yet none of them—"

He was overlooked. Since his birth, he had cultivated merit, yet none of it was recorded. Is this not a case of injustice? The official asked the registrar, "What merit does Ke have that it is not being recorded?
The registrar replied, "His merits were indeed all recorded. However, we weigh the amount of his offenses against them.

If his merit is great and his offenses few, we order him to experience his merit first. If his offenses are great and his merit few, we order him to experience his offenses first. In Ke’s case, his merit is slight."

"His sins are many; therefore, his merits have not yet been discussed. The official said in anger, "Even though he first received punishment for his sins, why did he not proclaim his merits to show them?
He ordered the chief officer to be whipped one hundred times. In an instant, the whipping was finished, and blood splashed upon the ground.

Thereafter, he proclaimed all the merits that Daokē had cultivated throughout his life, leaving nothing out. The official said to Daokē, "You ought to have received punishment first; I shall now further [grant you...]"
"You shall return in seven days; you must diligently cultivate merit. He then sent someone to escort him out, whereupon he revived.

Sengke convened a great assembly of monks and nuns to perform rites of repentance and practiced asceticism with diligent devotion. He recounted his own experience, and when the seventh day arrived, he took leave of his family and suddenly passed away.
His elder brother served as an official under the Suifu, which was why he had been entrusted to him.
Li Shanlong of Fengyi served as a Left Gate-keeper Cavalier (Zuo Jianmen Jiaowei). During the Wude era, he died suddenly;
however, the area of his heart about the size of a palm did not grow cold. His family members could not bear to enshroud him for seven days, at which point he revived.

He recounted that at the time of his death, he was apprehended by the underworld authorities and brought to an official office hall, which was extremely vast and magnificent. Within the courtyard were prisoners.
There were several thousand people, some with neck-fetters and others with cangues and shackles, all standing facing north to fill the courtyard.

The official Shan Long was led by his attendants to the foot of the hall, where the Celestial Official sat upon a high couch, attended by guards like those of a sovereign. Shan Long asked the attendant, "What office is this?"
The official said, "This is King [Śuddhodana]. Śāṇakavāsin approached the foot of the steps. The King asked, "What meritorious deeds did you perform throughout your life?
Śāṇakavāsin replied, "Whenever the people of my village established vegetarian feasts or gave lectures on the Dharma, I always contributed goods equal to theirs.

The King said, "What good deeds did you yourself perform? Śāṇakavāsin said, "I recited two fascicles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The King said, "Excellent! You may ascend the steps. Having done so...
They ascended the hall. In the northeast corner was a high seat, like that used for lecturing. The King pointed to the seat and said to Śāṇakavāsin, "You may ascend this seat and recite the sūtra.
Śāṇakavāsin obeyed the command and approached; the King immediately stood up and said, "Please, Dharma Master, ascend the seat.
Once Śāṇakavāsin had finished ascending the seat, the King sat down facing him. Śāṇakavāsin opened the sūtra and said, "The Sublime..."
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter One: The Introduction. The King said, "I request that the Dharma Master stop. Shanlong immediately ceased.
Descending from his seat, he stood again at the foot of the steps and looked toward the courtyard; the prisoners were already gone, not a single person remaining.
The King said to Shanlong, "The merit of your recitation of the sutra is not merely for your own benefit; it has caused all the prisoners in the courtyard to hear the sutra as well."
It was fortunate that he was spared; how excellent! The King now releases you and sends you back.
Shanlong bowed in farewell and walked some dozen paces when the King called him back and said to his official, "Take this man and lead him through all the hells.
The official immediately led Shanlong eastward for over a hundred paces, where he saw an iron city, vast and immense, with a roof covering the top of the city and many [towers] by its side.
There were small windows, some as large as small platters and others like bowls or basins. [The officer] saw men and women flying from the ground into these windows, never to emerge again.
Shanzhong asked in wonderment, and the official replied, "This is the Great Hell; it contains many separate compartments, and the offenses for which beings are judged vary.
These people are each following their own past karma to enter the hells and undergo their retribution. Shanzhong—

Upon hearing this, the dragon was filled with grief and fear; he invoked "Namo Buddha" and requested the officials to let him out. When he reached the gate of the courtyard, he saw a great cauldron, its fire fierce and its broth boiling.
Beside it sat two men, fast asleep. Shānlong questioned them, and the two men replied, "We are here as a retribution for our sins, having entered this cauldron of boiling water.
Because we were graced by the worthy one’s invocation of 'Namo Buddha,' all the sinners within the prison have attained [relief]."
He rested for a day, merely from exhaustion and sleep. Shanlong again recited "Namo Buddha. The official said to Shanlong, "The government offices have been frequently transferred and reorganized.
Now that the King has released you, you should request a certificate of release from the King. If you do not do so, I fear other officials will not know of it and may pursue and detain you again.
Shanlong immediately went to the King to request the certificate. The King ordered paper and wrote a line of characters, which he then gave to him.

The official said, "Go and fetch the official seals for the Five Paths and the others. Having received these orders, the official led Shanlong through two ministries, visiting each of their respective halls;

the ceremonial guards likewise followed in this manner. The King then dispatched the official to take all their official seals, and once each had been inscribed with a single line [of authority], they were complete.
He was handed over to Shanzhong. Shanzhong carried him out to the gate, where three men said to him, "The King has released you;
would it not be fitting to give us something? Before Shanzhong could speak, the official said to him, "The King’s release of you did not depend on them.
However, those three men were the ones who previously arrested and detained you: one is the master of the ropes, and he ought to be given a red [cord]."
"The one who bound you with rope is the master of the staff; he intends to strike your head with the staff.
The one who bound you with the sack is the master of the bag; he intends to suck your breath with the bag. Seeing that you have returned, we merely requested these items.

Shanlong was terrified and apologized to the three men, saying, "I am ignorant and did not recognize you gentlemen. I request that you come to my home to prepare the goods, but I do not know where to send them. The three men—

Shanlong said, "Burn it by the water's edge or beneath a tree. The mountain dragon granted his request. The official escorted him back home, where he saw his relatives weeping as they prepared the funeral equipment.
Shanlong entered until he reached the side of the corpse and immediately revived.

On the following day, he cut paper to make money and silk, along with wine and food, and personally took them to the water's edge to burn them. Suddenly, he saw three men come to thank him, saying, "We received your kindness..."
He broke his word and repeatedly sent me gifts; I am both ashamed and deeply grateful. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Shanlong then went to tell the Abbot of Zongchi Temple, who in turn transmitted the account to Lin. (The above three accounts are from the *Mingbao ji*).
The monk Śunhyǒng of Silla was a native of Nang-gun. He belonged to a local clan and a lineage of the Eastern Barbarians (Dongyi).

While residing in his own country, Hyǒng produced many writings, some of which were transmitted to the Central Plains. The Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang) school he followed adhered to the definitive teachings of the Mahāyāna.
As seen in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, from the very first arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one immediately attains Buddhahood.
Having said this, he gave rise to slander and disbelief, saying: "He shall now reveal his hands and feet. He then ordered his disciples to support him as he descended to the ground.
Suddenly, the earth split open, and Master Jing’s body fell into it instantly. At that time, people said that he had been reborn alive within hell.

Even today, the pit can still be seen, measuring over one *zhang* in both width and length; it is called the "Hell of Zhishun Jing" (*Shunjing-naraka*). (From the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*. Since Jing was a follower of the Mahāyāna sūtras and teachings, how could he not have seen [this]?).

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Even those who have merely once called out 'Namo Buddha' have all already attained the path to Buddhahood. The *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (or *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*) states: "Sentient beings are originally Buddhas. Yet you alone harbor doubts regarding the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Since you do not know the school of the "separate transmission outside the teachings," how could you possibly recognize the purport of the Perfect and Sudden?
You, Jing, have not yet deeply awakened to the teachings of definitive meaning; you merely rely on literal interpretations and intellectual views, thereby falling into a pitfall of your own making.
Ren Yifang of Le’an, the Regional Governor (Cishi) of Kuozhou, died during the Wude era. After several days had passed, he revived and said that he had been led into an audience with King Yama.
The King ordered an attendant to lead him to show him the various places of hell; what was described did not differ from the Buddhist scriptures.
He further stated that beneath the earth it is perpetually dark and gloomy, as if one were walking through a mist. At that time, his family...
Because Yi-fang’s mind was imbued with righteousness and propriety, there was a slight warmth remaining in his heart. He immediately invited monks to perform rites.
Yi-fang then heard the sound of chanting sutras and hymns from beneath the ground. The King inspected the records and said to his officials, "It was not yet time for him to die;

for what reason was he summoned by mistake? He then released him to return home. As Yi-fang emerged and passed through the three checkpoints, the checkpoint guards were all asleep. His escort said, "Just..."
Following the sound of the chanting, he arrived at the house immediately. As he was walking along, he saw a large pit in the road and intended to leap over it, but he fell into the pit.
He rose from it instantly and began to discourse on the hells, drawing figures on the ground as illustrations. Subsequently, the stipends and emoluments he received...

They all commissioned the production of scriptures and images; they once transcribed more than a thousand scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. This was recounted by Yifang himself (*Extracted from the Míngbào Shíyí*). The *Suìyuàn Wǎngshēng Jīng* states:

Bodhisattva Puguang addressed the Buddha, saying, "If good men or women, before their death, proactively prepare for the seven-day rites after birth—lighting lamps, hanging banners, and inviting monks to recite scriptures—will they obtain much merit? The Buddha said, "Their merit shall be immeasurable.

He further asked, "When parents or kinsmen have passed away and are suffering in the afterlife, if one performs meritorious deeds on their behalf, will they obtain much merit? The Buddha said, "One may obtain only one-seventh of it, because in their previous lives they did not believe in the Way and its Virtue. [If one uses the deceased's] ornaments for the body...

[It is] complete. Even by giving houses, gardens, and groves to the Triple Gem, one can extricate oneself from the sufferings of hell; this is because the deceased, knowing that these were their own possessions, gives rise to joy. According to the *Yijian zhi*, there was an old woman named Wang from E-zhu who regularly purchased paper money to deposit in the "storage" (ji-ku).

She had her servant Li Da write and sign for her on her behalf. After the woman died, Li suddenly fell ill and lay prostrate on the ground for three days. Upon recovering, he said: "I was captured by the authorities of the underworld and brought to the storage office. They ordered me to identify my signature. Li replied: "This was written by me on behalf of my mistress. [He was then led away.]

She saw a high official wearing the purple robe and gold insignia. The exchange of questions and answers was as before. The official said, "Simply pursue this matter for verification, and you may then return. As she was about to leave, the old woman arrived in great joy and said, "I am grateful that you have come; my money deposited in the treasury now has a way to return.

Nowadays, there are those who zealously engage in preparatory merit-making, yet they all act in this manner. However, when engaging in preparatory merit-making, one should follow the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Wǎngshēng jīng) to perform genuine meritorious deeds, personally observe the precepts and cultivate goodness, and pray to be reborn among humans or devas, or single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name to be reborn in the Pure Land and escape the cycle of birth and death. How could it be otherwise?

Can one prepare for hell in advance? If there are grave offenses, King Yama is impartial; how can paper money redeem or release one from them? Thus, those who commit evil often purchase much paper money to atone for their sins—this may be done by the wealthy, but even for the poor, though their offenses be small, they cannot escape.
Let the wise examine this carefully.

At Da-zhuangyan Monastery in the Western Capital, there was the Dharma Master Huien. Endowed with a spirit that was gentle and generous, he possessed clear discernment and thorough mastery of the classics.
In the eighth year of the Taian era of the Chen dynasty, at the commencement of the summer retreat, he was suddenly visited by a mysterious messenger who said, "The King invites the Dharma Master.

As the attendants made a clamor and the sounds of stringed and wind instruments resounded together, the Master immediately relinquished his life-breath while remaining as composed as on any ordinary day. Seven days passed in this manner.

When he emerged from a profound meditative absorption, his disciples questioned him, whereupon he said, "Try looking inside this chest; see what is there. Upon searching, they found two bundles of silk.
He then remarked, "This is my alms-offering (dakṣiṇā). When asked again for the reason, he said, "Deluded thoughts and inverted views—what is the use of knowing them?
I was commanded by King Yama to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. While in the realm of the underworld, I saw the ground..."
The various characteristics of the hells and the sequence of the five sufferings are not encompassed by a great compassion that reaches both the hidden and the manifest;

yet when practice reaches its ultimate, it moves through resonance and penetration—how else could one cause those spirits of the underworld to travel their divine journeys to other realms? He passed away in the first year of the Zhenguan era at the age of eighty-nine (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Tang*).
In Suizhou, Zhao Wenxin died suddenly in the first year of the Zhenguan era. After three days, he revived and recounted his experience, saying:
"On the day I first died, I was surrounded by people who drove me along. Ten companions were all with me as we proceeded until we reached the abode of King Yama.
There, I saw a monk; the King first called for the monk and asked him, 'Master, one..."
"Since birth, what merit have you cultivated? He replied, "Since my birth, this poor monk has done nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Upon hearing these words, the king suddenly sprang up in alarm, joined his palms, and praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!

Master, if you truly recite the *Prajñāpāramitā*, you ought to ascend to heaven and transcend the world. For what reason have you come here by mistake? Before the king had finished speaking, suddenly—
Tiantong came down and led the Master up to heaven. Later, the King called Wenxin forward and asked, "Since your birth, what meritorious deeds have you cultivated?
He replied, "Throughout my life, I have not cultivated any merit; I have only been fond of collecting the literary works of Yu Xin.
The King said, "This Yu Xin was a great sinner who is currently undergoing suffering here. You see Yu..."
"Yi Xìn? Have you ever known him? He replied, "Although I have read his writings, I do not know the man. The King immediately sent someone to bring Yi Xìn out to show him.
When they saw him, he was like a tortoise with one body and many heads. A short while after the tortoise departed, [the apparition vanished].
Suddenly, a man appeared and said, "I am Yu Xin. Because during my life I was fond of composing literary works, I recklessly cited Buddhist scriptures and mixed them with secular texts;
I slandered the Buddha-dharma, claiming it did not equal the teachings of Confucius and Laozi.
Now I undergo this retribution for my sins, suffering as a tortoise in the extreme of misery. Once Wenxin has been revived, tell your relatives in detail that in the land of Suizhou, the people..."
He was very fond of hunting and would catch insects and fish; those who heard of this from near and far all admonished one another, forever severing their karmic acts of killing.
Each gave rise to a sincere heart and upheld the Prajñāpāramitā, a tradition that continues uninterrupted to this day.
Liu Zhigan of Hedong was serving as the Magistrate of Changju County at the beginning of the Zhenguan era. One night he died suddenly, but revived at dawn.
He recounted that he had been abruptly summoned by an official of the underworld and brought before a great office.
After the messenger presented Zhigan, the official said to him, "There is currently a vacancy in an office; therefore, I have deigned to appoint you to it. Zhigan declined the offer, saying—

His parents were elderly, and he himself declared that his meritorious karma had not yet reached its end, so he ought not to die. The king ordered an investigation of the registers, and it was found to be true.

The king then said to him, "Since you have not yet reached the time for death, you may temporarily serve as the Recorder. Zhigan gave his assent and withdrew with thanks; the officials led him back to his office.
The Cao administration had five judicial officers who were held jointly liable for their actions; Zhi Gan was the sixth. His office was where the senior officials sat;
it consisted of three bays, each with its own couch and desk. The workload was extremely heavy and complex. At the western end, there was one seat that lacked a judicial officer.
The clerks led Zhi Gan to this vacant seat. The various officials brought documents, registers, and accounts, placed them upon the desk, and then withdrew to stand below the steps.
Zhigan questioned him. He replied, "An evil influence is pressing upon you; simply answer by referring to the matters in the case files from afar.
Zhigan examined and read them, and they were exactly as they were in the human world. Thereupon, he composed the legal judgments and texts. After a short while, food arrived.
The various judges ate together, and Zhigan also wished to join them. The judges said, "Since you have acted as the provisional judge, it is not appropriate for you to eat this. Zhigan [refused].
He followed this advice and ultimately did not dare to eat. Every day, an official would escort Zhigan back home, where he would regain consciousness only at dawn;

yet by the time he returned home, it would already be dusk. The official would come again to fetch him, arriving there at daybreak. Thus, one knows that the day and night of the hidden realm and the manifest world are reversed.

Consequently, he adjudicated matters in the underworld at night and presided over his county duties during the day, which became his constant routine. After more than a year had passed, while Zhigan was [at home]—
Zhiguan was about to rise from his seat to go to the latrine when, to the west of the hall, he saw a woman approximately thirty years of age.
Her features were elegant and her clothing bright; she stood there weeping. Zhiguan asked, "Who are you? She replied, "I am the wife of the Assistant Magistrate of the Storehouse in Xingzhou.
I have been brought here and am now parting from my husband, which is why I am so sorrowful. Zhiguan...
Zhigan asked the official about this. The official said, "The authorities have taken her in for interrogation; it is merely to corroborate her husband's case.
Zhigan then said to the woman, "I am the Prefectural Magistrate of Changju. If you are questioned, I urge you to speak clearly for yourself; do not involve others.
If the Director of the Granary should die, it will be of no benefit to you. The woman replied, "Truly, I—"
"Please lead him away; I fear only that the officials will press him. Zhigan said, "Madam, please do not drag him along;
then there will be no danger of being coerced. The woman agreed. Subsequently, Zhigan returned to the prefecture and first asked the Director of the Granary, "Is the lady ill?"
