The steward said, "My wife is young and free from illness. Zhigan informed him of what he had seen, describing her clothing and physical appearance, and further exhorted him to cultivate merit. The steward ran home and saw his wife weaving at the loom.
Wuhuan did not believe this very much. More than ten days later, the wife of the Director of the Granary died of a sudden illness.

Only then did the Director become afraid and perform meritorious deeds to avert the calamity. Zhigan would frequently see the names and appearances of his relatives and acquaintances in the registers of the netherworld;

he would inform them of the dates of their deaths and instruct them to cultivate merit so that many might be spared. Zhigan served as an acting official for three years when an officer from his department came to him.
He informed him, saying, "Li Sihù of Lóngzhōu has already been appointed to a regular official post to replace you; you shall no longer hold judicial authority.
Zhìgǎn arrived at the prefecture and reported this to the Prefect, Lí Fèng, who dispatched a messenger to Lóngzhōu to inquire. By then, the Sihù had already passed away.

When asked about the date of their deaths, it was the very time the officials had come to inform him; from that point on, the matter ceased. The provincial administration dispatched Zhigan to escort the prisoners to the capital.
Upon reaching the borders of Fengzhou, all four prisoners fled. Zhigan was filled with anxiety and fear; though he searched for them, they could not be captured.
While staying overnight at a roadside inn, he suddenly saw his former subordinate official appear and report, saying, "The prisoners have all been found. One.
"The man is dead. Three men are in the western valley of Mount Nan; they have all been captured and bound. I pray that you, sir, do not worry.
Having finished speaking, he took his leave. Zhigan immediately requested soldiers to enter the western valley of Mount Nan.

Indeed, they found four prisoners. Knowing flight would not save them, the prisoners rose up to resist. Zhigan overpowered them, killing one prisoner while the other three were taken captive—exactly as had been foretold.
[The Master] said: "I know that Jiǎng Gǎn is currently serving as the Judicial Official of Cízhōu in the South. Liú Héng, the Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, recounted this to me.
Héng, who served as the Regional Inspector of Yǎngzhōu, personally questioned Jiǎng Gǎn about it. Furthermore, the Censor Páitóngjié also stated that several people had told him the same thing.

(The above two accounts are from the *Míngbào jì*. Alas! Even before people have died, their souls have already entered the dark paths; such cases are not limited to one. Formerly, there was a man who was violent...)

After dying, he entered a prison where he saw a fellow country monk who had been imprisoned; the monk’s crown of the head was being driven with iron nails. Having regained consciousness, he went to the temple and found that the monk’s head was afflicted with a large ulcer, causing him extreme agony. He then recounted to him the events that had occurred while in prison.

At the Da-zhuangyan Monastery in the capital was the Śramaṇa Zhixing, a native of Luozhou. He accomplished his duties with humility and restraint, and his cultivation of conduct was steadfast and clear.
Following Master Shou, he recited the sūtras and upheld the Vinaya, his mind and mouth in constant harmony, never ceasing from dusk until dawn.

In the middle winter of the fifth year of the Daye era, it was his turn to serve as the *vina* (steward); he struck the bell according to the proper hour, and the assembly of monks remained undisturbed. The monks of the same monastery...

Regarding those named as having attained the third fruit: there was an elder brother who followed Emperor Yang on his southern journey to Jiangdu. He died along the way, yet at first there was no report of his demise.
He appeared in a dream to his wife and said, "I traveled as far as Pengcheng before unfortunately falling ill and dying; this was because I failed to maintain my fasts and precepts."
I have now fallen into hell and have fully experienced the five types of suffering; its bitterness and acridity cannot be described in detail—who knows my pain?
Fortunately, on the first day of this month, I was graced by the monk Zhixing of Chanding Monastery, who struck the bell and produced its resonance, the sound of which shook through hell.
Those suffering together with me were all liberated at once and have now been reborn in a place of bliss. Reflecting on how to repay his kindness, you may provide ten rolls of silk.

I presented him with a roll of silk early on and explained my intentions, hoping that through such profound courtesy and sincerity, he would wake from his sleep startled by the cause of his strange dream and speak of it with others;
yet at first, no one believed me. Soon after, I entered a deep dream once more and recounted what I had previously said.
Ten days later, the ominous news arrived suddenly, exactly as in the dream. Indeed, I did present the silk to him, but Xing himself stated that he had none.
The virtuous ones all bestowed [their merit] upon the great assembly. The abbot, Chan Master Gong, and the other great virtuous ones of the entire monastery all asked Daoying:

"By what cause did the sounding of the bell result in such a response? Daoying replied: "I have no other skill. I saw it stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fufa zang zhuan) that King Kaniṣka’s suffering was brought to an end by the sounding of a bell;
furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* contains verses on the blessings of ringing the bell. Out of reverence..."
In accordance with this matter, I have diligently put it into practice. During the severe winter, as I ascended the tower, the wind cut through my skin and flesh.

Although the monks provided me with sheepskin sleeves for holding the bell and mallet, I resolved to encourage myself; I struck the mallet with my bare hands until my palms were wounded and broken, yet I did not consider it a hardship.
Furthermore, at the beginning of ringing the bell, I first made a virtuous vow: "May all the worthy sages enter the Dharma hall together and partake of the Dharma-food together."
Then strike three times. As you are about to strike the long roll, pay homage as before and make this aspiration:

"May all those in the evil realms, upon hearing the sound of this bell, be freed from suffering and swiftly attain liberation. Constantly practice such vows and deeds with wisdom; how could one fail to do so with sincere devotion?

He was thus able to exert a far-reaching influence, and the multitude marveled at his words, finding them doubly verified and free from error. In the third month of the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he fell ill for a short time;
knowing that his future rebirth was near, he relinquished all his worldly possessions and summoned his teachers and friends. While eating, he took his leave, and shortly thereafter passed away.
(From the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan*) Formerly, there was a king of Kaśmīra who was by nature fond of slaughter; as a result of this evil retribution, he was destined to fall into hell. Because...
Upon hearing the Dharma preached by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, his transgressions became lightened. After death, he fell into the great ocean and was reborn as a thousand-headed fish.
Blades of swords circled his body, severing his heads; as soon as one was cut off, another grew in its place. In a mere instant, his severed heads filled the vast ocean.

Hearing the sound of the monastery’s *ghanṭī* (wooden gong), the blades of swords suspended themselves in mid-air and his suffering subsided slightly. At that time, there was an Arhat serving as the *karmadāna* who struck the gong.

Regarding the *gandi*: the King sent a messenger ordering it to be struck for a long duration. The Arhat then struck it for a long time, causing the sound to prolong itself until the end of seven days, at which point his suffering came to an end.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "If the bell is struck, may all sufferings of the evil realms be brought to a halt.
If one hears the sound of the bell and recites verses of praise, one shall be freed from [the retribution of] five hundred billion kalpas of birth."
A Grave Crime Regarding Xianyang.
During the Zhenguan era, there was a woman surnamed Liang who died and returned to life after seven days.
She said that she had been taken by others to a large courtyard where she saw a great hall. Inside, an official sat at a desk.
He took up his pen. His attendants were very numerous. He ordered an official to investigate, asking: "Should this woman be put to death?
Someone else brought forward another case and investigated, saying: "She has the same name as one who is destined for death; that is why she was pursued. The magistrate commanded his subordinates:
"I wish to release her immediately. Liang addressed the magistrate, saying: "I do not know what other crimes I may have committed; I beg [of you]..."

He immediately underwent his punishment and returned home. The officials then ordered an investigation of the records, which stated: "Throughout Liang Sheng's life, he committed only the offenses of double-tongued speech and abusive cursing;
there were no other crimes. They then ordered one man to pull out his tongue while another held an axe to hack it away.

This was done several times each day for a total of seven days, after which he was sent back home. At first, it felt as though he had fallen down a deep precipice, but after a short while, he fell asleep.

Upon awakening, his family looked at his tongue; it was still greatly swollen and ulcerated. From that time forward, he permanently abstained from wine and meat, a practice he maintains to this day (from the *Mingbao Shiyi*).
Dai Tianzou, the Minister of the Ministry of Revenue and Duke of Wuchang, had long been on friendly terms with Shen Yu, the Vice Governor of Shuzhou.
Tianzou passed away in the seventh year of the Zhenguan era. In the eighth month of the eighth year, while Yu was in his provincial post, he dreamed that he was walking through the capital.
At that time, he saw Tianzou on the street southwest of Yining Ward, wearing tattered and worn-out clothes, his complexion [extremely]— (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at this point.)

Zui saw Yu and was moved by both grief and joy. He asked, "What meritorious deeds did you perform throughout your life? What is the reason for your current state? Yu replied, "I once mistakenly reported that someone had committed murder.
After my death, others slaughtered a sheep to sacrifice for me. It is because of these two matters that I have been subjected to such bitter and exhausting interrogation."

"It cannot be fully recounted. Now its momentum has also reached its conclusion. He then said to Yu, "Throughout my life, I have been a close friend to you, yet in the end I was unable to advance your official rank; this remains a deep regret in my heart.

Since you have now obtained the documents for the fifth rank and have already passed through the Heavenly Office, I rejoice in assisting you and thus inform you of this. Having finished speaking, he woke up and told it to others, hoping—
The dream had been a sign. That winter, Sengyu entered the capital to seek office, but he was punished with a fine in copper and failed to obtain a post.

He told others that his dream had proven false. In the spring of the ninth year, as Sengyu was about to return south to Jiangnan, while traveling through Xuzhou, he suddenly received an imperial decree appointing him to the fifth rank as the *zhizhong* (Administrator) of Wuzhou.
When his elder brother, who served as the Minister of Personnel (*libu shilang*), heard of this, he summoned him.

Yu asked: "As for the people of today who slaughter living beings for sacrifices and establish *zhēngcháng* (vapor-offerings), they may reflect upon themselves by looking at Lord Dai. Therefore, the *Commentary on the Ullambana Sūtra* states:

'Though one may express filial thoughts by tending to the graves for a lifetime and performing *zhēngcháng* throughout one's life, this cannot assist the spiritual consciousness of one's ancestors in the dark path; ultimately, it is of no benefit. If one had honored and supported them while they were alive, there would still have been some small benefit; but once they have passed away, performing *zhēngcháng* provides no assistance at all.

Even if one performs offerings of water plants and vegetables during the *yòu* and *dì* seasons, these do not fall short of serving one's parents; yet if one slaughters living beings for *zhēngcháng*, it instead brings calamity upon one's parents. It merely spreads an empty reputation and does not assist the divine way. Only if one's parents are in the realm of ghosts can such sacrificial food truly nourish them.'"

If one is reborn in another realm, how could one receive sacrifices? Furthermore, there are many obstacles among the hungry ghosts; when they see food, it turns into ashes and charcoal, as was the case with Maudgalyāyana’s mother. The end of the *Xiaojing* says: "In life, serve them with love and respect;

in death, serve them with grief and sorrow. The fundamental duty toward the living people is fulfilled; the principle of life and death is complete. The service of a filial son to his parents is finished. Since we know that while the body perishes, the spirit does not perish, how can one value the physical form while disparaging the spirit? When the body is present, to show reverence and provide nourishment, and to feel anxiety when it is ill—this is what is meant by "valuing the form.

To offer sacrifices to the spirits of one's parents because of the grace of Heaven is, in effect, to disparage the spiritual essence of those very parents. Reasoning from this, do not be dogmatic about Confucian teachings; rather, establish sacrificial rites provisionally and follow the Buddhist way to repay their kindness.

According to the true principle, one should accumulate merit to support one's parents; pray do not kill living beings for sacrifice, thereby adding to the suffering of your parents in the unseen realm.
○ Zhang Fayi of Huazhou was a native of Zheng County. In his youth, he was poor and rustic, and did not observe the rules of propriety.
In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, while entering Mount Hua to fell timber, he encountered a monk sitting within a cave on a cliff. Fayi then approached him...
Yu said, "The day has grown dark and gloomy; we cannot return home. We shall stay overnight in this rocky cave. The monk provided powdered pine and cypress for them to eat as provisions.
He said to Fayi, "I have long wished not to let outsiders know of my presence. When you leave, be careful not to mention that you saw me.
I shall therefore explain to you that worldly people have many karmic burdens and sins, and upon death all enter the evil realms. You must repent with a sincere heart."
They extinguished the fire and ordered him to bathe for purification. He donned monastic robes and performed a ritual of repentance;
at dawn, he departed. In the nineteenth year, Fayi fell ill and died. Having no coffin due to his poverty, he was buried in the wilds and interred with miscellaneous timber.
He then revived and pushed himself out from the wood to return home. His family was struck with amazement; when they questioned him and learned he was alive, they rejoiced. Fayi himself—
He said: "At first, two men came to take me away. We traveled through the air to the government office and entered the main gate.
We proceeded south along the lane for about ten li; on both sides of the lane were government offices with gates facing one another, beyond counting.
When Fayi reached one of the offices, he saw an official who reprimanded the messengers from afar, saying: 'This is Zhang Fayi of Huazhou. His original deadline was...'"

Three days passed. "For what reason have you delayed for seven days? the messenger asked. Dharmaya replied, "The dog of the Dharma-teacher's family was fierce, and there were also sorcerers and priests.
When the priest struck me while I was invoking the deity, I was severely exhausted. I bared my back to show him; it was swollen and bruised green.

The official said, "Your detention has been too long; you shall receive twenty lashes. Having finished speaking, the lashes were administered, and blood flowed, spilling across the ground. The official said, "Take Dharmaya away and record his testimony."

Matters. The Secretariat for Administrative Affairs issues a document and orders it to be sent to the Judicial Official (*pan guan*). The Judicial Official summons the Chief Clerk (*zhu dian*) and requests the legal dossier (*fa yi an*).
There are a great many files and registers, filling an entire bed. Facing the Legal Specialist (*fa yi*), the Chief Clerk opens and examines them, saying:
"Most of the dossiers have already been marked with red ink; those that have not yet been marked, I shall record. He says: "In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, the Legal Specialist..."

His father sent him to reap rice. Fayi looked back and glared with wide eyes, cursing his father privately. [The judge declared,] "For this lack of filial piety, he deserves eighty blows of the staff.
As the first case was being recorded, a monk from a mountain cave in the past appeared. The official rose to welcome him and asked why he had come. The monk said, "Zhang Fayi is my disciple;
his offenses have all been repented and erased from the records of the Celestial Office."
[The case] was settled. Now you have been summoned here in vain; it is not fitting that you die. The official in charge said: "As for those who have performed repentance, this case is settled.
But as for one who stares at his father and reviles him, even though he has received repentance, the matter is not yet settled. The monk said: "If it were not like this..."
"You should take him and interrogate him; there will surely be some spiritual benefit. The Judge was ordered to have the master, Zhang Fayi, pass by the eastern side of the royal palace.
The halls and buildings were magnificent, and several thousand guards stood in attendance. The monk also followed to the King’s presence.
The King rose to greet him, saying, "Is the Master coming for his regular turn of duty? He replied, "It is not yet my turn; it is my disciple Zhang Fayi who has been arrested."

"Come. This man's past offenses have been fully accounted for by this poor monk; he does not yet deserve death. The chief official then looked at his father with wide-open eyes as the matter was presented to the King.
The King said, "He looks at me with wide-open eyes while confessing; this does not merit exemption. However, since you, Master, have come on his behalf to request it..."
"You may be granted leave for seven days. Fayi addressed the Saṃgha, saying, "Seven days is not a long time; I fear that when they return, I shall no longer see my teacher.
I beg you, let me remain here to follow him. The Teacher said, "Seven days is like seven years. You should depart early. Fayi earnestly requested to stay with the monks.
Consequently, the monks requested the King’s brush to write a single character upon Fayi’s palm, and further requested the King’s seal to stamp it.
He said, "You must leave home immediately. Relying on your karmic merit, you shall not see me again hereafter. You should present this hand-seal to the King;
the King himself will surely release you. Fayi then took his leave and departed. The monk ordered him out, and when they reached his home, it was pitch black inside.
Fayi did not dare enter, but the messenger pushed him in, whereupon he came back to life. He realized he was within the earth, yet the soil felt very light.
It was thin; he pushed it away with his hand and emerged. Thereupon, he entered the mountains to cultivate merit under a mountain monk.
The marks imprinted upon the palms of Fayi’s hands could not be recognized as characters, yet they all became sores that could never be healed;

they remain to this day. Longxi Wang Bochā entrusted Fayi with matters concerning his neighbors. The King personally explained [the matter] to him. (The above two accounts are from the *Mingbao ji*. [Regarding the entry on "Zhangmu sima": one encountered...])

Even when noble monks performed repentance on his behalf, he could not yet escape [retribution]. How much more so now, when one insults and reviles one’s parents and teachers face-to-face—what shall be the nature of such sin? Quickly impose self-reproach and deeply feel shame while repenting; perhaps you may avoid the heavy retribution of the hells.

Fu Yi of Fufeng was originally a native of Taiyuan. During the late Sui dynasty, he moved to Fufeng. From his youth, he was fond of extensive learning and was skilled in astronomy, calendrical science, and mathematics.
During the Sui, he served as a Daoist priest (huángguān) and was deeply dissatisfied with his position.

When Yu Jian, the Director of the Imperial Observatory, took offense at holding office based on his technical skills, he recommended Fu Yi to replace him. Having received the imperial mandate, Fu Yi attained his ambitions at court from the Wude and Zhenguan eras onward.
He served as the Director of the Grand Historian’s Office (*Taishiling*). By nature he did not believe in Buddhism and frequently held monks and nuns in contempt;
he even used stone statues for the purpose of bricks and tiles. Yan Yi, along with his fellow Daoist practitioners Fu Renjun and Xue Yi, all served as Directors of the Grand Historian’s Office.

They colluded and submitted seven memorials requesting the abolition of the Buddhist teachings. Consequently, Emperor Gaozu came to favor Yan Yi, praising the Way (*Dao*) and disparaging the Buddha (*Fo*), thereby aligning himself with their private interests.
Your servant, having no other recourse, subsequently integrated and implemented both teachings. One day, Emperor Taizong summoned Yi to grant him a meal and said to him:
"The Buddha and the Way are subtle and profound; their sacred traces are worthy of emulation, and moreover, their retributions are manifest."

"Numerous signs and proofs have repeatedly appeared. Why is it that you alone do not realize their underlying principle? Yi replied, "The Buddha is a clever rogue from the West who deceives the barbarians.
When his teachings flowed into China, those who venerated them were all perverse and petty men who imitated the profound words of Zhuangzi and Laozi to embellish his own delusions and falsehoods.
This provides no benefit to the state and only brings harm to the common people. The Emperor detested this.
When Renjun spoke these words, he did not answer; from that time on, [Xue Yi] never spoke with him again for the rest of his life.
Previously, Xue Yi had owed Renjun five thousand coins but had not yet repaid them when Renjun died. Later, Yi dreamed of Renjun, who spoke to him as usual.
Yi asked, "To whom should the money I previously owed be paid? Renjun replied, "It can be paid to the clay man. Yi asked, "Who is the clay man?"
The answer was: "It is Fu Yi, the Director of the Grand Astrological Bureau. He then awoke.

That night, Feng Changming, the Supervisor of the Office of the Imperial Household, dreamed that he arrived at the Netherworld and saw many deceased persons. Changming asked the deceased, "The scriptures speak of retribution for sins and blessings;
I do not yet know if these are truly fixed realities. They replied, "They all certainly exist. He asked again, "As for someone like Fu Yi—"

[The Emperor] said, "In my life I have never believed [in such things]. What retribution shall I receive after death? He replied, "Fu Yi has already been banished to Yuezhou as a *niraya* (hell-being).
On the morning of Changming, he entered the palace and saw Xue Yi, whereupon he recounted his dream. Xue Yi also spoke of his own experience regarding the hell-beings.
The two men’s accounts coincided perfectly during that dark night, and they both marveled at it together. The matters of sin and merit are not... [to be trifled with].
He did not believe it. When Yi saw the evidence, he sent money to Yi and recounted his dream to him. A few days later, Yi contracted a malignant disease;
his entire body became festering and putrid, and he died crying out in agony. At that time, in the autumn of the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, Yi passed away at the palace court.

[The Emperor] personally witnessed two officials recounting the dream, and their accounts were identical. (From the *Mingbao ji* and the *Tongji tongzai*. This is what is meant by "desiring to obtain...")
"Do not incur the karma of the Avīci Hell; do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata. "So it is," [said] Huangguan (the title *huángguān* was the ancient designation for a Daoist).
Wei Zhou’s Qi Shiwang was a native of Wuqiang. In the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era, he died and after seven days returned to life.
He said that at the time of his initial death, he was led before the King and immediately handed over to the judicial officials, who were separately dispatched to conduct an investigation. After...
After four or five days, the examination of the records revealed that he shared the same name as those who were due to die; however, it was not yet his time to die.
The judge said to Shi Wang, "In your lifetime you were fond of roasting chickens; you ought to undergo punishment and then return. He immediately ordered someone to escort him out the gate.
After traveling one or two li from the office, he saw a city. From within the city, the sound of drums and musical instruments could be heard.
Shi Wang hurriedly entered with joy. Once he had entered, the city gate was already closed;
there were no dwellings within, and the entire ground was covered with hot ashes. Shi Wang was distraught, not knowing what to do, as his feet were scorched by the heat.
He experienced extraordinary suffering. As he looked about in all directions, the city gates were all open; yet as he rushed toward them, the doors would close immediately.
This continued for an entire day, until someone commanded the gatekeeper, saying, "Open the gate and release the criminal from yesterday. Once he had emerged, [he was free].
He immediately ordered someone to escort him back. The messenger excused himself on the grounds that the road was too long and delayed his departure, refusing to send him.
Shi Wang then began to request money and silk; the messenger consented, and so they traveled across rivers and roads, treading through thorns and brambles.

Upon reaching a certain place, there appeared a walled enclosure like a small courtyard, within which was a deep, black pit. Shi Wang was terrified by it, but the messenger pushed him, and he fell into the pit.

Unaware, he gradually regained consciousness. He immediately prepared paper money and waited for him. When the messenger arrived at the appointed time to collect it, Shi Wang’s wife saw him as well and said so.
(From the *Mingbao ji*). Furthermore, during the Liang dynasty, there was a man who regularly used the whites of chicken eggs to wash his hair, saying it made his hair lustrous and smooth.
Every time he washed his hair, he would break twenty or thirty eggs. At the moment of his death, he heard only the sound of [hair being washed].
[From] the *Hongming zashi zhuan* (Miscellaneous Records of Propagation and Clarification).
Pēi Zé of Líhú in Cáo Zhōu was a man who died at the end of the Zhèngguān era on the twenty-first day. After three days had passed, he revived.
He said that when he first died, he was led by a person to the presence of a King. The King wore white robes that were extraordinary [in appearance].
It was fresh and clean. The King dispatched this man to plow the land with oxen. The man petitioned, saying, "My brothers are young; there is no one to attend to my two parents.
The King took pity on him and immediately sent an envoy to lead him southward. Upon reaching the third gate, he entered and saw boiling cauldrons, as well as mountains of knives and trees of swords.
He further saw the heads of several thousand people, all of whom had been beheaded and were laid out strewn across the ground.
[The King] said, "Above. As for these heads, they all cried out with their mouths, "Great hunger! In that village, there was an old woman nearly seventy years of age who had not yet died;
she was seen tending the fire before a cauldron of boiling water. Having finished her watch, she returned before the King and saw Zhang Cheng of the same village, who also had not yet died.
Someone accused Cheng, saying, "He destroyed my house. The King dispatched a messenger.
He had it investigated, and the report confirmed that it was indeed so. Cheng said, "I was plowing the land; I did not realize I was breaking open his tomb. It was not done intentionally.
The King said, "Although you did not do it intentionally, you were ultimately lacking in care. He then ordered someone to strike him seven times with a staff at the waist.

After a short while, the king said, "Since you have no further business here, release him so he may return home early. The king then dispatched men to escort him away, sending him out through the north wall.
As he climbed over the wall, he caught sight of his house from afar and heard the sound of wailing; he then leaped down from the wall. Suddenly, he felt himself sit up.
After regaining consciousness, he recounted the events in detail to the people of his village. When the villagers looked at Zhang Cheng’s waist, they saw...

Seventh, there was a footprint where a staff had been left behind; the mark was an intense blue-black. When asked about the desecration of the tomb, he replied, "It is not false. The old mother soon fell ill and died shortly thereafter (*from the *Mingbao Shiyi*). [Someone asked:

"Once a person dies and enters the six realms of existence, how could they still remain in a tomb guarding their old remains? [The answer was: "Although they have entered the realm of ghosts (*preta-gati*), their karma of sin and merit is not yet fixed.

Therefore, they are neither constrained nor restricted, yet they likewise have nothing to rely upon; thus they remain among the tombs. As the *Abhiṣeka Sūtra* says: 'A youth of the Śākya clan asked the Buddha: "Why do ordinary people have graves? Upon what do the various ghosts and spirits rely?"'"*

The Buddha said: "These are all the essences of the five grains, or transformations produced by malevolent spirits and phantoms, or ghosts of those who died untimely. Having no place to which they may attach themselves, they rely upon these [objects] to manifest their numinous power. Or they may be the essences of trees, forests, or mountains; because their bones have not yet decayed, they possess a subtle spirit."

If the bones have rotted away, this spirit will immediately perish; it will lack any vital power or influence and will be unable to bring about various blessings or calamities for people. Alternatively, it may be the spirit of one who has recently died but lacked merit while in the world, or who practiced deceit and flattery, such that they ought to fall among the ghosts and spirits, or become a numinous essence of trees or miscellaneous objects.

Having no celestial merit to enjoy and not being contained within the hells, they wander aimlessly through human villages. Since they lack celestial food or any other sustenance, they consequently terrify people by manifesting various strange portents and supernatural transformations, agitating the minds of ordinary folk when they hear of them.

Upon seeing this, they immediately perform meritorious acts, claiming it is a deity; or else, practitioners of sorcery rely upon such things as deities to seek blessings and long life. Driven by ignorance and false views, they slaughter living beings for sacrifice;
consequently, after death they enter the hells, or become hungry ghosts or animals from which there is no escape. How can one not be cautious?
Yongzhou: Liquan County. Yang Sicao was a native of Dongyang County. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he served as the Director of the Bamboo Park (Sizhu Jianshi).

Later, due to official business, he was transferred to the post of Magistrate of Lantian County. In the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era, having grown old in years, he returned to his home village and took up farming as his livelihood.
However, by nature, Sicao was malicious and violent in speech; throughout his life, he had taken pleasure in...
He observed the transgressions of others; whenever a villager had a matter, he would immediately record it and report it to the authorities.

Without regard for whether the offense was great or small, he constantly instilled fear and intimidation. Within his own village community, he would arbitrarily create matters where none existed and attempt to "rectify" them;
people took no pleasure in seeing him. Possessing a naturally malicious character, he also told others: "My nature is prone to haste and violence of speech. Since the Wude era, four times..."

She observed the eight precepts, performed prostrations, recited sutras and hymns daily, and exhorted others toward goodness. However, when those of high or low status encroached upon her, she was unable to endure it.
Later, on the night of the seventh day of the fourth month in the first year of the Yonghui era, a person suddenly appeared.
He came from the east, riding a white horse and wearing green robes; he went straight to Cao’s gate. Having met with Su, they exchanged pleasantries.
The man said, "The Great Inspector of Dongyang has specifically sent me to pursue you because, from the time of your birth, you have been bound by a poisonous heart."

Unable to endure or relinquish [faults], they encounter people and immediately speak of them to encourage virtue. Yet their own observance of the precepts is incomplete; they are stingy and do not practice giving.
They claim to themselves, "I possess a virtuous heart and make offerings to the Triple Gem," yet they have never bestowed even a fraction of their wealth. Although they say with their mouths:

Feeling shame and remorse, a separate consciousness immediately arose within his mind, which deluded and confused the ordinary person. For this reason, he called out to you; yet for a moment, no one came.
Cao was standing at the gate when he suddenly fell to the ground, unable to speak. Only his heart remained slightly warm.
His family carried him on a litter into the house, where he lay for a night without recovering. However, Cao had already arrived at the office of the Eastern Yang Prefectural Registrar. At that time—

At that time, while the Prefect’s official business had not yet concluded, Cao proceeded to travel privately. The various offices were all furnished with desks, tables, beds, and mats—extremely large and exquisite.
There were also prisoners there; some wore cangues and shackles, some had their heads bared and their waists untied, and some were sitting, standing, walking, or staying still.
Prisoners such as these were beyond counting. Cao walked toward the east until he reached a certain place, where the hollow was extremely deep.
It was small; one could see only sparks streaming out, with foul-smelling smoke and flames crackling so fiercely that they would not allow a person to stand nearby.

Furthermore, two men stood at the entrance of the gate, holding iron clubs in their hands. Cao asked the men holding the clubs, "What place is this? The officials replied, "This is the Hell of Fierce Fire.
It is intended for those who did not maintain the precepts completely, or those who ceased their cultivation of goodness mid-course. Cao understood.
Yet he deliberately committed offenses again and died to enter this place. I have heard that there was once a Master Yang Sicao who delighted his entire life in discussing the faults of others;

he would constantly report their shortcomings to the authorities and, whenever encountering anyone, would feign shame and remorse. Yet if there was even the slightest slight against himself, he could not truly endure it.
Now I wish to dispatch him here to this place, so I am repairing [the path] for him. That person’s birthday today is the eighth day of the fourth month.

One day, Yang Sicao’s family died while he was away. They performed offerings of alms and feasts for the deceased. The officials deliberated and intended to release him back home, yet they had not yet decided whether to grant his request.
While waiting here for Master Sicao, Sicao bowed his head in gratitude and said, “I, the disciple Yang Sicao, am that very person.
I pray you will provide a skillful means so that I may be released. The man replied, “You simply—”

With a sincere heart, he prostrated before the Buddhas of the ten directions and earnestly repented, reforming his poisonous mind; he was then immediately able to attain rebirth there and would no longer return to this place.

Although he harbored evil intentions, because he was able to repent for the duration of one life, he acted like a Bodhisattva who does not spare body or life, and thus attained birth in the Pure Land.
Having received these words, Master Cao followed the instructions, confessing with great sincerity and diligence, and then released [the animal].
He returned home and recovered after three days. Once he had regained consciousness, he recounted this matter in detail.
Later, Cao went to the place of Chan Master Huìjìng to reform his ways and repent. He remains alive today at the age of seventy-five.
Cao observed a long-term fast and performed repentance rituals during the six periods of the day. While inspecting the wheat field, he saw three oxen greedily devouring the young shoots.
Cao approached the oxen with a sense of shame and did not drive them away. On the following day, when he returned to inspect the field, he saw that the wheat had not died;
there were only the tracks of the oxen. That night, he dreamed of a man who came and said to him, "I am an envoy from the Cao family."

"I am a human being. Therefore, I have come to test you. Since you have ceased your evil ways, I shall no longer pursue you. However, as you diligently and sincerely cultivate goodness, you need not worry about this.

A monk who saw Cao reported this to Lin. (This official was a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to Master Cao; he instructed him to punish evil and cultivate goodness, showing him the way to be born in the Pure Land.

He returned to test him by appearing in a dream, admonishing him with repeated and earnest exhortations. Were it not for a Great Bodhisattva using skillful means (*upāya*) to guide and advance sentient beings, who could apply their mind in such a manner?)
Song Xingzhi of Boling, serving as the Minister of Justice (Xingbu Langzhong), was by nature a non-believer in Buddhism and spoke words of contempt and slander.

On the fifth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Yonghui era, he died of illness. On the ninth day of the sixth month, Wang Shu, a clerk in the Department of Judicial Review (Shangshu Duguan Lingshi), suddenly died;
after two days had passed, he revived and said that at the moment of his initial death, he saw four men arrive.
When they reached the place where it was said the government officials were pursuing him, Xu followed them into a large gate.
He saw a hall that was very grand, facing north. In the western wing of the hall sat a man whose appearance was stout and dark.
In the eastern wing of the hall sat a monk, who faced the official; both were oriented toward the north. Each had a bed, a table, a desk, and a mat, with attendant youths nearby.

There were about two hundred people, some wearing caps and others with braided hair, all of whom had handsome features. (Below this follows an interrogation and the revision of the registers; these matters are omitted as they are too numerous.
After walking east-southeast for several dozen paces, he heard a voice calling "Shu. Shu turned back and saw the Court Gentleman Song Xingzhi.
His face was a dismal black, appearing like damp earth; his head was bare and his waistband loose. He wore a worn crimson robe, and his hair hung down short, like...
The Hu people stood at the foot of the steps in the main hall, where an official was stationed to guard them.

To the west, near the city wall, there was a large wooden sign about one zhang and two chi in height. Inscribed upon it in large characters, each more than a chi square and very clearly legible, were the words:
"This is for the examination and preliminary screening of the king's envoys. Inside the main hall were beds, seats, and desks and tables, arranged like those of an official’s residence.
When they reached the prefecture, there was no one sitting at the gate. Xingzhi saw Xu and was moved by both grief and joy; he said aloud, "Why have you come here?
Xu replied, "The authorities summoned me for interrogation regarding the change of my registration, but I have been released without incident. Xingzhi took him by both hands and said to Xu:
"I have been summoned by the authorities for questioning regarding my ledger of merit. I do not possess such a ledger in my possession; because of this, I suffer great distress.

Furthermore, I am beset by hunger, thirst, and the bitterness of cold, beyond all description. You must make every effort to go to my home and urgently urge them to perform meritorious deeds on my behalf.
Thus he earnestly instructed him four times. After Sŏk had taken his leave and walked some tens of paces, the spirit called out to him again.
He was returning when, before he had even had time to speak, an official came and sat in the hall. Enraged at Xù, the official said, "I am currently conducting an interrogation;
who are you to arrive uninvited at the place of confinement? He ordered his guards to grab Xù by the ear and push him away. Xù fled until he reached another gate.
The gatekeeper said, "Since you were grabbed by the ear, your ears ought to be deaf. I shall restore their function for you," and then he used his hand to probe them.
He listened to his ears; the ringing within them was indeed a sign. He immediately went out the door and found himself as black as lacquer.
Xushu did not know where he was, so he felt with his hands toward the west and south, finding nothing but walls. Only the east was unobstructed, yet it was so dark that he could not proceed.

He stood waiting for a short while when he saw the same official who had previously pursued him coming out through the gate. The official said to Xu, "It is very good that you were still able to wait for me;
please give me one thousand coins. Xu did not respond, but thought to himself, "I have been released without fault;
why should I bribe this official? The official immediately said, "You must not lack integrity. If I had not [acted as I did] just now..."
"I shall have you brought before the authorities early tomorrow and have you bound for two days; will that not be exhausting?
Xu agreed with this in his heart and apologized with shame, saying, "I shall follow your instructions. The official said, "I do not want your copper coins; I wish to have white paper money.
Come to collect it on the fifteenth day. Xu gave his word. He then asked for the way back, and the official said, "Simply walk east for two hundred paces, and you will see a..."
He was at a spot where a breach in the wall revealed light; [the monk] said, "You may push it down. He then went to the Master’s house.
As he followed the instructions, after a long time at the wall, he emerged from the collapsed section and arrived at the southern gate of Longzheng Ward, where the Master resided.
Thereupon, he returned home and saw people sitting there weeping. He entered the door and revived. On the fifteenth day, Sù forgot to give the money.
The next day, he again fell into a state of illness and unconsciousness. He saw an official arrive and said angrily, "You truly have no integrity!

You promised me money and then failed to give it. Now I shall take you away. He then drove him along, out through the Golden Light Gate (Jinguangmen), and ordered him to enter a pit. Sù prostrated himself.

He apologized and performed more than a hundred prostrations, whereupon he was immediately released and returned home. He revived again. Xushu told his family members to purchase a hundred sheets of paper and make money-offerings for him.

On the following day, Xushu was again suffering from illness and exhaustion; once more he saw the official, who said, "It is fortunate that you were able to provide me with money, but the money was not of good quality.
Xushu apologized and requested that they be made anew. The official granted this. He revived again. When the twentieth day arrived, Xushu ordered that six... [sheets] be used.
With ten coins, he purchased a hundred sheets of white paper to make money-offerings, along with wine and food. He burned them himself on the canal waters at the West Gate in Longzheng Ward.
Thereupon, his body became light and his strength restored, and he was able to continue his recitations without interruption.

When this matter was reported, Liu Yanke, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, and Xin Maojiang, Junior Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, were then presiding over a legal inquiry in the Court of Judicial Review.
Please summon Liu Zhaoxu to come; he shall be questioned alongside his elder brother Xin and the others, and the account shall be as follows. (The above two accounts are from the *Mingbao ji*.

Formerly, while I was practicing meditation at Mount Xilai in Yingde, the people of the valley below frequently took small bamboo from the mountain to manufacture coarse paper. There was a man surnamed Hua, nearly fifty years of age, who was by nature miserly. On the day of the Cold Food Festival, he went to the mountain to offer sacrifices at his grave. He used a knife to hack down bamboo and burned it, saying:

"Paper money and silver are originally made of bamboo; this bamboo is itself the stem of silver. That very night, he dreamed that his father came and severely rebuked him, saying: "I bought coarse paper for the grave, which is why I said the money was not good. How much more so to use actual bamboo? )

Is it permissible to speak of the silver stem? The *Treatise* says: "The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. This is indeed not false. Take, for example, a single piece of paper: it can become currency, treasures, silks, and even chests and boxes.

All of these are produced by the consciousness of the human mind. Ghosts perceive objects differently from one another; thus we know that the three realms and the six paths are all formed by the mind. According to records, this currency and silk originated with Sui Renqian of the Tang dynasty, who commissioned Cen Wenzhen to create them as gifts for the Grand Scribe Cheng Jingchang. It is uncertain whether they existed prior to the Tang.

As for what generation this originated from, some claim it was used by those of antiquity; thus, ancient sacrificial rites employed jade *gui* and *bi* tablets, as well as furs and silks. Yet the *Changshi* (Director of the Imperial Secretariat) stated that even these were not as effective as the paper substitutes. As the *Tongji* (Comprehensive Records) states: prior to the Tang dynasty, there were no paper offerings.

Those who adopted the practice began with Emperor Mingzong of the Tang, who appointed Wang Yu to oversee sacrificial rites, and this method became widespread. Consequently, paper money accumulated in the netherworld—made of gold, silver, embroidery, and silk—was no different from the currency used in the world, all being created through the transformative power of the mind.

Thus, the gates of the celestial treasury and the netherworld also shift according to the human mind. Regarding the spirits and ghosts who use paper money to enter the human realm and purchase goods, there are those who have seen wax coins piled up at Mount Tai that are of no use, remarking: "The wealth transformed in the human world must be spent by lighting oil lamps to pass through the fires."

As for those who defile [the practice], such instances of evidence are manifold. "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise"; this applies not only to the single method of paper money. It is further said that one should not collect offerings near pomegranate or peach trees, for ghosts fear them.
Li Siyi of Longxi currently resides in Fuyang County of Xiangzhou. On the first day of the first month in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, he died and was revived after one day;
the account of his speech is recorded in the *Mingbao ji*. In the fifth month of the third year of the Yonghui era, he died again and was revived after one night.
He said that because his life span was not yet exhausted, he had been released by the King and returned to him.
Previously, I saw the monk Bian Gui of Faguang Temple in Fuyang County, Xiangzhou;
I also saw the monks Hong Liang and Hui Bao of Huifukong Temple—these three were all present before the King, answering his questions. The official of the underworld stated:
"The time for Hui Bao’s death has not yet arrived; he should cultivate merit. As for Bian Gui and Hong Liang, they will certainly die this year. Bian Gui and the others indeed died that very year.
They passed away one after another. Later, a monk at the temple had a medium go to the former quarters of Huilang to summon two monks and question them.
Biangui said, "I broke my fast, and now I am undergoing great suffering. He also told his disciples, "Perform a fast for me to rescue me from this hardship.
The disciples immediately prepared the fast. The medium further said, "Biangui has already attained..."
He was exempted from punishment. Hongliang said, "I broke my fast and furthermore spoke falsely of others' long and short comings;
now I am being tormented by the extraction of my teeth, so I cannot speak much. This was told by the monk Huiyong and others of Zhili Temple in Xiangzhou (from *Mingbao Shiyi*). [Note:
"Breaking the fast" refers to eating after noon, which violates the precept against eating at improper times; it does not refer to consuming pungent or fatty meats.]
Yongzhou: In Xizhouzhì County, to the northwest, there was a person from Yuancóng Fāng whose surname was Chéng and given name Pǔlè. In his youth, he had been fond of music.
On the seventh day of the fifth month in the sixth year of the Yǒnghuī era, he died suddenly due to a slight illness.
For five days, his heart remained warm and his body did not smell; his family did not dare to bury him. On the morning of the sixth day, he regained consciousness and returned to his normal state.
Śāṇakavāsin said: "At the moment of death, two men dressed in blue garments come before the bed and say, 'The King summons you.
Pūrṇa asked, 'Which king? They replied, 'King Yama. He asked, 'For what purpose? They replied, 'We have recently been sent to conduct an interrogation; we must depart at once.'"
"There is no need for further talk. One man grasped Pule by the hand and they departed through the southern gate of the monastery.

Gradually heading toward the southern mountains, they reached a desolate patch of overgrown grass where there was a small area of salty, barren soil that produced no vegetation. There was a large hole there, as wide as the mouth of a great jar.
He said to Pule, "Enter! Pule was afraid and refused to enter. One man pushed him inside; he did not notice any injury and saw directly before him the Great King.
In the hall, there were a great many staff-bearers. The King, together with his ministers, queens, and consorts, sat on a high throne within the main hall, separated from the assembly by a screen.

Before the hall, there was a great clamor of sound as performers engaged in various entertainments. An attendant led the musician forward and informed the King, "The person we were seeking has arrived.
The King asked, "Who is this? He replied, "Cheng Pu Yue. The King asked, "Are you skilled in dramatic recitation and storytelling? Yue replied:
"He does not understand. (This refers to comic performance, such as singing and acting. The King turned his head and asked a performer named Zhang She'er.
"This man does not understand comic performance; for what reason was he summoned? He replied, "Throughout his life, She'er and I were companions in the 'Universal Joy' troupe.
Later, we became embroiled in a mutual grudge. She'er has now used that grudge as a pretext to drag this man along. She'er would not dare deceive Your Majesty; he has returned [the man]."

According to the factual account, the King became enraged and ordered them to perform before the Hall of Amusements. All the musical instruments were struck simultaneously; they were seen beating drums and performing dances while climbing a vertical pole.

As the pole-climber first ascended to the top and descended, he would insert the base of the pole directly downward, causing it to emerge from behind him as he reached the ground, only to ascend once more.
Thus, as he climbed up and down the pole, his six sense organs were all shattered and blood flowed from his nine orifices. It was thus throughout.

It was all like this. Furthermore, he saw performers from the time of the Yellow Emperor and the Tang dynasty, such as Qi’s Yanzi, Tuchu Lang, Duzhu, and Chaobang, numbering several dozen, who were made to perform comic recitations.

At that time, they spat fire from their mouths and extended their tongues to circle the arena, which was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of iron birds and various venomous insects that flew down from the sky and all at once pecked and sucked at their tongues.
They undergo extreme suffering, their cries shaking the earth; they are unbearable for others to hear.

The other performers of miscellaneous entertainments and the various small iron insects, upon seeing them clap their hands and raise their wails all at once, are as if struck by smoke or fire and are simultaneously consumed by flames.
They are burned to death and then restored to life; they undergo suffering one after another without a moment’s rest. Their cries do not cease, and their endurance of pain knows no end.
Although the King has lowered his staff, he dispatches jailers who surround and guard them, clutching iron clubs, sharp spears, and iron bows and arrows.
He was sent to perform music, yet his suffering did not cease. When Pule (Universal Joy) arrived at the prison on the fifth day, he saw this musician suffering in such a manner.
On the morning of the sixth day, the King summoned Pule and said to him, "It is not yet time for you to die; examine the records again.
Two years hence, your lifespan will be exhausted, and you shall come here to suffer. Such people are born [into this state] because of their past deeds.

They habitually practiced false speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; they mocked and teased monks and nuns, treated the Buddha-dharma with contempt and derision, and feigned association with the Triple Gem to deceive others out of their wealth.
They devoted themselves solely to supporting their wives and children, took pleasure in slaughtering pigs and sheep, and consumed wine and meat.

Furthermore, they would enter temples for the purpose of eating and thereby defile the property of the Sangha with filth and impurity. Because of such transgressions as these, and because they did not observe the fast or the precepts, they have now received this [retribution].

"Disaster! Although you do not have such grave offenses as these, it is not that you are without other faults; you likewise deserve to receive this [retribution]. For now, we release you to go, but when the time of death comes, we shall take you back.
We shall have those same two men deliver you to your home. They saw a bed of thorn trees with dense branches and leaves. The two men ordered him to enter this bed.
Pule (Pūrṇa) at first refused to enter, but the two men pushed him urgently until he closed his eyes.

He entered [the water] and immediately awoke to find himself back on his bed, restored to life. Because Pule had witnessed this omen, he went to the capital, visiting various monasteries to receive the precepts.
He maintained them strictly without transgression, observed a vegetarian diet and perpetual fasting, and paid his respects without fail. Consequently, he went before the Sangha to perform repentance.
He recounted these words in full.
Master Pyeon, the Right Adjutant of the Guard of the Eastern Office, Jeong Sibi, died suddenly before reaching the age of twenty.
After three days, he revived and spoke of his own experience: "At first, several men seized me and led me away into a great government office."
Upon entering the gate, he saw more than a hundred prisoners, all standing in double file facing north, arranged in six rows.

Those in the front row were plump and fair-complexioned, dressed in fine garments like men of noble rank; those in the subsequent rows gradually became thinner and more wretched, some even wearing cangues and shackles.

Some merely removed their head-wraps and belts, and they all walked with arms linked together as strict guards kept watch over them. When Master Bian arrived, he was assigned to the third row and stood at the third position from the east;
he too removed his head-wrap and belt and linked arms with the others. Bian was filled with anxiety and fear, so he concentrated his mind on reciting the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, he saw a monk he had known since childhood enter the ranks of the guards; the soldiers did not stop him, and he proceeded to where Bian was. He said:
He said, "In my life I have not cultivated merit; how shall I fare now? Bian lamented piteously, entreating him for salvation. The monk said, "I can now rescue you so that you may escape.
Will you observe the precepts? Bian promised to do so. In a short while, they led the prisoners out to the magistrate's presence.
As they were questioned in turn, when they reached the gate, [the monk] conferred the Five Precepts upon him. He poured water from a jar onto Bian’s forehead and said, "The sun is setting."
He was restored to life. Furthermore, [his mother] gave Bian a yellow shroud, saying, "Wear this until you reach home;

remove it once you arrive at a clean place. She then pointed out the way back. Bian put on the shroud and returned home; upon arriving, he removed the shroud and placed it in the corner of the bed. Shortly thereafter, his eyes opened and his body moved.
The family members scattered in alarm, believing him to be a *vītaśava* (a reanimated corpse), but only his mother did not leave. She asked, "Are you alive?"
"Ya! Bian said, "The sun is setting; you shall live. Bian had suspected at the time that it was noon, so he asked his mother. His mother replied, "It is midnight.

Only then did he realize that life and death are contrary and that day and night are opposites. When the sun finally set, he was able to eat and recovered. He still saw the blanket on the head of the bed;
when Bian was able to rise, the form of the blanket gradually vanished, yet there was still a radiance. It lasted for seven days before it finally ended. Bian—
He subsequently observed the five precepts. Several years later, a friend urged him to eat pork; unable to refuse, Bian ate a single slice.
That night, he dreamed that he had transformed into a rākṣasa with claws and teeth each several feet long, seizing and eating a live pig.

When dawn broke, he felt a fishy odor in his mouth and spat out blood. When he sent someone to look, his mouth was entirely filled with clotted blood. Bian was terrified and did not dare [to eat meat again].
He resumed eating meat. Furthermore, after several years, he took a wife; his wife’s family pressured him to eat it again, after which no further signs occurred.

However, Bian had smelled a foul odor for five or six years, and he constantly suffered from large, festering sores that could not be healed throughout his life. It was perhaps due to his violation of the precepts.
Formerly, when [the author] was on duty at the Eastern Palace alongside Bian, he heard Bian recount these things himself. (The above two accounts are from the *Mingbao ji*).
In Fangzhou, there was Wang Huai-zhi, a Shangzhuguo. He passed away at the beginning of the Xianqing era.
His mother, Lady Sun, along with his younger brothers Huai-shan and Huai-biao, all survived.

In the sixth month of the fourth year, a man in Gaoling, Yongzhou—whose name has been lost—died and after seven days had passed, his back was already decomposing when he revived. This man saw Huai beneath the earth.
Zhìyún, currently serving as the Registrar of Taishan, sent this man to take up the brush and dictate a letter for him. He said to him:
"Although you deserve death, I shall now use skillful means to release you and allow you to return home. You should take this letter of mine to Fángzhōu."
Please visit my home and inform my mother that I, Huai-zhi, am currently serving as a Recorder-Attendant (Lu-shi Can-jun) for Mount Tai. I am fortunate to be in good health and peace.
However, our family previously borrowed timber from the monastery to construct a gate; as this was material intended for religious merit, I request that it be repaid at the earliest opportunity.
My younger brother, Huai-shan, has already passed away and cannot remain long in this world; please quickly commission scriptures and images to aid him in his rebirth. Otherwise—

It was feared that there would be no way to resolve the matter. After this man had revived, he immediately delivered the letter to the house; the family affairs discussed therein matched the reality perfectly, without exception.
When three days had passed, Huai-shan suddenly died of a sudden illness. Those among the clergy and laity throughout Hezhou who heard of this were struck with wonder.
There were none who did not increase their cultivation of merit. Xunwei Hou Zhi Chun of Fuzhou recounted this (from the *Mingbao Shiyi*).
In Xuanchuan Village, Xiaoyi County, Fenzhou, Liu Mo’er fell ill and passed away on the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month of the fourth year of the Xianqing era.
His son, Shi Bao, died the following day. The conduct of father and son throughout their lives—
They were all treacherous and perverse. A neighbor of theirs, Qi Longwei, was killed by being run over by a carriage while gathering firewood.

After several days, he revived and saw Ma’er’s son, his teacher, and his guardian in a cauldron of boiling water. In an instant, their skin and flesh were completely consumed until they no longer had human form;
only white bones remained. After this state persisted for a long while, they returned to their original forms. Longwei then asked:
The man asked, "What is the reason for this? He replied, "Because I went out hunting for him, I have incurred this punishment.

He asked Bao again, "Where is your father? He replied, "My father’s offense is grave; he cannot be seen immediately. Once you have returned, please inform my family so that they may perform vegetarian feasts and meritorious acts on his behalf.
Having finished speaking, he was urged by the messenger and proceeded to the official residence. There he saw that the buildings were lofty and imposing, and those who held staffs...
There were more than twenty people. An official asked one of them, "What meritorious deeds have you performed recently?

He replied, "Last year in the first month, while staying in Duku Village, I read and recited the *Sarvadharmaparyāya* (or all the sutras). I offered a single shirt as a gift and also received the five precepts."

To this day, he has not committed any transgression. The official then said, "If it is as you say, that there is immeasurable merit, why did you need to come here? He then requested the register for inspection.
Looking at the register, he saw that the man was indeed destined to die; however, there was a marginal note stating:

"Due to the merit and assistance provided by receiving the precepts and making offerings, his life span should be further extended. Thereupon, he sent someone to escort him back, and the man immediately revived. (From the *Mingbao ji*; *bi* pronounced as *mi*, meaning treacherous and biased.)
This is what is meant by "being dissatisfied.
In Chang’an County, Yongzhou, there was Gao Fayan, the great-great-grandson of Gao Ying, the Minister of Works during the Sui dynasty.
On the twenty-fifth day of the first month in the third year of the Longshuo era, he went to the Central Secretariat to register for official service; at noon, he returned home to his residence.
He resided in the southern corner of Yining Ward, with his gate opening toward the street; it was to the east of Huadu Monastery and belonged to the Gao family.
When he wished to exit through Zixi Gate on the west side of the city, two riders on horseback encountered him from behind inside the city.
Once he had exited the city, they gradually drew closer and pressed upon him. Outside the city gate, to the north of the road, was Puguang Monastery. One of the men spoke to the rider, saying:
"You run and seize the gate of Puguang Monastery; do not let this man enter. I fear he will be difficult to capture.
Following these instructions, the man galloped there to guard the gate. Fearing him, Fayuan was unable to enter the monastery and fled toward the west.
He arrived at Changcheng Ward on the West Street, to the west of the road by the South Gate, where Huichang Monastery was located. Four more horsemen were added, and they spoke to the two men ahead.
The man on horseback said, "Hurry and guard the gate of Huichang Temple. The man followed these words and ran to seize the temple gate.
Fearing for his life, Fayen immediately said to the man on horseback, "Who are you that dares to press me so? The man on horseback replied:
The King sent me here to take the Dharma-eye. When asked, "By which king were you sent? the horseman replied, "I was sent by King Yama.
Upon hearing that he had been sent as a messenger by King Yama, Dharmākṣa knew for certain that he was a ghost and immediately resisted him.
The ghost became enraged and said, "Quickly cut off his hair! Then another ghost seized a knife and cut off both of Dharmākṣa’s topknots. Attached [to the narrative].
His flesh fell to the ground, and he immediately proceeded to the west street. There he fainted and fell from his horse, dying a sudden death without awareness.

Having reached a major thoroughfare, while he stood hesitating, more than a thousand people looked on. At the head of the west street was a noble residence; he called for his family to carry him to their home.
Only at dawn did he revive, whereupon he spoke to those in his household, saying: "I entered hell and saw King Yama."

O King, he ascended the great high seat and reproached me with anger, saying: "For what reason did you go to the Huadu Monastery and eat the fruits belonging to the resident monks in the room of Master Mingzang?
As a result, you must swallow four hundred pellets of glowing iron. At the moment of swallowing them, your throat will contract and close;
your body will become scorched and shriveled, turning crimson. Only after swallowing them all will you regain consciousness. Once revived, twenty..."
On the sixth day, when he regained consciousness, various spirits came again to seize his Dharma-eye and bring him before the king.

The king said to him, "For what reason did you fail to revere the Triple Gem and speak of the faults and evils of the Saṃgha? Now that you have swallowed the iron balls, you must endure having your tongue ploughed by iron plows.
On the twenty-ninth day of the first month, having finished swallowing the iron balls, he revived and awoke. It was the beginning of the first month.
On the thirtieth day, at dawn, he died again and was cast into hell. Once more, he underwent the punishment of having his tongue plowed by an iron plowshare;
the tongue was several li long, yet bystanders saw it protrude only about one chi. The King spoke again to the hell-warden:
"Because this man has spoken ill of the Triple Gem, cut off the root of his tongue with a great iron axe. The warder hacked at it, but it would not break. The King spoke again, saying:
He had his tongue finely minced with an axe and cast into a cauldron of boiling water to be boiled; yet it would not soften. The King again questioned him in wonder about the reason for this.
Fayen replied to the King, saying, "I once read the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. The King still did not believe him and ordered an inspection of the register of merits.
Seeing that the record contained one volume of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the King verified that it was indeed true, and only then released him from prison.
This person is still living today. Those who observe him are as numerous as those in a marketplace; those who see him give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*);

his entire family believes and honors him, exerts themselves with diligence, and maintains sincere earnestness without weariness. This is known to both the clergy and the laity throughout the capital, so there is no need to cite further evidence.

(From the *Fayuan*, recorded by Dharma Master Xuanyun. Furthermore, at Shengguang Temple in the Western Capital, there was the śramaṇa Xiaozhi. His relatives and acquaintances would frequently visit him and he would feed them temple fruits. Before long—

He contracted a disease that caused him to vomit blood. He said of himself: "Whenever the illness was about to flare up, I would see a messenger in red robes leading me toward a black forest, where a great wind blew my limbs asunder. After a short while, I was led again toward a terrace and pavilion.
A man of terrifying appearance rebuked me in a harsh voice, saying: 'How can you feed the fruits of the monastery to your relatives? Having finished speaking, he vanished. Zhi.

Fearing this, he immediately calculated the value to compensate the Sangha. It was only after more than a month that he was released. (From the *Mingbao ji*. Question: Nowadays, many speak of the faults and evils of the Sangha;

there are many who steal monastic property, and even those who use monastic goods to provide for their relatives and friends. Why do we not see immediate retribution? Answer: Because evil karma is so abundant, it is like a black cloth upon which stains cannot be seen. One will only perceive it when one’s life comes to an end.)

In Tonggui Ward within the city walls of Chang’an, in the third year of the Longshuo era, Liu Gongxin of the Three Guards’ Guard, his wife Chen, whose mother had previously died, suddenly passed away from illness.
She saw people leading her into hell and witnessed all manner of sufferings, which cannot be described in full detail.
Finally, she saw a hell with a solid stone gate, where two great ghosts stood, their forms massive and imposing.

The gatekeepers on either side glared with wrathful eyes at Chen, asking, "Who are you to come here? When she saw the stone gate suddenly open, she found her deceased mother suffering within in ways that cannot be fully described.
As her suffering momentarily abated, she drew near the gate, and mother and daughter met. From afar, they were able to speak together;
the mother said to her daughter, "Return home and exert yourself for my sake by copying the sutras. The daughter asked, "Mother, which sutra do you wish for me to copy?"
The scripture says: "Write the Lotus Sūtra for me. As soon as he had finished speaking, the stone gate closed. Chen regained consciousness and related everything to her husband.
Her husband then relied upon his sister’s husband, Zhao Shizi, who wished to copy the *Lotus Sūtra*. Zhao Shizi was formerly skilled at transcribing scriptures.

There was a certain sutra-copyist who possessed a newly transcribed copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that had not yet been decorated. This man had previously been hired by another to copy a scripture;
the owner of that scripture was surnamed Fan. The copyist took that other person’s *Lotus Sutra* and went to Zhao Shizi’s place to pawn it for two hundred coins.
The original donor did not know the scripture had been panned. Zhao Shizi then said to his wife’s maternal uncle: "I have now lent this scripture."

While living at home, there was a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* belonging to a certain family. Her elder brother intended to redeem this scripture for a price of one thousand coins, but her husband, Chen, managed to redeem it for four hundred coins.
Having completed the decoration and restoration, he kept it at home to offer to his mother.

Later, Chen’s wife had a dream in which she saw her mother demanding the scripture from her daughter, saying: "I previously sent you to transcribe a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* for me; for what reason..."
To this day, she has not obtained it. The daughter replied to her mother, saying, "I have already ransomed a copy of the Lotus Sutra for you;
it is now fully adorned and being venerated at home. The mother said to her daughter, "It is precisely because of this sutra that I am undergoing further suffering in the realm of the dark paths."
"The wardens of hell beat my back until it was broken; look at the sores upon my body.
The prison official said, "For what reason did you take the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* belonging to the Fan family and claim it as your own? What merit do you possess? This is a most grievous transgression!
Seeing her mother speak thus, the daughter once again transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* for her. Before the transcription was finished, she saw her mother again in a dream, coming to urge her on.

In the sutra, she immediately saw a monk holding a scroll of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in his hand, who said to her mother: "Your daughter has already finished copying the first scroll of the sutra for you;
the merit is complete. For what reason do you come again to urge her so persistently? Wait until it is finished; why such haste?
Later, when the copying of the sutra was completed, the mother came to inform her daughter: "Because of your having copied the sutra for me, I have now been able to leave the underworld."
"May you attain the Way and receive a favorable rebirth. It is by virtue of your meritorious power that I have been able to do so; therefore, I come to repay your kindness.

May you dwell in well-being and perform the duties of a wife with excellence. Let faith be your foundation. Having spoken thus, they wept sorrowfully as they parted. Later, when inquiries were made, it was found that the former master of the *Lotus Sūtra* was indeed surnamed Fan.

Although the Fan family had not obtained the scripture, the sūtra had already been completed, and their merit from the act of giving was fully realized. Subsequently, others continued the transmission.
The collateral himself incurred guilt and misfortune. Liu’s wife redeemed him and thereby obtained a small measure of merit; however, her deceased mother did not benefit from it.
Chen’s husband, Liu Gongxin, recounted this in detail to Yuanxiu (from the *Mingbao Shiyi*).

Lady Xiao... was the wife of Cui Yiqi, the Minister of the Office of the Prime Elements (*Siyuandafu*). She was the daughter of Xiao Keng, who was the nephew of the Minister of the Household (*Puyue*).
Lady Xiao was by nature jealous and prone to anger; she enjoyed beating her male and female servants and did not believe in the retribution of karma.
In the first year of the Linde era, she accompanied the imperial entourage to Luoyang. By the first month of the second year, she passed away. After death, Lady Xiao was reborn in hell. Lady Xiao...

He had a handmaid whom he always loved, named Yunyu, about eighteen years of age. Although she was a slave from the *liao* tribes, her appearance was upright and her nature was intelligent and quick-witted;
she believed in and delighted in the Buddha-dharma. In the second month, the household held a seven-day vegetarian feast for the monks on behalf of the lady.
At the time of the main meal, the lady came in person to observe, her neck bound by a cangue and her waist shackled with chains, escorted by jailers and attendants. The rest...
No one knew [of her arrival], except for this maidservant who saw the lady’s spirit.

The spirit had taken possession of the maidservant’s voice, speaking with a tone no different from that of her lifetime, and sent a message to the members of the household, both great and small, saying: "Since I first entered the house of the Cuis, I have been here."
By nature he was prone to great anger and would recklessly give rise to jealousy; he delighted in beating his servants and slaves and furthermore did not believe in cause and effect.

Now he has reached hell, where he undergoes extremely heavy punishment and endures all manner of sufferings that cannot be fully described. He heard that within his family, the twenty-first day of the seven-day mourning period had now arrived.
"Prepare a vegetarian feast for me. Request leave from the prison officials for one day so that I may come briefly to observe the feast.

Tell your sons and daughters, and all members of the household, that since the time I have lived together with you, my body, speech, and mind—driven by the three poisons—have frequently been prone to anger and striking you, as well as harboring jealousy toward the maidservants and concubines overseen by the Great Officer. Through these various unwholesome acts, I have initiated evil karma, which I now must undergo."
I report this suffering to you. I pray that you, your sons and daughters, your entire household great and small, and all your internal and external kinsmen, will grant joy following your repentance.
Furthermore, may your sons and daughters remember the kindness of my nursing and providing milk; take these belongings and utensils used throughout my life.

Quickly abandon [this] and cultivate merit, hoping to be delivered from the sufferings of the underworld. Upon reaching the seventh week, hold a vegetarian feast for me, so that this merit may be swiftly accomplished.
On the day of the feast, I shall further invite the officials, hoping they may return. [Speak thus] to the Great Officer and his children:
"Throughout your life, the Great Officer has been quick-tempered and prone to anger; you must not excessively scold or beat your servants. Thus he exhorted them.
Have faith in the Three Jewels; show reverence to those above and below; observe the precepts and fasts; practice generosity and patience without negligence.
When the time of departure arrives, say to your sons and daughters: "I shall take Yunyu with me to the hells so that she may witness me undergoing punishment and see what my suffering is like.
After five or six days, I will release her and bring her back, so that you, my sons and daughters, may know the bitterness of my suffering."
She felt pain whether [the body] was empty or full. Having spoken these words, Yunyu died immediately; only her heart remained warm, while the rest of her body was cold.
