Her body lay on the ground, and they did not dare bury her. This servant girl then arrived at hell and saw a great palace courtyard with its gates guarded by strict soldiers, who said, "This is the King’s palace;
you must not peep inside. She proceeded to the eastern courtyard and saw another hall. Upon it—

There was a high-ranking official who claimed to be a judge of criminal cases. Passing further to the east of the hall and courtyard, there was a hell with various instruments of torture, exactly like the depictions of hells found in worldly paintings. The lady said to her maidservant, "Look at the suffering of my punishment.
Having spoken these words, various hell-wardens and rākṣasas immediately pounced upon and threw the lady down, slaughtering her.
He had his own flesh cut away; he was boiled in cauldrons of boiling water. Once cooked, he returned to life; once revived, he again passed through various hells.
Iron tongs pulled out his tongue; iron birds pecked at it. He was then laid upon an iron bed, where flying birds and fierce fires simultaneously descended upon his body.
After dying, he returned to life; after reviving, he again endured various sufferings that cannot be fully described. When the man finally regained consciousness, he immediately saw his father, Xiao.

*Keng*. He arrived, riding upon a purple-gold lotus throne, soaring through the air. From his birth until his tenure in various official posts, Keng had never consumed alcohol, meat, or pungent vegetables.
He constantly recited the Lotus Sutra once every day, revering the Triple Gem and performing prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day and night without fail.
Having now been born in a favorable realm, he came because he saw the woman suffering and thus wished to assist her.
Jiù addressed his daughter, saying: "Throughout my life, I have constantly exhorted you to cultivate faith and cease your anger.
You did not heed my words, and now this calamity has befallen us. For what reason have you brought this maidservant here? The daughter replied to her father:

"Because I lacked faith throughout my life, I am now suffering these punishments. I have brought this maidservant to observe the severity of my own punishment, so that she may convey [the message]..."
He directed his words toward the men and women of the household to inspire faith in them. Upon hearing this and granting his approval, the father spoke to his daughter, saying:

"Though I have been born in a favorable realm, I am unable to fully save you from your suffering. You must strive with diligent self-exertion to resolve your mind [for awakening], and by relying upon the merit and virtue of our household, we shall assist one another so that you may certainly hope to escape and ascend to the realms of humans and devas. Having spoken these words, suddenly there appeared—
A Brahmin teacher, young and handsome, also arrived through the air. He said to the lady, "Because you did not believe in cause and effect, you now undergo this suffering of retribution.
I do not yet know what the nature and character of this maidservant are like; I wish to instruct her in the recitation of the scriptures."

He sent her back into the household to inspire faith among the people of the world. The lady replied, "Please, Master, teach her yourself; this maidservant is clever and will be able to recite the sutra.
The Master then first taught her the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. When he first gave her two or three lines and she forgot one or two phrases, he subsequently taught her again.
Gradually, she was able to recite half a sheet and then a full sheet; in a short time, she could recite it from memory.
He forgot it. Later, when he was taught to recite the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he did not forget them after being taught once.

These three sections were all recited in the Sanskrit (*brahmā*) voice; they were not rendered in the Chinese vernacular. The phrasing was classical and correct, the intonation clear and resonant, and every word and phrase was mastered.

He then sent him back home, saying at their parting: "When you arrive home, recite these for anyone you encounter. Whether they be Chinese people, whether lay or ordained, they will not distinguish your accent."
"Have a Brahmin who is skilled in the Sanskrit language seek him out to test his recitation; only then will we know whether he is good or evil.

Many people in this world believe in heterodox matters and paths, taking no pleasure in the Buddha-dharma. Now that they have seen you, a tribal slave girl, yet still able to recite three versions of the Sanskrit scriptures, how can they not give rise to faith?
If even one person can be turned from the heterodox toward the orthodox, it is not merely for the sake of the lady."

"You shall obtain merit, and it shall also cause your future retribution not to enter the three evil paths. Having received these words, she was released and returned home, regaining her full consciousness as before.
She immediately gathered the elders and inferiors within the household and recounted in detail the matter of the lady suffering in hell.
Fearing that her sons and others might still disbelieve her, she lay down upon the ground and acted out the lady’s suffering in hell.
The events were as follows: some said, "Behold the lady swallowing glowing iron balls; she opens her mouth and swallows them, her mouth turning crimson and her belly burning like fire.
Others said, "Behold the lady having her tongue plowed by an iron plowshare; she extends her tongue for more than two or three feet.
Still others said, "Behold the lady suffering upon an iron bed; her body is scarlet red, and its heat is like fire. Such were the various manifestations of suffering.

After experiencing the sensations of suffering, she then regained consciousness. She further recounted seeing her husband’s father issue his instructions, and she also described seeing the Brahmin teaching and reciting the meaning of the sutras.

The lady was thus able to escape from hell and ascend to receive a reward in heaven. This maidservant immediately took her place as the presiding head of the household and recited the scriptural texts;
every phrase and every sentence was rendered in the Sanskrit language, with her voice and breath [perfectly attuned].

It was clear and resonant, causing those who heard it to rejoice. When the members of the household, both great and small, witnessed these signs of the efficacy of good and evil, they had rarely heard the like.
Men and women, young and old, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, wailing and lamenting with such grief that it surpassed even the sorrow of a recent death.

Monastics and laypeople, as well as local officials, who heard of this, all exhorted one another to change their minds and take refuge in faith, observing the fasts and precepts without ceasing. In the second year of the Linde era, there were four [monks] from the Western Regions...
The Brahmins arrived and presented the Buddha’s cranial bone. Because of their kinsmen, General Xue Renguī held a vegetarian feast at his residence where all his relatives gathered.
The various officials deliberated together, saying, "Although this maidservant can recite the Sanskrit scriptures, none of us can distinguish them.
Therefore, we have invited these four Brahmins to attend the feast at the General’s house. Furthermore...

He summoned this maidservant and said to the four bhikṣus, "She has recited [these scriptures] while in hell. He then falsely claimed, "There was another brāhmaṇa who taught her to recite these three sections of scripture.
To secretly test whether this was true or false, he immediately had the maidservant recite them before the four bhikṣus.
She first finished reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, whereupon the four brāhmaṇas all rose at once, joined their palms, and were struck with wonder.
He marveled at this rarity, exclaiming, "This is unprecedented! For what reason can a person of Han origin attain such [proficiency]?

Having finished reciting the *Bhaiṣajyaguru* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he was even more filled with joy. Treating her with the reverence due to a teacher, he immediately asked through an interpreter: 'For what reason has this woman attained such skillful diction?
Her phrasing is classical and correct; she is well-versed in the scriptures and commits no errors. I am well-versed in the Western Regions [of India], yet I cannot match her.'"
The reciter replied, "I am not yet able to do so; it is no ordinary person who can attain such [ability]. You officials have only now begun to speak the truth.
The four monks wept, saying, "Were it not for the secret empowerment of the power of the sages, how could our words be so refined and correct?"
The officials and laypeople who witnessed this were moved to grief and admiration; they came to have deep faith in the Buddha-dharma and did not dare to treat it with contempt.

The General, having observed these events, memorialized the Emperor, and his report reached the Imperial Throne. The Emperor then issued an edict to the hundred officials, stating that one may now truly know that the Buddha-dharma is supreme among all the sages.
That we are sustained by such profound protection—how could anyone dare not believe it? The hundred officials prostrated themselves in gratitude, celebrating what they had never heard before.

This is truly because the Three Jewels bestow magnificent blessings and their grace is weighty, providing compassionate shade for the four modes of birth; this is beyond the capacity of our humble subjects to fathom. Both the holy and the mundane have received these benefits.
How could one not believe this? (From the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
At Fahai Monastery in the Western Capital, Chan Master Ying, during the Xianheng era, dreamed that the Lord of Mount Tai summoned him to preach the Dharma.
Later, while sitting alone in his quarters, he saw a strange man of magnificent appearance and attire who came forward and addressed him, saying: "I am your disciple."
I have recently visited the Lord of Mount Tai and beheld your venerable countenance; I learned that your compassionate virtue benefits all things to a great extent.

Your disciple has heard that there is a Great Water and Land Repast (*shuilu daizhai*) which can benefit those in the netherworld. Its liturgy was compiled by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, and it was obtained at Dajue Temple by the monk Yiji of Wu.
I pray that you, Master, will go to seek it and perform the rite according to the dharma. *Ying* (英) [Note: This appears to be a signature or seal mark.]

The Master granted his request. He then went to Dajue and indeed obtained the text. When the ritual fast had been completed on the full moon, he again saw the strange man from before, who gave him ten more scrolls.
Approaching him, he thanked him, saying, "I am the former King Zhuangxiao of Qin."
He further pointed to his disciples, saying: "These are Fan Sui, Rang Hou, Bai Qi, Wang Jian, Zhang Yi, and Chen Zhen—all were ministers of Qin.
They have all been imprisoned in the underworld for their original crimes. Long ago, when Emperor Wu of Liang established this ritual feast at Mount Jinshan..."
The ministers of King Zhou of a former age were all able to escape and be liberated. At that time, this disciple also briefly ceased his suffering;

however, because the judgment on his case in prison had not yet been decided, he did not obtain liberation. Now, having received the Master’s ritual of repentance for his transgressions, this disciple, along with these others and the rulers and ministers of the various states, all rely upon the power of the Dharma to be reborn among humans. Fearing that the world has changed and the nations are different, we have come here.

"Thank you. Having finished speaking, he vanished. From then on, the Duke Ying regularly established this *zhāi* (fasting ritual), which spread throughout the world. (From the *Tongji* and the *Water and Land Ritual Manual*.
[Zhuangxiang was the father of the First Emperor of Qin. It has been nine hundred and forty years until the Xianheng era of the Tang dynasty. )
Fenzhou. In the first year of the Tiulou era, Huicheng, the abbot of Qifu Temple, fell ill and passed away with the sound of a "bull's roar.

Later that night, the monk Changning saw Cheng appear; his appearance was haggard and emaciated. He said, "Because I misappropriated the property of the Triple Gem, I am suffering from an indescribable agony.
While my various other sins are somewhat light, the misuse of temple property is the gravest. I pray that you will grant me deliverance. Ning then acted for him...
They recited sutras and performed repentance rituals for over a month, after which they returned and said, "We have received your benefit and our suffering has already ceased.
We now dwell in a separate place, yet we do not yet know the day we shall be liberated."

Deng Yuan-ying of Huayin had a close relative who died suddenly. After seven days, the person revived and informed Yuan-ying, saying, "I saw the officials of the underworld leading my father to be pursued.
You should urgently cultivate merit to ward off this fate. Yuan-ying asked in astonishment:
"What meritorious deed must one cultivate to escape this? [Yuan Ying] replied, "Quickly transcribe one copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Yuan Ying immediately purchased paper and summoned many scribes from neighboring monasteries; before ten days had passed, the scripture was already completed, and he ultimately escaped this calamity.

Furthermore, a lotus flower sprouted from the burial site of his mother. Empress Wu was struck by this marvel and issued an imperial edict to establish a "Gate of Filial Piety" (Xiaomen) there to honor him.
The Censor Feng Zhong died suddenly in the third year of the Jinglong era; two youths led him to the courtyard and stood before him.
The judge reviewed the records of his offenses and saw the name of his deceased maternal uncle, Zhang Siyi.

He said, "You should make a vow to transcribe a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and cast a bell; in this way, you may eliminate your past transgressions. As for the commentary, it was composed by Master Lizong Chan;

this master personally witnessed its transmission from Zhiyi, and it is always guarded by celestial deities. Zhong followed his uncle’s instructions and consequently succeeded in being released. Soon thereafter—
He had not yet obtained the commentary when he was again rebuked by a spirit from the underworld. Zhong requested three days to seek it out and transcribe it; the spirit then allowed him to return.
With sincere intent, he searched for it and indeed found the original text. He then hurriedly managed the transcription, after which he passed away (the above three accounts are from the *Tongji*).
Su Gui, the Vice Magistrate of Wugong County, regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. His entire family of fifty members all abstained from meat.
Su’s wife, Lady Cui, became so emaciated that she secretly ate meat. She subsequently suffered from a bone-thorn obstruction (*gu-keng*) and died. Ten days after her burial, she revived.
Upon seeing King Yama, he was reprimanded, who said: "Your husband is a flesh-body Bodhisattva; why did you steal and eat his meat?
It is only thanks to the merit of his recitation of the sutras that his life has been extended by twenty years. You may return and tell these matters to the people.
When Emperor Xuanzong heard of this, he too resolved to uphold the sutras, and those who followed his transformation were very numerous.

During the Southern Tang (the Li clan), in the city of Jinling, Upper Yuan County in Jiangnan, a commoner died suddenly and revived after three days. He went to the ruler of the Tang dynasty to report his experience.
Having entered the underworld, he saw the former Emperor, who was bound with five wooden stocks most severely. Startled, the man asked the Emperor why he was in such a state. The Emperor—
He said, "I was deceived by Song Qiqiu. I killed over a thousand surrendered people from Hezhou, and because of their grievances, I am being prosecuted.
Entrust you with this message to return and tell the successor: whenever a temple bell is struck, let its sound be prolonged.
When I suffer, hearing the bell alone will grant me a brief respite; it would be even better if you could have a bell cast for me. The man asked, "How shall I verify that this is true?"
The Emperor said, "During my reign, the King of Khotan once presented me with a jade image of a Heavenly King (*Devaputra*).

It was enshrined within the left knee of the Buddha statue at Waguan Temple, and no one has known of its existence. You may take this as proof. The Tang ruler personally went to Waguan Temple and cut open the Buddha’s knee;
indeed, he found the jade image there. Overcome with emotion, he wept and immediately commissioned a bell for Qingliang Temple, upon which he inscribed [the following]:

The Emperor said: "To recommend my late ancestor, the August Emperor Gaozu, who was delivered from obscurity and rescued from peril, I shall enshrine a jade image and erect a pagoda, and bury him at Jiangshan" (as recorded in the *Tong sai zhi*).

During the reign of Emperor Shizong (surnamed Chai) of the Later Zhou dynasty, he demolished the bells, chimes, gongs, cymbals, and bronze drums of all monasteries and observatories throughout the empire, and melted down the Buddha images to cast "Zhou Tong" coins.

At that time, the Great Compassion (Dabei) image in Zhenzhou was extremely efficacious; when the imperial edict was issued, no one dared to approach it. When the Emperor heard of this, he went there in person, wielding an axe.
He gouged out his own face and chest; those who witnessed it were struck with horror and trembling. Subsequently, an abscess broke out on the Emperor’s chest, and he passed away.

In the capital of Bian, there was a soldier named Zhou Baisheng who, in his old age, lived at home, subsisting on vegetarian food and reciting the Buddha’s name. One night, he dreamed that an official in yellow robes pursued him into a great city.
Upon arriving at the seat of government, the presiding official ordered an attendant to lead him on a tour of the hells. There he saw a person of black complexion.
He lay upon a great iron bed. The hell-wardens took up chisels and split open his chest, pouring molten copper into it; his cries were beyond hearing.
Baisheng was terrified and called upon the Buddha, seeking to withdraw. The official said, "You are a disciple of the Buddha; you need not fear. Baisheng asked:
"Who is this prisoner? he asked. The answer was, "It is Caidiya; he has been punished for this because he defaced a statue. Bai-sheng said, "I am his former king.
When shall I be released from this? The official replied, "Only when the currency circulating throughout the world is exhausted will you be freed from this offense."

The official then led him out of the city by the old path; upon hearing the sound of the temple bell, he suddenly regained consciousness. Baisheng often spoke of this to others, and those who heard it were moved to sorrow and lamentation.

(Emperor Taizu and Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty personally witnessed his miraculous recovery and their reverence and faith became even firmer; thus, at the beginning of their reigns, they restored Buddhist affairs throughout the empire. [This account is from the *Shenyi lu*].)

Ouyang Xiu (1007–1072) of the Song dynasty styled himself the "Six-One Recluse. While traveling to Mount Lu, he entered Donglin Temple and paid his respects to Chan Master Zuyin, requesting the master’s instruction.
The master revealed to him the Dharma-gate of the mind-nature, through which Xiu attained realization.
In the sixth year of the Jiayou era, Ou-yang Hsiu was appointed as a Participant in State Affairs (*Ch'eng-pan*) and concurrently served as the Editor for the Translation of Scriptures.

Having ascended to office, he suffered from frequent illness and once dreamed that he arrived at a certain place where ten men, wearing ceremonial caps and robes, were seated in a row. One man said, "Participant in State Affairs, how have you come to this?
You ought to return to your residence at once. Hsiu stepped out several paces, then went back to question them, saying, "Are you not perhaps those of the Śākya clan?"

"Are you one of the Ten Kings of the Netherworld? He replied, "Yes. He then asked, "When people of the world provide meals for the monastic community and recite sutras to perform merit-seeking rites for the deceased, is there truly any benefit?
He replied, "How could there not be benefit? Upon awakening, his illness was completely cured. From that time on, he gained deep faith in the Buddha-dharma.

While residing in Yingzhou, he renounced alcohol and meat, withdrew from sensory pleasures, and sat in silent meditation with a heart extinguished of worldly desires, ordering an old soldier— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available fragment.*
He went to a nearby temple to borrow a copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. He recited it up to the eighth fascicle when he passed away (as recorded in the *Tongji* and the *Jintang bian*).
Among the scriptures in the canon, there were originally ten *Yanluo Wang* (Kings of Yama) texts, but these have long since been lost.
Those currently transmitted in the world are: first, King Yanluo; second, King Qinguang; third, King Chujian; fourth, King Songdi; fifth, King Wuguan; sixth, King Biancheng; seventh... [text ends].
1. King of Mount Tai; 2. King of the Eight Equalities; 3. King of the Nine Capital Cities; 4. King of the Wheel-Turning (Cakravartin); 5. King Yama.
To claim that the Heavenly Son Yama constitutes the fifth court is an error. As the *Tongji* states:

"It is traditionally said that the Venerable Tang Daoming traveled spiritually through the underworld and saw the Ten Kings presiding over the governance of the deceased, from which their names were subsequently transmitted. This may be verified in the records of the Buddhist canon.

These are the six officials of the Five Offices of Yama. Guo Sheng of Chi Prefecture dreamed that he entered the Netherworld. Initially, King Chujiang (the River King) greeted him and invited him to sit, saying:

"I am Wang Lang of Ximen. Because the records of the Netherworld office noted my loyalty, filial piety, integrity, and my abstention from harming living beings, I was appointed as King Chujiang for one *jì* (twelve years).
Later, after Chen Sheng of Nanjian died, his younger sister saw two ghosts leading her [to the underworld].

Upon arriving at the palace, they said, "This is King Qin Guang. The king said to the woman, "If you wish to save your brother from suffering, you may recite the *Eight Masters Sutra* (*Ba Shi Jing*).

The woman awoke, and her family obtained the sutra and requested a monk to recite it one thousand times. Her younger brother dreamed that his elder brother came to thank him, saying, "I have already attained rebirth in heaven.
As with the ten kings above, with the exception of King Yama, most of the remaining nine kings have variations; therefore, they are called "officials" (*guan*).
"The number of prefectures has shifted.
(Question: "From the Han and Jin dynasties onward, we have not seen anyone who entered hell and returned to report; why is this? Answer: "...")
The scriptures and teachings have not yet reached them; who among them would recognize the name of *niraya*, the hell realms?

Even those who enter the underworld and return to life find it to be merely a dream-like or illusory state. Question: Why is it that since the Song and Yuan dynasties, such accounts have been rarely seen? Answer:
From my youth until now, I have often heard of people entering hell and recording the couplets posted before the Hall of King Yama.
[End. As for those who do not take pleasure [in these matters], I have recorded them. Had I not composed this, there would be no one to record even the subsequent sections;
how much more so now, when I constantly hear that they exist everywhere? Fearing prolixity, I have not recorded them all.
Furthermore, among the various ancient biographies, the details are exceedingly numerous; however, because people weary of complexity and prefer brevity, I have not recorded them in their entirety.

In Ming Gānzhōu, Tàohé County, there was Liu Xūwēi. During the Wànlì era, he served as the Governor of Náncháo and Shàocháo. He was fond of hosting guests and drank heavily, daily slaughtering countless living beings.
When he died, his son’s master, a certain Mr. Chén, suddenly died and then revived, saying: [...the rest of the narrative...]
King Yama said to me, "Since you have committed no great evil, I shall release you to return home. Standing before the hall of King Yama, I saw a man hanging from an iron mast;
it was my father-in-law, Xue Fu (Sūmī). He said to me, "Master, when you return, please convey a message to my son:
tell him that because I did not believe in the causality of good and evil during my lifetime, my karma of killing is heavy, and my suffering is unbearable."
He said, "Now my body is entirely covered with the fur and feathers of a beast. I fear that my son, not believing in the Buddhist rites, will surpass me.
I have a chest of silver buried at such-and-such a place; the key is hidden beneath such-and-such a tree. You may take this silver to invite monks to perform repentance rituals on my behalf.
Having said this, the master of the household went to Liu’s house and told him of the matter. His son indeed did not believe it, and he spoke again, saying:
"Burying silver is something your family has always done; however, you did not know where the key to the hidden store was kept.

Your father showed it to you specifically as proof of this. The son followed his teacher's words and indeed obtained the key. Thereupon, he believed that the underworld authorities do not speak falsely.
Consequently, he practiced great acts of charity, recited sutras, and performed repentance rituals. From then on, all was harmonious, and he followed the Way ever since.

Zhao Dingyu’s *Three Notes from the Bamboo Window* states: The late Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Zhao Dingyu, was a fellow graduate of the same year as Chen Yutai, the Governor-General of Yunnan.
On the full moon day of the third lunar month in the Wanshili year (1608), the Minister passed away. At that time, Chen Yutai was still in office;

because a member of his inner circle was ill, he invoked the spirits through spirit-writing (*fujin*), whereupon the deity declared that [the patient] would die. Consequently, he earnestly entreated for divine rescue.

The deity said, "The Lord of the Fifth Court, Yan Jun, has only recently assumed his post. He is upright and incorruptible; one cannot influence him with private interests. There is nothing that can be done.

When asked who his successor would be, he replied, "It will be a certain Zhao from Changshu. Shortly thereafter, news of a death arrived, and the date of the appointment coincided exactly with the date of the funeral announcement.
Chen was greatly astonished. Someone remarked, "Only one who possesses both merit and karma can hold such an office."
"Dingyu is a man of profound virtue; does he also have karma? Alas! The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said: 'I observe the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa;

every lifting of a foot and every movement of a step is nothing but sin. How could they be without transgression? Formerly, I heard of a monk who received a celestial tally summoning him to serve as a King of Yama.
The monk was terrified and exerted himself with great diligence, single-mindedly contemplating the Way. Consequently, the emissary of the tally ceased to appear."
Alas! The ancients said that Han Qintu was a Shangzhuguo during his life and became King Yama after death.
Furthermore, according to recent accounts, the Vice Minister of Justice Zheng Danquan became King Yama after death, and Lord Zhou, the Grand Governor of Hangzhou, became a City God after death;
such things are common occurrences. As a virtuous master of old said: "Though a monk may possess good conduct, if he does not realize the Way, he will mostly become a water spirit."
The various deities on land—how could their words be mere idle talk?
Regarding the image of Master Yongming, his name was Yanshou. When the King of Wuyue was stationed in Hangzhou, the Master served as a storehouse clerk in Yuhang County.

He frequently used the treasury funds to purchase fish, shrimp, and other creatures to release them. Later, he was prosecuted for embezzlement while acting as a guardian of the stores and faced the law.

He was to be executed by public decapitation. The King, who was somewhat aware of his practice of releasing living beings, instructed the executioners to observe his facial expression and demeanor as a test.
When the Master faced death, his countenance showed no sign of sorrow. People marveled at this, and the Master said: "I have not used a single cent of the treasury funds for my private benefit;
I have spent it all to purchase the release of living beings, beyond counting. Now that I die, I shall go directly to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss."
"Is this not joyful? Upon hearing this, the King released him. He then left the household life to become a monk, where he practiced dhyāna and repentance, attaining unimpeded eloquence.
After his master entered nirvana, a certain monk entered the underworld and saw King Yama. The king was seen bowing repeatedly before a certain image.
When the monk asked about it, [the king replied: "This is the Chan Master Yongming Shou of the world above; he has already been reborn in the Western Pure Land as one of the highest grade."

He was reborn in the higher realms. Because the King revered his virtue, he would pay him homage from time to time. (From the *Cloud Dwelling Text on Releasing Living Beings*. Formerly, when the King of Wu-Yue fed the monks, he questioned Master Yongming.)

"Is there a holy monk here? The Chan Master replied, "The Monk Long-ear is the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. Long-ear said, "Amitābha is too talkative; he will depart and no longer appear. He is not Amitābha; he has already attained the highest grade of rebirth in the Pure Land and will soon ascend to the rank of Buddhahood."
In Qinghuang County, Hengshan Prefecture, Hunan: Kang Yuandu delighted in practicing almsgiving. At the beginning of the Great Qing dynasty, he died of illness one day.
He saw two dragons swirling around his body as he proceeded all the way to the underworld and appeared before Lord Yan. The first hall was presided over by one surnamed Pan; the second—
The third hall is surnamed Zhang; the fourth hall is surnamed Qiang; the fifth hall is the father of Yuan Guang; the sixth hall is his grandfather; the sixth [hall] is surnamed Jiang;
the seventh hall is surnamed He; the eighth hall is surnamed Luo; and the tenth hall is surnamed Wang. Among those I know, these are the most numerous.
He also saw a woman from his neighborhood with her feet festering outside the hall. He asked her father, "Why is this woman here? The father replied, "Her karma has not yet been exhausted.
If someone were to establish a *dharmadhātu* (place of practice), she could be healed. After being dead for three days, she revived.

She traveled through various realms and witnessed those undergoing retribution, recording these experiences in a book. At times, she would also die for several days and then return, going about as before.
Upon their return from the Offices of the Underworld, they recounted matters that were truly terrifying.

This is as recorded in the *Mingpan Ji* (Record of Judgments from the Netherworld) by Dong Xujun of the past, which was circulated throughout the world to let people know that the retribution of sin and merit between the realms of Yin and Yang is not far removed. (The two preceding accounts are from the *Tieqiao Ji*.

These Ten Halls are like the prefectures and counties of the secular world; they are not the Heavenly Son King Yama himself. In the world, people only hear of "King Yama," but do not know there are also Prefectural Governors and Jail Masters. Therefore, when those returning from hell see any of the prison officials, they all call them "King Yama").
In Longjiang Village, Shunde County, Guangzhou, there was Yu Guining, whose wife, Cai Shi (Dharma name Dengshi), had a younger brother who had renounced the world at Mount Dinghu.
At that time, her brother returned home and instructed her to observe the fast and take refuge in the Triple Gem. Consequently, she resolved to maintain a lifelong vegetarian diet.
Whenever her paternal aunt or uncle caught fish or shrimp, she would secretly release the living ones into a well; she also frequently purchased [living creatures for this purpose].
She had released snails and clams as an act of merit. Her husband had gone abroad on business and died. Her aunt, Lady Liu, pressured her to remarry;
she truly hanged herself by a rafter to maintain her vow of chastity. At that time, the cord around her neck snapped and fell away. When her aunt heard of it, she rescued her.
Later, her elder sister and a female sorceress repeatedly urged her to abandon her vegetarian fast; she eventually complied. This occurred in the third month of the Wuzi year of the Shunzhi era.
She entered the Chen family as a secondary wife. The following year, she gave birth to a daughter. On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the *Renchen* year, she gave birth to a son.

After her delivery, she fell ill; she died after one day and night, yet her heart remained warm. When her former husband was about to leave for a journey, she entrusted him with these words: [...text continues...]
"You should remain firm. His wife said, "If I were to remarry, I would personally suffer the grave retribution of hell. On the morning of the twentieth day of the seventh month, she revived;
by the afternoon, she saw her former husband beating her and saying, "You said that if you were to remarry, you would personally suffer the grave retribution of hell.
She replied truthfully, "I will go with you. Her husband said, "There is no need for me to go with you; there is already someone else."
"Come and take you," he said, and so forth. That evening at the second watch, a ghost-judge came and bound him away.
He asked earnestly, "For what reason am I being bound? The judge replied, "To take you to suffer punishment. Upon arriving at hell, he saw heaps of dead people piled up.
He asked, "What place is this? The judge replied, "This is hell. Furthermore, on the first day of the seventh month, the good and evil deeds of all shall be examined."
During the day, he interrogated the living; at night, he interrogated the dead. At that time, the judgment tally (the *bandai*) fell upon the corpse.
He was seized with great terror and could think of nothing but recollecting the Buddha. By the end of the fourth watch, he regained consciousness.

On the second watch of the twenty-first day, the judge came again and bound him, scolding him, "Go quickly! Go quickly! You shall be cast down into the Blood Lake (*rakta-hrada*). You have lived and raised two..."
Next, he should descend for six years, yet [the being] truly refuses to go. He becomes enraged and strikes with an iron mallet, saying, "Go quickly! Go quickly!

Whenever he strikes, he sees snails and clams covering the being's entire body. Upon reaching the Blood Pond, he sees various sinners, half-sunken and half-floating, weeping in a state of suffering so unbearable that it cannot be endured to look upon.
Reaching the edge of the pond, he mindfully recites the Buddha’s name at every thought, and then he sees—
A dog said, "Noble lady, you understand how to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; thus you will avoid falling into the Blood Pond.
If you wish to go out, you should walk on the right side. On the left side there are venomous snakes, crows, and magpies that harm people.
She then walked along the right side and saw Chen’s former wife, Lady Zhang, who said, "Little sister, why have you come? She wept with such extreme bitterness that she said, "I am a concubine..."
"You have given birth to your fifth son and have fallen ill, which is why I have come. Your husband was previously performing a vegetarian feast for you;
will you also receive its benefit? She replied, "My husband lacks faith; it has not been effective at all. The two of them wept bitterly. At the end of the fourth watch, she then revived.
On the twenty-second day, at the second watch, Fan came again to lock her up and take her down to the boat. On the boat, there were four...
The men rowed the oars; truly, it was a cry of suffering reaching the heavens. He pleaded with the jailer and the men on the boat.
They said, "We know you are ill in body, yet we shall use things to screen you from view and row you with all our might across to West River. At the end of the fourth watch, he finally awoke.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the second watch, the jailer came and bound him in chains, leading him to the dark places of hell.
He saw Mount Aśoka. At that time, a ghost came with a garment to exchange for him; he truly refused to exchange it.
Again, the ghost brought "soul-confusing broth" to feed him; he truly refused to eat it. He was judged and led to the third hall before the throne of the King of Hell.

There, he knelt and pleaded, saying, "I am indeed a person from such-and-such a county and such-and-such a place. The King was greatly enraged and struck his desk; the sound shook like thunder as he said:
"You swore an oath with your former husband that you would not remarry. Why have you now violated that vow?

As for the five horses being dismembered—immediately the five horses were seen with their heads severed at five locations, and her liver and gallbladder were shattered; she did not know which part was hers.

The King consulted the registers of good and evil deeds and ordered the judge to summon her. When the corpse was restored, the King asked, "For what reason did you revile your son from your former marriage?"
Ya-yin. Ya-hui. How loathsome! How loathsome! Truly loathsome! One should be cast into a pit of fire; one shall see this for oneself.

At that time, he saw a ghost who seized Shi and pushed him down into a pit of fire. The suffering from the burning flames was great, but by single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name, he was able to escape.
He saw blisters on his own hands and blisters on his shoulders—five in number, about the size of fish-bladders, one inch wide and two inches long—remaining upon his body.
At that time, his family members all witnessed this; the retribution was unfailing.
On the fifth day, at the second watch of the night, he was brought before the judge and taken away in shackles. One ghost said, "You cursed Ya-hui until he became deaf," and immediately...

Molten copper was poured into both his ears, causing him extreme agony. He focused his mind solely on reciting the Buddha’s name. One ghost said, "If you understand how to recite the Buddha’s name, you may be spared.
He then blew into the ears with a bellows three times; immediately the pain subsided and he revived.
On the twenty-sixth day at the second watch, the judge again took him away in chains. Seeing the darkness of hell, he did not dare move forward. The judge grew angry and seized an iron staff.
As the blows fell, the pain was unbearable. He saw a chicken and said, "Give me back my life! The chicken replied, "When did you ever kill me?
You killed me when you were sixteen years old because of an illness. You did not eat my flesh; you ate my broth," and so on.
The man said, "Wait until I return to the world of the living, and I shall recite sutras and mantras for your sake. Only then did the vision vanish. Immediately—
She revived. On the twenty-ninth day, during the third watch of the night, she saw the Great Being Avalokiteśvara bringing a child to exchange for the one she had given birth to.

At that moment, her own child cried out with a piercing wail and fell to the ground. Distressed by the intense sorrow of its weeping, she pleaded with the Great Being, saying, "I do not yet know whether this child will be nourished and protected.
The Great Being replied, "If, when this child cries, you stroke its head with your hand and recite the sacred name several times..."

The sound was naturally without substance. At the end of the fourth watch, he regained consciousness. On the morning of the first day of the eighth month, at the hour of the Dragon (辰), he saw his father manifest his form and said to him:
"My son, you still ought to fall into the womb of a pig for three days and nights, and into the realm of hungry ghosts for two days and nights.
[The son] truly said: "I now do not wish to fall into hell; its agonies are unbearable. I pray that you will devise a skillful means so that I may be spared from this punishment. His father said:
"You shall reap what you have sown; no one can take your place. However, after the period of falling [into that state] has ended, you will gradually find peace.
He further said, "If you fall into the womb of a pig, you must take good care of yourself. The son asked, "I do not understand how to take care of myself.
His father said, "Pigs must eat clear rice gruel water; you must filter it through cloth before drinking. When eating, do not eat in pairs, for fear it may harm your life."
He asked, "How much may I eat? His father replied, "Either three, seven, nine, or even fifteen [mouthfuls].
He drank fifteen bowls at each of the three times of the day, and thus he revived. He then said to his family members, "I have now fallen into the womb of a pig."
"You may take a new summer shirt from my chest. Filter out the dregs of the gruel and let me drink the water.
When he ate, his family members all saw him as being no different from a pig drinking water. When the three days were over, he immediately fell into the realm of hungry ghosts;

he then had his hair disheveled like a ghost. When he wished to eat a small amount of tea, it was like eating chaff and husks; it blocked his throat and would not go down, remaining only in his mouth.
He moaned and lamented within himself, shaking and dancing with both hands for two days and nights; bystanders did not dare to approach and look at him.
After several days had passed, he saw the Great Being (Mahāsattva) once more, his entire body clad in white robes, holding a willow branch in his hand, and saying:
"From the mind, from reality it arises; when the mind is clear, karmic offenses are light. He also saw a duck saying: "Return my life to me! [The man] replied: "I..."
"When did I kill you? The duck replied, "At that time, Mistress Luo wanted me dead; she gave me a needle to swallow, yet I did not die.
Originally, this had nothing to do with Mistress Luo; it was you who were drying salted fish. I ate the salted fish and died of thirst.
You should have given me water to drink. To save one life is worth more than a thousand pieces of gold. Shiyan said, "Since I have wrongly caused your death, wait for me—"
He returned to life. [The monk] said, "How would it be to recite sutras and mantras to assist you? Thereupon, his form vanished.
Now, in the Jiwei year of the Kangxi era, that person is still alive, observing the fasts and reciting the Buddha’s name; he is sixty-two years old.

His younger brother who left the household, Juexing, having heard of my collected works, returned to his hometown and recorded this for his sister as she dictated it. I have therefore included it here. (This refers to the fact that a man lacked faith and established a vegetarian feast.)

There is absolutely no one who attains efficacy. In the world today, there are many who do not believe in the matter of the deceased being recommended for transcendence from the netherworld; they merely wish to conceal the eyes and ears of their relatives and friends by inviting monks to establish a *zhāi* (fasting/feasting rite).

Since they lack faith, they incur the fault of slighting the Buddha and disparaging the Sangha, yet even so they cannot avoid transgression—how, then, could efficacy be attained? Perhaps the monks lack compassion or the intention to benefit the deceased; perhaps they recite spurious scriptures such as the *Xuèhú Jiùkǔ* (Blood Lake Salvation from Suffering); or even if it be a true scripture spoken by the Buddha, they lack sincerity, treating it like the rote recitations of children.

The *Three Character Classic* says: "Some invite Daoist priests to perform incantations (*jiao*). Lacking the utmost sincerity, and the scriptures being inauthentic, these rites consist entirely of vulgar speech. After three days, they slaughter living beings, falsely claiming it is to 'thank the generals' and privately seeking to fatten their own bellies.

The people of the world have long been deluded, drinking this poison with pleasure. How could the killing of living creatures ever surpass the suffering of the deceased? Or, when setting up vegetarian feasts, they are stingy with wealth and do not provide abundant offerings; they only insist on chanting mantras while drums and music resound through the heavens. They pay no heed to whether the ritual site is clean or whether the vegetarian dishes and utensils are pure.
Consequently, both the living and the dead suffer loss; such rites are truly established in vain, resulting only in needless toil."
Yingde County, Shaoyou Prefecture. A rural area with winter waters. Yang Shuyi once observed the six fasts.

During the Shunzhi era, there was Cheng Huahan, who, at the time of his death, entrusted Shuyi, saying: "You possess faith; after I die, you should establish a vegetarian feast and serve as my attendant for the incense and candles.
At that time, a monk from Leizhai Temple, leading a novice boy, went to pour wax over candles and entered the inner chamber.
While eating and drinking, a dog licked the oily residue from a cauldron, causing a candle to break. When the boy returned and saw it, he immediately poured the oily residue over the candle.
As soon as the vegetarian feast had concluded, he slaughtered a pig right before the altar. The next day, Shuyi fell ill and went to hell, where he met Hua-han; they went together to see King Yama.
The King asked Hua-han, "What meritorious deeds did you perform while in the world? He replied, "I once performed the *yù*..."

He was asked to cultivate merit. The King examined the records and found that neither possessed any merit. He then said to Shuyi, "You serve as the official in charge of incense and candles for others;
why do you offer defiled candles to the Buddha? Shuyi replied, "When this humble servant was in charge of the incense and candles, those candles were not pure."

This was the fault of the attendant boy. The King said, "The sacrificial altar is impure; this is the crime of those who manage the incense and candles. He was then punished with five strokes of the bamboo and subsequently revived.

Later, both his thighs swelled and rotted until the bone was visible. He then sought out the *Mahākaruṇā-mantra* water from a monk at Bailing Monastery, and after washing with it, he gradually recovered.
He passed away in the thirteenth year of the Kangxi era. Shu Yi personally recounted this, and as all his fellow villagers spoke of it, I have recorded it here for praise.
Luling ○ Chen Zhongchi suddenly died at the end of the sixth month in the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era. On the seventh day of the seventh month, he revived and said:
"A certain person is undergoing punishment in the underworld; another person has now come to preside over a certain place;

furthermore, a certain person sent a message and left an object in a certain location. Everything was exactly as he had described. He further stated that he saw three paths in the underworld, the first of which...
He was heavily bound with many strips of leather and shackles. There is one path for virtuous people; the other leads entirely to the conduct of beasts.
He said of himself: "I shall live for only three more years. Thereupon, he resolved his mind upon a long-term fast. After three years, he died without illness (from the *Tiēqiáo jí*).
In Huanggang Village, Gaoyao County, Zhaoqing Prefecture, Guangdong, there lived Liang Zhiqiu, whose courtesy name was Chaodong.

He had long since refrained from sexual misconduct and killing, and he encouraged virtue while concealing others' faults. He resided in a private academy as a tutor. In the ninth year of the Kangxi era, Zhiqiu was forty-one years of age.

On the eighth night of the sixth month, he dreamed of two ghost messengers, one of whom was accompanied by a servant. They held a tablet and seized him by the ball (the *qiú* [ball] used as a metaphor for the person).
He pleaded with them, saying, "My family is poor and my children are young. The ghost messengers then departed. Five days later, the *qiú* dreamed that the two messengers came again to summon him.

He begged to be excused, but the ghosts did not grant his request. He then awoke and died without illness, having no time to leave a final testament. When he first set out on the path, the two messengers...

He said to Qiu, "The mountains and rivers along the main road are steep and obstructed; traveling there is not easy. There is a shortcut here, but it is difficult to cross because of karmic creditors.
Since you are a virtuous man, I am consulting with you about it. Qiu replied, "I have long practiced releasing living beings and abstained from killing;
I have no other concerns. The messenger said, "If this is truly so, you may cross. They then passed through a marketplace, and the two messengers went into a shop to eat.
The two messengers raised cups and dishes to encourage Qiu to eat, but Qiu thought to himself, "This is not the food and drink of the human world," and declined to partake.
The two messengers said, "This man is extraordinary; he may yet return to life. We only fear that he will be hastily interred.

They sent a servant to Qiu’s house in haste to tell his corpse, "I shall certainly return to life; please do not enshroud me. Having finished speaking, the spirit immediately returned. Together they went to Baoyuanjing, and indeed—
He saw six domesticated animals and wild beasts filling the path; those who passed through were mostly bitten or pecked by them, yet Qiu alone walked across in peace.
Having passed this, he caught sight from afar of a magnificent palace. As evening fell, the two messengers stayed with Qiu overnight in a temple.

A golden plaque was inscribed there: "Imperially Enfeoffed Temple of the Dragon Mother. Rising at dawn, they went together to the court gate, where the hundred officials stood in solemn attendance. The two...
He was made to kneel with the ball beneath the steps. The Recorder opened the register and reported to the King that under the name "Ball" there was but one transgression.

Ball wept and pleaded, saying, "My wife and children are orphaned and young; I beg for release back to the world of the living. The King said, "Your allotted lifespan has already ended; it is difficult to spare you for the sake of wife and child.

However, I am pleased that you were able to remain content in poverty and encourage goodness, and that you have committed no great sin or evil. Now, in the secular world of the living, many commit great [sins]..."

"Your sins all stem from a lack of faith in the laws of the underworld. You should read these couplets on penal statutes thoroughly before returning to the living world, and transmit them to others so that they may do good and abandon evil.
Qiu received this command and, together with the two messengers, read through the couplets and the various lists of offenses.
He then stayed overnight in the temple again. The following morning, he went to the hall and prostrated himself, taking the couplets and the statutes...

He recited [the scriptures] clearly and fluently. The King was greatly pleased and ordered the two envoys to escort him back. On the way, they passed through a military training ground where he encountered his deceased disciple, Mo Huan-yuan, who was practicing archery with a group of companions.
Seeing the ball, [Mo] dismounted from his horse; grief and joy welled up within him as he said to himself, "Even after death, I have no transgressions.
Now, for the sake of the military inspection, I shall be subject to the discipline of the generals. I trouble you to convey my words to my elder brother, sister-in-law, wife, and children."

"Serve your parents well. I previously possessed a handwritten critique of the *Wujing Ce Lun* (Treatise on Military Strategy); you may burn it and give it to me. Having spoken thus, he bowed twice and departed.
After traveling several more li, he caught sight of his hometown; the two ghost messengers took their leave and went away. After three days and nights, he finally revived.
He has recorded in full the inscriptions on the door couplets and the laws of retribution; these are now set forth below.

Couplet for the Hall of Retribution for Vengeance: "Roasting and carving to fill the bellies—birds and beasts harbor grief as they seek retribution; Slaughtered and offered as feasts—oxen and sheep drink in their resentment, awaiting the repayment of their grievances.
Couplet for the Bridge over the River Nai: "The bitter sea is boundless; one must recognize that turning back is the shore. The Nai River has a ferry;

if one can turn their thoughts, they will not be deluded. Couplet for the Path of Separation: "This road leads to Heaven; virtuous men all pass through here. This path sinks into Hell; the wicked all travel along it."

Couplets for the Main Gate: "Three feet of solemnity—how could one here pervert the law as easily as in the world of the living? Four knowledges, stern and fierce—indeed, the underworld brooks no leniency.
Couplets for the Second Gate: "Born in the world of the living, your evil was grave; having reached the underworld, you wish to repent, but it is too late.
Couplets for the Imperial Steps: "The hearts of iron and stone—your stubbornness is hard to change; the furnace of the nether laws—let your obstinacy melt away by its own force."

Couplet before the seat: "Blessed is he who follows the auspicious, and calamitous is he who follows the perverse; the retribution for good and evil is decided on this very day. Accumulate goodness and blessings will follow; commit evil and disaster will ensue. The distinction between blessing and disaster is clearly manifest before one.
Red placard on the left corridor of the hall: "Confessions of Offenses and Penal Statutes:
Disloyalty, unfiliality, rebellion, immorality, plotting for wealth at the cost of life, and the unjust or excessive taking of life."
Regarding the aforementioned offenses of robbery, theft, sexual misconduct, killing, and harming others' families: their punishment reaches the ultimate penalty.

Regarding the offenses of cursing Heaven and Earth, slandering the sovereign, resenting one's parents, reviling teachers and elders, abducting others' wives and children, and committing adultery with improper lust: these offenses are reduced by one degree from the ultimate penalty.
For those who commit any of the following offenses— damaging waterworks, setting fires to mountains, practicing subterfuge to violate the law,

using heterodox paths to delude the masses, killing living beings or harming things, or exploiting the orphaned and the widowed— the punishment shall be reduced by two degrees from the ultimate penalty.
Sowing discord among kin, inciting litigation, casting blame upon others, framing the innocent, selling living beings for profit,
forging counterfeit currency, trafficking in human beings, forcing the virtuous into prostitution, coercing servants and maidservants, kidnapping people,
acting as a pimp for gamblers and thieves, and indulging greedily in food and drink while scheming to defraud others of their wealth.
Those who seize fields and lands, exercise arbitrary power in their local districts, incite killing and promote lewdness, violate the precepts of fasting and purification,

amass wealth without satiety, exploit perilous situations for profit, act wantonly with authority and power, indulge in licentiousness and hunting, abuse their influence to act with impunity, or betray the trust placed in them—
those who commit such offenses as these shall be subject to three grades of punishment, commensurate with the severity of the crime, falling short of the ultimate penalty of death.

The categories of the five punishments number three thousand; here, only those of the utmost severity are singled out to serve as warnings, so that people of the world may know them with awe and refrain from transgressing them.
These include the mountain of knives, the iron bed, and even the hells of wind, fire, and submersion.

Each receives their retribution according to what they have committed; form and shadow follow one another, all of which is self-inflicted. Only by reforming one's faults and accumulating virtuous deeds can one escape it.
To slander the Triple Gem, to destroy monks and nuns, to defile and despise the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and to propagate teachings that rebel against the Sages—[these lead to such consequences].
All of these are more severe than the ultimate punishments; therefore, they are listed separately. Those who commit them may not be absolved through repentance.
On the right corridor of the hall is the Golden Banner of the Text for Releasing Living Beings (the text on abstaining from killing by Master Lianchi of Yunqi Monastery in Hangzhou).
It is heard that among all things in the world, life is most precious, and slaughter and injury are most grievous. Therefore, when encountering capture, [beings] flee.
Even wax-lice know how to avoid death; they migrate when rain is imminent. Even ants still cherish their lives;

why then do you net them on the mountains and set snares in the depths? Employing myriad methods to capture them—bending hooks and straightening arrows—you scour them with a hundred stratagems, causing their courage to fail and their souls to flee.
Mothers are separated from their offspring, or they are imprisoned in cages and enclosures as if in a dungeon, or they are struck by blades.
The butcher’s block is no different from the site of execution and slaughter. The deer, pitying its young, licks the scarred wound until its tender entrails break in pieces;
the monkey, fearing death, gazes at the reflection of the bowstring until twin streams of sorrowful tears fall. To rely on one's own strength to oppress the weak is surely contrary to reason;
to consume the flesh of others to nourish one's own body—how can the heart endure such cruelty? For this reason, the Great Heaven bestowed compassion, and the ancient sages...

Practicing benevolence, Cheng Tang is renowned for untying the nets; fostering fish, Zi Chan rose to eminence. How sagely is the flowing water, moistening the withered and parched by its hidden springs!
How tragic was Śākyamuni, who cut his own flesh to save those in peril of death. Zhiyi of Tiantai excavated a pond for releasing living beings;
the Rishi of the Great Tree protected the birds that took refuge within it. By redeeming scaly creatures, they attained deliverance; this is the longevity of the Chan [tradition].
The Master’s enduring compassion remains: he saved the dragon’s offspring and transmitted the secret methods. The compassionate spirit of the Realized Man Sun has not faded:
he restored life to a single ant. Thus, the novice monk was transformed from a short lifespan into long years, and the scholar was changed from an humble name to the highest degree.
First was the release of the tortoise. Mao Bao escaped peril by releasing it from danger; Kong Yu was enfeoffed as a marquis for his minor official service.
Qu Shi released the carp at Yuancun, and his lifespan increased by twelve years. The Marquis of Sui saved a snake in the fields of Qi, and the pearl repaid him with a thousand pieces of gold.
By rescuing a fly that had fallen into wine, the wine-maker’s death sentence was commuted; by sparing a turtle about to be cooked, the kitchen [was spared].
The chronic illness of a maidservant was cured; one traded his life for that of a butcher. The soul of Judge Zhang transcended to the celestial realm;
another exchanged his remaining life for a fishing boat. Li Jingwen’s poison was neutralized by cinnabar; Sun Liangsi was delivered from the peril of the hunting net.
When the burial was divined, feathered creatures gathered to assist; when Magistrate Pan established prohibitions against fishing and hunting, the aquatic life wailed as he left office.
Xinxiao exempted the common people from sacrificial offerings, and sweet rain fell in response; Caoxi kept hunters from casting their nets.
The Way has spread throughout the land of Zhōushén. A magpie understood how to bring a ring to repay its kindness; a fox was able to appear at a well to bestow secret arts.

Even those with but a remnant of life regained their lives; one offered a white jade disc to hear the scriptures. In a perilous place, one sought to survive; another appeared in a dream wearing yellow robes.

Every act of giving receives its retribution; how could such matters lack evidence? These are recorded in the annals and made manifest to our ears and eyes. May all universally vow that, according to the objects they encounter, [they may attain liberation].

Arouse a heart of compassion. Sacrifice insubstantial wealth to perform acts of skillful means. Whether your kindness encompasses many lives, thereby accumulating great hidden merit, or whether your benefit extends to even a single insect, how could that not be a virtuous deed?
If this increases daily and accumulates monthly, one’s own practice will broaden and blessings will become sublime.
When compassion fills the human realm and one’s reputation reaches the celestial offices, karmic obstacles and grievances will be swept away, and manifold blessings will converge upon you.
In this life, one cultivates and accumulates roots of goodness; the remaining blessings extend to future lives.

If one can assist them by reciting the Buddha’s name and chanting sutra texts, dedicating these merits toward rebirth in the Western Paradise, so that they may forever leave the evil realms behind, then one’s resolve becomes even greater and the virtues planted become all the more profound.
Through such support, their spiritual practice will be swiftly perfected, and they shall be born in a superior lot upon the Lotus Throne. (Recorded by Zi-qiu).
In the second month of the Xinhai year of the Kangxi era (1671), there was a woman in Yangcheng (Guangzhou) who poisoned her husband to death and pushed his former wife’s mother-in-law into a well;
no one knew of it. Later, during the night, the woman saw ghostly soldiers who seized her and brought her before the City God.
The City God, together with a figure wearing a *guàn* (official cap) and a *fùtóu* (headband), conducted an interrogation and immediately applied the iron *jiāgùn* (torture rack) to her.
The feet of the wicked woman were severed and she was ordered to show them to the living world. There is no discrepancy between good and evil.
When Pingfan heard this, he provided her with food and placed her outside the West Gate in front of the horse stable. Crowds went there to watch; the woman ate her daily meals as usual.
Her severed foot was placed on a tray before her, and she said to the people herself, "In two days I shall be cast into the oil cauldron. As the time approached, she suffered great pain.
The appearance of his body was unbearable to behold. It was further said that after two more days, his body would be hacked into pieces, and he would die within a few days.
Lord Ping then ordered his head to be severed and his remains cast away in the wilderness to be devoured by dogs (from the *Tiexiao ji*).

In Xi Yong Village of Shunde County, there was Zhang Zaiming, whose wife was Lady Li. They had two sons. By nature she was malicious, prone to anger and jealousy, and took pleasure in beating her servants and slaves.
Whenever she struck them, she never felt satisfied unless they were subjected to extreme agony; she would force them to kneel before the steps and douse them with urine.
He continued to burn iron tongs and cauterize his own body and face. Neither his husband nor his son dared to approach him.
In the *Ren-yin* year of the Kangxi era, he stole a neighbor’s chicken and killed it for food. When the neighbor questioned him, he immediately made a vow, saying:
"If I have stolen and eaten your chicken, may both my eyes fall to the ground. The following month, while he was free from illness, one eye suddenly burst open. This occurred by the *Yi-si* year.
In the year [X], he again tore out one eye. In the year Ding-si, while lying alone in his room, he broke the planks of his bed at midnight.
He then placed a wooden collar around his neck and knelt on the ground. At dawn, his family heard the sound of groaning; they rushed to him and asked, "Why are you like this? He replied:

"I am now bound by the shackles of King Yama; though my suffering is still light, after two days I must be placed upon the bed of iron spikes and cast into the cauldron of boiling oil," he said (and so forth).
He died within a few days. This was known by all the people of his home village and neighboring districts.
His son, Duanzhong, also personally recounted this to others, and I have therefore recorded it here.
In Shangzhi Village, Shunde, there was a man named Lu Yeqing who served as a district official for Guangzhou Prefecture. He was a follower of the Wuwei (Non-Action) sect;
though he claimed to observe a vegetarian diet, his conduct was unwholesome and his deeds were improper, such that they cannot be fully recounted.
In the fifth month of the Jiwu year of the Kangxi era, he intended to sell a pig to a butcher. The butcher offered a price of five cash, whereupon the official himself...
He killed it and sold the meat for eight cents of silver. A few days later he fell ill.

On the morning of the twenty-third day of the sixth month, he saw a pig come to him and say, "My life was destined to end today; why did you greedily take three more cents of silver and slaughter my neck with a knife?
I have already lodged a complaint with the local authorities. At the hour of Wei (2–4 p.m.), a ghost indeed appeared and bound him, leading him before King Yama.
He saw three officials; one was named Lord Deng. They all testified that he had killed pigs. The King said, "For what reason did you greedily kill these pig lives?
You shall receive sixty strokes of the rod. For now, I shall spare you and strike you with thirty for the time being;
we shall re-examine the case later. Thereupon, he revived and returned home, telling his wife everything. When his wife examined both his thighs, they were swollen and covered in dark bruises.

For several days, it festered and rotted. Thereafter, he was repeatedly pursued by messengers from the underworld and subjected to various sufferings of retribution; upon his return, he recounted these events.
However, his family home allowed only followers of the Wuwei (Non-action) sect to enter and exit, while others were barred.

His wife and children, as well as the members of the Wuwei sect, were so fearful and ashamed that they concealed the matter and did not speak of it; only a neighbor managed to hear a fragment or two. This continued until the seventh month.
He died on the ninth day. Before his death, a foul stench permeated the air outside his door;
passersby could not bear to smell it. At that time, a villager asked the practitioner of non-action (Wuwei tu): "The people of this world kill many creatures, yet why do they receive no retribution?
Why is it that only you, Master Ye, must alone suffer this? He replied: "In my teaching, we take a vow three times every day. At each session, I recite [the name of] one..."
The names of the two officials of the Bureau served as witnesses. Now, because they killed living beings and violated the precepts, they have received this retribution.

They used this to deceive people, while concealing all other [transgressions]. My fellow villagers and neighbors told me of this (the names of the remaining two officials of the Bureau have been forgotten).
The End of Volume Five of the *Liùdào jí* (Collection on the Six Realms).
Phonetic Explanation:
*Féngyì Jùn* (Prefecture of Fengyi); *yì* is the same as *yì* (wing).

The name of King Yama is fully rendered in Sanskrit as *Yamarāja*. This is translated as "Quelling Dispute" (*xi zheng*), meaning that he brings to rest the disputes of those who have committed offenses.
Regarding the *gaṇḍī*:
the character *zhì* (稚) is sometimes erroneously written as *zhuī* (椎). It refers to any object made of wood, stone, copper, iron, or other materials that can be struck to produce a ringing sound.
It is called a *ghanṭā*. A question was asked: "Is the wooden fish used today the same as this? The answer was: "The sound of the wooden fish is small;
it cannot be called a *ghanṭā*. Question: "Why do the monastics use the wooden fish? Answer: "The wooden fish is an ancient musical instrument found only in this country and nowhere else.
Because its sound is harmonious and its resonance is tranquil, the monastics have adopted it for their recitations."
Regarding the rhythm of recitation, it is intended that the assembly chant with one voice in unison.

Furthermore, in the past, Cao Zijian once traveled to Mount Yushan and heard the resonance of Brahma in the sky—clear, lofty, and plaintively beautiful. He subsequently imitated those sounds and transcribed them as *fanbai* (Brahma chants).
Today, the wooden fish is used to represent the Brahma sounds of Mount Yushan.
*Gai* (刈) is pronounced *yi*; it means "to reap.
*Du* (堵) is pronounced *du*; it means "a wall.
*Zhouzhi* (盩厔) has the first character pronounced *zhou* and the second pronounced *zhi*; it is the name of a commandery located in Jingzhao.
*Wàn* (惋): Pronounced like *wàn* (wrist). To express astonishment and admiration.
*Yú* (漁): Pronounced like *yú* (fish). To catch fish; it also means to encroach upon or seize. This refers to what is called "fishing for beauty," which is sexual misconduct.
*Zēng* (矰): Pronounced like *zēng* (increase). A fletched arrowhead tied to an arrow. *Yì* (弋) refers to shooting with an arrow; it also refers to a short arrow.
The character for "jiao" (矯) is pronounced with the third tone. To straighten an arrow is called "jiao.

Regarding the Great Water-Land Repast (*shuìlù dàzhāi*) during the Tiānjiān era of Emperor Wǔ of the Liáng dynasty: the Emperor dreamed of a divine monk who said, "Sentient beings of the four modes of birth (*sìshēng*) undergo great suffering;
why do you not perform the Great Water-Land Repast to rescue and deliver them? The Emperor questioned Master Zhìgōng, who then exhorted the Emperor to seek it out.
The sutras must have their causes and conditions. He then personally examined the Tripitaka and composed the ritual texts; it took three years to complete them.

At night, while reciting the texts, he extinguished the lamps and candles and addressed the Buddha: "If these principles accord with those of both the sages and the ordinary, I pray that upon my rising from prostration, the lamps and candles will spontaneously brighten."

"Perhaps the ritual procedures were not yet detailed, and [the darkness] remained as before. Having finished speaking, he prostrated himself once on the ground, whereupon the lamps and candles all became bright.
Consequently, on the fifteenth day of the second month in the year of Yiyou during the Tianjian era, he established a Water and Land (Shuilu) Dharma Assembly at Jinshan Temple.
The Emperor personally attended the assembly site and issued an edict appointing Vinaya Master Sengyou to preside over the proceedings. This is excerpted from the Weijiang Ji.
